China has said that it would safeguard its interests after Washington unveiled new measures while laying out plans for the “economic asphyxiation” of Beijing’s economic partner Iran.
Speaking at a regular news briefing in Beijing on Tuesday, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian rejected Washington’s expanding pressure campaign, calling for an immediate end to unilateral measures.

China has advocated for a ceasefire, insisting US sanctions will not resolve the conflict.

Iran has weathered sanctions for decades, using complex international financial networks to evade restrictions. Before the war, it continued to export millions of barrels of oil, mostly to China.
‘We will see a lot of resistance’ from China
Amid the US’s latest move, some analysts say threats to sanction Chinese entities over trade with Iran are unlikely to materialise. Diplomatically, Parsi pointed out that Beijing helped avert a severe economic crisis during the height of the war by halting its oil purchases just as prices spiked, cratering demand and keeping crude under $100 per barrel for extended periods.
“They did this because the Chinese objective was to make sure this crisis would not bring about a global recession, which would be bad for China,” Parsi said, suggesting the move indirectly spared Washington from an energy shock that would have hurt the US economy.
Beyond that, Beijing is unlikely to accept US attacks on its companies or economic interests without pushback. “I suspect that we will see a lot of resistance from the Chinese if the US actually ends up going after Chinese companies,” Parsi said.
Separately, the president of the Iran-China Chamber of Commerce and Industries, Majidreza Hariri, also criticised US policies, warning that Washington has entered into an economic war with Tehran.
“What Trump has said makes it clear that he has entered into an economic war with us and considers it a new phase of military and security wars!” Hariri wrote in a post on X.
“With this same reasoning, all of America’s economic targets and its partners around the world, and especially in the region, are considered military targets of the enemy and are targetable!”

Tehran, Dushanbe open virtual exhibition highlighting shared decorative arts

Unknown Publisher

Tehran, Dushanbe open virtual exhibition highlighting shared decorative arts
TEHRAN – A joint virtual exhibition showcasing Iran’s Qajar-era tilework and Tajikistan’s traditional Kundal decorative art has opened simultaneously at the Golestan Palace World Heritage site in Tehran and the National Museum of Tajikistan.
The exhibition, titled “One Heritage, Two Lands,” features about 20 digital images of Kundal artworks from Tajikistan alongside 10 images of Qajar-era tilework from the eastern and southern sections of the Golestan Palace complex.
Speaking at the opening ceremony on Tuesday, Golestan Palace Director Imam Ali Emami said high-quality digital images of Tajikistan’s Kundal works, accompanied by relevant information, had been provided by the National Museum of Tajikistan. They are being displayed alongside digital images of tilework from Golestan Palace.
Kundal is a traditional decorative art in Tajik architecture whose roots date back to the 14th and 15th centuries. The technique uses vegetal, arabesque and geometric motifs on plaster and wood and is used to decorate walls and ceilings, in ways comparable to the decorative role of tilework in Iranian architecture, Emami explained.
Alisher Zarifi, first deputy director of the National Museum of Tajikistan, who addressed the ceremony online, said the exhibition provided an opportunity to introduce the two countries’ shared historical and cultural heritage to an international audience.
He said the National Museum of Tajikistan has organized 22 exhibition halls dedicated to presenting the country’s history and culture, including historical and cultural artifacts, artworks and representations of the customs, traditions and rituals of the Tajik people.
The museum seeks to portray Tajik history from ancient times and the formation of states to the contemporary era, while introducing different aspects of Tajik culture and civilization to visitors, Zarifi added.
He said the joint virtual exhibition was organized as part of the museum’s international cooperation program and ahead of Tajikistan’s 35th anniversary of state independence. The exhibition focuses on Tajik Kundal art and Iranian tilework.
Zarifi said the initiative would allow both sides to present their historical and cultural collections to a global audience, noting the longstanding historical and cultural ties between the peoples of Iran and Tajikistan.

Cultural event to spotlight Iran’s Dareshuri horse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25

Cultural event to spotlight Iran’s Dareshuri horse
TEHRAN – A cultural and artistic event dedicated to Iran’s Dareshuri horse is scheduled to be held in Semirom, Isfahan province, bringing together horse experts, breeders, riders, researchers and artists to promote the breed and highlight its cultural and heritage significance.
Negar Mohammadi Kashkoli, a member of the board of the Fars Equestrian Federation and a tourism professional, said the event aims to introduce the capabilities of the Dareshuri horse, help safeguard the cultural heritage associated with it, expand knowledge and experience in horse breeding and equestrianism, and create a forum for specialists and cultural, artistic and tourism practitioners, Miras Aria reported.
The Dareshuri is an Iranian riding horse of oriental type native to Fars province in southern Iran. It is closely associated with the Turkic Qashqai people, particularly the Dareshuri tribe, and is also sometimes known as the Shirazi horse.
Mohammadi Kashkoli said the Dareshuri horse could be regarded as the product of a long interaction between people, the environment, culture and selective breeding. The population has been bred for generations within the geographical and cultural setting of the Qashqai tribe and has retained characteristics shaped by the needs of nomadic life and riding.
She said the breed’s significance extends beyond its physical characteristics and riding abilities, encompassing important historical, cultural and social dimensions.
“Scientific documentation and more detailed study of its phenotypic, genetic and historical characteristics, as well as traditional breeding practices, can contribute to a better understanding and preservation of this heritage,” she said.
One of the event’s main objectives is to provide a platform for dialogue and the exchange of knowledge and experience among horse specialists, veterinarians, researchers, breeders, riders and professionals working in the cultural, artistic and tourism sectors.
Mohammadi Kashkoli said the event would examine the Dareshuri horse and efforts to document and safeguard it from different perspectives.
The program will also have an artistic dimension, with visual artists taking part in workshops focused on traditional handicrafts and cultural expression, including textile weaving, calligraphy, painting, music and singing, as well as Shahnameh recitation.
She said the artistic programs would seek to present the story and cultural identity of the Dareshuri horse to a wider audience through different art forms.

A ‘serious violation’
Israel also claimed that UNRWA had fenced off the land for decades despite having no ownership rights over it.
The ministry cited legislation passed by the Israeli Knesset in October 2024 banning the agency’s activities in Israel.
UNRWA, however, maintains that the Qalandia Training Center is a UN facility and is protected under international law.

US removes Syria from 'state sponsor of terrorism' list
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
14:41:17 UTC
23:41:17 KST

Breadcrumb
US removes Syria from 'state sponsor of terrorism' list in 'historic' step
The United States on Monday removed Syria from its blacklist of "State Sponsors of Terrorism" after over 40 years, in a move described as a "historic step" for the country.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement that the removal "will help foster additional investment in Syria to promote political and economic stability".
Bessent added the moves were "in line with President (Donald) Trump's promise to deliver sanctions relief to Syria".
Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa welcomed the move, saying: "Today, Syria shakes off a dark stain and tears away a painful chapter of its past to embark on a path of development, reconstruction and rebuilding".
Al-Sharaa thanked US President Donald Trump, as well as countries that have supported Syria.
Syrian Foreign Minister Assad al-Shaibani described Washington's delisting as a "historic milestone", while Finance Minister Mohammed Barnieh described the move as a "success for Syrian diplomacy".
The designation made Syria a high-risk, heavily restricted jurisdiction in the US-led financial and trade system, impacting it on all fronts, including legal, economic, diplomatic and humanitarian.
"It's really the last piece of the puzzle when it comes to trying to not only provide the boost to the post-war Syrian economy and Syrian reconstruction efforts, but additionally, the boost that many of Syria's security and political agencies will need to build capacity after the fall of the Assad regime," Caroline Rose, Senior Director at The Soufan Center, told The New Arab.
"The designation carried a lot of weight when it came to providing dual-use items, military assistance, also collaborating directly with Syrian defence and security agencies and forces, and so as a result, this is going to, I think, open up a whole new portal, so to speak, when it comes to US security and defence collaboration with the new Syrian administration."
Syria was subject to restrictions on US foreign assistance, a ban on defence exports and sales, strict controls on exports of dual-use goods and technology, and financial and other miscellaneous restrictions.
Yazan Al-Saadi, The New Arab's International desk editor, says the move "will untangle a lot of the day-to-day challenges that Syrians and Syrian institutions face when they try to work within the international financial sphere".
"There is hope that this will alleviate a lot of the economic pressures facing the country at the moment after 15 years of a brutal civil war uprising as well as the fallout from what's going on worldwide with price increases, gas increases," Al-Saadi added.
"This is another obstacle removed for them."
The US initially announced in July its intention to delist Syria as a state sponsor of terrorism, in a move seen as a vote of confidence in Sharaa.
The US Department of State has also removed the designation of al-Nusra Front, which later became known as Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), as a global terrorist organisation. HTS rebels, led by al-Sharaa, overthrew Syria's long-running ruler Bashar al-Assad in December 2024.
The Treasury Department announced corresponding sanctions relief, while asserting that its removal of restrictions on Syria "does not change Treasury's posture with regards to countering global terrorism and our commitment to hold bad actors in Syria accountable".
Fadel Abdulghany, founder of the Syrian Network for Human Rights (SNHR), cautioned that the moves by the US "must not be portrayed as full normalisation".
"Delisting does not remove targeted sanctions against individuals and entities implicated in serious human rights abuses, illicit finance, terrorism or other destabilising conduct," Abdulghany said.
"Nor does it resolve the structural challenges that continue to deter responsible investment, including weak public institutions, uncertainty over property rights, lack of judicial independence, corruption, damaged infrastructure and ongoing insecurity."
Syria was first blacklisted by the US in 1979, making the designation one of the longest-standing, lasting throughout the Assad family's rule.
Al-Saadi notes that the blacklisting had a negative impact on how Syrians were perceived, and hopes that the new move will change this.
"With Syria being on such a list and so forth, Syrians have been vilified for a long, long time and they continue to be, I would say, as terrorists, as Barbarians, as savages," he said.
"For Syrians in particular, they've been dehumanised for so long that maybe it's time to start humanising them more and more in a very natural and much needed way, just like other people, Palestinians and so forth."
The blacklisting concerned successive Syrian governments' support and logistical assistance for armed groups that Washington classified as terrorist organisations. The listing was also not internationally agreed.
Other countries on the list include Iran, North Korea and Cuba. States included in the list are accused of providing support for "acts of international terrorism".

At UN conference, Türkiye showcases policies to fight desertification and drought
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
14:40:10 UTC
23:40:10 KST

Fatma Sevinç Çetin Obuz, Beril Çanakcı
25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
- Türkiye highlights its policies and projects on desertification, drought, and sustainable land management at UN Convention to Combat Desertification conference in Mongolia
- Country is also using COP17 to build international partnerships ahead of COP31 UN climate change conference, which Türkiye will host in Antalya in November
Türkiye is showcasing its efforts to combat desertification and drought at the 17th UN Convention to Combat Desertification, or UNCCD COP17, in Mongolia.
The conference is being held in the capital Ulaanbaatar on Aug. 17-28 under the theme "Restore land, revive hope." Representatives of 197 countries, as well as scientists, civil society groups, young people, local communities, and other stakeholders, are attending the meeting.
Land degradation, drought resilience, desertification, sustainable land management, pasture management, and the protection of water resources are among the key issues of the gathering.
Türkiye set up a pavilion at COP17 to present its policies and projects in these areas, including efforts to prevent land degradation, improve drought resilience, promote sustainable land use, and protect ecosystems.
Panels and other events at the pavilion also address environmental monitoring, early warning systems, and education, while meetings with representatives of countries and international organizations are exploring opportunities for joint projects and cooperation.
Türkiye aims to share its experience in combating desertification and drought while using the contacts established at COP17 to strengthen international cooperation ahead of COP31, the UN climate change conference set for this November in Antalya, Türkiye. 
Rio Synergy initiative
Türkiye is also advancing work on "Rio Synergy," a priority of its COP31 Action Agenda that treats climate change, biodiversity loss, and desertification as interconnected global challenges.
The initiative seeks to improve coordination among international efforts under the three environmental conventions and turn existing commitments into joint action.
A Rio Synergy Working Group is expected to be launched during COP17. It will seek to develop actions aligned with countries' national priorities and commitments and boost international cooperation on climate change, biodiversity, and desertification.

First modernized Ulan fighting vehicle delivered to Austrian troops
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
14:38:38 UTC
23:38:38 KST

- Austria's Bundesheer received its first modernized Leopard 2A4 tank and Ulan infantry fighting vehicle on August 25, 2026, in Großmittel.
- The upgrades are part of Austria's Aufbauplan ÖBH 2032+ force-development plan, covering 58 Leopard 2A4 tanks and 112 Ulan vehicles.
Austria’s Bundesheer received its first modernized Ulan infantry fighting vehicle and Leopard 2A4 tank at a handover ceremony in Großmittel on August 25, Austria’s Ministry of Defense announced. Defense Minister Klaudia Tanner attended the event.
The modernization program is part of a broader force-development plan the ministry calls Aufbauplan ÖBH 2032+. Work on the armored fleet began in 2023.
The Ulan fleet is undergoing a separate, comprehensive upgrade at GDELS Steyr. That work includes renewed optics and electronic components, an overhauled electrical system, and replacement drivetrain parts. Austria has said the Ulan program covers 112 vehicles at a cost of 460 million euros ($537 million). The first modernized Ulan vehicles are being delivered directly to troop units, while the upgraded Leopard tanks go to the Army Logistics Center for final adaptation work before fielding.
“With the modernized tank fleet, we are strengthening the capabilities of the Austrian Armed Forces exactly where they matter most for national military defense. Our soldiers need modern, mission-ready systems to carry out their duties. The handover of these vehicles makes the 2032+ development plan visible,” Tanner said.
The Leopard 2A4 upgrade replaces outdated components and restores the tank’s night-fighting capability. The vehicle’s turret hydraulics are being replaced with an electric drive system. KNDS Deutschland, formerly Krauss-Maffei Wegmann, is carrying out the modernization; Austria previously disclosed a contract value of 305 million euros ($356 million) covering 58 tanks.
The Leopard 2A4 serves as the primary weapon system of Austria’s tank force, relying on its main gun and engine power for mobility across varied terrain. The Ulan is the combat vehicle used by Austria’s armored infantry, built to keep pace with the Leopard across difficult terrain while carrying an onboard cannon, a squad of infantry and its crew.
Austria’s Ministry of Defense described the mechanized force, combining tank and armored infantry units, as central to the country’s conventional military defense.

At least 306 people in Belgium have fallen ill after consuming eggs contaminated with salmonella, the Federal Agency for the Safety of the Food Chain (FASFC) said on Tuesday, according to The Brussels Times.
The outbreak was traced to egg producer Laerco in Geel, with authorities blocking the entire poultry farm.
As a precaution, eggs from the producer are also being recalled in eight other European countries, including the Netherlands, France, Italy and Portugal, FASFC spokesperson Helene Bonte said.
Salmonella was first detected at the site in late April, prompting a large-scale recall in May covering all eggs from the company’s Geel facility.
Authorities initially believed the contamination was limited to one of the farm’s four sheds.
However, further testing detected contamination in a second shed after the number of newly reported cases failed to decline as expected.
The eggs were distributed through several supermarket chains, including Aldi and Carrefour.
Consumers have been urged not to eat the recalled eggs and to return them to the stores where they were purchased for a refund.

Spain formally requested emergency EU funding to address the migration situation in its North African enclave of Ceuta, the European Commission said Tuesday.

Around 72,000 people irregularly crossed from Morocco into Ceuta on July 30-31, according to the Spanish government’s official estimate.
The unprecedented influx briefly brought a number of migrants almost equivalent to the enclave’s population.
The crisis triggered sharp criticism of Madrid from other European governments. A group of 22 EU countries signed an open letter saying Spain’s relatively open migration policies acted as a “pull factor.”

====================================================================================================

Israel is exporting its West Bank land seizure model to colonize new territory in Syria, using 140 cattle to do it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
14:34:07 UTC
23:34:07 KST

In May 1943, David Ben-Gurion described the failure to settle Hauran, a geographic region spanning southern Syria and northern Jordan, as “a dream that had stayed a dream.” Almost a century later, locals of that region say a new push is underway to make that Zionist dream a reality. The dream may be coming to life at the expense of local pastoralists at Wadi Toemm, on the western edge of the Hauran plain, where a group of Israeli settlers, supported by the Israeli military, have spent the past six months fencing off thousands of dunams of Syrian grazing land for an Israeli cattle colony.
In the village of Ma’ariyah, one of three major villages in the region, 44 kilometers from Daraa’s urban center, Muhammad al-Hafri, a Syrian farmer who relied on the valley’s natural pasture to graze his herds, says that in recent months, the Israeli military and Israeli settlers have effectively cut him and his fellow villagers off from their land.
“The economy of our village depends entirely on herding and early-season crops,” al-Hafri explained. “Ever since the settlers showed up, they have been firing live rounds at anyone who comes near the valley.”
Ma’ariyah is located near the official “buffer zone” that sits on the border of Syria and the Israeli-occupied Syrian Golan Heights. Under the 1974 disengagement agreement, the buffer zone is a demilitarized strip inside Syrian territory, under Syrian civil administration and UN supervision, where no forces other than UN peacekeepers are permitted. Two lines bound it: Alpha, to the west, is the limit Israeli forces may not cross, and Bravo, to the east, is the limit for Syrian forces.
Wadi Toemm runs outside the zone, marking the divide between the occupied Golan and Daraa, though the ground seized for the cattle colony lies within it. Since the fall of the Assad regime in 2024, Israeli forces have pushed past the Alpha line and taken control of Syrian land inside the zone.
Seven months ago, the Israeli military moved 140 head of cattle into the valley floor in Wadi Toemm, pushing Syrian farmers like al-Hafri from their historic pastureland. The land has now been effectively occupied by an Israeli settler named Yoel Zilberman, founder of HaShomer HaHadash, or the New Guard, the movement that pioneered the doctrine of “presence” as territorial control. The Israeli army is aiding him with a reconnaissance unit and nearly 22 kilometers of livestock fencing, parts of it electrified and running alongside minefields.
HaShomer HaHadash was founded in 2007 with the stated aim of reconnecting Jewish Israelis to agricultural land. Under Zilberman’s leadership, it has increasingly functioned as a vehicle for settler land seizure, deploying herds and farming operations to establish a presence in contested areas.
According to the Syrian monitor Sijil, HaShomer HaHadash’s appearance in the region marks the most significant of three attempts to establish outposts there over the past 18 months.
This method of colonization has been exhaustively documented in the occupied West Bank, where so-called “shepherding” or pastoral outposts, composed of small herds that can cover maximal terrain with minimal people under military protection, have helped settlers take over more than 1.1 million dunams (110,000 hectares) of land — close to a fifth of the entire West Bank. Of that, roughly 750,000 dunams (75,000 hectares) have been effectively seized by settlers since December 2022.
This practice of using herds to take over land, coupled with violent settler attacks and restrictions placed on Palestinians to access their own property, has displaced Palestinians across 97 communities and areas since January 2023, most of them Bedouin and herding communities.
Residents of southern Syria now say that Israel is using the same West Bank model to displace them from their land.
The most dangerous attempt yet
Since Israeli forces seized the demilitarized buffer zone in Syria after the fall of the Assad government in December 2024, Israeli forces have been documented seizing and demolishing homes, razing forests, and firing on Syrian herders approaching their own land. Since June 2025, there’s been an average of 17.5 Israeli ground incursions per week, according to Syria monitor Karam Shaar Advisory.
Khaled al-Asaad, who heads the farmers’ association in Ma’ariyah, says the land Israeli forces have seized contains around 40 dunams (4 hectares) of olive groves and 140 (14 hectares) dunams of early-season vegetable fields that produce zucchini, cucumbers, and tomatoes.
“Another 1,200 dunams [120 hectares] of irrigated land are gone, and of the 6,800 dunams [680 hectares] the village once grazed in the valley, 2,000 [200 hectares] remain. Israeli forces have also seized 200 goats and 50 cattle,” he adds.
The economic impacts on farmers and the local community have already been devastating. FEWS NET, the famine early warning network, reported in April that Israeli incursions into Quneitra and Daraa involving checkpoints, detentions, livestock losses, and the destruction of agricultural assets had undermined household livelihoods and pushed families into greater dependence on borrowing. After this farming season was lost to the land seizures, residents were left carrying accumulated debt. Farmers have had to borrow cash flow from agricultural supply offices — local entities that distribute essential farming inputs — to cover lost income.
“I had to sell my car to pay off what I owed,” al-Hafri says. “Others have sold much of their livestock.”
In addition to the loss of land and income, farmers in Quneitra and Daraa said they face mounting restrictions on water sources used to irrigate crops and provide drinking water for livestock. They have also faced an increase in settler gunfire, nighttime military raids, shelling around their villages, road closures, and deliberately damaged electricity infrastructure, including cut power lines and disabled transformers – obstacles which residents say Israeli settlers enforce to make life miserable.
Khaled Khalil, an expert on Syrian-Israeli relations, describes the pastoral cattle colony as the most dangerous settling effort yet in Syria, a product of the growing dominance of Israel’s far right.
“The trio of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir has driven vertical splits inside Israel and energized the extreme religious current, represented by Bashan Pioneers and the New Guard organization, both of which are working to build settlements in the West Bank and southern Syria under the protection of the Israeli army,” he told Mondoweiss.
Founded in April 2025, Bashan Pioneers is a group of Israeli activists named after the biblical region that covers what is now Quneitra, Daraa, and Sweida in Syria. Amos Azaria, a computer science professor at Ariel University — the largest Israeli settlement university located in the West Bank — who leads the group, has said it wants a corridor running from Israel to the Druze areas of Sweida, with the Sunni-majority districts in between emptied and settled by Jews.
The group’s most recent incursions have intensified in recent weeks. In July, members of the Bashan Pioneers repeatedly crossed into southern Syria, including through Mount Hermon, with some remaining inside Syrian territory for hours before being detained and returned by Israeli forces.
The cattle unit
According to a Yedioth Ahronoth report in July, the Israeli army had brought in the cattle to create a reality on the ground as a prelude to settlement. Khalil argues that Israel is replicating the West Bank model in southern Syria through land confiscation, arrests, abuse of residents, and the enclosure of farmland, and that this is underway in every village in the south, from northern Quneitra to western Daraa.
The model, approved in January 2026 by Brig. Gen. Yair Palai and Col. Benny Kata, was deployed by Zilberman, who told Yedioth Ahronoth that the army handed him an operational plan marking the ground it wanted held, and that officers pressed him to “seize the ground faster and restore sovereignty to the area.” The Israel Land Authority is now working with the military to develop procedures regulating civilian use of what remains a closed military zone.
Bassam Alyan, a researcher at the Center for Palestinian Studies, tells Mondoweiss the introduction of cattle herds in the Wadi Toemm area cannot be read as pastoral activity isolated from the political and security context in the West Bank. “Multiple reports,” he says, “have documented how grazing and farming have been used in the West Bank in recent years as a means of entrenching an Israeli presence, particularly in open rural areas that Palestinians find difficult to reach freely.”
One example from Nablus shows how these methods effectively empty villages. In late December 2025, the last six families in the hamlet of Khirbet Yanoun left the village after more than 60 years there, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA). OCHA attributed the ethnic cleansing of Yanoun to Israeli settlers from the Itamar settlement and nearby outposts that blocked grazing areas, stopped Palestinian residents from planting fodder, and cut off access to olive groves. Seven days before, on December 21, settlers had taken over two abandoned houses in the village and plowed 130 dunams of Sahel Yanoun, the community’s own cultivated plain.
The last family was given a few short hours to leave, as reported by Mondoweiss in January 2026. Once Khirbet Yanoun was empty, Israeli forces installed a gate across the road, effectively putting an end to the existence of an entire village.
With settler incursions and attacks on Palestinian communities in the West Bank on the rise, Alyan adds, steps like the introduction of a cattle unit raise fears of effective control expanding over further tracts of land in Syria, whether through the establishment of pastoral outposts or by limiting the ability of farmers and herders to make use of their own land.
Tracking the mounting violations by occupation forces in southern Syria, the Sijjil center documented 187 violations in July and 239 in June, ranging from ground incursions and checkpoints to raids, detentions, and air sorties. In one striking escalation in the humiliation of residents, a patrol at a temporary checkpoint on al-Rafid road stopped a group of passers-by and ordered them to remove their clothes.
All of this, according to Mahmoud Ismail, head of the farmers’ association in al-Rafid, a village abutting the border strip in Quneitra, is meant to create “an environment that drives people out.”
“Residents of the border strip feel no stability, and what they fear most is conditions that push them to leave by indirect means,” he told Mondoweiss. “What is needed is an end to the incursions and a return to security, so that people can stay on their land. If present circumstances do not allow for that, then residents must at least be enabled to remain through aid and compensation for the losses the occupation has inflicted on them”
Not the West Bank yet
Yet, Alyan draws a distinction between the Syrian and Palestinian cases.
“In Palestine, and especially the West Bank and East Jerusalem, millions of Palestinians live on the land itself, and settlement interlocks directly with their communities, their towns, and their villages. Its effect on territorial contiguity and on the establishment of a connected Palestinian state is therefore far greater,” Alyan explained.
“Can what is happening in southern Syria turn into a model resembling settlement in Palestine?” he added. “I’d say the danger exists, but it is not correct to say the outcome is settled.”
Khalil disagrees. He believes Israel is carrying out the same occupation measures in southern Syria that it is carrying out in the West Bank. But he places his hopes in legitimacy, international law, and Syria’s diplomatic efforts, crediting Syrian negotiators with shifting the confrontation from the battlefield to the area of international law — a success he says was reflected in the UN Secretary-General’s visit to Damascus in July.
However, he notes that Guterres’s affirmations regarding Syria’s security and stability, and his emphasis on the international resolutions bearing on the conflict with Israel, “count for little against Israel’s defiance of international legitimacy” and the repeated statements by senior Israeli leaders that they will not withdraw from southern Syria.
Damascus has repeatedly condemned the incursions into Quneitra and Daraa as a violation of Syrian sovereignty. Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa said in July that Syria was working toward a U.S.-mediated security agreement with Israel, avoiding confrontation in the meantime, and pressing for a withdrawal to the 1974 disengagement lines.
For farmers, this debate does not matter. What matters is that they are seeing their land being taken before their very eyes, with seemingly no way to stop it.
In Ma’ariyah, the village has lost around two-thirds of its livestock, al-Hafri says, sold off as fodder prices climbed and the animals died of thirst. Residents can no longer move between the last house on the valley’s edge and the al-Jazeera base, taken after Assad fell.
“First, we sold the animals,” he says. “If things stay as they are, the land goes next.”
Residents of the southern villages insist, however, that they will not let these attempts succeed.
“They are holding on to their land despite their meager means,” Ismail from al-Rafid told Mondoweiss.

Colombia to treat all illegal armed groups as terrorists under new security strategy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
14:31:34 UTC
23:31:34 KST

Mariam Ashalem De Andres
25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
Colombian President Abelardo De La Espriella announced a comprehensive security strategy that will treat all illegal armed groups as terror organizations, regardless of their name or structure.
“When it comes to combating crime, there are no differences in the action of the State or in the response of the State, and much less in an organization designed by those seeking to protect these bandits so that the State cannot exercise the legitimate force as it should. All are terrorists and we are going to treat them as such,” De La Espriella said in a statement by the presidency.
The president ordered the immediate creation of a National Search Bloc to combat extortion, bringing together the army, police, navy and Aerospace Force in coordination with the Attorney General’s Office and the judiciary.
He also ordered the reactivation of the Financial Information and Analysis Unit (UIAF), which will be headed by former prosecutor Marta Lurreyes, and will have access to banking information from the last four years.
The unit will work with police and financial institutions to identify and dismantle the financial structures supporting criminal organizations, according to the statement.
The strategy also includes the reactivation of a rewards system, police raids and a network of civilian informants, as well as urgent transfers of prisoners to prevent prisons from continuing to operate as centers for extortion.
On migration, De La Espriella instructed Migration Colombia to launch coordinated operations with police in Barranquilla this week to target irregular migration and foreign criminal activity.
He also ordered the Colombian Public Force to operate as a “single and unified body,” without institutional rivalries, and announced the creation of elite teams of prosecutors and judges specializing in organized crime in each city.
The teams will target the so-called land cartel and the “gota a gota” system of informal, high-interest lending, which De La Espriella described as a modern form of slavery affecting millions of Colombians.
Colombia continues to face threats from armed and criminal groups, including the National Liberation Army (ELN), FARC dissidents and the Gulf Clan, which authorities link to drug trafficking, extortion, kidnapping and illegal mining.
Security has been a key priority for De La Espriella’s government, which has stepped up military and police operations against armed groups and criminal organizations.

Sex sells and wins votes – and the Democrats know it | Arwa Mahdawi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
14:30:25 UTC
23:30:25 KST

Despite being a card-carrying member of the International Order of Confirmed Homosexuals, I have spent quite a lot of time lately thinking about Abdul El-Sayed’s biceps. I mean, have you seen them? The progressive Michigan senate nominee is jacked and he knows it. He almost always wears a tight black T-shirt to show off his muscles and incorporates a lot of fitness content in his campaign.
I’m not the only one who has noticed El-Sayed’s prominent muscles. They have had a lot of coverage, and are seen as part of a wider attempt to rebrand the Democratic party. Which, I don’t need to tell you, has a serious image problem; a poll in March found that the party is looked on even less favourably than the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency. So, to make it look less like a party that is full of out-of-touch technocrats who sound as if they are reading from a 500-page PowerPoint presentation every time they try to explain anything, Democrats seem to be trying to up the sex appeal.
“Democrats enter their thirst trap era,” News website Axios recently declared, summing up the phenomenon. The piece observed that the Democrats’ main TikTok page has given “the thirst trap treatment” to big names including El-Sayed, Zohran Mamdani and senator Jon Ossoff (“nicknamed ‘Senator My Boo’ by internet fans”), by posting flirty photos and videos. Axios quotes a political analyst who explains that while female Democrats such as Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez have had their share of screen time, the Dems’ TikTok page has made a “very intentional choice to feature the most attractive male members”.
Fox News would appear to reluctantly agree with the assessment that Democrats are leaning into good looks to win the midterms. “El-Sayed is out in these tight T-shirts,” Fox News host Ainsley Earhardt said in a discussion last week. “AOC with her pretty smile. She’s beautiful. She’s got the red lipstick. You have Mamdani, always smiling … It doesn’t make their philosophy any less dangerous, right?… even with a tight T-shirt, it’s still socialism and it fails.”
Over on CNN there was a little more jubilation about the Democrats’ vibe shift. “Dems are hot again,” strategist Yemisi Egbewole proclaimed. “They’re coming out of the closet as hot people and I’m so excited.” Egbewole added that it wasn’t just about physical attractiveness: “I think they’re learning from Trump. Entertainment really sells.”
Sex sells too: it’s well established that voters around the world prefer good-looking candidates. But, while we may all be shallow deep down, some of us are shallower than others. A 2016 study found that rightwing politicians in Europe, the US and Australia tended to be more attractive than their progressive counterparts. That’s partly because “low-information” conservative voters are particularly prone to choosing attractive candidates. “In low-information city elections, a beauty increase of one standard deviation attracts about 20% more votes for the average candidate on the right and about 8% more votes for the average candidate on the left,” an analysis of the study by the Washington Post noted. Which raises the question: if looks really are so important to low-information rightwing voters, how did we end up with Donald Trump as president? (Woke 1.0 is over, haven’t you heard? It’s OK to say things like this now.)
Social media may have brought a new visual element to politics, but the most famous anecdote about how looks can sway an election is almost 70 years old. In September 1960, 70 million Americans watched Richard Nixon debate John F Kennedy in the first nationally televised debate between presidential candidates. Nixon had been the favourite going in but he had just been in hospital for a couple of weeks and looked terrible. JFK, on the other hand, was tanned and rested and had good stage makeup.
You can quibble with the conventional wisdom that Nixon lost that election on looks, but it certainly played a part. In his memoir, Nixon wrote: “What hurt me the most in the first debate was not the substance of the encounter between Kennedy and me, but the disadvantageous contrast in our appearances. After the program ended, callers, including my mother, wanted to know if anything was wrong, because I did not look well.”
In short: if thirst traps are what it takes to get the US on a better path, then so be it. Jacked candidates in tight T-shirts may seem like a cheap trick, but even Nixon’s mother would agree that it’s a sound political strategy.
Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

Ukraine mapped Russia’s Su-35 down to individual control units—and found 22 firms nobody has sanctioned
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
14:30:23 UTC
23:30:23 KST

Ukraine's military intelligence has named the Russian companies that build the Su-35S fighter jet and singled out those no country has sanctioned, according to the Main Intelligence Directorate of Ukraine's Defense Ministry (HUR). The unsanctioned suppliers make parts as ordinary as wheels and fuel-system units, and one of them helped develop the aircraft. Kyiv wants sanctions efforts synchronized across every link of Russia's military-industrial complex.
The 22 firms no one has sanctioned
HUR identified 79 companies in the Su-35S production chain. Of those, 22 face no sanctions from any country restricting Russia over the war. The agency highlighted three. Rubin Aviation Corporation supplies the aircraft's braking and non-braking wheels. Gidroavtomatika builds the AU46-05 control units inside the fuel system. The Oktava research institute carried out design and development work on the Su-35S itself.
What the rest of the network builds
The 79 firms develop and produce the engines and fuel system, the control, communications, and guidance systems, the electronic warfare suite, and the main aviation missiles the jet carries into the war against Ukraine. HUR set the data out in the "Components in weapons" section of its War&Sanctions portal. The page carries a rotatable 3D model of the aircraft whose parts open onto the firms behind them, alongside directory listings and a profile for each company.
Ukraine mapped Russia’s Su-35 down to individual control units—and found 22 firms nobody has sanctioned
Three sanctions regimes, loosely aligned
The gaps HUR points to exist because the restrictions are not one list. The EU legislates in packages, the US and other G7 states maintain their own designations, and Ukraine issues sanctions by presidential decree, each covering a different set of firms. Kyiv has spent years asking partners to synchronize those lists, and its own designations often run ahead of them. A company can therefore supply a frontline fighter and still trade freely under most of them.
Previously, HUR ran the same exercise on the Su-34, where a third of the production network was still unsanctioned. The same pattern shows up above the component level, with Russia's largest arms conglomerate covered by EU measures while hundreds of its subsidiaries are not, and Western machine tools still sitting inside Russian missile plants.

Rare tornado rips through southern France (VIDEOS)
A rare and violent tornado has run rampant through the village of Pomas in southern France, injuring 39 people, including two critically, and damaging around 300 homes, according to the local authorities.
The tornado struck the village in the Aude department on Monday evening, with footage showing a large funnel swirling over the settlement, with gusts of violent winds wreaking havoc, ripping apart roofs, and smashing windows.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez called it a “tornado of rare intensity” while praising firefighters, security forces, and volunteers involved in the response.
Rescue operations continued through the night, the prefecture said on Tuesday, with 75 firefighters deployed alongside specialist reinforcements to check damaged buildings and search affected areas.
Residents forced from their homes were sheltered in a multi-purpose hall with help from the Red Cross, while others were temporarily relocated with relatives or to neighboring communes.
🌪️Eyewitness footage recorded from the village of #Verzeille captured a #tornado forming and swirling beneath a violent supercell thunderstorm south of the southern French city of #Carcassonne. https://t.co/tL5GfNBnxLpic.twitter.com/oGurjJdrxi
📌Authorities reported at least 26… pic.twitter.com/U5AVlVP0iw
While no people were reported killed or missing, among the injured was a pregnant woman who was hurt when her house collapsed on her, according to AFP.
The storm also battered electricity infrastructure across southern France. Grid operator Enedis said about 21,000 households were without power across the south on Tuesday morning, including around 1,600 in Aude. The prefecture later put the number still without electricity locally at about 1,400.
The tornado appears unusually powerful by French standards. Emmanuel Wesolek, president of the Keraunos severe-weather observatory, told HuffPost that an initial assessment indicated “gusts of more than 200 kph” and potentially as high as 240 kph.
The tornado would likely rate somewhere between the upper end of EF2 and the lower end of EF3 on the Enhanced Fujita scale, he added.
According to Meteo-France, while not as frequent as in the US, a few dozen tornadoes occur in mainland France in an average year, and most are of low intensity. According to figures cited by HuffPost, EF2 tornadoes occur only once or twice annually, while an EF3 is recorded roughly once every four years.

UNRWA urges international community to protect training center after Israeli raid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
14:29:13 UTC
23:29:13 KST

Serdar Dincel
25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
The UN agency for Palestinian refugees (UNRWA) on Tuesday called on the international community to act “immediately and decisively” to safeguard its Qalandia Training Center north of Jerusalem after Israeli security forces raided the facility. 
“Today at approximately 10:00, Israeli Security Forces forcibly entered” the center in occupied East Jerusalem, UNRWA said in a statement. 
At least four armored vehicles entered the premises, accompanied by more than 50 Israeli security personnel, it added. 
Approximately 20 UNRWA staff members were present at the site at the time of the incident, the agency noted. 
“The entry of armed security forces into a United Nations facility, without the authorization or consent of the United Nations, is unacceptable,” it added. 
Earlier Tuesday, the Israeli army carried out raids in the village of Kafr Aqab and the Qalandia refugee camp north of Jerusalem, forcing agency staff to vacate the training center. 
Israeli forces also issued demolition warnings for several Palestinian structures in the area. 
Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir boasted about the raid on the training center, while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he had directly ordered the operation, contravening UN protections and international warnings. 
The raid came a day after representatives of 49 diplomatic missions accredited to the State of Palestine visited the center to assess conditions facing refugees and Israeli restrictions on the agency’s work. 
Ben-Gvir personally took part in the raid, posting a photograph of himself at the center’s entrance on social media and showing an Israeli flag that had been hoisted over the facility by Israeli forces. 
“UNRWA is in our hands,” Ben-Gvir crowed in the social-media post. 
The raid on the facility comes as Netanyahu’s government seeks to appease its far-right constituency amid mounting domestic political pressure, according to political observers. 
Netanyahu, for his part, said the evacuation of UNRWA staff from the center had been carried out on his direct orders. 
“In accordance with my directive and following the law we passed, the evacuation of the UNRWA compound in Kafr Aqab, Jerusalem, began today,” he said in a  statement. 
He added that his government would not allow UNRWA to operate and “will act against it by all means at its disposal.” 
Netanyahu’s actions come despite the fact that UNRWA facilities are protected -- in theory at least -- by rights and privileges granted to the UN under international law. 
Facility protected under international law 
Earlier this month, UNRWA said the Qalandia training center was a UN vocational training facility. 
It stressed that all the agency’s facilities, including the Qalandia center, were protected by UN privileges and immunities under international law. 
The agency noted that the center was established in 1952 as its first training center, adding that it provides technical and vocational training to about 340 young Palestinian refugees each year. 
At the beginning of 2025, Israel closed UNRWA’s main headquarters in the Sheikh Jarrah neighborhood of occupied East Jerusalem and later announced its seizure by the authorities. 
UNRWA was established in 1949 by a UN General Assembly resolution, and was tasked with providing assistance -- and extending protection -- to Palestinian refugees in Jordan, Syria, Lebanon, the West Bank and the Gaza Strip.

CIA Director John Ratcliffe on secret trip in Russia

It appears to be Ratcliffe's first known trip to Russia as CIA director, though he has maintained contact with Russian intelligence counterparts.

The CIA has also played a role in recent U.S.-Russia detainee exchanges, including the April 2025 release of a U.S.-Russian dual national Ksenia Karelina, whose case Ratcliffe personally negotiated. Former CIA Director William Burns traveled to Moscow in November 2021, when he met with senior Russian officials and spoke directly with President Vladimir Putin to warn him against invading Ukraine.
Ratcliffe's visit comes as U.S.-mediated peace talks with Ukraine remain mostly stalled, with the sides still far apart on core issues.

European Commission announces new decisions and defense payments for Ukraine in coming weeks
Ukrinform reported this, citing European Commission spokesperson Balazs Ujvari as saying at a news briefing in Brussels.
At the same time, he noted that the European Commission had not received an official request from Ukraine for the early disbursement of the allocated funding.
“We have allocated €45 billion for this year and around €45 billion for next year. This year, €28 billion is allocated for defense and around €17 billion for budget support, and this is also the plan for next year. As far as I know, we have not received an official request to accelerate this process. So, we are focused on implementing this plan,” the spokesperson said.
Of the €28 billion earmarked for Ukraine’s defense support this year, the EU has already allocated €22 billion, of which €8.5 billion has already been disbursed, the official went on to say.
“In the coming weeks, you will see more decisions, more payments. Over the next few weeks, we will be very busy on defense because we know what is at stake, we know there is an incredible sense of urgency, and accordingly, we are accelerating our work,” Ujvari said.
Asked whether the European Commission had rejected Ukraine’s request for early funding, Ujvari clarified that the EC had not received such a request. “We have not been informed bilaterally that Ukraine wants early funding, so we are focused on the plans we have in place,” he added.
At the same time, the spokesperson emphasized that the European Commission remained open to considering any requests from Ukraine.
“There is a continuous exchange of information between us and Ukraine about the latest developments. And we are ready to meet Ukraine’s requests to the maximum extent possible. But again, we have a plan that has been put in place, exchanges of information with Ukraine are ongoing, and we will conduct our work on that basis,” he explained.
Responding to a question about the contribution of other international partners toward covering Ukraine’s defense needs, Ujvari said that the EU’s contribution was significant but insufficient to fully meet Ukraine’s needs.
“That is why we use every opportunity to raise this issue with our partners, like-minded countries in the G7 and in ad hoc formats,” the spokesperson said.
He added that the EU was focused on implementing its share of the contribution to Ukraine’s defense, but “it is important that other partners also follow this example.”
For her part, European Commission chief spokesperson Paula Pinho praised several of Ukraine’s partners for their additional bilateral commitments and offers of defense assistance to Ukraine.

Punctuality at Zurich Airport improves, SWISS stagnates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
14:28:00 UTC
23:28:00 KST

Punctuality at Zurich Airport improves, SWISS stagnates
Punctuality at Zurich Airport improved during the peak summer season of 2026. Swiss International Air Lines (SWISS), on the other hand, had to contend with more cancellations and diverted landings, meaning that its punctuality did not improve.
Across Zurich Airport as a whole, departure punctuality in June and July was significantly higher than in both of the previous two years, the airport’s chief operating officer, Stefan Tschudin, told the media on Tuesday.
In July, for example, 56% of flights took off with a delay of less than 15 minutes. That is five percentage points more than in July 2025. Since the start of the year, punctuality at Switzerland’s largest airport has averaged 66%.
“We’ve made a great many improvements,” said Tschudin. For example, staff numbers have been adjusted and the airport has hired its own meteorologist to provide local weather forecasts. This enables the airport to take operational measures in the event of adverse weather conditions, such as the Bise wind or thunderstorms.
Similarly, the docking stations at the gates have been fitted with cameras. The aim is to analyse and improve aircraft handling processes. Nevertheless, Tschudin admitted that the airport had not quite met its own punctuality target of 65% for July.
More
Flying in Switzerland set to become even more expensive
SWISS stagnates
The same applies to SWISS, where punctuality has shown no improvement. Throughout the summer, 59% of flights departed with a delay of less than a quarter of an hour. Punctuality thus remained at the previous year’s level. The airline failed to meet its own target of 65%.
The main cause was the weather, said SWISS’s Chief Operating Officer, Oliver Buchhofer, in an interview with the AWP news agency. “The thunderstorms were stronger and more intense than last year.” The thunderstorm on June 30 alone – which raged over Zurich Airport for two-and-a-half hours without moving – accounted for a third of all last-minute flight cancellations at SWISS this summer.
As a result, 26 aircraft had to divert to other airports. In total, over 10,000 passengers were affected by the thunderstorm on June 30.
SWISS also faced difficulties due to strikes abroad and technical issues. The cancellation of flights to Tel Aviv and Dubai due to the war in Iran also had an impact, said Buchhofer. Flight schedule reliability fell to 97.1% from 98.5% the previous year.
The number of last-minute cancellations was 80% higher than in the previous year. A total of 337 flights were cancelled at short notice. However, in 2024 the figure had been just over twice as high.
More
SWISS flight makes emergency landing on the Azores
Series of peak days
Zurich Airport and SWISS struggled to cope with the high passenger numbers: from mid-July to early August, over 120,000 travellers passed through the airport on each of five peak days.
The busiest day was August 2, with just under 122,000 passengers, around half of whom were travelling with SWISS. That was only around 500 fewer than the all-time record set on October 5, 2025.
The pressure was high, said Tschudin. There were almost no breaks at all. The heatwaves had been an additional strain. When it was 35°C outside, it was 55°C on the tarmac near the aircraft and, in the belly of a plane, sometimes over 60°C.
This placed an enormous strain on the baggage handlers. To cool them down, the aircraft de-icing machines were used, said Tschudin.
Despite the mixed results this summer, SWISS manager Buchhofer believes the annual target of 70% punctuality is still within reach. “At the moment, things are still looking good.” SWISS is currently still slightly above last year’s level. “I haven’t given up on the target yet. It would be too early for that. We’re working on it,” Buchhofer told the AWP.

‘Not an isolated incident’: Russian drones stalk Ukraine’s civilians in ‘human safaris’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
14:27:23 UTC
23:27:23 KST

‘Not an isolated incident’: Russian drones stalk Ukraine’s civilians in ‘human safaris’
The video of a Ukrainian cyclist being targeted and killed by a short-range drone posted – and later deleted – by the Russian military Friday left viewers outraged and shaken. But it’s not the first time that Russian drone operators have been accused of terrorising Ukrainian civilians by deliberately targeting them in “human safaris” denounced as a war crime by an independent UN commission.
First, he freezes, caught off guard. Then the young Ukrainian cyclist begins to backpedal awkwardly, his eyes never leaving the Russian drone that hovers ahead of him. It moves closer, and he swings his leg over the bike and tries to run. He doesn’t make it.
Even though the footage, posted Friday on the official Telegram account of the 3rd Army Corps of the Russian armed forces, cuts off before the moment of impact, the video’s description leaves no doubt of the outcome. The Russian soldiers congratulate themselves on having taken out an “enemy combatant” in the Ukrainian district of Kramatorsk, not far from the front line in the northern Donetsk region.
Two years of ‘human safaris’
But the cyclist was visibly unarmed, wearing civilian clothes and looked like any other young man riding his bike down a country road. Independent Russian media outlet Astra quickly accused the Russian military of trying to pass off an unarmed cyclist as a Ukrainian combatant.
The video spread swiftly across social media as influential accounts, including prominent Kremlin critic and former world chess champion Garry Kasparov, reposted the footage to denounce the Russian military’s apparent cruelty.
Less than 48 hours and hundreds of outraged comments later, the 3rd Army Corps took the video down.
It’s far from the first time that Russian drones laden with explosives and controlled from a distance have targeted civilians in Ukraine’s frontline regions. The Ukrainians have even found a term for these deadly drone hunts – “human safaris”.
“On the one hand, I'm very happy that there is more attention on this,” said Olga Tokariuk, a specialist in Ukraine at the British think-tank Chatham House. “On the other hand, this is not something new. This has been happening for two years. And the impunity that Russia faces for these attacks just means it can continue.”
Watch moreKherson under fire: The reality behind the Russian drone strikes
The “human safari” carried out by Russian drone operators seems to have begun in July 2024 in Kherson, a city on the banks of Dnipro River in the country’s south.
“Kherson in 2024 was the point at which isolated incidents developed into a sustained campaign,” said Will Kingston-Cox, a specialist in Russia and the Ukraine war at the International Team for the Study of Security in Verona. “Initially, small quadcopters followed individuals and vehicles and dropped explosives. Since then, we have seen FPV (first-person view) impact drones expanding the practice in scale, frequency and geography. Documented targets include pedestrians, cyclists, private cars, buses, ambulances and rescue workers.”
In Kherson, Russian forces installed on the opposite bank of the Dnipro can easily use short-range drones to target the population who had either remained in or returned to the city following its recapture by the Ukrainian army at the end of 2022.
‘Those seconds are so precious’
Numerous eye-witness accounts, including several reported by FRANCE 24’s Observers team, describe a climate of constant fear of being targeted and killed by a Russian drone.
Read moreHow Russian drones are terrorising civilians in Ukraine
Tokariuk, who wrote a report on the “human safaris” in 2025, said that people she’d interviewed in Kherson had spoken of being under a state of almost permanent tension.
“Something really striking that they told me was they would only go out there if the weather was bad – because drones cannot really operate in rain or snow or fog,” she said. “And they would also tell me they would drive really fast in their cars, because that maximises your chances of survival if you're hunted by a drone … People wouldn’t use their seatbelts when they're driving, because those seconds are so precious when they see a drone hovering above their car about to hit them, and they need to get out of the car really quickly.”
For its part, the UN’s Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine condemned these “human safaris” as a war crime, for deliberately targeting a civilian population, and a potential crime against humanity, for its possible use as a tool to carry out forcible population transfers.
“They are targeting precisely not only civilians in their day-to-day life, but also hospitals and shops and very basic things that sustain day-to-day life for people,” said Ivan Klyszcz, a specialist in Russia at the Centre of Defence and Security in Tallinn, Estonia. “So there's definitely a pressure on the civilian population, and inevitably this leads to people to relocate. I cannot say that this is part of a larger plan for population transfer – but it is working out that way.”
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
The UN commission reported that roughly 150 civilians had been killed and hundreds more wounded in Kherson region by short-range drones since the end of 2024.
Veronika Hinman, a specialist in the Ukraine war at the University of Portsmouth who has studied the use of drones in the conflict, said that while she wasn’t convinced the practice could be described as official army tactics, it certainly seemed tolerated by the military brass.
“I've been trying to think whether this could be just an isolated incident, whether we could consider these drone operators as 'bad apples' or rogue soldiers acting independently – or whether, if you look at the company itself that, they are remnants of an informal militia integrated into Russian forces later on,” she said. “But no, it doesn't seem anything like that. It's not an isolated incident.”
Cutting promos
Although Kherson remains ground zero for this grim practice, the fact that Friday’s cyclist was targeted by a drone in the distant Kramatorsk district shows that these “human safaris” have spread beyond the battered city.
Tokariuk said similar attacks had also been reported in Ukraine’s border region of Sumy, as well as in Kharkhiv, which sits across the border from Russia’s Belgorod region.
She maintained it was impossible that the drone operators didn’t know the people they were targeting were civilians.
“They know exactly what they’re doing,” she said. “The operators of these drones, they can see the real-time footage of who the drone is chasing.”
The practice is also likely a macabre way to train Russian troops to pilot the remote-controlled drones, Hinman said.
“Civilians are not protected. They are easy targets because of what they are wearing, as opposed to soldiers on the battlefield,” she said.
It may be that these “human safaris” can also allow Russian officers to made sure that the drone operators under their command won’t be overcome by remorse during combat operations. After all, soldiers who are apparently prepared to target old people leaving their homes and children playing in the street – cases documented by the UN commission – would likely be ready to carry out any other order.
Read moreZelensky calls on allies to cover €27 billion gap for Ukraine’s air defence needs
Hinman said that these videos also served encourage Russian viewers to donate money for the production and purchase of more drones to deploy at the front.
“One of the reasons why they post these on social media, why they make these social media posts, can be to show off what these drones are being used for to the people who fundraise for them,” she said.
By seemingly trying to pass off an unarmed civilian for a hardened Ukrainian soldier, Kingston-Cox said, Friday’s video appeared to have backfired – possibly, he said, explaining why it was later taken down.
“That discrepancy made the video both a propaganda liability and potentially important evidence,” he said. “Operational security concerns cannot be excluded, but reputational and legal containment appears more plausible – particularly because the footage appeared on a channel associated with the army rather than an anonymous pro-war 'miliblogger' (Russian military blogger) account.”
But Tokariuk said she didn’t think the controversy the video had caused would have any real impact on the Russian army’s use of these tactics.
“These drones are cheap to operate – they are flying the distances that they need to,” she said. “In those border regions they use drones because it works. It really keeps civilians in terror. It makes people flee.“
She said the seeming impunity that Russia had enjoyed for more than two years now over its “human safaris” made her worry that other states or actors could start to carry out their own version of the low-cost war crime.
“It is very easy to replicate elsewhere,” she said. “And civilians are completely defenceless against it.”

Steady, locally heavy rain and thunderstorms are expected

Moderate northeasterly winds will prevail, bringing cool air to the country; its chill will be most noticeable in the northern part of the country, especially at night. Variable cloudiness. Moderate, locally heavy rain and thunderstorms in the central regions, Zakarpattia, Chernivtsi, as well as in most southern regions and the Kyiv region during the day; no precipitation in the rest of the country

Zelensky also said Ukraine expects to receive a schedule for the FREYJA initiative within seven to 10 days, including information on meetings and areas where cooperation with defense companies is currently blocked.
Norway has confirmed $9 billion in funding for Ukraine for 2027, according to Zelensky.
He said Norway could also help finance the development of an office dedicated to the FREYJA initiative.
“Thank you to our partners for all this support,” Zelensky said.
Zelensky asks for 300 Patriot missiles
Zelensky told reporters on Saturday that Ukraine is seeking 300 Patriot missiles for the winter. He has previously said that if Kyiv could buy 5% of US Patriot missile stocks, it would survive the winter, and if it could purchase 10%, it could destroy all of Russia’s ballistic missiles.

At least 437 Ukrainian civilians were killed in July 2026, a 30% increase from a year earlier, according to the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine.

Trump ignored top-level warnings before launching Iran war: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
14:26:33 UTC
23:26:33 KST

Muhammed Yasin Güngör
25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
US President Donald Trump launched the February offensive against Iran despite explicit warnings from his intelligence chief, vice president and senior military advisers that the conflict could trigger a global energy crisis and lead to a more hard-line Iranian leadership, The Wall Street Journal reported.
According to people familiar with pre-war meetings, then-Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard told Trump that killing Iran’s supreme leader would likely “usher in a more hard-line” successor and force the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic waterway through which one-fifth of global oil and gas trade passes.
US Vice President JD Vance also advocated a more “cautious,” negotiation-first approach, arguing that a diplomatic deal would be less costly than a war with “unwieldy consequences.”
While top military officials, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine, briefed Trump on “decisive” strike options, other officials raised concerns about munitions shortages and risks to an “overstretched force.” Trump reportedly dismissed those concerns, suggesting the military could “handle any problems” as they arose.
The report said Trump was initially pleased with the start of the war and “puffed out his chest” at a Mar-a-Lago fundraiser when informed of the killing of then-Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei.
However, as fuel prices soared and the war stalled, regional leaders from Saudi Arabia and Qatar pressed the White House for a diplomatic solution. Internal polling showed nearly 80% of Americans favored an agreement to end the war, prompting Trump to pursue the June interim truce.
Some Republicans also warned Trump about the potential impact of a prolonged war on their chances in the November midterm elections.
The 60-day window for nuclear negotiations ended on Aug. 17 without a final settlement.
The administration has since shifted back to Operation Economic Outcast, a campaign of economic warfare aimed at weakening the Iranian government through a sustained naval blockade and sanctions.

How an Election in Okinawa Will Impact East Asian Security
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
14:25:00 UTC
23:25:00 KST

Okinawa Prefecture will hold its gubernatorial election on September 13. Incumbent Governor Denny Tamaki, in office since 2018, is seeking a third term. His main challenger is Koja Genta, a former deputy mayor of Naha backed by the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP). While local elections in Japan typically center on issues like the local economy and social welfare, Okinawa’s pivotal geographic location means this election could become a critical variable influencing the future security situation of East Asia.
Okinawa sits at the heart of the First Island Chain and is the Japanese territory closest to both Taiwan and mainland China. Consequently, since the end of World War II, Okinawa has served as the U.S. military’s “Keystone of the Pacific,” bearing a heavy military burden. Currently, nearly 70 percent of U.S. military bases in Japan are located in Okinawa.
Beyond the U.S. presence, Japan’s Self-Defense Forces (SDF) are also expanding their deployments in Okinawa as the country accelerates a defense strategy known as the “Southwest Shift.” For instance, the Ground Self-Defense Force’s 15th Brigade, stationed in Okinawa, is set to be reorganized into a division by March 2027, increasing its personnel from 2,300 to 3,900. Furthermore, over the past decade, the Japanese government has deployed SDF units to Yonaguni, Miyako, and Ishigaki, islands located west of Okinawa Island, while bolstering radar, air defense, and rapid-response capabilities to counter the People’s Liberation Army’s (PLA) growing military activity in the East China Sea and the Western Pacific beyond the First Island Chain.
In fact, the PLA and the SDF have frequently engaged in standoffs in the area in recent years. On December 6, 2025, a fighter jet launched from a Chinese aircraft carrier locked radar on an Air Self-Defense Force fighter while flying over the high seas southeast of Okinawa Island, sparking a strong protest from Tokyo. Additionally, Chinese naval fleets and joint Chinese-Russian fleets have frequently transited the waters surrounding these islands. These developments underscore how Okinawa is increasingly becoming a frontline for great power confrontation.
For the people of Okinawa situated at the eye of the storm, the issue of U.S. and Japanese military deployments is not a simple matter of support versus opposition. It involves conflicting inner sentiments.
On one hand, as China increases its activities near Okinawa – particularly with frequent patrols by its coast guard vessels in the waters around the Senkaku Islands (known in China as the Diaoyu Islands) – Okinawan perceptions of the military forces stationed there are shifting. According to public opinion polls, a greater number of Okinawans now view the presence of the SDF and even the U.S. military as necessary compared to the 1970s, shortly after the islands’ return to Japan.
On the other hand, this shift does not alleviate Okinawans’ collective anxiety. For Tokyo, the deployment of missiles, radar systems, and SDF units may signify enhanced deterrence and situational awareness. However, for the local residents, these facilities also imply a higher likelihood that their home could become a frontline in a conflict or a target for attack. This has sparked a contradictory mindset and an enduring debate among the Okinawan people: Do military assets guarantee their safety or bring greater danger?
Since taking office as prefectural governor in 2018, Tamaki has made opposition to the construction of the new U.S. base at Henoko and the reduction of the base burden on Okinawa the core of his political agenda. However, the LDP’s victory in all four of Okinawa’s electoral districts during the February 2026 House of Representatives election clearly served as a warning sign for Tamaki. Furthermore, a capsizing incident in March involving boats participating in protests against the Henoko base, which resulted in two fatalities, including a student on a school trip, triggered criticism directed at Tamaki, a staunch opponent of the base. The upcoming election will serve as a critical test of Tamaki’s stance against the Henoko base, the expansion of SDF deployments in Okinawa, and joint Japan-U.S. military exercises.
This is why the contest between Tamaki and Koja holds significance that extends beyond local politics. If Tamaki is re-elected, Tokyo may continue to face political resistance from the Okinawa prefectural government. While a governor cannot single-handedly halt the Japanese government’s national defense policies, a local government opposed to Tokyo’s military agenda can still raise the political costs of implementation and engage in ongoing bargaining regarding the burden of military bases and local interests. Under these circumstances, although Japan may proceed with the military deployment in the Nansei (Southwestern) Islands, the rift between Tokyo and Okinawan society could widen further.
For Tokyo, another challenge lies in preventing the discord with Okinawa from undermining Japan-U.S. alliance operations in the region. Clearly, the United States expects Japan not only to sustain investment in military deployments on Okinawa, thereby sharing security responsibilities, but also to effectively manage tensions between military forces and Okinawan society.
In September 2025, U.S. forces and the SDF conducted “Resolute Dragon 25,” a large-scale exercise spanning a vast area that included Okinawa. This sparked widespread protests among local residents. Some protesters took to the streets, directly forcing the SDF to alter its operational plans. This underscores that the Japan-U.S. alliance cannot be sustained by military facilities alone: It requires the understanding and support of the communities hosting them. If Tamaki wins re-election, the friction between Okinawan society and the military presence will be difficult to resolve over the ensuing four years.
Conversely, a victory for Koja could present a significant political opportunity for Tokyo. His election might mark a turning point in the relationship between the Okinawan prefectural government and the central government, potentially opening up greater scope for local cooperation on base policies and defense infrastructure in the Nansei Islands.
If Okinawan society increasingly perceives itself as bearing the risks of war solely for the strategic interests of Tokyo and Washington, the expansion of their military capabilities could exacerbate tensions with the local population. However, if Tokyo can convince Okinawa that strengthening defenses serves not only Japan’s national security but also the protection of Okinawa itself, then the military deployment in the Nansei Islands might secure a more stable political foundation. Ultimately, the outcome hinges largely on who leads Okinawa for the next four years.
Furthermore, this election also has implications regarding China. In recent years, Beijing has paid increasing attention to Okinawa, attempting to leverage the Okinawan people’s historical memories and anti-base sentiment to construct political narratives directed against both Japan and the United States. For instance, following Tamaki’s visit to China in July 2023, Chinese state media highlighted the historical ties between China and Okinawa (Ryukyu), as well as the tensions between Okinawan society and the U.S. military.
Furthermore, in recent years, Beijing has increasingly used its state media to question Japan’s sovereignty over Okinawa, which is a stance Tamaki has generally sought to avoid criticizing. Regarding the upcoming election, Beijing likely hopes that Tamaki, who holds a relatively moderate view toward China, will remain in office, thereby allowing for continued propaganda efforts challenging the Japan-U.S. military presence in Okinawa. However, this is clearly an outcome that neither Tokyo nor Washington desires.
In conclusion, this election will shape the relationship between Tokyo and Okinawan society over the next four years. More importantly, it will determine whether the Japan-U.S. alliance can maintain a solid foundation in Okinawa amidst China’s rise and escalating risks in the Taiwan Strait. This is precisely why the election is bound to draw intense scrutiny from Washington, Beijing, and Tokyo alike.
