China sends archaeologists to South America to trace ancestral links for the first time
Joint project with Peru will start with field surveys in the Caral zone, which is home to the oldest known urban centre in the Americas
Chinese archaeologists are heading to South America for the first field project on the continent in search of ancestral bonds between ancient Chinese and native American civilisations.
The joint archaeological team will start the project with field surveys exploring the basins of the Chancay-Huaral and Supe rivers and key sites such as the Sacred City of Caral and the coastal settlement of Aspero.
Jia Xiaobing from the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences’ Institute of Archaeology, who led the Chinese delegation in Supe, said the collaboration would cover field surveys and excavations, the use of advanced technologies in archaeology, heritage conservation and researcher training.
The archaeological community believes that Chinese and American civilisations descended from the same ancestor.
Despite being separated by vast oceans, Chinese and Peruvian civilisations share interesting similarities in areas such as astronomical observation and spiritual beliefs, according to a statement from Jia’s institute.

How memories may survive hibernation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
14:00:00 UTC
23:00:00 KST

How memories may survive hibernation
Changes in the brains of hibernating mice reveal surprising resilience
How do you fit a human life’s experiences into 1.3 kilograms of brain? Neuroscientists have searched for the cells that generate and store our memories for decades. Now, some surprising hints have turned up in the brains of hibernating mice.
Over two days, hibernating mice temporarily lost nearly half of the connections between their brain cells in a key brain region for memory. But after this ordeal, the mice retained their memories. Imaging shows that key connections between brain cells had regrown, often in exactly the same place that they had disappeared from. The researchers also identified hub-like clusters of brain cell connections that were preserved during the cull.
The findings, published August 13 in Science, bring scientists closer to understanding how memories are acquired, lost and preserved.
The human brain is constantly recording new memories, yet still manages to retain some of this information in the long term. Reconciling these two abilities is a challenge, says Kazumasa Tanaka, a neuroscientist at the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology in Japan.
The hippocampus, the center of episodic memory, is “one of the most dynamic structures in the brain,” Tanaka says. There, synapses — connections between brain cells integral to brain function — grow and shrink almost constantly, but allow the brain to remember these episodic memories, like a a particularly significant meal or sunset, years later.
No animal demonstrates this mystery better than the ground squirrel. In a classic neuroscience experiment, Russian researchers showed that hibernating squirrels lost brain connections during their dormancy. But these structures were fully repaired within hours of their hibernation ending.
Rather than waiting out the winter with squirrels, Tanaka’s team induced a form of artificial hibernation in mice. The researchers imaged the mice’s brains before, during and after using electron microscopy, which reveals synapses and related structures called dendritic spines in vivid detail. During hibernation, activity in the mice’s hippocampi dropped by 70 percent.
Countless experiments have shown that the strength of a newly formed memory depends on the strength of linked synaptic connections. Tanaka says his team expected large dendritic spines, and the stronger synaptic connections they make, to be preserved during hibernation. That’s not what they saw.
As their brains shut up shop, the mice’s neurons withdrew more than half of their synaptic connections compared with mice that didn’t undergo hibernation. But just two days after hibernation ended, these connections had been restored. Many spines that persisted through hibernation were found in busy brain junctions called multisynaptic boutons. Synapses have two components — an axon that sends chemical messages and a dendrite spine that receives them. At multisynaptic boutons, one single axon joins onto several spines, like a multisocket adaptor that directs electricity into multiple devices.
In different experiments, anesthetized mice were given a drug known to impair memory formation. These mice lost their multisynaptic boutons — and their memories.
“It seems that the multisynaptic boutons, they are the key to preserving this structural connectivity,” says Michele Pignatelli, a neuroscientist at MIT who wasn’t involved in the study.
Another surprising finding was that over 80 percent of the lost dendritic spines reappeared in the same locations as before hibernation. “That says to me that although the spine is lost, the synaptic machinery … is still there,” says Cliff Abraham, a retired neuroscientist at the University of Otago in Dunedin, New Zealand, who was not involved with the research. It’s unclear how these connections get restored with such accuracy.
After the mice emerged from their hibernation, Tanaka’s team assessed their ability to remember locations linked to food rewards or mild electric shocks that they had learned about before their rest. Despite the huge changes in their brains, these mice could still remember the fear of a shock or the location of a treat.
The new findings, experts say, challenge the idea that individual connections formed during a memory must be maintained throughout their lifetime. Instead, the architecture of the wider brain network appears to preserve the memory.
Tanaka’s focus now is to see if there is a secret recipe that gives the spared spines their strength. “We are now working … to see if there’s any unique molecular profiles that makes these surviving spines under hibernation special,” he says.

Waymo will introduce its self-driving taxis in Munich by the end of 2027, the American autonomous driving company announced today.

Advertisement
The news marks Waymo's first foray into the European Union. It already operates in 11 cities in the United States and has applied for a license in the United Kingdom to launch its robotaxis in London this year.

Other self-driving taxi companies are also looking to enter Germany, with American ride-hailing company Lyft announcing last year that it would partner with Chinese AI firm Baidu to put autonomous cars on German roads in 2026.
German authorities gave autonomous vehicles the green light in 2021 to operate in the country in approved geographical areas. Other countries are looking at following suit, though the EU's broader autonomous driving rules are set by the U.N.

Economy minister responds to new US sanctions: Offensive economic strategy prepared
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
13:58:46 UTC

Economy minister responds to new US sanctions: Offensive economic strategy prepared
TEHRAN – Iran's Minister of Economic Affairs and Finance, Seyed Ali Madanizadeh, has stated that the government has formulated an offensive economic plan to counter US sanctions against the Iranian nation.
Marking Government Week, he emphasized that the 14th administration had been planning for such scenarios well in advance and is fully prepared for new sanctions.
Madanizadeh noted that enemies have long sought to test the resolve of the Iranian people and officials through various means, including military threats, territorial disintegration, and political destabilization. However, he asserted that these conspiracies have failed due to the steadfastness of Iran's military forces, people, and officials, combined with diplomatic efforts. While acknowledging damage to the economy—including attacks on steel and petrochemical facilities—he stated that recovery efforts have been swift, with damaged units returning to operation and market shortages being addressed.
Regarding recent US Treasury statements, the minister dismissed the notion that new sanctions could sever Iran's economic and financial arteries, emphasizing that the unipolar world order has ended. He argued that such claims are not new, as previous attempts under similar circumstances had failed. "We have endured a full-scale war and defeated them on both the economic and diplomatic fronts," he declared.
However, Madanizadeh acknowledged the hardships imposed on the Iranian people, including high inflation and currency pressure resulting from enemy actions over the past year. He stressed that the government remains fully aligned with the people's struggles and is committed to preventing enemy attempts to halt the country's financial and economic flows.
The minister outlined that all government bodies—including economic ministries, the Central Bank, the Budget and Planning Organization, and ministries of industry, agriculture, transport, and labor—have developed coordinated programs. Continuous coordination meetings are held to address various scenarios, including disruptions in finance, trade, or goods imports. He cited examples where alternative routes were successfully established when maritime routes were restricted, and measures were implemented to counter efforts to halt oil exports or impose budget deficits.
Madanizadeh reported tangible improvements in customs efficiency, noting that goods clearance time had been reduced from up to 10 months to just eight days, with further reductions to three days expected. Taxation revenue exceeded 90 percent of commitments last year despite wartime conditions. The banking sector also fulfilled its obligations regarding housing, childbearing, and marriage loans, while allocating substantial resources to working and fixed capital facilities.
The minister emphasized that enemies are now conducting an economic terrorist operation targeting patients, cancer sufferers, children, and even infant formula supplies. While Iran does not seek war, it will respond decisively to attacks—whether military or economic. "They should not think our approach is merely defensive this time; they should also expect offensive actions from us," he warned.
Madanizadeh noted that two major world powers have already refused to accept the new sanctions, and many other nations are expected to follow suit, either officially or unofficially.
The minister detailed a seven-pillar government program to combat inflation. Key pillars include:
· Monetary and banking policy adjustments
· Production and employment support through investment project financing
· Capital market reforms, which have already enabled businesses to raise approximately 55 trillion tomans through debt issuance
· Household livelihood support, including the continuation of the food basket subsidy program (Kala-Barg), with expanded support planned for the second half of the year
Addressing energy imbalances, Madanizadeh outlined plans for combined-cycle power plant development and modernization of existing facilities. Notably, solar energy investments have shown significant results through private sector participation. Public cooperation in consumption management has been remarkable, with energy consumption growth not only halted but reduced in some sectors—contrary to previous annual increases of 6-7 percent.
The government's reconstruction approach emphasizes modernization rather than mere restoration, with 20 major national projects identified for financing through capital markets, banking, and public participation. Reconstruction of damaged homes, hospitals, and schools is also underway.
A comprehensive trade facilitation and production barrier removal package is awaiting final government approval. The minister highlighted that cumbersome regulations identified during wartime conditions are now being made permanent to facilitate business operations. The former "Foreign Investment Organization" has been transformed into the "Iran Investment Organization," tasked with identifying and removing investment obstacles across the country.
Regarding recent currency market volatility, Madanizadeh attributed it largely to media-driven sentiment but expressed confidence that Central Bank policies would restore stability. He reiterated that the government remains firmly committed to managing economic conditions, controlling inflation, protecting employment, and ensuring the supply of essential goods for the Iranian people.

India’s National Security Adviser Ajit Doval and Chinese foreign minister Wang Yi on Tuesday held the 25th round of special representatives’ talks on the India China boundary question in Beijing, with the discussions focused on maintaining peace and tranquillity along the border and advancing bilateral ties.Earlier in the day, Doval met Chinese vice president Han Zheng ahead of the boundary talks. According to the Indian Embassy in China, the two discussed ways to strengthen peace and tranquillity in the border areas and further improve India China relations across economic, political and multilateral forums, in line with the consensus reached by Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping.Chinese Ambassador to India Xu Feihong said Han highlighted the momentum in bilateral ties, noting that Modi and Xi had met twice over the past two years in Kazan and Tianjin and reached a series of important understandings. Doval arrived in Beijing on Monday for a two day visit at the invitation of Wang Yi. His visit comes amid a gradual thaw in India China relations following a series of high level engagements between Modi and Xi.The two leaders had met on the sidelines of key international summits, including the SCO Summit in Tianjin, following their October 2024 meeting in Kazan. Vondelkerk fire investigation ends in mystery, police say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
13:57:14 UTC
22:57:14 KST

Vondelkerk fire investigation ends in mystery, police say
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
How the Vondelkerk in Amsterdam went up in flames on New Year’s Eve is still unknown, police have said, after months of trying and failing to establish a criminal cause for the blaze.
Investigators had looked into whether the fire was started deliberately and whether fireworks were to blame. Local residents were interviewed, video footage examined and tips about possible arson followed up, but none of it produced any evidence, police said.
It could also not be established whether fireworks caused the fire. Much of the forensic evidence was destroyed in the blaze itself, police said, and no traces of fireworks were found. With no leads left to pursue, the investigation has stalled.
Years to rebuild 
 The monumental church on Vondelstraat, close to the Vondelpark, was largely destroyed in the early hours of January 1, when its tower collapsed and much of the roof was lost. It was designed by Pierre Cuypers, the 19th-century architect behind Amsterdam’s Centraal station and the Rijksmuseum, and completed in 1880.
The building served as a Catholic church until it closed in 1977 and has since been used for concerts, offices and community events, with church services returning in 2017. It has been owned since 1996 by heritage restoration body Stadsherstel Amsterdam.
Several fundraising drives were launched after the fire. Stadsherstel said more than €180,000 had been raised within a week, and other appeals brought in tens of thousands of euros more. Rebuilding the church is expected to take years.

Will Volkswagen's crunch week decide Germany's auto future?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
13:57:00 UTC
22:57:00 KST

Will VW's crunch week decide Germany's auto future?
August 25, 2026
1. Why is Volkswagen holding crunch talks with workers?
Volkswagen's management is holding extraordinary meetings with workers this week amid an unprecedented cost-cutting drive, including reports of up to 100,000 job losses and the possible closure of several German car factories.
Germany's auto industry faces a deep structural crisis due to intense pressure from Chinese rivals, the transition to electric vehicles (EVs), higher production costs and other challenges.
As Europe's biggest carmaker by volume, VW has the heaviest exposure to overcapacity in its German plants, high fixed costs and its reliance on China.
Workers have been particularly concerned by how the restructuring was communicated so far, which representatives have described as "disastrous."
Nine separate meetings will be held, starting on Tuesday at VW's headquarters in Wolfsburg, with talks at other sites including Emden, Zwickau, Braunschweig and Hanover before the end of the week.
Workers had already agreed to around 50,000 job cuts, mainly through voluntary redundancy schemes. But management now thinks a further 50,000 jobs will have to be lost.
2. Why does Volkswagen need to make such drastic cuts?
CEO Oliver Blume has stressed that VW is in a "more than critical state" and that the measures adopted so far are not enough to restore competitiveness.
"We are oversized. That often makes us too slow and too complicated," he told staff in an interview on the company's intranet last week.
With nearly 630,000 workers, VW has grown more bloated than its peers over decades after choosing to control more stages of production — including components and software — while mopping up rivals such as Skoda, Porsche, SEAT and Bugatti.
The automaker was also slow to transition to EVs just as Chinese competitors gained ground, causing a large sales drop in its former number one market — China.
Blume warned that VW is currently over-producing around half a million vehicles in Europe every year.
While closing German factories would be a last resort, Blume said management "cannot currently see any way of them remaining profitable in the 2030s."
Other automakers have criticized Germany's high operating costs, including Mercedes-Benz CEO Ola Källenius, who last month spoke of a 70% cost gap between the firm's Hungarian and German operations.
3. What reaction is expected from workers?
Blume is expected to face an angry reaction from VW employees, who rank as some of the best-paid auto workers in the world thanks to the power and influence of unions and the works council.
After already accepting VW's earlier restructuring plans, Christiane Benner, the head of the IG Metall union, said workers "are getting another slap in the face."
During the meeting with workers in Wolfsburg on Tuesday, VW works council chair Daniela Cavallo said "trust" in Blume and the executive board "has been damaged," but "not yet beyond repair."
Last month, VW's supervisory board — which includes shareholders and worker representatives — rejected the second round of cost-cutting proposals.
The move is further complicated as VW is part-owned by the state of Lower Saxony, which holds 20% of the voting rights. The state has refused to sign off on the plans, according to German media reports.
"Lower Saxony is automotive country ... and this must remain so," said Olaf Lies, the state's premier on Monday. "Now it is important to me that we find joint solutions."
4. How is Volkswagen planning on getting back on track?
Blume told the Bild am Sonntag newspaper last weekend that he had drawn up "the largest transformation plan in the history of the Volkswagen Group."
His Target Vision 2030 plan aims to cut VW's model lineup by half and lower overheads, particularly in Germany. The automaker will also reduce its global production target, which peaked at about 11 million vehicles in 2018, to 9 million a year in the future.
Faced with rising competition from China, along with US tariffs, geopolitics and red tape, Blume warned that VW management has to "assume the risks will get worse, worldwide."
Most global automakers are struggling to react to Chinese EVs flooding global markets, increasingly unpredictable markets and the mounting pressure of EU net-zero rules, which include fines for not hitting emissions targets.
Blume told the newspaper that the next few years would be "decisive" in determining which carmakers remain viable.
He said although VW achieved a solid 3.8% operating margin, the profits are not enough to invest in new technologies, products and maintain the company's sites.

Daily Update: Russia Loses 1,230 Troops, 2 MLRS and 48 Artillery Systems
Russian forces lost an estimated 1,230 personnel over the previous 24 hours, bringing their total personnel losses since the start of the full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022, to approximately 1,479,300, Ukraine’s General Staff reported on August 25.
Over the same period, Ukrainian forces destroyed 48 Russian artillery systems, 9 armored combat vehicles, two multiple launch rocket systems, one air defense system, 10 unmanned ground vehicles, and 1,555 operational-tactical drones.

The General Staff also reported the destruction of 448 vehicles and fuel tankers, and seven pieces of special equipment.
According to Ukraine’s latest estimates, Russia’s cumulative equipment losses include 12,293 tanks, 25,220 armored combat vehicles, 48,567 artillery systems, 2,058 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,587 air defense systems, 440 aircraft, and 354 helicopters.
Russia has also lost 2,378 unmanned ground vehicles, 479,882 operational-tactical UAVs, 5,052 cruise missiles, 35 ships and boats, two submarines, 139,221 vehicles and fuel tankers, and 4,582 pieces of special equipment.
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s General Staff reported 209 combat engagements across the frontline during the previous 24 hours.
The latest battlefield losses come as Ukrainian forces continue targeting Russian communications equipment along the front. On August 24, Ukraine’s 1st Separate Assault Brigade named after Dmytro Kotsiubailo reported destroying a rare Spirit-030 portable satellite internet terminal on the Huliaipole front.
Russian forces use the Spirit-030 satellite communications terminal as an alternative to Starlink. Its compact antenna measures just 30 centimeters (12 inches) in diameter, making the system relatively difficult to detect on the battlefield.

Polish far-right leader charged with Holocaust denial for calling Auschwitz gas chambers “fake”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
13:54:18 UTC
22:54:18 KST

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun has been charged with denying Nazi crimes, a criminal offence in Poland that carries a prison sentence of up to three years.
The charges relate to statements last year in which Braun, who has a long history of promoting antisemitic conspiracy theories, suggested that the gas chambers at Auschwitz, which was the Nazis’ main killing centre during the Holocaust, are “fake”.
Komunikat o przedstawieniu posłowi do Parlamentu Europejskiego zarzutów publicznego i wbrew faktom zaprzeczania zbrodniom ludobójstwa popełnionym w niemieckim nazistowskim obozie koncentracyjnym i zagłady KL Auschwitz-Birkenau w Oświęcimiu. https://t.co/nLq3XKnXCK
— IPN Kraków (@ipn_krakow) August 25, 2026
On Tuesday morning, Braun was summoned to appear as a suspect at the Kraków branch of the Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), a state historical body that has the power to prosecute crimes relating to the periods when Poland was under Nazi and communist rule.
A group of his followers gathered outside the building to express their support for Braun, who finished fourth in last year’s presidential elections. Since then, his Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) party has risen to around 9% in polls, making it a potential kingmaker after next year’s parliamentary elections.
After meeting with Braun, IPN prosecutor Robert Janicki announced that they had presented Braun with charges for “publicly and contrary to the facts denying the crimes of genocide committed by officers of the Third Reich in the German concentration and extermination camp KL Auschwitz-Birkenau”.
The charges relate to two interviews Braun gave in July last year. He declared that “Auschwitz with its gas chambers is unfortunately a fake” and said that claims about the use of gas chambers are part of a “propaganda narrative” supporting a “quasi-religious cult”.
In actual fact, gas chambers were used at Auschwitz, which was located in German-occupied Poland, to kill around 900,000 people, the vast majority of them Jews.
Janicki noted that Braun’s remarks “clearly contradict common historical knowledge based on documents, witness accounts, perpetrators’ statements and findings from past criminal proceedings”.
Far-right leader Grzegorz Braun says the gas chambers at Auschwitz are “fake” and it is a “fact” that Jews have committed ritual murder.

When Braun originally made his remarks, they were widely condemned in Poland, which suffered enormously under German occupation during World War Two. Justice minister Waldemar Żurek asked the European Parliament, where Braun sits as an MEP, to lift his legal immunity so he could be charged.
“For me, it is a scandal that, in a country that suffered such enormous war losses, there is a politician who can deny historical facts that are so painful for Poles,” said Żurek at the time, quoted by the Onet news website. “I won’t let this go. We must bring such people to justice.”
In March, the European Parliament approved Żurek’s request, allowing Braun to face charges in relation to his Auschwitz comments, as well as for other alleged crimes.

On Friday last week, the district prosecutor’s office in Warsaw charged Braun with those other crimes, including the theft of Ukrainian and EU flags he tore down and vandalism of an LGBT+ exhibition being displayed in parliament.
In a separate case, in February this year, Żurek also asked the European Parliament to strip Braun of immunity to face charges of denying Nazi crimes over another incident in which he called the gas chambers at both Auschwitz and Majdanek, another Nazi-German camp in occupied Poland, “fake”.
Meanwhile, Braun is already on trial in Poland for four other alleged crimes, including using a fire extinguisher to attack a Jewish Hanukkah ceremony in the Polish parliament in December 2023.

Taiwan: A Growing Economic Partner for the EU in Troubled Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
13:54:00 UTC
22:54:00 KST

Much has changed since September 2021, when the European Union launched its Indo-Pacific strategy. In less than five years, armed conflicts in Ukraine and in the Middle East have shocked Europeans who know they can no longer fully rely on the close protection of their traditional ally, the United States. Although the U.S. remains NATO’s largest military power, Washington’s recent signs and messages have brought confusion to Europe. In some ways, East Asia faces a similar situation, where Japan and South Korea are now looking at diversification options.
Meanwhile, the EU is trying to “pivot” toward Asia, and has developed multiple ties with Japan, India, South Korea, and ASEAN. In that context, Taiwan remains a special case due to its unique situation as the world’s premier producer of high-end semiconductors. As Europe seeks to diversify supply chains and reduce vulnerabilities in strategically important sectors, Taiwan’s comparative advantages have become increasingly aligned with European interests.
Within this broader transformation, Taiwan has emerged as a significantly more important partner for the EU than at any previous point since diplomatic relations between the EU and the People’s Republic of China were established, 41 years ago. Once viewed primarily as a trading partner constrained by the EU’s adherence to the “One China” policy, Taiwan has increasingly been incorporated into European discussions on semiconductor resilience, critical technologies, cybersecurity, digital governance, and Indo-Pacific stability.
In the past five years, Europe has become acutely aware of the importance of Taiwan. European delegations, from Brussels to EU member-states, have visited Taipei frequently; the number of engagements has surged by 20 percent since the COVID-19 pandemic, according to the EU-Taiwan Tracker by CEIAS. Cooperation projects in technology and education have multiplied. The Taiwanese authorities have been welcoming and open to collaboration.
In addition, the EU also started to engage with Taiwan through costly commitments. On December 1, 2025, Taiwan and the German manufacturer Merck announced a “Semiconductor Solutions Site” in Taiwan’s Kaohsiung city. Similarly, in July 2023, the ribbon was cut for ASML’s Linkou campus in Taoyuan city. This shows that while geopolitical uncertainty lies ahead, economic ties still manage to form.
Despite the tricky waters both countries find themselves in, the numbers are clear: Taiwan’s Overseas Community Affairs Council (OCAC) announced that between 2016 and 2025, Taiwan investment in the EU amounted to US$13.88 billion, a 650 percent surge compared to just US$1.85 billion between 2006 and 2015.
As the EU is facing an increasingly challenging conversation with China over a trade deficit that reached 360 billion euro in 2025, Taiwan can stand out as a promising dialogue partner in the matters of technology and economic security. However, figuring out how to make the EU-Taiwan collaboration sustainable is more important than simply pouring in truckloads of investment.
While EU-Taiwan interaction is built on commercial activity, China has a long history of punishing any actor who shows the slightest friendliness toward Taiwan. Take the example of Japan: since a comment made by Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae in November 2025 suggesting that a Taiwan crisis might be a question of national survival for Japan, Beijing continuously slapped sanctions on Japanese companies. China added 20 Japanese firms to its export control list in February 2026, with another 20 added to the watchlist in June 2026. To use the Chinese axiom, Beijing is “killing the chicken to scare the monkey” – not only punishing Japan, but sending a warning to any country that might be tempted to follow suit.
Takaichi has refused to back down. However, there is a major difference between the EU and Japan: the EU is not one single country, but a conglomerate of sovereign states. Whether the EU could handle such pressure by Beijing without scattering apart is not only under scrutiny by Taiwan but also a potential weakness to exploit for China.
Although the EU will probably never become a conventional security actor in the Taiwan Strait, increasing concerns regarding economic coercion, supply chain disruption, cyber threats, and hybrid warfare have expanded opportunities for cooperation in non-traditional security domains and led to a shift in thinking. Consequently, EU-Taiwan relations increasingly resemble a form of functional strategic partnership, whereby cooperation develops through economic security, technological resilience, and institutional coordination, despite the lack of either formal diplomatic recognition or collective defense agreements.
As Europe is gearing up for multiple economic and technological conflicts in the months to come, Taiwan could become a promising partner for the EU in key areas. It is time for both the EU and Taiwan to use their respective strategic leverage and seize the opportunity.
However, that is easier said than done. Not only is the EU divided by country, but attitudes toward China are also polarized in terms of party affiliation in each EU member state. Take Germany’s CDU/CSU-SDP coalition for example. While both governing parties support continued economic engagement with Beijing, their approaches differ. The SPD, with longstanding ties to trade unions and traditional industries heavily exposed to the Chinese market, places greater emphasis on balancing “de-risking efforts” with preserving commercial interests. By contrast, the CDU/CSU has adopted a stronger focus on industrial competitiveness, supply-chain resilience, and technological autonomy. Consequently, it has been more supportive of deeper semiconductor and high-tech cooperation with Taiwan, increasingly viewing Taiwan as a strategic partner in Germany’s economic-security agenda. This exposes another layer of complexity in terms of the heterogeneity of China-dependence on both inter- and intra- state levels.
Hence, building on the above-mentioned observations, the issue is the underlying proposition of tying EU-Taiwan relations to EU-China relations. The argument here is that EU countries should pursue EU-Taiwan relations in parallel with EU-China relations, not subsequently. Taiwan, on the other hand, has sought to separate its cross-strait relations from its foreign policy since the Tsai Ing-wen presidency (2016-2024), emphasizing establishing international relations despite the cross-strait situation. However, this will only become effective if allies reciprocate the endeavor by showcasing support for Taiwan, disregarding the incrementally mounting pressure from Beijing.
Taiwan has shown that the establishment of so-called non-red supply chains is possible, if one doesn’t lose the support of close allies. Economic deterrence is now even more effective than military and political coercion. The idea of resilience might vary by country, but for Taiwan, raising the cost of invasion for China could most effectively balance power asymmetry in the strait. With Chinese efforts to cut off Taiwanese international engagement rising and becoming more diverse and intricate, the EU should stand firm on its policy of competing on fair ground and not having to swim between two great powers during times of murky waters.
While what lies ahead seems uncertain for the EU and Taiwan, one thing is for sure: a friend in need is a friend indeed.

China warned that it would defend its interests in response to new U.S. sanctions against Iran
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
16:53:59 EEST
22:53:59 KST

China warned that it would defend its interests in response to new U.S. sanctions against Iran
Kyiv • UNN
Beijing promised to protect its interests after the U.S. plans to expand sanctions against Iran and its partners. China buys most of Iran’s oil.
China has promised to defend its interests after the US announced plans to expand economic sanctions against Iran and its trading partners, including Beijing, UNN reports, citing the BBC.
Details
Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian said that China strongly opposes what he called "illegal unilateral sanctions" and would take "all necessary measures" to protect its rights.
This came after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced new measures on Monday, warning that any country financially cooperating with Iran would be isolated.
China is the largest buyer of Iranian oil, although trade has declined due to the US blockade of Iranian ports.
Lin said: "Cooperation between China and Iran has always been conducted within the framework of international law and should not be obstructed or disrupted."
Bessent called the sanctions plans "the largest financial offensive in history" against Iran, warning that banks and businesses would share Iran's isolation if they refused to sever ties with the country.
He declined to focus on specific countries, but said that US President Donald Trump would call world leaders "with specific requests to end their engagement with the regime".
However, responding to a question about Chinese banks, Bessent said he wanted to make it clear that "no one is beyond the reach of US sanctions".
The statement came ahead of planned talks between Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping next month.
Washington will likely be concerned about potential retaliatory measures by Beijing, which processes most of the world's rare-earth elements and other critical minerals essential to the production of many high-tech products, the publication notes.
Beijing has already tightened export controls on rare-earth elements as part of previous trade negotiations with the US.
China's response came after Iranian Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh said that Tehran was "fully prepared" for broader sanctions, which he said would result in "another defeat" for the US.
Iran says it is ready for "tough sanctions" from the U.S. and has a plan25.08.26, 07:58 • 5172 views
"The government is ready and has been ready, and has a two-year plan to manage these events," he told state television.
"We also have our own tools and know how to play this game," he said, adding that Tehran had "been waiting a long time for these plans".
The US has called its latest sanctions "Operation Economic Outcast" and described them as an "economic D-Day" against Iran.
This came nearly six months after the start of the war with Iran.
Since then, the conflict has led to rising oil prices worldwide, with Tehran effectively blocking exports through the Strait of Hormuz—a waterway vital to the global economy. The US has also slowed shipping through its own naval blockade.
Recent attempts to end the conflict diplomatically have failed, and the 60-day ceasefire officially ended last week with no signs of a settlement.
Announcing the new sanctions, the US Treasury Secretary said that America "is no longer managing the Iranian threat; we are ending it".
Iran is already under severe US sanctions, but Bessent said these sanctions go further.
He said the US Treasury had tracked the financial channels, intermediaries and networks that Iran uses to evade sanctions on oil trading, imposing sanctions on nearly 60 organizations, individuals and vessels.
But analysts questioned the latest measures even before China's response.
David Oxley, chief economist for climate and commodities at Capital Economics, told the BBC that the direct impact on Iran's energy revenues would be "somewhat weak".
"We suspect that the new package will have only a limited direct impact on Iranian energy flows in the short term," he added.
This is partly because approximately 90% of Iranian oil goes to China, he said, "which has not recognized U.S. sanctions in the past and is unlikely to be intimidated this time either".
Ali Vaez, deputy director of the Middle East and North Africa Program at the International Crisis Group, said: "Generally, the Chinese oppose unilateral sanctions. They will comply with multilateral or international sanctions, but unilateral sanctions, once imposed by the United States – they have always considered them illegitimate".
And although Iran's neighbors, such as Pakistan, Turkey and Iraq, want to maintain good relations with the United States, they "cannot afford to sever ties with Iran", Vaez said on the Today program on BBC Radio 4.
He said that economic pressure on Tehran "does not work", as the Iranian regime is prepared to "absorb any pain" and pass it on to the people.
Other trading partners that could be affected by the U.S. announcement include India and Russia, which have not yet responded, the publication notes.

Slovak police thwart planned arson attack on drone factory
Aug 25 - Police have thwarted a planned arson attack on a factory producing unmanned aerial systems in eastern Slovakia and detained three foreigners suspected in the attempt, police said on Facebook on Tuesday.

Police investigators charged the suspects with public endangerment committed on commission.
They did not name the factory targeted, nor its precise location, and the suspected commissioning party was not named.

Indian national security adviser holds border talks in China
Indian National Security Adviser Ajit Doval held talks with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi on Tuesday on the border issue between the two countries and improving relations.
”We are meeting in keeping with the guidance of our leaders, Prime Minister Narendra Modi and President Xi Jinping, who have given clear and positive direction to our relationship, both at the highest and working levels,” Doval said in his remarks, reports said. “I am happy that, over the past year, our relationship has been steadily returning to normalcy.”
Doval noted that the talks are “particularly important against the backdrop of the BRICS Summit.” The summit will be held in New Delhi next month and Chinese President Xi Jinping will reportedly attend.
The two officials are the designated special representatives for the border talks mechanism, which was established in 2003. It is the main channel for negotiations between the two countries on the border issue and communication on issues of mutual interest.
Doval, who is on a two-day visit to China, met with Chinese Vice President Han Zheng on Monday and discussed ways to strengthen peace in the border areas and improve economic, political, and multilateral relations, the Indian Embassy said in an X post.
National Security Advisor Ajit Doval held the 25th round of Special Representatives’ talks on the India-China boundary question with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi in Beijing.
During his visit, NSA Doval also met Chinese Vice President Han Zheng, with discussions focusing on… pic.twitter.com/QyEcnOaYN3
Ahead of the talks, Indian Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar reiterated that “peace and tranquility” along the border areas are a prerequisite for good relations with China.
Relations between the two nuclear-armed neighbors froze after a skirmish between their troops in the Ladakh region of their common Himalayan border in 2020, which left 20 Indian soldiers and at least four Chinese soldiers dead.
The two countries have been rapidly normalizing relations recently, with the resumption of direct flights and updates to the visa regime. India has started allowing Chinese investments into critical sectors of its economy. Border trade, which once connected remote Himalayan communities to the Silk Route, was also resumed earlier this month.
Chinese President Xi Jinping is expected to attend the BRICS summit in New Delhi next month with a 400-strong delegation, Reuters reported, citing three unnamed sources.
Xi’s participation in the summit, which Russian President Vladimir Putin will also attend, has not been officially confirmed yet. India, which holds the rotating chair of the BRICS group, has engaged in intense diplomacy ahead of the summit.

Brazil slaps TikTok owner with $38m fine over data use
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
13:53:00 UTC
22:53:00 KST

Brazil slaps TikTok owner with $38m fine over data use
- Brazil fined TikTok owner ByteDance S$38 million for mishandling children's and teenagers' personal data without proper legal basis or safeguards.
- TikTok must delete improperly collected data and face new restrictions for unregistered users, including suspending ads and limiting features.
- ByteDance agreed to a compliance plan with stricter privacy settings for under-16 users, including parental authorisation and stronger content controls.
AI generated
Brazil’s government fined TikTok owner ByteDance 153.7 million reais (S$38 million) over its handling of children’s and teenagers’ personal data, reflecting scrutiny of how online platforms protect minors.
The government’s National Data Protection Authority, known as ANPD, said TikTok processed minors’ personal information without an adequate legal basis and failed to put effective safeguards in place to prevent improper data collection. The decision, which was published in Brazil’s Official Gazette on Aug 25, requires ByteDance to delete data collected improperly.
The company can appeal within 10 business days. TikTok’s press office in Brazil did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has pushed for stronger online protection for children and teenagers as he seeks a fourth term in October’s election. In March, Brazil implemented a law requiring companies and digital platforms to restrict minors’ access to illegal or potentially harmful content. Earlier in August, ANPD ordered chat app Discord to halt live streaming in the South American country after the death of a teenager.
The violations occurred when people used TikTok through registered accounts and also when they accessed a feed without creating an account, according to the Brazilian regulator. ANPD said the company’s technical and organisational measures were not enough to comply with the nation’s data protection law.
TikTok will face additional restrictions in Brazil for people who use the platform without registering. The company must suspend advertising for those users, disable live streams and direct messages and sharply reduce the personal data it collects. Unregistered users will also face time limits on the platform.
ANPD separately approved ByteDance’s compliance plan while requiring the company to follow new age-verification rules under Brazil’s Digital Child and Adolescent Statute. The regulator said the measures are intended to reduce risks to children and teenagers that were identified during its investigation.
ByteDance committed to a compliance plan that will impose TikTok’s most restrictive privacy settings by default on accounts belonging to users under 16, with changes requiring parental authorisation. The platform must also strengthen controls and introduce stricter content filters, regulators said. BLOOMBERG

Dutch foundation plans to build underground hospital in Ukraine

Dutch foundation plans to build underground hospital in Ukraine
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
A Dutch organisation is trying to raise funds to build a reinforced underground hospital in Ukraine so soldiers can be treated nearer the front line.
Protect Ukraine and a Norwegian foundation, HMM Healthcare, say they have already secured €750,000 in donations for the project, which is expected to cost €2.5 million in total.
The 600 m2 hospital will be built 8 m below ground and made entirely of concrete, allowing wounded service personnel to be treated in what is effectively a giant bunker.
The organisers hope to have the building fully equipped and operational by February 2027.
Jaap Scholten, a Dutch writer and co-founder of Protect Ukraine, said: “The fact that we have raised three-quarters of a million euros in such a short time shows that people in the Netherlands have not forgotten Ukraine.
“But we are not there yet. Every donation brings us closer to a hospital and stabilisation point that can save many lives.”
Protect Ukraine has around 100 volunteers who run regular trips to Ukraine to deliver goods such as medicines, pop-up tents and pick-up trucks.
Scholten, who lives in Hungary, told NOS he started the organisation after watching people in his neighbourhood handing out fresh fruit, energy bars and blankets to Ukrainian refugees.
“Arranging supplies for Ukrainians is the most effective thing you can do to help,” he said. “That’s why I started Protect Ukraine.”

Yemen's increased violence leaves thousands hungry, displaced
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
13:50:44 UTC
22:50:44 KST

Breadcrumb
Yemen's increased violence leaves tens of thousands displaced and hungry
The increase of military conflict in Yemen is not limited to traditional front lines, with the fighting impacting different aspects of life.
The UN-sponsored de-escalation agreement reached between the conflicting parties in Yemen in April 2022 failed to protect what remained of the necessities of life amid a new threat of all-out war, bringing the spectre of the ongoing humanitarian disaster to the fore since the Ansar Allah group, also know as the Houthis, took control of the capital Sanaa in September 2014.
During the current military round, infrastructure and service facilities are direct targets in attacks, almost completely paralysing local trade, disrupting supply chains and leaving millions of Yemenis, particularly displaced people, facing a daily struggle for survival in a country where even the most basic rights are an unattainable luxury.
The present fighting also affected Mocha Port, one of the most important arteries for the flow of food supplies along Yemen's western coast, which has come under repeated shelling.
According to port director Abdulmalik Al-Sharaabi, the attacks caused extensive damage to vital facilities, with direct losses estimated at $16 million, as well as deaths and injuries among workers and civilians.
This disruption immediately impacted living conditions for thousands of people, particularly due to the halt of basic goods flows, foremost among them food and fuel products.
Wide areas under the control of the internationally recognised government along the western coast and parts of the neighbouring highlands have been hit by severe shortages.
In addition to the alarming figures related to living conditions, this paralysis has another particularly harsh dimension.
Hundreds of workers at Mokha port suddenly found themselves deprived of their only sources of income, accompanied by severe food shortages and sharp price increases that have placed a heavy burden on all citizens exhausted by years of prolonged war.
Meanwhile, residents of Marib province are facing immense suffering being the largest refuge for internally displaced people.
The province, which carries significant demographic and humanitarian weight, is facing repeated and intense waves of ballistic missile and drone attacks, threatening the lives of hundreds of thousands of civilians, particularly those living in dilapidated tents in informal displacement camps.
Displaced from Al Mahwit province, Umm Ziad told The New Arab, "We are living in a catastrophic situation, as we have no food to live on away from our homes since we were displaced while fleeing the Houthis' brutality. We depend on aid, and we have begun to fear that we will be forced to flee to another province because of the continued shelling of Marib."
The danger of further war extends to harming the main lifeline of livelihoods by targeting energy facilities and domestic gas supplies that serve most Yemeni provinces.
This direct threat risks causing a complete paralysis of supply chains, early signs of which have already emerged in the shortage of domestic gas cylinders in several cities.
From Taiz, Abdu Saif Al-Bakari told TNA, "I have been trying for four days to obtain a gas cylinder. I searched all the petrol stations in Taiz and all the cylinder shops, but I could not find one. They told me that gas was unavailable because of the shelling of Marib, and I was forced to buy it on the black market for 20,000 rials, although its official price is 9,500 rials (One dollar is equivalent to 1,550 rials in areas controlled by the internationally recognised government.)."
The repercussions has also suffocated the capital, Sanaa, under the Houthis' control.
As commercial activity at Mokha port has halted and major supply lines have been cut, Sanaa's markets have suffered severe food shortages, immediately reflected in unprecedented waves of price rises that have consumed what little money remains in residents' pockets.
In a city already suffering a chronic humanitarian crisis because salaries have remained unpaid since 2016, with no prospect of an end to the crisis, the latest escalation has closed the last avenues of survival for millions of families unable to afford food or medicine.
"We have reached a situation in which we can no longer bear living," From Sanaa, Ibrahim told TNA. "For more than 10 years, we have lived without salaries and suffered fear, repression and security crackdowns to the extent that if a person says he is hungry, he is threatened or kidnapped. Despite this, the Houthis impose financial levies on citizens under the pretext of celebrating the Prophet's birthday."
As the health, education and other basic services sectors collapse under the strain of shortages of supplies and fuel, Sanaa is now living through an extremely harsh reality.
Citizens find themselves trapped between the burden of excessive price rises and the complete helplessness imposed by a parallel economy that is draining the resources needed for their daily lives.
Residents are also facing heavy financial levies imposed under the name of commemorating religious occasions, alongside a growing wave of online protests launched by citizens on social media platforms under hashtags denouncing escalating policies of starvation.
Experts warn the current conditions is pushing the country towards extremely dangerous territory.
Wafik Saleh, executive director of the Taiz Centre for Studies, told TNA that Mokha Port going out of service would inevitably trigger a rapid wave of inflation, leading to unprecedented increases in the prices of food and basic goods at a time when markets are unable to absorb the shock or provide sustainable alternatives.
"The spectre of collapse does not stop at food. It extends to the most basic necessities of survival," Saleh explained. "Targeting the vicinity of energy facilities in Marib is emptying markets of their supplies of domestic cooking gas and other petroleum products, automatically fuelling black and parallel markets whose prices double the burden on Yemeni families."
"As people's purchasing power collapses, thousands find themselves forced to exhaust what remains of their income to cope with harsh living conditions, driving a catastrophic deterioration in humanitarian crises on the ground," he added. "These accumulating crises are outlining the features of a comprehensive disaster that is undermining the efficiency of the health and food sectors as a result of interruptions to cold chains and rising hospital operating costs, threatening to increase the number of people in need of urgent assistance to unprecedented levels," Saleh concluded.

Russia Steps Up Recruitment of Women for Ukraine War – Vot Tak
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
13:49:51 UTC
22:49:51 KST

Russia is increasingly recruiting women for the war against Ukraine amid signs that its pool of potential male recruits is shrinking, according to an investigation by the Poland-based news outlet Vot Tak.
At least 50 Russian women serving in the war have been killed, with the annual death toll rising the longer the war has gone on, the outlet found.
Vot Tak identified each of the 50 women and examined how Russia recruits women, what motivates them to enlist and how their roles have expanded from medical and support work to operating drones, firing sniper rifles and taking part in assaults.
Women have traditionally served mainly in civilian and support positions in the Russian military. In early 2022, 310,000 women worked in the armed forces, but only about 40,000 were service members. By March 2023, 1,100 women were deployed in Ukraine, according to then-Defense Minister Sergei Shoigu, the only official figure released during the war.
Vot Tak found that women are now being recruited for a wider range of combat duties, including as drone operators, snipers, machine gunners and assault troops.
One of the women interviewed by Vot Tak was Yelizaveta Tsybina, a 24-year-old drone operator with the call sign “Bayana” who signed her fourth volunteer contract this summer. She is now based at a barracks in the southwestern Kursk region.
“They present it all beautifully and patriotically,” Tsybina told Vot Tak. “But when you arrive, the situation, the way you are treated and the work itself are completely different.”
She said that although she did not initially want to enlist after Russia invaded Ukraine, many of her friends did, and her boyfriend signed a contract in June 2024. A military enlistment office rejected Tsybina because she lacked medical training. Her boyfriend was killed that August.
She then trained as a drone operator and joined the St. George volunteer assault brigade, formed largely from former Wagner mercenaries and Russians who had fought in eastern Ukraine since 2014. A week after signing a six-month contract, she was sent on her first combat mission.
“I didn’t think I would survive my first contract,” she said.
In late 2024, Tsybina was deployed near Soledar in Ukraine’s Donetsk region, where she used drones for reconnaissance and later helped direct artillery fire. Her unit was subsequently sent to Chasiv Yar, where she said she dropped munitions on a dugout after seeing Ukrainian soldiers enter it.
Tsybina returned to her home region of Krasnoyarsk in May 2025 with a minor wound and concussion. Four months later, she was back in the military.
“It draws you in. Unfortunately, I can’t get out of it anymore,” she told Vot Tak. “When I return to civilian life, everything feels wrong — the environment, the routine, the people, the relationships. It feels as if I’m not where I belong.”
Tsybina has since signed three more fixed-term contracts with volunteer formations. She said she avoided signing with the Defense Ministry because its contracts are effectively impossible to terminate while the war continues.
“If I had the choice, I would choose not to start down this path,” she said. “I am afraid to say this openly, but disappointment with the Russian Armed Forces is the view of most Russian soldiers.”
Short-lived recruitment drives
Women can sign military contracts in any Russian region and are offered the same bonuses, salaries and benefits as men, according to Vot Tak. Advertisements generally seek Russian citizens aged 18 to 45 with at least a secondary education and no criminal record, though the criteria vary.
Like men’s contracts, women’s agreements with the Defense Ministry are automatically extended until the war ends.
Since late 2025, students have been targeted at universities in at least five cities, as well as the Ulyanovsk region, Vot Tak found. A college in Krasnoyarsk held a closed recruitment meeting attended only by women.
The recruitment drives are often short-lived. One in the Tomsk region lasted 10 days. A Telegram channel reopened recruitment in March 2026 and expanded it in June to drone, communications, logistics and supply roles. Two weeks after Vot Tak contacted the channel, a recruiter said applications had closed because of an “extremely large influx” of candidates.
Recruiters also made misleading promises, the outlet reported, including telling prospective recruits that contracts could be terminated after one year and that women would not be transferred to assault units or sent to the front. In practice, Defense Ministry contracts are extended indefinitely and women have served in frontline and assault roles.
Russia had initially tried to recruit women as medics and cooks early in the war. By 2023, volunteer formations were advertising for female snipers, drone operators, electronic warfare specialists and assault troops.
The Defense Ministry has also reportedly recruited female prisoners in exchange for expunging their convictions. More than 80 may have left Siberian prisons to work as medics in late 2024, Vot Tak reported, though the practice appears to have since been phased out.
Rising death toll
Vot Tak said it identified 50 female service members killed since February 2022. The annual toll rose from five in 2022 to 15 in 2025. Twelve were killed in the first half of 2026 alone.
Most were between the ages of 31 and 49. The oldest, Irina Anisimova from the Saratov region, was 57 when her death was reported in October 2024. The youngest was 23-year-old Yana Koshkina, who volunteered in 2023 and was killed in a drone strike near Bakhmut while commanding a casualty evacuation team.
One of the first was Valentina Galatova, 27, who was killed during a combat mission in Mariupol on April 14, 2022.
Galatova first traveled to Russian-occupied eastern Ukraine with humanitarian aid in 2014 and later settled in Donetsk with a commander from a Russia-backed formation. After he was killed in 2020, she joined his regiment.
Officially listed as a paramedic, Galatova worked as a political officer and therapist, her mother told Vot Tak. During the full-scale invasion, she joined assaults and died in mortar fire in Mariupol.
Women have also been implicated in abuses. Vot Tak previously reported that an assault platoon commander with the call sign “Witch” allegedly ordered subordinates to shoot five Ukrainian prisoners of war in May 2024. A female sniper called “Ripley” told a pro-Kremlin correspondent that she would be willing to shoot foreign fighters who try to surrender.
Some women now enlist as soon as they turn 18, while others try to flee after encountering withheld pay, violence by commanders or indefinite contracts, Vot Tak said.
Sofya, who asked that her name be changed, signed a Defense Ministry contract at 19 after graduating from medical college in 2023. Now 22, she trains soldiers in first aid and wants to leave.
She told Vot Tak that recruiters had promised her about 80,000 rubles ($967) a month but did not pay the agreed salary. She dismissed recruitment into drone units as another lure to send young people into Ukraine.
“I am disappointed in today’s army and want to leave as soon as possible,” she said. “Everyone is waiting for the war to end so they can get out — young people and older people alike.”
“At 22, I have no desire to die because of politicians’ wars.”

Sexual Assault Rates Decline in Latest Pentagon Survey Following Reforms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
13:49:19 UTC
22:49:19 KST

Sexual assault reports across the military decreased last year, according to the Pentagon’s latest official figures released Aug. 21.
The Department of Defense received 7,998 official reports of sexual assault involving service members in fiscal 2025, a decrease from 8,195 in 2024 and 8,515 in 2023, according to the U.S. military’s annual congressionally mandated report on the issue. The Pentagon said it found sufficient evidence for disciplinary action in 2,220 of those cases.
The Pentagon also estimated that sexual assaults involving service members decreased to 4.3 percent from 6.8 percent for Active-Duty women. It dropped to 1 percent from 1.3 percent for Active-Duty men since the latest available data from 2023.
The Air Force and the Space Force had the lowest rates of sexual assault among the services—2.8 percent for female Airmen and 3.5 percent for female Guardians, and less than 1 percent of male service members for both services.
Those figures come from the Pentagon’s biennial Workplace Experiences Survey, which asks service members whether they have been sexually assaulted, sexually harassed, or experienced sex discrimination in the past year. The total number of reported sexual assaults across the military is released annually. The anonymous survey, which asks about incidents that occurred in the past 12 months, captures a broader set of data and is the primary marker for the Pentagon on how prevalent sexual assault is within the ranks. Responses were collected in the fall of 2025.
“Dignity, respect, and discipline are foundational to the warrior ethos and the overall preparedness of the force,” Undersecretary of Defense for Personnel and Readiness Anthony Tata said in an Aug. 21 statement. “Sexual assault and sexual harassment undermine these values, eroding trust and threatening the mission.”
The U.S. military estimated that one-third of sexual assaults were reported in 2025, compared to one-fourth in 2023, according to Pentagon data.
Military personnel experts said the trends are an indication that the process for reporting and addressing sexual assaults has improved during the Biden and Trump administrations.
“We’re seeing increased trust in reporting and in the systems that are available,” said Katherine Kuzminski, the director of studies at the Center for a New American Security, which she attributed to “deliberate policy decisions and investments.”
“Not only was that something that was started in the last administration, but this administration also gets to claim credit for continuing on,” she added of the recent reforms.
At the end of 2023, each of the military services established an Office of Special Trial Counsel to prosecute serious crimes, including murder, sexual assault, and domestic violence. The aim was to remove the chain of command from the process to lessen fears of retaliation.
That followed the establishment of an Integrated Primary Prevention Workforce, which has focused on preventing sexual assault, suicide, and other harmful behaviors in 2021. President Joe Biden also ordered that sexual harassment be added as an offense under the Uniform Code of Military Justice.
Alex Wagner, who served as the assistant secretary of the Air Force for manpower and reserve affairs under Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin in the Biden administration, said the latest figures showed recent reforms, particularly the hiring of the prevention workforce and the implementation of the Office of Special Trial Counsel, have started “to sink in and demonstrate success.”
Wagner said the survey results represented “clear, strong evidence that the focus on reducing unwanted sexual contact in the military by Secretary Austin and the service secretaries has resulted in a real and positive reduction in harmful behaviors that impact the lived experiences of members of the military.”
This year’s report, under the Trump administration, appears to support continuing many of those efforts.
“[E]ngaged leadership, a fully resourced Integrated Primary Prevention Workforce, and the active mitigation of stressors are critical readiness multipliers that preserve and support our Total Force’s warfighting capability,” the Pentagon wrote in the report released Aug. 21.
According to the Pentagon, trust in the military to handle sexual assault has increased. Still, less than half of Active-Duty women trust the military to “protect their privacy, ensure their safety, and treat them with dignity and respect” compared to around two-thirds of Active-Duty men.
Asked about the new military justice process, 44 percent of Active-Duty women and 64 percent of Active-Duty men said they would trust the Office of Special Trial Counsel to be fair in a hypothetical sexual assault scenario.
Preventing sexual assault, the Pentagon says, is not just a personnel matter but is vital for the military’s combat effectiveness.
“The Department’s commitment to a disciplined, professional fighting force is fundamental to maintaining a lethal, ready, and mission-focused military,” the latest report concludes.
“This commitment is grounded in standards, accountability, and mutual respect across the Total Force. Conduct that undermines that trust—including sexual assault—directly degrades unit cohesion, readiness, and overall warfighting effectiveness. Preventing and responding to sexual assault is therefore a readiness imperative.”

How to Break Up With Your Therapist Without Ghosting Them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
13:48:11 UTC
22:48:11 KST

Your therapist has probably encouraged you to have difficult conversations, advocate for your needs, and resist the urge to avoid things that make you anxious. That’s all well and good—until, one day, the difficult conversation is with them.
If therapy doesn’t feel useful anymore, or if you’ve realized that you and your therapist simply aren’t the right match, it can be tempting to outsource the breakup to the cancel-appointment button. Yet unless there’s an ethical, boundary, or safety concern, experts say it’s usually worth having a conversation with your therapist before ending the relationship. It might improve the therapy. It might also help you find someone better suited to you, or simply allow you to leave without feeling guilty about ghosting the person who knows exactly why you tend to ghost people.
Speaking up could also save you from having to begin the search from scratch. “Your therapist could be the gateway to your next great therapist,” says Ryan Culkin, a licensed professional counselor and chief counselor officer at Thriveworks, which provides therapy and psychiatry services. They might be able to adjust their approach—or recommend someone who would suit you better.
Even if you already know you’re finished, breaking the news doesn’t require a dramatic confrontation or an elaborate defense. Here’s how to decide whether it’s time to call it quits—and how to do it painlessly.
Figure out what kind of discomfort you’re feeling
Good therapy isn’t necessarily easy. “Sometimes therapy can be really uncomfortable, but it can be incredibly productive,” says Eli Kraiem, a clinical psychologist in New York. A therapist might challenge an assumption you’re attached to, point out a pattern you’d rather not see, or encourage you to do something that scares you. Feeling unsettled after a session doesn’t mean it went badly.
Michael G. Wetter, a clinical psychologist in Los Angeles, prefers this question: “What is the discomfort accomplishing?” Productive discomfort generally leads to insight, reflection, behavioral change, or progress toward goals you and your therapist have agreed on, he says. If it’s a poor fit, you might notice you leave therapy feeling misunderstood or have the same conversation week after week without much meaningful movement.
Juliann Siwicki, a licensed clinical professional counselor in Vero Beach, Fla., thinks about it this way: “Are you uncomfortable because you’re talking about something hard? Or because you feel like you’re having coffee with someone and not getting help? Those are two different things.”
You should be able to name what you're working toward—a pattern you're trying to break, a decision you're stuck on, a reaction you'd like to change—and to notice how much airtime your therapist is taking up. "A therapist can share something about themselves if it helps the client," Siwicki says. "It becomes too much when the client is spending the session listening to the therapist's stories, or feels like they need to take care of the therapist."
Kamran Eshtehardi, a clinical psychologist in Pasadena, Calif., has heard the far end of that spectrum. One client described a previous therapist who "thought it would be helpful to tell me about when they cheated on their wife"—including that his wife left him, and that he later saw an escort. "And I'm like, ‘What? Like, a therapist told you?’" Eshtehardi says. "Those are major red flags."
What was once a good fit can also change over time. A therapist who helped you through a crisis might not be right for your next stage. "A great therapist might not be great for you," Culkin says. "It's kind of like dating—you're not going to get it right the first time every time."
Even finding that “the therapist gets on your nerves” doesn’t necessarily mean you should quit, says Eshtehardi. A rupture doesn’t mean the therapy has “rotted on the vine,” he says, and progress sometimes develops “underneath the surface” before reaching a tipping point. But if you’ve explained what you need and nothing changes—or there’s no sense of progress—your frustration deserves attention.
Serious boundary violations, unethical behavior, or anything that makes you feel unsafe are different. You don’t need to attempt a repair before leaving, nor do you owe the therapist another session.
Say what isn’t working
If you’re open to continuing with your therapist, with the appropriate changes, describe what you’ve noticed and need—without turning the conversation into a performance review.
Try: “Our sessions have started to feel conversational, and I need more structure, feedback, and therapeutic insight. Can we talk about that?” Or: “I’m not sure what I’m working toward. Could we revisit my goals?” Culkin suggests language as straightforward as: “That didn’t land with me,” “I want to try something different,” or “I really liked when you did this.”
Eshtehardi recalls a client telling him that the usual sympathetic responses—“I’m so sorry to hear that” or “That must have been so hard”—didn’t work for them. “I just want to get stuff on the table and say, ‘OK, what’s going on here? How do we work with this?’” the client told him. That feedback helped Eshtehardi calibrate his approach. “I’m not saying it’s necessarily the client’s job to help train the therapist,” he says, but clients can explain what they’re looking for and how they prefer to work.
If you know you’re ready to leave
Sometimes you’re not interested in recalibrating the relationship—you’ve already decided to end it. In that case, the goal isn’t to persuade your therapist that you have a good enough reason to go. It’s simply to communicate your decision in whatever way feels most manageable.
You don’t have to deliver the news face-to-face. A call, email, or text is fine: “I don’t want therapy and the therapeutic relationship to be another source of anxiety for my clients,” Eshtehardi says. For someone accustomed to conflict or pushback, sending “I’m sorry, this isn’t working for me” and receiving a calm response can itself be therapeutic. You might realize, he says, that “maybe there’s a way to connect with people that doesn’t feel like I’m always doing the wrong thing.”
Eshtehardi also encourages clients who feel guilty to view the conversation as an opportunity to “practice trusting that someone else is going to be OK,” and trusting themselves to make the right decision. Your therapist’s response will provide useful information. A therapist who responds with openness and a willingness to adjust is giving you one kind of information; defensiveness or guilt-tripping gives you another. If the therapist acts wounded, Eshtehardi thinks of it as a “double whammy.” It might hurt, but it also “confirms that you’ve made the correct decision to stop therapy.”
You don’t need to build a case for your decision. “When it comes to trying to find the right fit, I don’t think clients should have to worry about having to justify their perspective,” Eshtehardi says. He suggests keeping the message simple: “I don’t think it’s the right fit. I’d like to stop sessions, and I really appreciate your time. Thank you.”
And try not to assume you’ve devastated them. Therapists are trained to handle patients leaving, Kraiem says. If yours can’t tolerate it, “then there’s a problem with the therapist, not with the patients.”
Make the transition easier on yourself
If you need consistent support, try to line up a new therapist before leaving your current one. Ask your therapist if they can recommend someone with a different style or specialty.
Before booking, confirm the new therapist accepts your insurance. “There’s nothing worse than getting through that first session” only to discover they don’t, Culkin says. You can also ask how they structure sessions, establish goals, and respond when a client disagrees. Be candid about what helped the first time around, what didn’t, and what’s important to you this time. Culkin encourages therapists to ask what clients appreciated about past providers and what they wish had been different. “Those are gold answers,” he says.
It’s not mandatory, but Kraiem recommends a wrap-up session, if you’re comfortable: “Let’s have one session to reflect on the experiences, process how you’ve improved, how you’ve grown through therapy, and maybe areas that still need improvement,” he says.
Ask the practices about transferring relevant records. You’ll typically sign an authorization specifying what can be shared. Whether you want a direct handoff depends on why you’re leaving, Eshtehardi says. If you felt misunderstood, the former therapist’s perspective could “muddy the waters,” and you might prefer a clean start. If your therapist is referring you to someone with more specialized expertise, a conversation could help them get up to speed more quickly. In that case, Eshtehardi tells clients, “I’ll tell you everything I tell them so you know what they know.”
Finally, cancel future appointments and settle outstanding balances or other loose ends. Eshtehardi suggests asking: “Are there any last things we need to do?” If medication is part of your care, coordinate with your prescribing clinician about refills.
Changing therapists isn’t proof that treatment failed. Sometimes successful therapy means repairing a strained relationship. Other times, it means recognizing that the relationship has run its course—and using the difficult-conversation skills you’ve practiced to say so.
