====================================================================================================

From "poor, corrupt Ukraine" to EU candidate: how Italy won over Germany and opened the EU’s door to Kyiv
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
12:56:00 EEST
18:56:00 KST

From "poor, corrupt Ukraine" to EU candidate: how Italy won over Germany and opened the EU’s door to Kyiv
Pier Francesco Zazo was one of the few ambassadors of EU member states who was in Kyiv on 24 February 2022. At the time he had headed Italy’s diplomatic mission in Ukraine for more than a year, and he remained in the position until 2024.
The Italian ambassador did not have a particularly high profile during his time in Ukraine, although everyone involved in supporting Ukraine and its path towards EU membership was aware of his personal role in backing the country and its European integration.
Now Zazo, who will soon turn 67, has left the diplomatic and public service.
"Now I am a free man, and I am happy to speak openly about what I know and what I think," he admitted during his interview with the editor of European Pravda.
We took advantage of Zazo’s visit to Kyiv to hear his candid recollections of how Ukraine has been perceived by its partners, how attitudes changed after the full-scale war began, how the negotiations over EU candidate status were conducted, and what we can expect going forward. And this isn’t just about Italy.
"There are Italians with a pro-Russian attitude, and I can't convince them with arguments"
You’ve heard the news about Iryna Mudra. How do people in Europe perceive the news that high-level Ukrainian politicians are suspected of such serious crimes?
It definitely doesn't help Ukraine. Being pro-Ukrainian, I always try to explain the positive side of these cases: I tell people that this proves Ukraine is really fighting against corruption; that the anti-corruption bodies work well; that it’s a process which is ongoing and needs time.
But still, this is a weak point.
People who sympathise more with Russia use this as a strong argument: "This proves that the Italian government shouldn’t give money to a corrupt Ukraine."
But it’s not a disaster. I see many articles explaining the positive side – that Ukraine is moving in the right direction. The mere fact that you’re able to investigate corruption at the highest level is definitely a good sign. And one more positive aspect which seems important is that Ukrainians are ready to go out into the streets and protest. That would never happen in an autocratic country like Russia.
Therefore you can see it in a positive way and in a negative way.
Do these explanations work in Italy?
It depends who you talk to.
Italian society is very polarised.
If you talk to pro-European Italians, they appreciate your fight for freedom and the rule of law. Also, those who have some knowledge about Ukraine and the war tend to recognise that Ukraine’s transition to democratic rules is happening.
Also, in my experience, these explanations work well with those who are neutral towards Ukraine, who don’t have any prejudice. I can tell you that because I often talk to this type of person. They want to understand; they listen to me very carefully, knowing that I have previous experience both in Ukraine and in Russia.
But there are also Italians with a pro-Russian attitude, and I'm not able to convince them with arguments. There are quite a few people in Italy who have never been to Ukraine, but they have a position based on the clear Russian narrative.
They would tell me that everything was staged in Bucha. And if I tell them that I have been there personally, that I’ve spoken with the mothers of people who were killed, that I saw a lot as an ambassador, they don't trust me. I see no way to convince them.
Fortunately, this type of person is a minority.
So Ukraine has to work more with the people who are in between – and they are ready to listen.
"Italians were really caught by surprise that Ukrainians resisted"
What does Ukraine mean to people in Italy today? And what did it mean to them a few years ago? I imagine that 10-15 years ago, the main things people in Italy associated with Ukraine were [the footballer] Andriy Shevchenko, perhaps Chernobyl, and the idea that Ukraine was somewhere near Moscow.
Yes, that's very true. This perception was formed under strong influence from Russia.
Since 1990, Ukraine had been perceived as a poor, corrupt country with a strong presence of oligarchic powers, plus Chernobyl and environmental disasters. The image was completely negative, and it persisted not just until 2014, but until the outbreak of the full-scale war in 2022.
One of the few positive aspects about Ukraine was the Ukrainian diaspora, which was respected in Italy, but it was not a very influential one. Many Ukrainians worked [as carers] for elderly people, and they never created problems with the justice system. Here comes a very important point, which may surprise you today, but in Italy Ukrainians were perceived as a community with a very weak national identity.
The community did not fight that stereotype, partly because Ukrainians abroad are quite individualistic.
This was also partially a Russian narrative, as Russia worked hard to convince Italians and Europeans that all the former Soviet Union countries basically have a Russian identity and sooner or later they will return to Great Mother Russia.
That created an incredibly simplified image of Ukraine, even among my colleagues.
Do you mean that even within the Foreign Ministry, some diplomats saw Ukraine as essentially part of Russia’s sphere?
Yes. Even in 2021, when I came here as an ambassador, there were very strong narratives against Ukraine. For instance, many people in Rome believed that Ukraine was suppressing Russian-speaking people, that people in South-Eastern Ukraine were being discriminated against because they spoke Russian.
The first thing I did on arriving in Ukraine was to go to Kharkiv and Odesa and start writing reports to my capital explaining that that wasn’t true: that many people speak Russian, but they feel Ukrainian.
Of course not every diplomat had that wrong image of Ukraine, but many did.
Russia really worked hard in the field of disinformation – it’s where they are strong. Also with all this narrative of "there's no Ukraine", "Ukraine is an artificial state", "they're just part of Great Mother Russia".
Therefore, the Italians were really caught by surprise not just by the fact that the war had started, but even more by the fact that Ukrainians resisted.
Everyone in Italy was convinced that in two or three days everything would be over. Even my colleagues thought so.
What other myths or misconceptions about Ukraine were widespread in Italy?
I would stress the underestimation of the economic potential of Ukraine.
For me, it was always clear that Ukraine has huge potential, but in Italy, it was never known. People were usually surprised if I said that Ukraine was the second most important republic in former Soviet Europe. No one knew before 2022 that you had a very strong defence industry, space industry. No one had heard about your success in digitalisation.
For the majority of people, everything good was related to Russia.
Everything bad could be Ukrainian.
Andriy Shevchenko played for AC Milan. Did Italians see him as Ukrainian, or simply as a talented footballer from the former Soviet Union?
Yes, and this contributed very positively, though it was never enough compared to the negatives.
By the way, I was among the first Italians who knew that Shevchenko was going to play in Italy. At the time, I was working here in Kyiv as a consul, and I issued him the visa to move to Milan. I remember it well – it was 1999.
I love football, and I used to watch the games of Dynamo Kyiv here. I knew that he was a great player.
I called some of my friends in Milan and said, "Look, you know who is moving to your team?" and my friends answered: "What? Ukraine? Do they play football?"
After a few months, they called me back saying: "Yeah, he's a great player!"
"Until 23 February, nobody in Rome believed there would be an invasion"
What changed in Italy’s perception of Ukraine after 2022?
As I said, your resilience was a huge surprise, and the attitude also changed completely. Ukrainians were admired.
Let me give you one example that demonstrates this change. Before 2022, there were no books about Ukrainian history available in Italy. There was only The Gates of Europe by Serhii Plokhy. Now there are many books about Ukraine available. Italians have discovered that there is a Ukrainian nation and a Ukrainian national identity.
What changed?
The Russian invasion came as a huge shock. Italian foreign policy changed immediately, in 24 hours. I always say that paradoxically, my work [as an ambassador] became easier after the invasion.
Italian business and public opinion quickly turned to being pro-Ukrainian. To some degree, it was sympathy for the victims (even if many did not believe Ukraine would manage to survive). It has slowly decreased. After four and a half years of war, people still support Ukraine politically, but they would rather go out into the streets to protest for Gaza, not for Ukraine.
But the political position has completely changed.
How did that change happen? Given that Russian narratives were quite influential, including within parts of the government and the Foreign Ministry, and that Italy had traditionally been relatively close to Russia, how did it become such a strong supporter of Ukraine? Was Mario Draghi instrumental in that shift?
Absolutely yes, but not only him.
I would say that first of all, it was Italian public opinion. People didn't even understand the difference between Ukraine and Russia, they used to have strong cultural links with Russia, and the invasion came as a shock to Italian public opinion.
In Italy, nobody expected full-scale Russian aggression.
I can tell you that until 23 February, nobody in Rome believed there would be an invasion. Nobody! I was here in Kyiv and I was sure that Russia would attack, but nobody even wanted to talk to me.
Up until 24 February, Italy perceived all the developments as: okay, we are G7 members, so we participate in joint sanctions and don’t block them, but we are not very enthusiastic supporters.
On the morning of 24 February, everything changed immediately.
I went to the embassy and everyone called me – the foreign minister, the prime minister. And the reaction was immediate, even if they were caught by surprise (although later I discovered that Mario Draghi had also expected the war to start). The Italian government immediately adopted sanctions, immediately confirmed support for Ukraine – political, economic, humanitarian.
Prime Minister Draghi played a very important role in the joint efforts to freeze Russian sovereign funds. You know, he is a former governor of the European Central Bank, and he knew the correct way to immobilise them.
Later I had a chance to talk to him about the events of those days, and he told me how he talked to Biden and agreed that.
Also, he told me about his contact with Putin [on 1 February 2022].
As an economist, he had the impression that Russia was preparing for the war, as they had started accumulating reserves. His conversation with Putin confirmed that feeling.
But even so, Italy did not believe that Russia would actually invade Ukraine. Why was that?
One of the reasons was that our foreign minister, Luigi Di Maio, paid a visit to Kyiv in mid-February, right before the invasion, and two days later to Moscow, where he was told by Lavrov that nothing would happen.
There was also a wishful desire not to believe in this scenario, so as not to jeopardise the strong economic relationship between Italy and Russia.
But thank God, later Italy completely changed its mind. And then we got the Meloni government, which cemented the role of Italy as a very responsible member of NATO, the EU and the G7 in supporting Ukraine – even if now, after four years of war, a certain fatigue has emerged.
"It wasn’t clear what Scholz would say until the joint press conference"
How did Italy become one of the key countries advocating for Ukraine to receive EU candidate status?
It started even in 2021, when our foreign minister, Luigi Di Maio, visited Kyiv and during that visit quickly agreed – to my surprise – to publicly support Ukraine’s European aspirations. He accepted much more positive wording than Italy had ever accepted: we accept Ukraine’s aspiration to join the EU, provided of course that you carry out the reforms.
But the person who really played the fundamental role was Draghi.
He was the most convinced supporter of Ukraine, and he played a decisive role in the decision to grant Ukraine candidate status in June 2022.
I was there, I accompanied him on the visit to Kyiv that he made with Macron and Scholz, and I saw that with my own eyes. There was a goal to convince Chancellor Olaf Scholz, and it started even before they arrived in Kyiv – on the train.
I was told that wine was involved. What happened?
Yes, that’s true. By the way, I just met your former foreign minister Dmytro Kuleba, and we were discussing whether it was French or Italian wine.
But wine was there, and it contributed a lot.
Still, during the visit to Kyiv, Scholz remained very cautious, and there was no clarity about what he would say up until the joint press conference. Draghi was saying that we have to support Ukraine, Macron was also in favour, although he was more interested in pushing his own initiative, the European Political Community.
And it was only during the press conference that Scholz finally declared: "Okay, we accept Ukraine as a candidate." He confirmed that only at the press conference, although he was probably preparing to accept it.
The role that Draghi played was immense – of course, with Macron’s support. By the way, there was also the Romanian president, Klaus Iohannis, but the key talks were only for three leaders.
Why was Draghi so convinced that Ukraine belongs in the EU?
I also asked him this question.
My impression is that Draghi was outraged by the aggression.
He felt betrayed by Russia.
When it happened, he took a very immediate decision: Russia had crossed a red line, and although the economic links were very strong, they had to be cut.
He told me that at the beginning, he was very worried about the economic consequences, but Italy was very quick in decreasing its economic dependence. Within a few months, Draghi and Di Maio paid visits to Azerbaijan, to Algeria, and Italy was much faster than Germany in getting rid of Russian gas and oil.
Earlier, you said that Russian propaganda had portrayed Ukraine as a poor and corrupt country. How then did Italy end up supporting EU membership for Ukraine?
Draghi did not buy that narrative, of course. Talk about a "poor, corrupt country" works with ordinary people. Not with those in the government.
Draghi was removed in July 2022, and then came Meloni.
"We don't want to have the same experience we had with Orbán"
Let me also ask you about Giorgia Meloni. In 2022, many Ukrainians were wary of her. She leads a right-wing party, so her strong pro-Ukrainian position came as something of a surprise. Why did she take such a clear stance in support of Ukraine?
First of all, Meloni is not a fascist, as some opponents depict her.
Yes, Fratelli d’Italia is a right-wing party, but not that right-wing. And yes, in 2022, she was absolutely not pro-European, although now she's becoming pro-European because of Trump. The way Trump is treating her is shifting her position more and more towards the EU.
Meloni’s party is a nationalist party; she personally believes in nationalism. And that’s why she respects countries that fight for their homeland. That’s a very important aspect of why she supports Ukraine.
And secondly, she used to be very pro-American and pro-NATO. The fact that Biden took a pro-Ukrainian approach was very important in forming her pro-Ukrainian stance. Even if now her relations with the US are changing, I’m confident that
Meloni will remain pro-Ukrainian.
Personally speaking now as a free citizen, I like her pro-Ukrainian approach, and I think for Ukrainians it's good that she is the leader of Italy. What I don't like, and where I disagree with her, is that she's still quite against changing the decision-making mechanism within the EU. She's in favour of the unanimity rule.
I believe in enhanced cooperation in Europe, or multiple speeds, like we have with the euro and with Schengen.
This is also in the interest of Ukraine.
Ukraine needs a strong Europe. We don't want to have the same experience as we had with Orbán again – if every country has a veto, it's very dangerous.
But also the European Union needs a strong Ukraine. Therefore, Ukraine must join the European Union.
Will Italy continue to support Ukraine?
I’m confident about Italian support for Ukraine in the political or humanitarian field. The way towards EU membership is also not really an issue for Italians.
The problem is military support. According to the latest polls, the majority of Italians are against military aid. Next year we have elections in Italy.
Also, within the coalition, two parties, the majority – Meloni’s party and Forza Italia – are pro-European and pro-Ukrainian, but the third party, Lega, is more loudly opposing military aid to Ukraine.
Let me put it bluntly: they are pro-Russian.
Yes. Lega even has an agreement with United Russia. They have received Russian money in the past.
Therefore Meloni, although she is still pro-Ukrainian, has to be very cautious. Even though she still supports Ukraine militarily, she doesn’t speak a lot about it.
You have to keep in mind that Italians are very pacifist people. It has always been in our DNA because of Christianity and the Vatican. It's very difficult to talk to pacifists, I tell you.
We also have a problem with the opposition, which is looking for a way to get more votes.
The third most popular party in Italy is the Five Star Movement led by former prime minister [Giuseppe] Conte. His position is: we condemn Putin, but we have to talk to Putin. The second most popular party, the Democratic Party, is divided on Ukraine. There is a minority which is strongly pro-Ukrainian, but the leader of the party, Elly Schlein, is different.
Therefore, we have to see the outcome of the next elections.
The situation could be dangerous. Russia will likely invest in its disinformation campaign, aiming to support the "sovereigntist" populist parties, whether they are left– or right-wing.
"Italy is perceived by Russia as a weak link"
Do you believe the EU will be brave enough to reach a consensus on membership for Ukraine?
It depends upon the outcome of the political elections. Next year there will be elections in Italy, in France, in Spain and in Poland.
These elections come at a time when Europeans are under attack both by Russia and by Trump.
People need to understand that it’s time to change, including our approach to Ukraine. It’s now or never, otherwise we are condemned to a steady decline.
Europe has shown its ability to surprise everyone.
Who would have expected Europe to increase its support for Ukraine to an extent that it is able to completely replace the US after it suspended financial aid? Who expected the EU to provide military assistance in the numbers we see now, including through the €90 billion support package?
Europe is doing a lot to reinforce the European pillar of NATO.
We’ve started accession negotiations with Ukraine. I’m sure it would be a mistake if Ukraine does not join the EU now. Of course the negotiations have to be finalised and reforms in Ukraine are needed, but it’s quite possible to do it in three years.
It also depends on when the war ends.
Absolutely. Also because of Article 42 in the EU Treaty about joint defence – nobody will dare to attack Ukraine if it automatically triggers Article 42.
To join the EU, you have to respect the Copenhagen criteria, where the main point is democracy. There should be elections, but it's impossible to hold democratic elections now.
You also have to prepare adequately for membership.
I want to stress that I’m very much convinced that Ukraine will join the EU because it's in the interest of Europe, even in terms of defence. Of course there will be obstacles, mainly from Eastern member states, but studies show there are much more advantages to Ukraine’s accession than disadvantages.
Will Italy support NATO membership for Ukraine? Given what you said about Italy being more cautious when it comes to defence and security issues, would that be a difficult position for Rome?
Italy is more cautious on military support, but NATO membership is not a very sensitive issue. Italy will support what the big countries decide.
You referred to Russian propaganda. How is Russia currently working to undermine Ukraine in Italy?
They are using all the weapons of disinformation in Italy.
Italy is perceived by Russia as a weak link.
For example, even Telegram is quite widely used here, as well as TikTok. Fake news, the spread of official Russian statements, interference in Italy’s internal affairs – all of this works. They are very strong in corruption. Just recently, two former agents of the Italian intelligence service were arrested because they gave confidential material to Russia.
I'm sure, but I can't prove it, that there are journalists and opinion leaders paid by Russia.
Unfortunately, Italy is not ready to accept how big the threat represented by Russia is.
We don't have a legislative framework to act against those who disseminate disinformation and fake news. We don't have a national agency coordinating the fight against it – some other European countries do have one.
Italian public TV shows and media have a lot of pro-Russian views. There's no proper fact-checking.
But I still hope we will avoid a U-turn in our policy. If you put together the votes for the different parties, you will see that the majority of Italians are pro-Ukrainian. I don’t see a risk of a pro-Russian majority emerging after the elections.
And again: Meloni is still in the lead, and she will not change her pro-Ukrainian stance after the elections. She is becoming more and more pro-European.
Sergiy Sydorenko,
Editor, European Pravda

Slovak police thwart arson plot targeting Ukrainian drone factory, media reports

Slovak police detained three foreign nationals on Aug. 25 over an alleged plot to set fire to a Ukrainian-owned Skyeton factory producing advanced surveillance drones, Dennik N reported.
The incident marks one of the first known attempts to target a military equipment manufacturer in Slovakia, according to Dennik N.
Two suspects were detained in Slovakia, while a third was arrested in Germany under a European arrest warrant. Slovak police did not disclose the nationalities of the detained individuals in its statement.
The alleged plotters' actions could have sparked a "large-scale fire" at the facility, where about 70 people were present at the time and property was valued at "tens of millions of euros," police said.
Police seized an incendiary mixture of gasoline and polystyrene — a homemade form of napalm — along with tools, cell phones, an action camera and a hand-drawn map of the facility they allegedly planned to set on fire.
Skyeton did not immediately comment on the reported arson attempt targeting the production facility.
Skyeton announced plans to open a production facility in Haniska, near Presov, Slovakia's third-largest city, in spring 2024. The Ukrainian company expected the new site to employ up to 200 people by the end of 2025, according to the statement.
Since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion, sabotage and arson attempts targeting industrial and logistics infrastructure have increased across the EU, particularly at facilities involved in weapons production.
Russia has regularly recruited both foreign nationals and its own citizens to carry out such operations in NATO and EU countries.
Similar incidents have been reported in other EU countries in recent months. In March, perpetrators set fire to a facility belonging to Ukrainian company Archer-LPP, which manufactured thermal imaging devices, in the Czech city of Pardubice.
Earlier in August, two suspects were detained in connection with an arson attack on a building belonging to Estonian defense company Milrem Robotics, which supplies unmanned ground systems to Ukraine.

Customers facing steeper electricity bills as Hong Kong firms raise fuel charges
CLP Power and HK Electric announce higher fuel-related charges, while offering rebates and subsidies to ease the burden on households
Customers will face higher electricity bills next month as Hong Kong’s two power suppliers will raise fuel-related charges, with the firms blaming geopolitical tensions and volatility in international energy markets.
As electricity costs rise, CLP Power and HK Electric have introduced rebate and relief schemes as grass-roots households face higher air-conditioning costs after a summer with an unusually high number of very hot days.
HK Electric, which supplies electricity mainly to Hong Kong Island and Lamma Island, said on Tuesday that its fuel clause charge would rise to 60.7 HK cents (7.74 US cents) per kilowatt-hour (kWh) in September.
The charge will increase by 3.4 cents, or 5.9 per cent, from August, marking the fourth consecutive monthly increase since May. The fuel clause charge has jumped 1.3 times from 26 cents per kWh in May.
Together with the basic tariff, the average net tariff will rise to 188.6 cents per unit in September, an increase of 1.8 per cent from August.
“International energy prices remain volatile, with spot prices for liquefied natural gas having more than doubled compared with levels before the geopolitical developments earlier this year and still rising,” HK Electric said.

U.S. Air Force C-17 lands in Moscow, no reason given
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
09:52:28 UTC
18:52:28 KST

- A U.S. Air Force C-17A Globemaster III flew from Riga, Latvia, to Vnukovo International Airport near Moscow on August 25.
- Neither the U.S. Air Force nor the Department of War has publicly confirmed the flight's purpose or destination.
A U.S. Air Force C-17A Globemaster III flew from Riga, Latvia, to Vnukovo International Airport near Moscow on the morning of August 25, according to flight tracking data reported by Flightradar24.
The flight, carrying the callsign REACH4555, landed in Russia at approximately 10:04 a.m. Moscow time, according to Russian outlet RBK, which cited Flightradar24 data.
The aircraft, tail number 07-7181, departed Riga at roughly 8:50 a.m. Moscow time. Flightradar24 posted images of the flight’s tracked path showing it crossing Latvia and Lithuania before continuing into Russian territory and landing at Vnukovo.
Flight tracking accounts on X initially questioned whether the aircraft had actually entered Russian airspace, noting that some position data appeared inconsistent with typical automated tracking. One account, Coffe Report, said the aircraft’s position was later confirmed through an ACARS initialization message and that Flightradar24 showed the full approach and landing at Vnukovo.
Neither the U.S. Air Force nor the Department of War has issued a public statement confirming the flight’s purpose or destination. Coffe Report, citing unnamed sources on X, described the flight as filed under a “SECDEF support code,” a designation that would indicate the mission was tied to Department of War leadership travel or logistics support, though this claim has not been independently confirmed.
Flight history data reviewed by Brit Brief showed the aircraft’s recent routing began in the United States on August 22, when it departed Joint Base McGuire-Dix-Lakehurst in Wrightstown, New Jersey, and landed at Joint Base Charleston in South Carolina. The following day, the aircraft flew from Charleston to Joint Base Andrews in Camp Springs, Maryland, before continuing to Riga.
Vnukovo International Airport, the third-busiest airport in Russia, has periodically served as a landing point for diplomatic and military flights during the war between Russia and Ukraine, though direct U.S. military flights into Russian territory have been rare since the war began in 2022.
The flight’s arrival was widely noted on social media given the current state of U.S.-Russia military relations, though no context has been publicly confirmed for the visit. The C-17 is a heavy-lift transport aircraft used by the Air Force for cargo, troop movement and, at times, VIP or diplomatic support missions.
What prompted the flight, who was aboard, and how long the aircraft remained at Vnukovo have not been disclosed by U.S. or Russian officials.

How to choose a tubular radiator for an apartment
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
12:51:45 EEST
18:51:45 KST

Modern radiators have long ceased to be exclusively an element of the heating system. Today, they combine functionality, energy efficiency, and an attractive appearance. That is why more and more apartment owners are paying attention to tubular radiators, which fit well into modern interiors and provide a comfortable microclimate in the room.
Why tubular radiators are gaining popularity
- The main advantage of tubular heating radiators is their modern and attractive appearance, thanks to which the battery is not hidden behind curtains or decorative grilles, but is boldly made an addition or even an accent of the interior.
- A large selection of sizes makes it easy to fit the heating device under the window and on the column near the panoramic window, providing the necessary heating.
- Hygiene - due to the fact that tubular radiators do not have closed hidden parts, they are easy to care for.
- Delonghi tubular radiators can withstand a working pressure of 10 bar, which is suitable for central heating in new buildings.
One of the main advantages is versatility. Tubular radiators look equally good in classic interiors as well as in modern apartments in the style of minimalism, loft or Scandinavian style. In addition, manufacturers offer a wide selection of sizes, shapes and colors. Learn more at the link: https://delonghi-radiators.com.ua/trubchasti-radiatori/
What to look for when choosing
Step #1 - Radiator power
Before buying, it is important to determine the required thermal power of the heating device. It depends on the area of the room, the height of the ceiling, the number of windows and the level of thermal insulation of the house. For a standard apartment, approximately 80 W of heat is required per square meter of area. For corner rooms or rooms with large windows, this figure may be higher, about 100 W per 1 m2. For example, for a room of 15 sq.m., 1200-1500 W is required (15m2*80W/m2=1200 W).
Step #2 - Dimensions and installation location
Tubular radiators are presented in a large number of options. For rooms with panoramic windows, vertical models are often chosen, which are installed on the side walls near the glazing so as not to block the view from the window. For rooms with standard windows, horizontal models with a height of 570 mm are perfect, and for small rooms or narrow walls, tall vertical structures with a small width are perfect. Before ordering, it is worth measuring the available space in advance and taking into account the location of the connection to the heating system.
Step #3 - Workingpressure
For apartments with centralized heating, it is important to check the working and maximum pressure of the radiator. The selected model must meet the parameters of the house's heating system and have a sufficient margin of safety.
Step #4 - Color
Modern steel radiators are covered with multilayer protective compounds and powder paint. High-quality coating not only improves the appearance of the product, but also protects the metal from corrosion and mechanical damage. The most polar colors remain white and black, although you can choose to paint in any color from the RAL palette upon request.
Vertical or horizontal radiator
The choice depends primarily on the characteristics of the room.
Horizontal models are considered a classic solution and are most often installed under windows. They create a thermal curtain and effectively compensate for heat loss through glazing.
Vertical radiators allow for rational use of space and become an interesting design accent. They are especially relevant for apartments with panoramic windows or non-standard layouts.
In addition, tubular radiators mwill become a full-fledged part of the interior design and harmoniously combine with the furniture and decoration of the room.
Conclusion
The choice of a tubular radiator for an apartment depends on the area of the room, the features of the heating system and the design wishes of the owner. It is important to pay attention not only to the appearance, but also to the technical characteristics that affect the efficiency of heating. For the correct selection, we recommend contacting the specialists of the Delonghi Radiators store for advice to ensure a comfortable temperature in the home and choose a stylish element of a modern interior for many years.

Upgraded Stryker variant debuts on NATO’s east flank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
09:47:40 UTC
18:47:40 KST

- The 2nd Cavalry Regiment fired live rounds from the upgraded ICVVA1-30mm Stryker for the first time in Europe on August 20.
- The Army ordered 269 of the 30mm-equipped Strykers from Oshkosh Defense for $356 million under a contract that began in 2021.
A Stryker squadron based in Vilseck, Germany, fired live ammunition from newly upgraded Stryker vehicles for the first time in Europe this week, Stars and Stripes reported.
The 3rd Squadron, 2nd Cavalry Regiment conducted the gunnery exercise August 20 at the Grafenwoehr Training Area, using the new ICVVA1-30mm variant of the Stryker Double-V Hull Infantry Carrier Vehicle.
The unit is the first outside the United States to receive the upgraded vehicles, according to Stars and Stripes. Twenty of the new Strykers began arriving in February and will be fielded across the rest of the regiment, Capt. Alexander Stamatiou, commander of the squadron’s Killer Troop, told the outlet.
The vehicles carry a 30 mm semiautomatic cannon in addition to M240 machine guns. Some are also equipped with self-contained 120 mm mortars, .50-caliber machine guns and mounted Javelin anti-tank launchers, Stamatiou said.
“Versus a peer adversary, for an infantry carrier vehicle these are unmatched,” Stamatiou said.
The Army selected Oshkosh Defense in June 2021 to integrate the 30 mm Medium Caliber Weapon System onto the Stryker ICVVA1, under a six-year requirements contract with partners Pratt Miller Defense and Rafael Advanced Defense Systems worth up to $942.9 million. The weapon system is based on Rafael’s SAMSON turret family. The Army has since ordered 269 upgraded vehicles for $356 million to outfit three Stryker Brigade Combat Teams, along with additional units for testing and logistics development. Oshkosh delivered the first upgraded vehicle to the Army’s Aberdeen Test Center in August 2022, and fielding began in 2023 with the 1-2 Stryker Brigade Combat Team at Joint Base Lewis-McChord in Washington state.
The new variant also gives infantry squad leaders independent sights that let them designate targets for the vehicle’s gunner, Spc. Spencer Riley told Stars and Stripes.
“There’s actually a feature where I can flip a switch and my gun will automatically move to what he’s looking at,” Riley said. “And then I can engage straight from there.”
Soldiers said the upgraded vehicle also lets crews reload weapons and perform maintenance from inside the vehicle rather than climbing outside it. Sgt. Oliver Estela demonstrated that capability during the exercise when a round jammed in his machine gun. Estela climbed into the vehicle’s unmanned turret, cleared the jam and resumed firing within minutes.
“It’s more convenient,” Estela said, calling the new Stryker variant “way more capable than our older platforms.”
The vehicles also feature improved engines, optics, communications and targeting systems compared with earlier Stryker models, Stamatiou said.
Separately, the Army has been testing vehicle-mounted and wearable counter-drone systems through an initiative called Project Flytrap, aimed at detecting, tracking and jamming hostile drones. Personnel transport vehicles have increasingly come under attack from first-person-view and commercial drones during the war between Russia and Ukraine.
“I’ll take one of these any day of the week,” Riley said of the upgraded Stryker. “You can reach out and touch somebody pretty far with these things. You got a nice armor-piercing round.”

What would justice look like if there were no Rohingya left in Myanmar?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
09:46:11 UTC
18:46:11 KST

What would justice look like if there were no Rohingya left in Myanmar?
Nine years after the 2017 atrocities, Rohingya are still being forced to flee because the genocide has never stopped.
August 25 is an incredibly painful day for the Rohingya. It marks the anniversary of the 2017 genocidal campaign by the Myanmar military. Babies and young children were thrown into fires. Women and young girls were systematically gang-raped and mutilated. Entire families were slaughtered as they fled. Others were trapped inside their homes and burned alive. More than 700,000 of our people were forced to flee to Bangladesh.
The Rohingya, who are an ethnic Muslim-majority group who speak their own language from the Indo-Aryan family, have long faced discrimination and persecution in Myanmar.
Today, about 1.2 million Rohingya remain trapped in camps in Bangladesh, while a new wave of persecution is forcing more Rohingya from their homes in Rakhine state. Others are risking their lives at sea in a desperate search for safety.
In this desperate situation, there is a ray of hope raised by international justice proceedings in Argentina and the International Court of Justice (ICJ). Still, the international community is falling short in fulfilling its commitments to ensure accountability and protect the Rohingya.
The genocide never stopped
Over the past two years, the balance of power in Rakhine has dramatically changed. The Arakan Army (AA), an ethnic Rakhine armed group, now controls most of the state, including the main Rohingya areas in the north. But the brutality and persecution Rohingya face have not ended.
As the AA has consolidated its control, evidence has mounted of mass killings and targeted attacks on civilians, documenting what Rohingya communities have been warning of.
Rohingya also face forced recruitment, forced labour, detention and severe restrictions on movement. Sexual violence, a hallmark of the Rohingya genocide, is continuing under AA authority.
Rohingya in Rakhine report that the violence and oppression they now face from the AA is just as brutal as the Myanmar military’s ethnic cleansing in 2017. Taken together, we see these abuses as part of a deliberate strategy to drive Rohingya from their homes and continue their erasure from Myanmar.
The same anti-Rohingya racism that drove decades of persecution by the Myanmar military is also at the heart of the AA’s treatment of the Rohingya. The perpetrators may have changed, but the dehumanisation and denial of our identity and rights continue.
The AA is completing what the Myanmar military started. Rohingya are being driven from their villages and prevented from returning, while their land is confiscated and new Rakhine settlements are built on it, sometimes by Rohingya coerced into forced labour. The possibility of return is being destroyed in real time.
Nowhere safe to go
More than 150,000 Rohingya have fled to Bangladesh since late 2023, just as international humanitarian funding for refugees is being slashed. Learning centres in Cox’s Bazar have closed and essential services are being cut. Children who fled genocide are growing up without education or hope for their future. Others were born in the camps and have never known a life outside them. The international community is allowing an entire generation of Rohingya children to be abandoned.
Rohingya are being forced to choose between continuing persecution in their homeland and hunger, insecurity and an increasingly desperate existence in camps.
For those forced to flee, there is often no safe route to protection. The very people forcing Rohingya to flee are often involved in and profiting from their trafficking as they try to escape. In July, two boats carrying more than 500 Rohingya, including children and young people, sank after leaving Rakhine. No one would put their children on such a dangerous journey unless staying was even more dangerous.
Meanwhile, there is growing anti-Rohingya sentiment in countries that host them as refugees. Governments talk about Rohingya returning home while more are being forced out and the land they would return to is being taken. We want to go home. But we want to go home with our rights: citizenship, equal rights and the right to return to our own land.
Nine years of impunity
For nine years, the Myanmar military leaders responsible for genocide against Rohingya have faced no real consequences. The architects of the genocide remain free, while the same military has gone on to commit atrocities against communities across Myanmar. Accountability is not only about the past. It is about stopping the violence happening now and preventing further atrocities.
The world cannot repeat the same failure with the Arakan Army. We have seen this pattern before and know where it leads. The longer the Myanmar military and AA are allowed to act with impunity, the closer we come to the complete erasure of the Rohingya from Rakhine.
Rohingya survivors and organisations have spent years documenting crimes, giving evidence and fighting for accountability. We had to pursue justice on the other side of the world because governments and international institutions failed to deliver it.
That fight is finally producing results. My organisation, the Burmese Rohingya Organisation UK (BROUK), brought a universal jurisdiction case in Argentina which has resulted in international arrest warrants for 22 Myanmar military officials and three civilians, including the military government’s leaders Senior General Min Aung Hlaing and General Soe Win, for genocide and crimes against humanity. We are also pursuing reparations for Rohingya survivors.
A judgement is also expected in the coming months in the genocide case brought by The Gambia against Myanmar at the ICJ.
Rohingya are getting closer to justice in international courts but at the same time are being pushed further from our homeland. Legal progress means little if Rohingya continue to be killed, forced out and stripped of the land to which they hope one day to return.
We have fought for years to get this far. Now governments must act. Every possible pressure point must be applied.
States must enforce the Argentinian arrest warrants whenever those wanted enter their jurisdictions, and Interpol must act on Argentina’s request for red notices. Governments must impose coordinated targeted sanctions on the AA and the Myanmar military, alongside restrictions on arms, aviation fuel and revenue streams that enable further atrocities. Maximum international pressure must be applied on the AA to end its persecution of Rohingya and ensure our protection and equal rights.
The United Nations Security Council must act. The United Kingdom, as penholder on Myanmar, must push for an urgent council meeting on the atrocities taking place in Rakhine and the continued failure to protect the Rohingya.
Governments must restore and increase humanitarian funding for Rohingya in Bangladesh and Rakhine, facilitate cross-border aid and pressure the Myanmar military and the AA to end restrictions on humanitarian access.
Governments must pursue every available route to justice and accountability for crimes by the Myanmar military and the AA. They must also be ready to respond to the forthcoming ICJ judgement.
Justice and accountability delivered years too late will mean nothing if there are no Rohingya left in Myanmar.
Justice is not only about what happens in courtrooms. For Rohingya, it means being able to return to our villages and our land. It means restoring the citizenship and rights that have been taken from us. Above all, it means being able to live freely and as equals in Myanmar, without ever again facing persecution and genocide.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

FSSAI crackdown: Food companies withdraw ‘100%’ and health claims after notices

FSSAI crackdown: Food companies withdraw ‘100%’ and health claims after notices
Edited by: Yashasvi Vasistha / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Aug 25, 2026, 15:15 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
FSSAI's crackdown on misleading claims (representative image)
The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) on Tuesday said several major food business operators (FBOs) had taken corrective action following notices issued over misleading labels, claims and other regulatory violations.In a post on X, the food regulator said the measures included withdrawal of misleading label claims and changes to product packaging to ensure consumer safety and regulatory compliance.Among the companies named by FSSAI were Amway India Enterprises, Juza Foods, Mondelez India Foods and Sapiens Labs, while another case involved a product marketed by Vichi Agro Products and processed and packed by J J Foods.
Amway removes 'Energy Drink' and '100%' claims
FSSAI said Amway India Enterprises Pvt Ltd had accepted its directions and removed the term "Energy Drink" from its XS product range.According to the regulator, the product was a caffeinated beverage licensed under food category 14.1, but carried the term "Energy Drink". Amway confirmed that it had removed the word "Energy" from its product artwork, website and promotional materials.
FSSAI said Amway had clarified that the descriptor was originally adopted in good faith following an FSSAI advisory issued in March 2024. The company said revised packaging would take effect from the next production cycle in August 2026.
Amway also requested permission to sell existing stock carrying the earlier artwork until the inventory was exhausted in the ordinary course of trade, while the revised packaging is introduced.In a separate case, FSSAI said Amway had also removed the term "100%" from its product name "100% Pure Coconut Oil", citing violations related to food labelling and advertising claims.The company submitted a compliance response confirming that it had removed the claim from its packaging and promotional material and discontinued old stock from sales channels.Revised packaging has been finalised and is in production, with the new packaging expected to be rolled out progressively from September-October 2026, along with updated website listings.
Juza Foods agrees to remove baby food claims
FSSAI also highlighted action taken by Juza Foods, Malappuram, Kerala, over multiple claims made for its baby food products.The regulator listed claims including "pure", "natural", "traditional", "no artificial colours, flavours or preservatives" and "Your baby's 1st taste of Real Nutrition".It also flagged health claims such as products being "ideal for sensitive babies", "easy to digest", offering "better absorption", and helping to "boost immunity" and "support stronger bones".FSSAI also cited claims including "100% Ragi", "100% vegan", "100% Kerala Banana powder" and "100% sweet potato powder", along with comparative claims that the products contained "10X the calcium of wheat and rice" and "3X the calcium of Milk".The regulator further said the company had been conducting its food business through an online website without having e-commerce listed as a Kind of Business in its licence.Juza Foods acknowledged the violations and agreed to remove the misleading claims, FSSAI said. Its selling website has been shut down until the rectification is completed, while the company has applied for modification of its licence and for an e-commerce category.
Products delisted, advertisements withdrawn
In another case, FSSAI said a product marketed by Vichi Agro Products Pvt Ltd and processed and packed by J J Foods was flagged over a misleading trade name.A response received from Flipkart stated that the food business operator had delisted the product from the platform.FSSAI also said Mondelez India Foods Pvt Ltd had withdrawn claims and advertisements from e-commerce platforms following action over misleading health claims and nutrient comparative claims.Sapiens Labs similarly submitted a response and withdrew all claims and advertisements after FSSAI flagged a misleading claim on its own initiative.
Action comes amid wider FSSAI enforcement drive
The latest update comes amid a broader FSSAI enforcement drive against misleading advertisements, false claims and labelling violations.
The regulator said recently that it had issued more than 150 notices to food companies, including Nestle India, PepsiCo, Abbott India, Red Bull India, Danone India, Monster Energy India, Hell Energy, Mondelez India, Coca-Cola India, Diageo, Pernod Ricard, Ferrero India and Kenvue.FSSAI has also issued notices to e-commerce companies and food service establishments over alleged regulatory violations..The regulator has separately been taking action against the use of "100%" claims on food labels and advertisements. In an earlier update, FSSAI said several companies, including Amway India, Emami, Bonn Biscuits, Apis India, Juza Foods and Masterchow Foods, had taken corrective measures after being asked to discontinue such claims.

Indonesia battles haze as wildfires rage across South Sumatra forests
Indonesia deploys prayers and emergency measures to combat South Sumatra’s raging wildfires and hazardous haze.
Authorities in South Sumatra, Indonesia, have turned to spiritual measures as wildfires rage across forests and peatlands, shrouding parts of the country in hazardous haze.
About 3,000 residents gathered on Tuesday in Palembang, the provincial capital, to perform salat istisqa, a special Islamic prayer for rain, in the courtyard of the governor’s office. Worshippers stood shoulder to shoulder as thick smoke reduced visibility and forced motorists to drive with headlights on during the day.
South Sumatra currently has the highest number of wildfire hotspots in Indonesia, with 1,429 detected by Environment Ministry satellites, followed by West Kalimantan with 1,226 and Central Kalimantan with 811. Nearly 940 square kilometres (360 square miles) of land burned in July alone, officials say, including more than 20sq km (8sq miles) in South Sumatra.
“We have done everything we can and worked closely with all relevant parties,” Governor Herman Deru said before the prayers. “As people of faith, we are also praying to God to send rain so that life can return to normal.”
Emergency crews are battling fires driven by an intensifying El Nino pattern and a prolonged dry season. The fires have generated smoke that has drifted into Malaysia and Brunei, according to the national disaster management agency. Authorities have deployed dozens of aircraft for cloud seeding and water bombing and arrested 72 people over allegations of using fire to clear land, while four companies are under investigation.
Seasonal fires and cross-border haze have long been a regional flashpoint in Southeast Asia.

Japan signs deal to begin mass-production of interceptor drone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
09:37:52 UTC
18:37:52 KST

- Japan's ATLA signed a mass-production contract with Terra Drone for its Terra B1 interceptor drone on August 25, 2026, after it was the only aircraft to pass demonstration testing.
- Trials of four interceptor drone models ran from July 15 to August 6, moving from solicitation to production contract in roughly three months.
Japan’s Acquisition, Technology & Logistics Agency has signed a mass-production contract with Terra Drone Corporation for an interceptor drone designated Terra B1, the agency announced August 25.
Terra Drone said Terra B1 was the only aircraft to pass the agency’s demonstration test among the systems evaluated, advancing it alone to the mass-production phase.
The contract followed trials that the Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force conducted on ATLA’s behalf between July 15 and August 6, testing four different interceptor drone models. ATLA has not disclosed the contract’s value or the number of Terra B1 units it plans to procure.
The award is the latest step in Japan’s Interceptor Drone Rapid Acquisition Program, which ATLA launched June 5 to field counter-drone systems capable of addressing long-range one-way attack UAVs such as Shahed-type drones. According to Terra Drone, the program was designed around the operational lessons of two different conflicts: in the Middle East, defenders have relied on comparatively expensive interceptor missiles against low-cost Shahed-type attack drones, straining missile stockpiles and cost-effectiveness, while in Ukraine, low-cost interceptor drones deployed against similar threats have achieved high interception rates.
ATLA received interceptor drone proposals from 38 companies after opening the solicitation, Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said in early July. The agency selected four companies, including Terra Drone, for the demonstration phase announced July 15.
ATLA’s published program materials called for demonstration tests in late July and early August, followed by a mass-procurement contract in late August and delivery around September 2026, compressing the process from demonstration to mass procurement into roughly three months. ATLA’s evaluation criteria covered effective range, flight duration, flight distance, maximum and cruising speed, guidance method, the number of aircraft that can be controlled simultaneously, launch and recovery methods, integration with other systems, safety measures, operational track record, and the time required from contract signing to delivery, according to Terra Drone.
Terra Drone said it will now move to commence mass production of Terra B1, establish domestic production and procurement systems, and strengthen supply chains for components, batteries, communications and control equipment. The company also plans to build out maintenance, replenishment and training support, along with system integration for operations at bases, vessels and other facilities.
Terra Drone said initial deployment is expected to begin with the Maritime Self-Defense Force, with the company also considering future expansion to the Air Self-Defense Force and Ground Self-Defense Force depending on operational needs.
Terra Drone entered Japan’s defense sector earlier in 2026, announcing plans in March to establish a U.S.-based subsidiary, Terra Defense, by the end of the current fiscal year. The company secured its first Japanese defense contract in May, a roughly $800,000 order from ATLA for 300 modular unmanned aerial vehicles, with delivery required by September 30.
That earlier contract built on testing Terra Drone conducted in Ukraine between April and May, when the company evaluated two interceptor models, the rocket-propelled, short-range Terra A1 and the fixed-wing, long-range Terra A2, in the country’s active combat environment. Terra Drone has invested in Ukrainian interceptor drone developer Winnylab and has said it plans to bring two Ukrainian interceptor drone companies into its corporate structure as consolidated subsidiaries.

Details
In Kyiv, a man will stand trial for fraud involving the apartment of prominent Ukrainian surgeon Oleksandr Shalimov. Prosecutors from the Obolonskyi District Prosecutor’s Office of Kyiv have submitted to the court an indictment against a man accused of fraudulently taking possession of the apartment where the renowned doctor lived and where his relatives later lived
According to the investigation, the apartment in Obolon was allocated to the academician at one time by the Mayor of Kyiv. After the surgeon’s death, his wife lived there, and after her death, a female relative of the woman lived there, but they never formalized ownership of the property.
Taking advantage of this situation, members of the fraudulent scheme forged documents according to which the accused had allegedly invested money in the apartment during its construction as early as 2005. On the basis of these documents and information that ownership of the apartment was not registered to anyone, in the summer of 2024 the accused registered ownership of the property through a private notary. The very next day, he sold the apartment, and some time later the new owner resold the property to a legal entity
According to an expert appraisal, the value of the apartment, which was supposed to become municipal property after the death of the doctor and his wife, amounts to more than UAH 4.8 million. The apartment has currently been seized.
The actions of the accused, who registered ownership of the apartment in his own name and immediately sold it, have been classified as document forgery, fraud on an especially large scale, and legalization of property obtained through criminal means

====================================================================================================

It Should Be Harder to Apply for a Job. No, Really
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Three years ago, Andrew Stockwell had his hiring routine down to a science.
As head of people for the software-buying company Vendr, Stockwell posted a listing, waited a few days, and then reviewed a few dozen applications—up to 100, if he was lucky. Recruiters identified other potential candidates, adding a few more applicants to the mix. Stockwell read résumés, conducted interviews, and passed along sterling candidates to hiring managers.
“It was really about finding that great talent, sussing out that talent, speaking with that talent, and identifying the best possible people,” Stockwell tells WIRED.
Sometime in the last year or so, Stockwell says, everything changed. The process started off the same way, but within a day or two, Stockwell wasn’t looking at 100 candidates. Instead, he was flooded with hundreds of applications. Sometimes, the incoming topped a thousand. A good chunk were “total bogus,” Stockwell says—fake candidates. Many more appeared to have been written using artificial intelligence, stretching the truth and making it difficult to distinguish one applicant from another. The sheer quantity was overwhelming. Stockwell says he found himself “paying my talent-acquisition professionals—who are high-paid, high-quality individuals—just to look through applications all day long.”
Stockwell is one of many recruitment professionals who believe looking for a job is fundamentally broken. In 2026, job hunting has become as easy as online shopping: AI can crank out tailored résumés and cover letters in seconds. Browser extensions can autofill applications, no human necessary. LinkedIn serves users dozens of jobs a day, many with the option to apply with “just a few clicks.”
“A year ago, every recruiter would tell me: We want to make it as easy as possible to apply for jobs,” offering candidates a “seamless experience,” Ophir Samson, the head of voice AI for Greenhouse, tells WIRED. Samson joined the recruiting platform earlier this year, when it acquired his startup, which used AI to conduct job interviews. “What they got was 2,000 applicants in 24 hours for a job. That is a shitty experience for everyone.”
Good applicants can’t stand out, while bad candidates slip through the cracks. Recruiters, Samson says, face the tortuous task of judging thousands of candidates, every single day. Instead of taking the time to search LinkedIn for dream employees, they spend hours in applicant tracking systems, tweaking filters to try to determine whose applications are worth a 30-second skim.
Now, recruiters are telling Samson, “actually, we kind of want friction,” he says. “The friction is good. We want to make it harder.”
The desire to remove pain points in the application process makes sense: If the highest number of qualified candidates apply for a role, it stands to reason that a company can maximize the chances of finding the best possible fit. So for years, recruiters have posted on job boards and LinkedIn; they signed up for LinkedIn’s “Easy Apply” feature; they promised candidates a “one-click” application process. Post-pandemic, recruiters’ efforts to simplify the process went into superdrive, as employers struggled to fill open roles.
“Everyone was job hopping, because you literally could have three offers in an afternoon,” Jane Curran, the chief transformation officer at real estate giant JLL, tells WIRED. Now, “it is the polar opposite.”
Openings peaked at a record 12.3 million in March 2022, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data, followed by two years of decline. Since mid-2024, openings have hovered at around 7 million, give or take 500,000.
But as the number of job openings contracted, the barriers to entry for applying declined even further. AI—which entered the mainstream in late 2022 with the public release of ChatGPT—allows applicants to rewrite résumés and track new postings almost instantaneously. Companies like JobAssist, Sonara, and Ladder’s Apply4Me promise applicants that their technology will handle all the busy work of applying for jobs, by submitting “10x as many applications with less effort than one manual application.” If you wanted to, you could apply for dozens of jobs a day.
This formula has led to ballooning candidate pools and laborious hiring processes. LinkedIn tells WIRED that submissions per applicant on the platform are up 46 percent compared to February 2020. Since the launch of ChatGPT, applications are up 22 percent. The explosive number of applications led to LinkedIn adding limits to cut back on automated and low-quality applications. This month, the platform is rolling out a feature that informs (seemingly) underqualified applicants that they probably aren’t a good fit for a role, and suggests other jobs.
“We're currently in a place where employers are complaining that they can't find good people, and people are complaining that they can't find jobs,” Tessa White, a former HR executive, tells WIRED.
White worked in HR for two decades before leaving corporate America in 2018. During the pandemic, she began posting on TikTok, where she has built a following of 800,000 by sharing advice and commentary on the job market. She believes the current situation is unworkable, and is a result of recruiters’ quest for speed and ease. “Every time we seem to strive for efficiency, we seem to give up quality,” she says.
Recruiters know they have a problem. Sure, an avalanche of résumés is welcome for some roles, such as skilled trades workers, where employer demand consistently exceeds employee supply. But for the typical unemployed white-collar knowledge worker, JLL’s Curran says, there “is not enough churn, not enough jobs coming into the market.” That means recruiters in these industries face a barrage of résumés every time they post a new role.
Many recruiters are turning to AI tools themselves, hoping to wrangle the sea of applications into something more manageable. Companies have used automated applicant tracking systems to screen résumés for at least a decade; now, many are using agents to conduct first-round interviews with candidates.
“We frequently hear from recruiters: They have 1,000 applications, but they know that only 30 of them are serious,” Greenhouse’s Samson says. An AI interview can sort the unserious from the serious, he says, offering recruiters context beyond a résumé.
While Samson says that these AI interviews are not friction for friction’s sake, they have the added bonus of weeding out bots and halfhearted candidates. Curran says she expects some companies to turn to knock-out questions that cut down the application pool via strict criteria. Others might add skills testing earlier in the process.
But White isn’t convinced these changes fix the underlying problem—that the frictionless résumé drop has rendered the first round of the application process essentially worthless. “Employers are having such a hard time hiring people with the current antiquated process,” White says. “Even AI and applicant tracking systems, which sound so high-tech, are an antiquated way to look at people and skill sets.” AI simply does not have the capabilities, she says, to accurately judge someone’s potential.
“I definitely think recruiting and the way we do it is due for a massive overhaul,” White says. “And I don't even know that I have the right answers.”
The deluge of applications has increased recruiters’ reliance on referrals and internal hires. While these human-to-human connections have always been important, today, some see them as the only ways to circumvent the glut of applications. Stockwell believes this benefits people whose backgrounds align with existing employees’, which isn’t conducive to a diverse workforce. “The whole thing is a big mess,” he says.
Stockwell is now dealing with the mess from the other side of the application portal. In February, he left Vendr, and is now on the job hunt. He treats the search like a job, “pounding the pavement” and attending in-person networking events. He knows that without a personal connection the chance of actually getting an interview is close to zilch. When he applies to jobs online, he estimates it only leads to a phone interview less than 2 percent of the time.
“I'm biased, of course, about my own capabilities,” Stockwell says. “But companies are missing out on fantastic talent.”

Children arrive late at Kutupalong hospital in Rohingya refugee camps
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
09:28:42 UTC
18:28:42 KST

In the sprawling, overcrowded refugee camps of Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, a crisis far from the headlines is taking a severe toll on the youngest generation of Rohingya refugees. Children arrive at medical facilities later, sicker, and with complex, overlapping physical and psychological health needs.
Nine years after fleeing extreme violence in Myanmar, children make up more than half of the 1.3 million refugees living in conditions of indefinite containment. In these camps, where international funding is volatile and shrinking, families struggle to secure basic food, healthcare, and education, placing children’s daily survival at constant risk.
Beyond physical hardship, children and their families carry the heavy psychological weight of a life in limbo, trapped by political dynamics that fail to deliver meaningful solutions or ensure long-term safety and dignity. At Kutupalong hospital – Médecins Sans Frontières’ (MSF’s) largest hospital and main referral hub for people in the camps – medical teams are witnessing the largely overlooked impact of this crisis.
What was once a hospital treating routine, seasonal illnesses has turned into an emergency facility managing children arriving in life-threatening conditions.
As general health posts scale back due to drastic international funding cuts, specialist referral facilities, like Kutupalong hospital, are left absorbing critical needs far beyond their original design. Today, severe physical disease, chronic malnutrition, and acute mental health distress are colliding, making children sicker and much harder to save.
Children admitted multiple times
Inside the paediatric ward of Kutupalong hospital, Yasmida sits at a hospital bed, holding her one-and-a-half-year-old daughter, Halima Sadia. Halima’s small body is fragile, weighed down by severe malnutrition, fever, and persistent infections that have left her too weak to sit or stand on her own.
Yasmida fled Myanmar in 2017, surviving a treacherous 15-day journey across mountains and rivers to reach Bangladesh. Today, living in the camp with a family of seven, her daily reality is consumed by her child’s relentless cycles of illness which sometimes result in multiple hospital admissions in a single month.
“My baby has been very sick for many days now,” says Yasmida. “Since her birth, we have frequented various hospitals and health facilities inside the camps around 10 to 12 times, and she was admitted to the MSF hospital four times.”
Since her birth, we have frequented various hospitals and health facilities inside the camps around 10 to 12 times, and she was admitted to the MSF hospital four times.
Yasmida’s experience navigating health emergencies in the middle of the night reflects the severe security and logistical barriers families face in the camps.
“Stepping out in the camp at night is terrifying because it is very dark, and I feel scared,” she says. “Once, at 2 am, my daughter became extremely ill. As my husband and I set off toward the hospital with our sick baby, after walking a short distance, we came across a group of men. They beat up my husband and looted everything he had.”
“Frightened that night, we returned home in that condition with our daughter and only took her to the doctor the next morning,” says Yasmida. “Because of these things, if the child falls ill at night, we cannot go out, and her health worsens further due to not receiving timely treatment.”
This delay in seeking care echoes across the camps. Dr Nadim Shahariyar, deputy hospital director at Kutupalong hospital, observes that Yasmida and Halima’s story is part of a broader trend.
“Over the last few years, we have seen significant changes in paediatric admissions to our hospital,” says Dr Shahariyar. “One thing we know for sure is that patients are arriving in more critical condition and with multiple illnesses at the same time. Previously, patients usually came in with a single illness and recovered well.”
“Recently, however, children are arriving at our hospital later in the progression of their conditions, often with multiple illnesses and complications,” he says. “This makes their clinical management much more challenging.”
Dr Shahariyar highlights how drastic cuts to humanitarian aid have forced families into desperate daily trade-offs that directly delay medical care.
“Within the camps, we have observed a significant reduction in funding,” says Dr Shahariyar. “As a result, families are struggling to meet their basic daily needs. When parents are forced to prioritise daily survival, like securing food or safety, they delay seeking hospital care for a sick child until it becomes a life-threatening emergency, leading to an influx of far more severe cases.”
“It is particularly difficult for a child to recover when their immune system is compromised, whether by malnutrition or other diseases,” he says. “Recovery can be extremely difficult, and despite treatment, the outcomes are not always successful. Malnutrition acts as an invisible amplifier, turning treatable childhood infections into life-threatening emergencies.”
A tipping point for adolescent wellbeing
Beyond physical illness, a mental health emergency is taking a devastating toll on young people. Chronic stress, severe poverty, a lack of education opportunities, and exposure to family disputes are driving a sharp rise in adolescent distress.
Beauty, 13-years-old, and Jasmine, 14-years-old, both reached a breaking point inside their overcrowded shelters, leading to suicide attempts before receiving psychiatric care and counselling at Shantikhana, an MSF mental health counselling room and safe space at Kutupalong hospital.
“With the rations we receive, we somehow get by eating just rice and lentils,” says Beauty, who attempted suicide following severe food scarcity and family conflict. “We cannot eat anything beyond that. Driven by so much suffering and deprivation, I made that decision.”
“After this incident, I came to Shantikhana,” they say. “A counsellor explained things to me and provided counselling. I now understand that dying is not a solution."
“Life in the camp is difficult for people our age," explains Jasmine, sharing how systemic hardship exacerbates tension at home. “The living conditions here are not good. Many people are crammed into small shelters, and families have barely any income, which causes a lot of distress. Overall, life here is barely manageable. If only the environment in the camp were better, perhaps we would feel better.”
The painful experiences of Beauty and Jasmine reflect stark admission trends recorded at Kutupalong hospital. Facility-based data between 2023 and 2025 reveals that children under 18 years of age accounted for 27% (160 out of 586) of all recorded suicide attempts, meaning one in every four attempts was a child.
Over the same period, 81% of these paediatric suicide attempts were directly attributed to family violence, exacerbated by severe crowding and relentless daily stress. This crisis is growing rapidly, with the proportion of children under 15 years old seeking MSF mental health support jumping from 9.7% (131 cases) in 2021 to 29.4% (232 cases) in 2025.
Shariful Islam, MSF’s mental health activity manager, emphasises that these acts are clear cries for help in an unviable environment.
“We are observing that both the volume of mental health patients and the severity of their conditions have increased significantly compared to five years ago,” says Islam. “Our team also observes that suicide attempts are driven by a complex interplay of factors rather than a single isolated cause. The root drivers stem from inadequate humanitarian assistance, lack of freedom of movement, and a pervasive loss of hope after nearly nine years of displacement.”
Beyond emergency response: An urgent call for systemic solutions
The findings from Kutupalong hospital demonstrate that paediatric illness and rising child mental health distress are not isolated medical issues, but indicators of a broader protection and public health emergency. Reduced funding across the camps has crippled general healthcare, compromised nutrition programmes, and eroded basic living conditions — forcing specialist facilities like Kutupalong hospital to absorb critical needs far beyond their original design.
A malnourished child with pneumonia, a young person in acute psychological distress, or a patient whose chronic condition is no longer controlled may appear as isolated medical emergencies. But together, they reveal the devastating health consequences of a system steadily contracting around people who are confined.
Emergency medical care cannot substitute for political responsibility. Humanitarian and health organisations, alongside international stakeholders, must sustain an adequate humanitarian response, ensuring that basic food, healthcare, and protection are reinforced, while a lasting political solution is sought.
