Pentagon awards Boeing $131.23 billion F-15 Eagle Crest deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
08:20:57 UTC
17:20:57 KST

- Boeing received a $131.23 billion ceiling IDIQ contract to support the F-15 Eagle Crest program, covering production, upgrades and sustainment.
- The sole-source award includes Foreign Military Sales to Japan, Israel, Saudi Arabia, South Korea, Singapore, Indonesia and Poland.
Boeing has been awarded a $131.23 billion ceiling contract to support the F-15 Eagle Crest program, the U.S. Department of War announced August 24. The indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity contract covers aircraft production, systems integration, modernization, upgrades, retrofits and sustainment for the F-15 fleet.
The contract also establishes organic depot maintenance capabilities intended to keep F-15 aircraft mission-ready for the U.S. Air Force, the Air National Guard and other Department of War customers. Work will be performed in St. Louis, Missouri, where Boeing has built F-15 variants for decades.
The ceiling figure represents the maximum value of work the government could order under the contract, not a guaranteed payment. At the time of award, the Department of War obligated $343,740 in fiscal 2026 research, development, test and evaluation funds, a small fraction of the total ceiling.
The contract’s ordering period runs through August 24, 2031, with an option to extend it through August 24, 2036. Work under the contract is expected to be completed by August 2037. The Air Force Life Cycle Management Center at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio, is the contracting activity, and the award was designated FA8634-26-D-B001.
The contract was awarded as a sole-source acquisition, meaning the Department of War negotiated directly with Boeing rather than opening the work to competitive bidding. It also covers Foreign Military Sales to Japan, Israel, Saudi Arabia, South Korea, Singapore, Indonesia and Poland. Japan, Israel, Saudi Arabia, South Korea and Singapore currently operate F-15 variants. The contract documentation does not specify the nature of Poland’s or Indonesia’s inclusion in the FMS scope; neither country currently operates the F-15.
The Eagle Crest program manages the broader F-15 fleet across its production and sustainment life cycle. Boeing has continued producing new F-15 variants even as the aircraft has been in U.S. service since the 1970s, including recent work on the F-15EX Eagle II for the Air Force and F-15IA aircraft for Israel.
Earlier this month, Boeing was awarded a separate $8.58 billion contract covering the F-15 Israel program, which includes production of 25 new F-15IA aircraft with an option for 25 more. That contract, also a sole-source award managed through the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center, is expected to run through the end of 2035.

Taiwan legislature strengthens penalties for patient privacy violations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
08:16:02 UTC
17:16:02 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The legislature passed amendments to the Medical Care Act Tuesday that strengthen penalties for patient privacy violations and violence against medical workers, CNA reported.
Under the revised law, medical institutions and their staff may not, without justification, secretly observe patients’ intimate body areas or listen to private medical information. They are also barred from secretly making audio or video recordings, taking photographs, or creating electronic records of such information or images, Rti reported.
People who illegally observe, listen to, or record patients’ private medical information or intimate body areas can face up to three years in prison and a fine of up to NT$300,000 (US$9,403). Items connected to the offense can also be confiscated, regardless of ownership.
People who provide facilities or equipment for profit to help others commit such privacy violations face heavier penalties. Those convicted can face six months to five years in prison and a fine of up to NT$500,000.
The same penalties can apply to people who produce illegally obtained recordings or information with the intent to distribute, broadcast, or sell them. Attempts to commit these offenses are also punishable.
The amendments also raise fines for using violence, coercion, intimidation, or other means to obstruct medical work. The previous fine of NT$30,000 to NT$50,000 rises to NT$50,000 to NT$250,000, per UDN.
Protection under the law is also expanded beyond medical and emergency medical personnel to include other related workers. Medical institutions that fail to take safety measures required by the central government can be fined NT$30,000 to NT$150,000.
The revised law also makes it an offense to publicly insult medical or emergency workers when the conduct disrupts medical, health care, or emergency services. Violators can face up to two years in prison and a fine of up to NT$200,000, per SETN News.

====================================================================================================

Pakistan Passes Legislation to Formalize New Military Command Structure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
08:16:00 UTC
17:16:00 KST

Pakistan’s National Assembly last week passed the Defense Forces of Pakistan Bill. The legislation is part of the ongoing broader set of reforms in the country’s senior military command structure.
The development is significant not merely as a procedural step but as a tangible move to operationalize structural changes that have been unfolding within the armed forces over the past year.
Defense Minister Khawaja Asif presented two related bills in the parliament, including the Defense Forces of Pakistan Act, 2026, and amendments to the National Command Authority Act, 2010.
Both bills had earlier been approved by the federal cabinet in a meeting chaired by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif. A statement issued by the Prime Minister’s Office after that meeting described the bills as a continuation of the adjustments introduced under the 27th Constitutional Amendment. The Defense Forces Act, the statement noted, aims “to determine the relevant administrative matters regarding the office of the Chief of Defense Forces and the Chief of Defense Forces Headquarters.” Similarly, the amendments to the National Command Authority Act were described as a “necessary process” following the constitutional changes enacted last year.
The 27th Constitutional Amendment, passed by parliament in 2025, essentially altered Pakistan’s higher defense structure. It abolished the long-standing office of the chairman joint chiefs of staff committee and created the new position of chief of defense forces (CDF). Both posts are occupied by the chief of army staff. Moreover, Field Marshal Asim Munir became the country’s first chief of defense forces under the revised framework. Furthermore, the amendment also established the commander of the National Strategic Command (CNSC), which is a four-star office responsible for the operational integration of Pakistan’s strategic forces. These changes marked one of the most significant overhauls of the country’s top military hierarchy in decades.
The legislation approved last week carries those constitutional provisions into legal form and introduces further refinements. Arguably, the Defense Forces of Pakistan Act is designed to give practical effect to the CDF’s role as the overall commander of the armed forces. The draft of the bill explicitly states that the changes are intended to ensure “multidomain integration, restructuring and optimum jointness of the Armed Forces.” In essence, the provision seeks to reduce compartmentalization between the individual services and create a more unified operational posture across land, air, maritime and other domains.
According to the draft, the proposed legislation also enables the establishment of the Defense Forces Headquarters, which will serve as the central headquarters of the Armed Forces. This has ostensibly created a single institutional center under the CDF for coordination, planning and oversight that previously did not exist in the same consolidated form.
Moreover, the legislation has significantly expanded the formal authority of the CDF in relation to both the armed forces and the civilian government. Under the revised arrangement, the Defense Forces Headquarters will function under the CDF’s command. The CDF is now formally designated as the principal military advisor to the prime minister of Pakistan on issues of national security, defense, and all matters concerning the armed forces. Besides, the CDF has been granted operational command and control of the Armed Forces and has been made responsible to the federal government for matters of command and control.
The act further elaborates the CDF’s powers and functions, stating that the office-holder “shall exercise such powers and perform such functions as are necessary for multidomain integration, operational cohesion, coordination and oversight of all matters which have joint, tri-services and strategic implications for the Armed Forces and national security of Pakistan.”
In addition, the CDF now possesses authority to “retire, release, accept, or reject resignation of, or discharge from service, or retain in service, or relax age, or service limit of retirement” of personnel subject to the laws of the Armed Forces.
This authority, however, does not extend to those appointed under Article 243 of the constitution.
Article 243 of the Pakistani Constitution governs the highest-level military appointments, including the chief of naval staff, the chief of air staff, the chief of defense forces himself, and the commander of the National Strategic Command. These positions are filled by the president of Pakistan on the advice of the prime minister, so their tenure, retention, and removal largely stay under constitutional executive authority and beyond the CDF’s internal administrative purview.
The distinction seemingly preserves a formal layer of civilian oversight at the very apex of the military hierarchy even as operational and administrative authority is concentrated in the new CDF structure under these reforms.
Taken together, the bills represent another step in the institutional redesign of Pakistan’s armed forces.
The changes reflect an effort to modernize command arrangements and improve joint operational capacity in the aftermath of the 2025 conflict with India. Whether these changes produce the desired improvements in cohesion and effectiveness will eventually depend on how new reforms are implemented in the years ahead.

The newborn began searching for her mother’s milk shortly after birth and successfully drank colostrum at about 5:30 a.m. on Aug. 18. Zookeepers later weighed and measured the calf while Putri was eating breakfast.
The calf measured 72.5 cm in body length and 23.8 cm in head length. She appeared somewhat nervous while being handled, but veterinarians found her appearance normal and confirmed that her umbilical cord had retracted properly.
The zoo said Putri and male tapir Moshu were paired again in 2025. Keepers and veterinarians confirmed Putri’s pregnancy during a routine ultrasound training session in November.
Veterinarians began conducting weekly prenatal examinations in early July to monitor the fetus’s heartbeat, size, and position. An ultrasound examination on Aug. 11 showed that the amount of amniotic fluid had decreased significantly, indicating that birth was approaching. Putri gave birth six days later, per the press release.
The zoo said the calf remained calm while a veterinarian treated Putri’s umbilical cord. After the veterinarian examined the newborn and found no abnormalities, keepers were reassured that both mother and calf were healthy.
Because the mother and calf are particularly sensitive to their surroundings following the birth, the zoo has prepared a quiet nursery where Putri can care for her offspring. Keepers will continue monitoring their condition.
The zoo said visitors can expect further updates as the calf grows, with another update planned in two to three weeks. Young tapirs of all species have brown hair with white stripes and spots, a pattern that enables them to hide effectively in the dappled light of the forest. This baby coat fades into adult coloration between four and seven months after birth.
Putri was born June 3, 2013, and arrived at Taipei Zoo from Singapore Zoo in 2021. Moshu was born May 30, 2014. The pair previously had a male calf, Treeda, born July 26, 2023.

Taiwan manufacturing index hits 4-year high in July
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
08:15:31 UTC
17:15:31 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s manufacturing business climate index reached a more than four-year high in July, but sustaining the AI-driven export boom will depend on demand for new products, according to a report published Tuesday by the Taiwan Institute of Economic Research.
TIER’s manufacturing business climate index rose 2.48 points from June to 101.09, per RTI. The construction-sector index also climbed for a fourth consecutive month to 110.55, while the services-sector index fell 1.29 points to 98.2, ending a four-month rise.
TIER Macroeconomic Forecasting Center Director Sun Ming-de (孫明德) said the first half of the year was marked by volatility in commodity prices amid conflicts in the Middle East, while strong AI demand supported economic growth in Taiwan, South Korea, and the US, per CNA. As conditions have stabilized, he said businesses have become less concerned about energy prices and other external risks.
Sun said the conflict’s greatest impact on international energy prices occurred in March, while government efforts to diversify energy sources and stabilize prices have helped limit the impact on Taiwan. Although uncertainty remains, he expects international and domestic oil prices to remain stable.
Taiwan’s economic growth is expected to exceed 10% this year, with the Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting, and Statistics raising its forecast to 11.05% in August, the highest in 39 years. Sun said AI demand remains strong and should make the forecast achievable, but the next phase of export expansion will depend on the success of new AI products.
Sun said Taiwan’s ICT exports to the US have gone through two major AI-driven growth waves, first after Nvidia’s H100 launch in 2023 and again in 2025 following the introduction of the Blackwell architecture. With the industry now entering another product transition, export values remain high but growth has become more stable.
Sun said new AI products have emerged roughly every one to 1.5 years, with strong demand potentially triggering another surge in Taiwan’s exports. However, he said doubts about returns on AI investments and concerns over whether new products can sustain market demand could weigh on the next growth cycle. Tighter liquidity could also raise companies’ financing costs even if the Central Bank leaves interest rates unchanged.

Low-Cost Patriot PAC-3 ACE Missile Gets Simplified Motor and Seeker
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
08:11:48 UTC
17:11:48 KST

The low-cost PAC-3 ACE missile, introduced by Lockheed Martin, features simplified components, particularly the motor and seeker.
Janes reported on this.
The main differences are a simplified seeker, the elimination of kinetic interception, and a simpler rocket motor.
In the standard PAC-3 MSE, these components are more complex and therefore more expensive, as the missile was designed to intercept modern ballistic missiles.
The missile was unveiled at the 2026 Farnborough International Airshow in the United Kingdom.
According to Lockheed Martin Vice President Jason Reynolds, the company aims to reduce the cost of the PAC-3 ACE to less than half that of the PAC-3 MSE.
To do so, engineers simplified several missile components. In particular, it will feature a simplified seeker system compared with the PAC-3 MSE. Lockheed Martin did not specify what type of seeker it will use.
The new missile will also omit the Attitude Control Motors (ACMs) used on the PAC-3 MSE. The company also simplified the missile’s midsection.
Another change will be the propulsion system. The PAC-3 ACE will use a single-mode solid-fuel rocket motor instead of the dual-pulse motor used by the PAC-3 MSE. Lockheed Martin is also considering the use of cheaper rocket motor casings.
A key difference will be the warhead. Instead of the hit-to-kill approach, which destroys the target through direct kinetic impact, the PAC-3 ACE will feature a blast-fragmentation warhead.
According to Reynolds, such a warhead reduces the need for terminal trajectory-correction systems, particularly ACMs or thrust-vector control systems.
At the same time, the PAC-3 ACE will retain the PAC-3 software used in the PAC-3 MSE. Lockheed Martin says the new missile is designed to counter aerodynamic targets, cruise missiles, and short-range ballistic missiles.
Militarnyi previously reported that the first flight test of the new low-cost PAC-3 ACE interceptor was expected in 18 months, with serial production set to begin “within a few years.”

Collins Aerospace completes altitude testing for F-35 cooling system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
08:10:57 UTC
17:10:57 KST

- Collins Aerospace completed altitude testing of its EPACS power and thermal management system for the F-35.
- The system is designed to more than double the F-35's current cooling capacity to support planned technology and mission-system upgrades.
Collins Aerospace has completed altitude testing of its next-generation power and thermal management system for the F-35, the company announced August 24. The Enhanced Power and Cooling System, known as EPACS, is designed to replace the fighter jet’s current cooling system.
The test campaign ran for several days at power levels meant to replicate operational mission requirements. Engineers pushed the system to its operating limits at multiple altitudes to collect performance data, and the tests also demonstrated EPACS’s ability to deliver emergency power during operation, according to Collins Aerospace, an RTX business based in Windsor Locks, Connecticut.
“Successful altitude testing validates system performance in real-world flight conditions,” said Ira Grimmett, vice president of Environmental & Airframe Control Systems for Power & Controls at Collins Aerospace. “Completing this phase of testing advances EPACS maturity and reinforces confidence in the system’s capability and performance.”
EPACS is intended to more than double the F-35’s current cooling capacity. Collins Aerospace has said the added thermal margin is needed to support the aircraft’s newer weapons and mission systems, which generate more heat than the jet’s existing power and thermal management system was designed to handle.
The Government Accountability Office has reported that the F-35’s current cooling system is already being pushed beyond its intended capacity, forcing the engine to operate outside its designed limits and accelerating wear. Collins has cited that strain as the rationale for developing a replacement system.
Collins Aerospace first demonstrated 80 kilowatts of cooling capacity from an EPACS prototype in 2024. In February 2025, the company said a fully functional demonstrator had met requirements for aircraft integration, a step toward working with Lockheed Martin, the F-35’s prime contractor, on installing the system on the jet.
The altitude testing announced this week builds on that integration milestone. Collins Aerospace said the technology is also intended for future defense and commercial aircraft with higher power and cooling demands than current platforms.
The F-35 is flown by all branches of the U.S. military and by international partners. Its manufacturer, Lockheed Martin, has continued adding capability to the aircraft under its Block 4 modernization program, which includes upgraded sensors, weapons and mission systems that Collins says will require additional cooling capacity to operate reliably.
RTX, Collins Aerospace’s parent company, reported more than $88 billion in sales for 2025 and employs more than 180,000 people globally, including roughly 80,000 at Collins Aerospace.

Global ocean temperatures hit record high as El Nino intensifies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
08:10:10 UTC
17:10:10 KST

Global ocean temperatures hit record high as El Nino intensifies
Copernicus warns of ‘unprecedented strain’ on world’s oceans as El Nino and climate change drive up sea surface temperatures.
The average global sea surface temperature has reached its highest level on record, a European Union agency said, warning that a rapidly intensifying El Nino and human-caused climate change were putting “unprecedented strain” on the world’s oceans.
In a statement on Monday, the EU’s Copernicus Climate Change Service said sea surface temperatures hit 21.1 degrees Celsius (69.98 degrees Fahrenheit) on Friday and Saturday, surpassing the previous record of 21.09C (69.96F) set in March 2024.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Iraq’s solar villages show how to build an energy transition that lasts
- list 2 of 3Where water conflicts pose the biggest threat in 2026
- list 3 of 3Can Kenya’s AI ambitions coexist with Naivasha’s water needs?
“This record is another clear signal of an ocean under growing stress,” said Samantha Burgess, the strategic lead for climate at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF). “El Nino is adding heat to the system, but it is doing so on top of decades of human-driven warming.”
Copernicus called the timing of the new record “particularly notable”. It said global ocean temperatures usually peak in March and April, when the summer in the Southern Hemisphere – which is mostly ocean – draws to a close.
But this year, the record was set in August.
Burgess told The Associated Press news agency that the oceans will keep getting hotter until the current El Nino – a natural temporary warming of parts of the Pacific that then warps weather and raises temperatures globally – reaches its peak, which is expected sometime between November and January.
The World Meteorological Organization, too, said it expects El Nino to strengthen in the coming months, and Copernicus said its seasonal forecasting system indicates that the event “could reach levels not seen for several decades”.
The added heat from El Nino comes as long-term fossil-fuel-driven warming has already raised ocean temperatures by 0.8C (1.44F), Burgess noted.
Copernicus also warned that rising ocean temperatures have “far-reaching consequences” for marine ecosystems and coastal communities.
Warmer oceans contribute to sea-level rise through thermal expansion, it said, and increase the likelihood and intensity of marine heatwaves, which can damage coral reefs and seagrass beds. This can in turn disrupt food chains and threaten industries such as fishing and aquaculture.
Warmer oceans are less able to absorb carbon dioxide, too, it said, weakening one of the planet’s key defences against climate change.
Higher ocean temperatures can also supply more heat and moisture to the atmosphere, enhancing the “potential for extreme weather events”.
Jane Lubchenco, an oceanographer and former head of the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, called the finding “very troubling”.
“An ocean this warm destabilises weather patterns and threatens food security, economic prosperity and marine life,” Lubchenco told the AP. “A warmer ocean is not our friend.”

The Philippines plans to expand its unmanned capabilities, including through the development and acquisition of drones as part of efforts to modernize its military, its defense chief said on Tuesday.
US defense ally the Philippines also plans to acquire additional guided-missile corvettes and other major defense assets to beef up its external defense capabilities, Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro told a budget hearing in the lower house of Congress.
The Philippines has shifted its security focus from internal threats to external security as tensions rise with Beijing in the South China Sea, where confrontations between them over disputed features inside Manila's exclusive economic zone have grown in frequency in recent years.
The armed forces currently operate a fleet of unmanned aerial vehicles that provide intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, Teodoro said.

Drone expansion is part of a proposed 50 billion pesos ($810.4 million) allocation for the Philippines' modernization program next year, 25% higher than that of the current budget.
Philippines seeking integration for drones
The priority was also developing the systems, connectivity, and operational know-how needed to use drones effectively, Teodoro added.
"More than the personnel, it is the integration into the operation, what do you do with them and how do you use them," he said. Developing secure communications and network capabilities was crucial, he added.
Teodoro declined to identify specific systems under consideration, saying the details were classified and highly sensitive.
"They are very, very sensitive to compromise, particularly with AI," he said, adding that the Philippines was in close contact with several countries with expertise in drone technology.
Yuliia Fediv, Ukraine’s ambassador to the Philippines, told Reuters in June that Kyiv has been in discussions with Manila over drone technology cooperation.
In June, the United States said it has given the Philippine military four solar-powered sea drones to boost its maritime surveillance.

Nearly a third of businesses’ complaints about law enforcement agencies concern the Economic Security Bureau (ESB) - the Business Ombudsman Council
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
11:05:04 EEST
17:05:04 KST

Nearly a third of businesses’ complaints about law enforcement agencies concern the Economic Security Bureau (ESB) - the Business Ombudsman Council
Kyiv • UNN
In 2025, the ESB received 29% of businesses’ complaints about law enforcement agencies, and the same share in 2026. Entrepreneurs complain about property seizures and investigative actions.
Almost one-third of business complaints about the actions of law enforcement agencies submitted to the Business Ombudsman Council concern the Economic Security Bureau. This trend has persisted for the second year in a row. The problems entrepreneurs raise include asset seizures and questions regarding the admissibility of investigative actions. The Business Ombudsman Council reported this in response to a request from UNN.
One in three complaints is against the ESB
The Business Ombudsman Council reported that complaints against law enforcement agencies consistently rank second among all business appeals.
In 2025, the Council received 129 such complaints in total, including 37 against the ESB, accounting for 29% of all complaints against law enforcement agencies. In 2026, the ratio practically remained unchanged: of 83 complaints concerning law enforcement, 24 related to the ESB—again 29%
For comparison, during the same period this year, 31 complaints were filed against the National Police, and 19 against the Office of the Prosecutor General.
Overall, according to the Business Ombudsman Council, 71% of complaints concerning law enforcement in 2025 were successfully closed. This year, the share of successfully closed complaints has already reached 52%.
What businesses complain about
A substantial portion of entrepreneurs' appeals is related to asset seizures and investigative actions carried out as part of criminal proceedings.
In particular, a significant share consists of complaints concerning the lifting of asset seizures or assessments of the admissibility of investigative actions authorized by a court. Under its Rules of Procedure, such matters do not fall within the Council's competence
In other words, some of the problems businesses bring to the ombudsman cannot be resolved through this mechanism at all, since they concern procedural decisions and actions within criminal proceedings, which may be assessed exclusively by a court.
The issue of using criminal procedure as an instrument of pressure on business has been repeatedly raised by entrepreneurs and experts. For companies, the seizure of accounts and assets, searches, and the confiscation of documents or equipment mean complications or even a shutdown of operations before a court has established that any crime was committed.
The scandal surrounding aircraft leasing taxation
Despite the fact that Ukrainian tax legislation, which has remained unchanged regarding leasing for decades, and international treaties clearly describe how taxes on helicopter and aircraft leasing should be paid, the Economic Security Bureau decided to change this approach at its own discretion. The ESB is investigating cases involving at least five air carriers, including MAU, "Constanta Airline," "Urga," N3Operations, and "Skyline," over the alleged failure to pay an additional 15% tax on income earned by nonresidents under aircraft leasing agreements into the Ukrainian budget. Investigators equate leasing payments with royalties and treat aircraft and helicopters not as means of transport, but as "equipment."
Law enforcement officers obtained the analytical conclusions after, in 2024, the previous team of the State Tax Service published an article proposing that leasing transactions involving transport with nonresidents of Ukraine be taxed as royalties. The documents, which according to aviation market representatives are similar to one another, as if written "using the same template," formed the basis for criminal cases against air carriers.
Lawyers interviewed by UNN point out that investigators ignore the effective international conventions on the avoidance of double taxation ratified by the Verkhovna Rada. According to them, the automatic assessment of an additional 15% tax in Ukraine without taking into account the provisions of a specific convention is at the very least debatable.
It is worth noting that, according to the State Tax Service, the airlines underwent tax inspections, and violations in the taxation of leasing were established based on only one of them. The remaining tax inspections did not reveal such violations.
Following one inspection of companies in the aviation sector, leasing payments were reclassified as royalties. Only one inspection—the deputy director of the Transfer Pricing Department of the State Tax Service of Ukraine, Viktoriia Kasian, noted.
However, the absence of violations did not prevent the Economic Security Bureau (ESB) from opening criminal cases against the airlines, believing that they had failed to pay 15% in royalties over the past seven years. At the same time, the list of airlines that law enforcement authorities have claims against over leasing may expand at any moment, since around 40 air carriers use leasing. Thus, the entire civil aviation industry could come under attack.
Representatives of the aviation industry have already publicly stated that they are facing pressure from the Economic Security Bureau. According to them, civil aviation has come under threat of destruction due to actions by state regulatory bodies, which could finally bring down companies that survived the closure of the airspace and relocation abroad because of the full-scale war. The Ukrainian Air Transport Association appealed to the Verkhovna Rada Committee on Transport and Infrastructure, as well as to the Public Council under the Ministry of Finance, calling for a unified approach to applying tax legislation in the field of aviation leasing.
The trend whereby, for the second consecutive year, almost one-third of business complaints about law enforcement agencies concern the Economic Security Bureau once again raises the question of the need for a complete overhaul of the Bureau. The results of the re-certification of its leadership demonstrated the scale of the personnel problem; however, simply replacing managers may not be enough. Genuine reform requires not only the re-certification of employees at all levels, but also an audit of ESB criminal proceedings, especially those in which entrepreneurs report unjustified prosecution, contentious interpretations of the law, and the use of criminal proceedings as an instrument of pressure on business.

Iconic Palestinian artist Sliman Mansour dies at 79
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
08:04:05 UTC
17:04:05 KST

Lina Altawell
25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
Iconic Palestinian artist Sliman Mansour, whose work became a symbol of Palestinian identity, memory, and resistance, has died at the age of 79, his family said late Monday.
“The final chapter has been written,” the family said in a statement. “With hearts heavy beyond words, we share that our beloved father has passed away.
“To the world, he leaves behind a life filled with beauty, memory, and a legacy that will continue to live through all those he touched,” it added.
The family said funeral and memorial details will be announced later.
Born in 1947 in the town of Birzeit near Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, Mansour was one of the most prominent figures in modern Palestinian art, working as a painter, sculptor, writer, and cartoonist.
For more than five decades, his works documented Palestinian struggle, displacement, attachment to land, and cultural memory, using symbols drawn from Palestinian history, heritage, and daily life.
In a 2024 interview with Anadolu, Mansour said he saw art as a way to “rehumanize” Palestinians amid attempts by “Israelis and the West” to dehumanize them.
“As artists and people who deal with culture, it’s our role to rehumanize the Palestinian people,” he said.
Mansour often placed land at the center of his work, saying: “Everybody is fighting about the land, and the land is my main inspiration.”
Among his best-known works is The Camel of Hardships, which depicts an elderly Palestinian man carrying Jerusalem on his back, an image that became one of the most recognizable symbols of Palestinian endurance.
In the same interview, Mansour said his message to Palestinians living outside their homeland was: “Don’t forget Palestine and Palestine is beautiful.”
“In my art, there is no message of hate. It’s beauty and love,” he said.

UFORCE Develops MV11 Naval Drone – Largest Member of the MAGURA Family
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
08:04:04 UTC
17:04:04 KST

Ukrainian company UFORCE has presented its newest naval drone, the MV11, as part of the MAGURA family during a parade marking Ukraine’s Independence Day.
The company shared details with Militarnyi.
The “drone parade,” held on the Dnipro River, showcased the full current MAGURA lineup, including the newly introduced MV11.
The MV11 was designed and developed by UFORCE’s design and R&D bureau in Portugal, with international investment and a focus on meeting the operational needs of the Ukrainian Defense Forces.
A key feature of the drone is its ability to launch a larger number of unmanned systems directly from its deck. This turns the platform into a mobile naval base for other unmanned systems.
The MV11 is the largest unmanned surface vessel (USV) in its class. Unlike previous models in the family, it is designed as a transport platform capable of carrying other unmanned systems and mission equipment.
With its larger size, a payload capacity of up to 2,200 kg, and an endurance of up to seven days, the MV11 can serve as a carrier platform, transporting, launching, and supporting other unmanned systems far from shore.
The platform is designed for reconnaissance, surveillance, support of amphibious operations, as well as the delivery of fuel and equipment to other unmanned surface vessels (USVs).
The drone is capable of performing all of these missions around the clock and in all weather conditions.
“We are proud to present the MV11 on Ukraine’s Independence Day. This is not simply the largest maritime drone; it is a multidomain platform – a single carrier capable of transporting and launching other unmanned systems far from shore for operations across all domains. The investments attracted by UFORCE are being directed toward the needs of Ukraine’s Defense Forces. We are confident that the MV11 will become the backbone of many successful missions and contribute to further pushing back the enemy,” Oleh Rohynskyi, CEO of UFORCE, shared.
UFORCE’s operations in Portugal were first reported in September 2025.
In July, it was also announced that UFORCE and U.S.-based ReconCraft had signed a memorandum on the licensed production of Magura-family unmanned surface vessels in the United States.

Belarusian delegation attends Baikal International Partners Forum in Irkutsk

2026-08-25

Photo courtesy of the Brest Oblast Executive Committee
                    
                    BREST, 25 August (BelTA) – A Belarusian delegation is taking part in the Baikal International Partners Forum in Irkutsk, Russia, BelTA has learned.
A delegation of Belarusian official and business circles, led by Governor of Brest Oblast Piotr Parkhomchik, is currently visiting Russia. The governor is responsible for coordinating cooperation with Irkutsk Oblast on the Belarusian side. At the Baikal International Forum, the Brest Oblast representatives took part in a plenary session, a presentation of investment projects, and a business matchmaking session.
“The platform allows businesses to find a partner and reach an agreement. Eventually, these partnerships can evolve into a major international company that will represent the interests of different states,” Piotr Parkhomchik said. He highlighted Belarus’ strategic location to attendees from Russia, China, and Mongolia, emphasizing that Brest Oblast acts as a crucial gateway linking East and West. “Belarus is an export-oriented country. We have established modern enterprises. We have long ensured our own food security. A significant share of what is produced in our country is exported,” the governor noted.
According to him, Belarus aims to maintain close ties with its partners in Russia and Asian countries. “For instance, we have long- standing, excellent relations with Irkutsk Oblast, which are systemic in nature. There is a working group that drives this development. We cooperate in many areas. Closer alignment is underway, opening up serious prospects,” Piotr Parkhomchik emphasized. He added that Belarus has long enjoyed good relations with Mongolia and China. “The plans and tasks facing our states are highly strategic. We want to be as close as possible in the economy, healthcare, and education so that this creates lasting ties. Such meetings are the key to developing relations between our countries,” the governor said.
The potential of Brest Oblast was presented at the forum. The region is home to around 2,000 industrial enterprises. Over the last decade, the output has nearly doubled, while the average annual inflow of investments has quadrupled. Currently, capital from 33 countries drives the economy of Brest Oblast.
“Together with partners from China, Cyprus, Germany, Canada, Italy, and Russia, the region has recently implemented projects in animal byproduct recycling, LED manufacturing, and hydraulic axial piston pump production. Production facilities for upholstered and solid wood furniture, as well as packaging for the meat and dairy industry, have been set up. The manufacturing complex for mushroom cultivation has been expanded, and a facility for processing and freezing berries and vegetables has been launched. A complex for the production of extruded aluminum profiles has been built and commissioned. Currently, these are stably operating enterprises that continue to reinvest profits into their development,” Deputy Governor of Brest Oblast Mikhail Batsenko said. The region’s enterprises export their products to 88 countries worldwide, with Russia, China, and Kazakhstan leading the list of top trading partners. Positive dynamics are observed in relations with African countries, while a presence in European markets is maintained.
A cooperation agreement was also signed during the forum between the Administration of the Free Economic Zone (FEZ) Brest and the Irkutsk Oblast Development Corporation on 25 August. The parties intend to provide assistance for the development of enterprises in the Belarusian and Russian regions. On the sidelines of the forum, the Belarusian representatives spoke with potential partners from Mongolia and China.

“Together with partners from China, Cyprus, Germany, Canada, Italy, and Russia, the region has recently implemented projects in animal byproduct recycling, LED manufacturing, and hydraulic axial piston pump production. Production facilities for upholstered and solid wood furniture, as well as packaging for the meat and dairy industry, have been set up. The manufacturing complex for mushroom cultivation has been expanded, and a facility for processing and freezing berries and vegetables has been launched. A complex for the production of extruded aluminum profiles has been built and commissioned. Currently, these are stably operating enterprises that continue to reinvest profits into their development,” Deputy Governor of Brest Oblast Mikhail Batsenko said. The region’s enterprises export their products to 88 countries worldwide, with Russia, China, and Kazakhstan leading the list of top trading partners. Positive dynamics are observed in relations with African countries, while a presence in European markets is maintained.
A cooperation agreement was also signed during the forum between the Administration of the Free Economic Zone (FEZ) Brest and the Irkutsk Oblast Development Corporation on 25 August. The parties intend to provide assistance for the development of enterprises in the Belarusian and Russian regions. On the sidelines of the forum, the Belarusian representatives spoke with potential partners from Mongolia and China.

AI startups are reshaping the US defense industrial base
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
08:03:33 UTC
17:03:33 KST

- Defense startups like Hadrian and Castelion are using AI-driven manufacturing to compress production timelines once dominated by legacy prime contractors.
- Missile stockpiles fell sharply during the Iran War, driving urgency behind AI-enabled efforts to accelerate rare earth processing and munitions output.
Procurement bottlenecks, rigid legacy contracts and a rare earth supply chain dominated by China have combined to slow the production of missiles and interceptors just as the Iran War has drained U.S. stockpiles to their lowest levels in years. Dr. Guy Kioni, critical minerals initiative fellow at the Cambridge Middle East and North Africa Forum and CEO of the geostrategy consultancy Missang, argues that artificial intelligence, applied from mineral separation through missile assembly, is the tool now compressing decades of slow, incremental progress into a matter of years, and opening the defense sector to a new generation of startups competing with the primes.
Historically, when gas prices go down, consumption goes up. Emissions go up too; people drive more, and the avenues of commerce accelerate. Consumers and entrepreneurs, alike, plan more and do more. Cheaper goods allow people to be more productive. That same relationship holds true for Artificial Intelligence in American industry, which allows more productive firms to grow, hire, expand and scale. In fact, US firms that have invested in integrating AI into their workflows have since expanded their entry-level headcount by 12%, defying expectations that AI would reduce jobs.
No industry shows this better than the Defense sector, where AI is being paired with government contracts that seek accelerated production. The American defense industry has historically been very slow. There are procurement bottlenecks, with long-running chains of bureaucracy that delay and dull innovation. Legacy manufacturers have become inflexible with long-term repetitive contracts and complex supply chains, often structured to appease Congressional constituents. The process has produced a variety of domestic and international chokepoints.
Another chokepoint sits entirely upstream of the factory floor. China refines close to 90% of the world’s rare earths and roughly 94% of the sintered permanent magnets used in missile guidance and radar systems, and it has shown it will restrict export licenses to US defense suppliers with little warning. AI does not change that concentration of power; it shortens how long it takes to build an alternative to it.
AI is doing similar work upstream, separating the critical chokepoint beneath the factory floor. Isolating individual rare earths from complex ore matrices is a chemical engineering challenge requiring dozens of solvent extraction stages, a craft China has refined across four decades. AI is improving the extent to which Western companies can change the calculus.
Aclara Resources and Argonne National Laboratory are now building an AI digital twin to simulate those stages instead of running them by trial and error, accelerate ramp-up timelines and reduce uncertainty at a planned Louisiana separation plant. A comparable AI-controlled rare-earth separation facility in Saskatchewan is now entering commissioning. Neither has replaced Chinese capacity yet. But it’s the same compression driving the factory floor. This is decades of learning curve compressed into years.
The same compression is happening downstream, where the minerals become missiles, and none of it is speculative. AI’s boost to production, jobs, the economy, and defensive readiness is already occurring. Business development within legacy companies like Raytheon and Boeing has been riddled with delays and procurement stagnation; however, at the startup level, entrepreneurship and accelerated manufacturing using AI have begun to reshape how the defense industry functions.
Many new companies stand out. Three-year-old company Castelion, for example, manufactures hypersonic missiles using AI-automated rapid iteration and vertical integration to build out industrial systems constructed for agility and scale. They joined a separate Pentagon agreement to scale production of the Blackbeard hypersonic missile. Manufacturing company Hadrian is another startup that has impressed the defense sector by creating its own AI model, named Opus, for integration into its ‘factory of the future‘ for defense production.
Hadrian provides automation tools that can be integrated across factories, for example, reducing lead times for production for Anduril Industries by over 50%. Hadrian, founded in 2020, prioritizes flexibility in the manufacturing process, using Opus to automate production on reduced timescales with sudden changes in procurement needs. The company has hit an $8 billion market cap as it rapidly expands production and its workforce, focusing on building parts for naval defense capabilities.
Zone 5 is another company working to rapidly produce low-cost cruise missiles and interceptors. Caracol AM, similarly, applies Large Format Additive Manufacturing (LFAM) and Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing (WAAM) to the defense sector. Both methods are robotic technologies for casting and forging complex and dual-use military components. The company can print parts directly from CAD models using AI, heavily reducing overall lead times.
Under the parallel LCCM program, new agreements and contracts with startups like these will help the Pentagon reach its goal of procuring more than 10,000 low-cost cruise missiles over three years, beginning in 2027. These are just a few examples among many of how AI is used to create real material increases in output.
The ambition is driven by urgency. The Iran War reduced stockpiles of Patriot missiles from 2,200 before the war to fewer than 827. THAAD missiles dropped from 452 to 278. Over 1,000 Tomahawk missiles have been expended since the war began, nearly half of the US’s global inventory. The number is striking considering the US only produced 207 Tomahawk missiles for FY2026. New requests for more will likely not arrive until 2030, after 34 months of production lead time, though a $22.9 billion contract awarded this month aims to ramp annual production past 1,000.
This is why companies that accelerate production are crucial for national security, and it is why AI will show its biggest successes within the defense sector first. Artificial Intelligence has become a tool for increasing productivity by finding efficient new workflows for manufacturing processes, offering substitutive solutions, and accelerating innovation by analyzing and tracking material production. Defense industries have been among the first to showcase these benefits of AI, and increasingly AI has empowered defense startups to receive government contracts in ways never before possible. In the past, they would have been quickly overlooked as incapable or too small, but now AI has advanced the competitive playing field, expanding the number of defense companies and government contracts.
AI is not simply automating the sector. It is one reason startups are now winning contracts once reserved for prime contractors, alongside a deliberate Pentagon shift toward faster, non-traditional procurement. Many economic benefits will stem from the Pentagon’s new strategy. The Defense Department has prioritized contracts that transform industry even amongst legacy companies like Lockheed Martin, which received $53.86 billion for tripling the capacity of PAC-3 MSE interceptors by 2030. They also broke ground on a new facility in Alabama in May of this year, preparing to nearly double production lines for THAAD interceptors. Using AI within the factory will allow Lockheed to produce more at a fraction of the cost while also employing more people to handle the increases in output.
They will undoubtably face heavy competition from startups. That competition, driven in part by the use of AI, should however, result in a more robust, efficient, and productive defense sector, benefiting both national security and the broader American economy.

Russia Equips Geran Kamikaze Drones with EW Systems to Counter Interceptors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
08:02:35 UTC
17:02:35 KST

Russia has equipped Geran-type kamikaze drones with an electronic warfare system designed to jam the analog video link used by Ukrainian interceptor drones.
Serhii Flash, an adviser to the President of Ukraine on the development of defense technologies, reported this after examining the system found in the wreckage of one of the drones.
The EW system found on the Shahed detects the video transmitter signal of a Ukrainian interceptor drone as it approaches. The system’s receiver identifies the interceptor’s operating frequency and instructs the EW transmitter to generate interference in the same frequency band.
According to a preliminary assessment, the jammer’s signal is approximately five times more powerful than the drone’s video transmitter, causing the ground-based operator to lose the video feed and the ability to accurately guide the interceptor toward its target.
The system consists of a VTX transmitter, a VRX receiver, and control electronics. It operates with an analog video signal in the 5.8 GHz band.
During testing, the system detected a test VTX and activated the jammer approximately three seconds later, causing the analog video signal to disappear. After the test transmitter was switched off, the system took about five seconds to enter standby mode. In this mode, it consumed approximately 2W, and up to 33W when activated.
Possible countermeasures include interceptor drones equipped with terminal guidance systems, digital communication links, or video transmitters operating on non-standard frequencies.

UNIFIL says ‘entire neighborhoods’ wiped out in southern Lebanon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
08:00:05 UTC
17:00:05 KST

Sahin Demir
25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
The UN Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) said Monday night that peacekeepers continue to report “extensive destruction” of civilian infrastructure across southern Lebanon, warning that entire neighborhoods have been wiped out and some destruction appears “systematic rather than selective.”
UNIFIL spokesperson Kandice Ardiel told UN Radio that peacekeepers had documented widespread damage and destruction from Kafr Kila to Khiam and Naqoura.
Israel has launched extensive attacks on Lebanon since March 2, claiming they targeted Hezbollah, while the Lebanese group responded with attacks against Israel, effectively ending the ceasefire that had been in place since November 2024.
“Homes and businesses, schools and hospitals and other critical infrastructure like roads, electricity and water networks” have been damaged or destroyed, Ardiel said.
“It’s hard to overstate the devastation that some communities have seen. Entire neighborhoods have been wiped out,” she added.
She also said peacekeepers had expressed concern about cases in which “the destruction appears to be systematic rather than selective.”
Ardiel warned that the impact goes beyond physical damage, pointing to displacement, loss of property and livelihoods, disruption of community networks, and a diminished sense of security.
She said the destruction could have long-term consequences for civilians’ ability to return to their communities and rebuild their lives.
“Any durable peace depends on strong and stable communities, communities where people can have hope for the future,” she said, warning that diminishing that hope would make the future more unstable for families living and working on both sides of the Blue Line.
Ardiel said UNIFIL’s primary role in southern Lebanon is to support the implementation of UN Security Council Resolution 1701 and help restore security and stability.
She said peacekeepers also support humanitarian organizations by coordinating their safe movement across southern Lebanon and, in some cases, providing escorts to help aid reach people in need.
UNIFIL also supports local communities through small-scale projects, including helping restore water infrastructure and providing school supplies, food, and hygiene items, she added.
“We firmly believe that Resolution 1701 remains the framework for achieving stability, but long-term stability can’t be built on rubble,” Ardiel said.

3 helpers sacked, issued warnings over use of employer data to secure loans
Hong Kong’s privacy watchdog highlights three cases and says helpers’ actions led to their employers being harassed by debt collectors
Three domestic helpers in Hong Kong have been sacked and issued warning letters after providing their employers’ personal data without consent to secure loans, resulting in the households being harassed by debt collectors.
Privacy Commissioner for Personal Data Ada Chung Lai-ling said on Tuesday that, in each of the three cases, the names, phone numbers and addresses of employers were originally obtained solely for work purposes.
“However, the domestic helpers in question subsequently provided the employers’ personal data to financial institutions for applying for loans,” she said. “And I would say that this went beyond the original purpose for which the data was collected.”
In one of the cases, which happened in 2025, the helper provided her employers’ phone number and address to a moneylender in the Philippines as proof of work, but later defaulted on payments due to the high interest rate.
The moneylender then texted the employer, requesting that the helper be reminded to make the payments, and threatened to send debt collectors to the address if the transaction was not completed by a deadline.
The other two cases took place in January and May this year and involved the helpers disclosing their employers’ personal information to several financial institutions without consent to apply for loans, resulting in their employers being harassed.

She reiterated the need for international cooperation, noting that international players take EU regulations into account.
"In this way, Europe is also helping to set the standards for AI," she said.

Hasina spat stalls Bangladesh-India reset. What would break the deadlock?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25

Bangladesh-India reset stalls over Hasina: What would break the deadlock?
Analysts say that an Indian commitment to not allow the ousted Bangladesh prime minister to engage in politics from their soil would help, as the two countries prepare for a visit to New Delhi by current Bangladesh PM Tarique Rahman.
Dhaka, Bangladesh — New Delhi and Dhaka had been quietly planning Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s first visit to India since taking office earlier this year, when a news conference shattered those efforts.
Former Bangladesh PM Sheikh Hasina, convicted of crimes against humanity in her country, addressed a news conference held in the heart of the Indian capital by video on August 5, where she, her son and their Awami League party colleagues criticised the mass uprising that had brought her down.
Bangladesh responded swiftly, saying it was “outraged” that Hasina had been allowed to speak publicly from Indian soil, where she has been in exile since her ouster in August 2024. Dhaka had specifically warned New Delhi against allowing political activities that could affect bilateral relations.
Bangladesh subsequently said a “propitious environment” was needed before the trip, while asking New Delhi to act on extradition requests involving Hasina and other fugitives.
India says the requests remain “under examination” through established procedures.
But interviews with Bangladeshi officials and analysts suggest the immediate dispute may be more nuanced than a simple extradition standoff.
The key question may be less when India hands Hasina over than what India allows her to do while she remains there.
The ‘megaphone’ problem
Faisal Mahmud, a former press minister at the Bangladesh High Commission in New Delhi, said extradition and Hasina’s political activities should be treated as separate issues.
“The stalemate between Bangladesh and India stems largely from New Delhi giving Sheikh Hasina a literal megaphone while she remains in exile there – something Dhaka had specifically asked India not to allow,” Mahmud told Al Jazeera.
Extradition, he said, was “an entirely different matter, and a far more complicated and lengthy one” that the Rahman government understood.
“At this point, the impasse over Tarique’s proposed visit to India, and over any broader reset of the frosty bilateral relationship, is not centred on Hasina’s extradition,” Mahmud said. “It is centred on India allowing her to conduct political activities from its soil.”
That concern predates the government under Rahman’s Bangladesh Nationalist Party.
During an April 4, 2025 meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus, then head of Bangladesh’s interim administration, asked New Delhi to prevent Hasina from making what he described as “incendiary statements” from Indian soil.
Humaiun Kobir, deputy head of Bangladesh’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, told Al Jazeera that Dhaka wanted “a good and working relationship with India based on trust and mutual respect”.
“But letting terrorists like Sheikh Hasina destabilise our country from India is not acceptable,” Kobir said, using the government’s description of the former prime minister.
He argued that relations could enter “a new phase” if the leadership of both countries wanted it, but said New Delhi must recognise Bangladesh’s changed political reality following the 2024 uprising.
“No one can conduct any terror activity from a sovereign land,” Kobir said. “It is unacceptable that the terrorists who killed our people are allowed to talk from their land and incite violence in Bangladesh.”
He said Dhaka wanted India to return other Bangladeshis accused of crimes, including suspects in the killing of Sharif Osman Hadi, an outspoken critic of Hasina and India who was murdered in 2025. His alleged killers were subsequently arrested by India, where they had crossed over.
Yet Kobir’s comments also suggest Dhaka does not want the Hasina dispute to indefinitely prevent high-level engagement.
Talks over Rahman’s visit remain under way, he said, describing a meeting between the Bangladeshi and Indian prime ministers as ultimately unavoidable. Over the weekend, in fact, India’s Rashtrapati Bhavan — the presidential palace — issued a notice suggesting that it was preparing to host Rahman, only to withdraw the document hours later.
“A meeting is a must,” Kobir told Al Jazeera. “But only when it aligns with our national interest.”
“It can be next week, two weeks later or two months later,” he added.
Will India extradite Hasina?
That distinction matters because restricting Hasina’s political activity and extraditing her present very different challenges for New Delhi.
Hasina was sentenced to death in absentia by Bangladesh’s International Crimes Tribunal after being convicted of crimes against humanity over the deadly crackdown on the 2024 uprising. She rejects the proceedings as politically motivated.
Bangladesh first formally sought Hasina’s extradition on December 23, 2024, through a diplomatic note sent under the countries’ 2013 extradition treaty.
After her death sentence in November 2025, Dhaka reiterated the request, and India subsequently said it was “under examination”.
On August 11, India’s Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said Bangladesh’s request for Sheikh Hasina’s extradition was being examined under India’s “established procedures”, adding that New Delhi would share an update when there was further progress.
The MEA did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for further details on the matter.
Pinak Ranjan Chakravarty, a former Indian high commissioner to Bangladesh, said the matter must proceed through treaty provisions and India’s legal system.
“All legal formalities have to be completed for obtaining a judicial order for extradition,” Chakravarty told Al Jazeera.
He said the treaty also contained grounds under which extradition could be refused.
Domestic politics shapes diplomacy
Some analysts see a political contradiction in the extradition demand.
David Bergman, a veteran observer of Bangladesh politics, argues that Dhaka is pressing India to return Hasina while potentially preferring that she remain outside the country.
“Bangladesh demands extradition knowing that the Indian government will never extradite Hasina,” Bergman told Al Jazeera, adding: “It is apparently playing to the gallery of Bangladesh public opinion.”
“At the same time, the government does not actually want Hasina to return,” Bergman said, referring to a dilemma that other analysts too have pointed to: Hasina’s return could create as many political and legal problems for Dhaka as it resolves.
Bangladesh would have custody of a former prime minister sentenced to death, forcing the government to confront the politically and internationally sensitive consequences of imprisoning, and potentially executing, one of the country’s most consequential political figures.
But the Hasina question is only one part of a broader recalibration of Dhaka’s relationship with New Delhi.
Shahab Enam Khan, professor of international relations at Jahangirnagar University, said Dhaka’s current posture should not be read simply as anti-India. Khan told Al Jazeera that Bangladesh still needs trade, defence, security and people-to-people ties with India.
He said the government’s stance reflects two pressures: asserting Bangladesh’s legal and sovereign authority, and responding to public sentiment shaped by what he described as New Delhi’s close alignment with Hasina’s Awami League over the past two decades.
Khan argued that India had invested heavily in the Awami League as its principal political partner in Bangladesh and had been slow to fully adjust to the country’s post-2024 political reality.
He said New Delhi was now “increasingly embracing the political reality in Bangladesh”, but added that Dhaka needed to see that shift translated into concrete outcomes.
Neither side wants a rupture
The political dispute has not halted practical engagement.
A Confederation of Indian Industry delegation visited Dhaka this month for talks with ministers and business leaders even as uncertainty over Rahman’s proposed India visit intensified. Bilateral merchandise trade remains above $12bn annually, with India exporting $10.56bn worth of goods to Bangladesh, according to the Indian High Commission in Dhaka.
For former Indian High Commissioner Chakravarty, that reflects an unavoidable structural reality.
“Geography is an immutable factor in geopolitics,” he told Al Jazeera. “It binds India and Bangladesh in a manner that cannot be ignored by policymakers in both countries.”
But he criticised Dhaka for attaching conditions to Rahman’s visit.
“I do not think that the larger national interest and bilateral ties should be held hostage to any individual,” Chakravarty said.
Sreeradha Datta, a professor specialising in South Asian studies at India’s OP Jindal Global University, pointed to another dimension of that interdependence: Bangladesh’s attempts to diversify its external relationships have not reduced India’s strategic importance.
She said Dhaka’s expanding engagement with the United States and China, growing defence cooperation with Turkiye and renewed outreach to Pakistan have added to New Delhi’s concerns about Bangladesh’s foreign policy direction.
China has become particularly important, Datta said, with Beijing’s sustained economic and strategic engagement giving it a growing role in Bangladesh’s development and foreign policy calculations.
Even so, she argued, Bangladesh’s broader external partnerships cannot diminish India’s structural importance.
“Neither side can stay disengaged for long,” Datta told Al Jazeera, noting that geography ensures India will remain strategically important to Bangladesh.
The two countries share a 4,096km (2,546-mile) land border.
Datta said Bangladesh also occupies a critical place in India’s eastern connectivity, security and neighbourhood strategy, adding that the relationship is supported by more than 70 bilateral mechanisms.
That structural dependence also helps explain why, despite the political standoff, New Delhi has stopped short of closing the door on high-level engagement.
As recently as August 18, the MEA said Rahman’s invitation remained open, while reiterating that New Delhi wants a “positive, constructive and forward-looking” relationship with Bangladesh based on mutual interest and reciprocity.
The unresolved question is what concession, public or private, could create enough political space for both governments to move towards a meeting without appearing to have backed down.

freddie mercury’s iconic costumes to enter the V&A galleries in london
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
07:45:12 UTC
16:45:12 KST

Freddie Mercury’s costumes span Queen’s rise and solo career
The V&A will trace Freddie Mercury’s evolving stage persona through eight costumes and personal accessories, placing the Queen frontman’s wardrobe across its South Kensington galleries from October 24th, 2026, to January 17th, 2027. Freddie Mercury | Splendid Things is developed with Mary Austin, Mercury’s former fiancée, close friend, and confidante of 20 years, who is lending seven of the looks for the display.
The free trail places the clothes within the V&A’s permanent galleries, architecture, and collections. Each of the six stops focuses on a different moment in Mercury’s career, creating connections between his performances and the museum’s holdings in fashion, design, decorative arts, theater, and performance.
The exhibition takes its title from Mercury’s 1978 remark: ‘I like to be surrounded by splendid things. I want to lead a Victorian life surrounded by exquisite clutter.‘ The phrase points toward the importance of objects and clothing within his public identity. His costumes were carefully considered components of his performances, helping translate his persona across increasingly large venues and audiences.
from the ‘mercury wing’ catsuit to the magic tour crown
The selection spans the 1970s and 80s, beginning with a monochrome ensemble worn for an early Queen gig at Imperial College and later featured on the cover of the band’s 1973 debut album.
Another key piece is the ‘Mercury Wing’ catsuit, designed by Wendy de Smet and worn during the A Night at the Opera tour in 1975–76. The costume also appeared in Queen’s groundbreaking Bohemian Rhapsody video, connecting Mercury’s stage wardrobe with the increasingly visual language of music performance during the period.
The exhibition continues through the later years of Queen with Mercury’s signature crown and cloak, designed by Diana Moseley for the 1986 Magic Tour, an ensemble worn for Mercury’s final stage appearance with Queen at Knebworth.
The trail also moves into Mercury’s solo career with the costume worn in the Made in Heaven music video. Accessories and pieces from his personal wardrobe provide a quieter counterpoint to the theatrical costumes, offering glimpses of the person behind the stage persona.
The installations are designed by Tom Piper, whose work spans theater, opera, and exhibition design. His previous projects include productions for the Royal Shakespeare Company, the V&A exhibition Alice: Curiouser and Curiouser, the Taylor Swift | Songbook Trail, and the Tower of London poppies. Piper has designed each intervention as a distinct setting. Costumes are presented alongside set dressing and, in some spaces, sound and light. Specially made mannequins are dynamically posed to evoke Mercury’s stage presence, making the body and its gestures part of the display.
The approach emphasizes the relationship between costume and performance. Mercury’s clothes did not simply decorate his appearances; they helped establish scale, movement, character, and atmosphere. As Mary Austin explains, he understood that he was ‘providing an image to match the scale of the space and the vastness of the crowd.’
Opening in what would have been Mercury’s 80th year, Freddie Mercury | Splendid Things also highlights the continuing cultural relevance of his visual legacy. His costumes remain recognizable because they were never separate from the performance and helped turn Mercury into a figure whose image could carry across music, fashion, film, photography, and popular culture.

'Withdraw existing questionnaire': Kharge, Rahul Gandhi write to PM Modi over caste census issue
Edited by: Abhishek Mishra / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 25, 2026, 13:20 IST

Rahul, Kharge write to PM Modi over caste census
NEW DELHI: Congress high-command Mallikarjun Kharge and Rahul Gandhi on Tuesday urged the PM Modi-led government to change the way caste information is being collected in the census, warning that the current method could result in inaccurate data.The grand old party leaders also called for withdrawal of existing questionnaire, terming those "misleading".Kharge, Rahul requested PM Modi-led government to opt for a different way to detail on caste.
In a letter to Prime Minister Narendra Modi, the two leaders said accurate caste data was necessary for implementing social justice policies. “The policies of social justice in India cannot be properly implemented without accurate data,” they said.Kharge and Rahul objected to the use of an "open-ended question" to record caste details. Under the system, people can provide the name of their caste, which is then recorded in that form.The Congress leaders said the same caste may be known by different names, sub-castes or local names in different parts of India. If these different names are recorded separately, “a single caste could end up being divided into thousands of names,” they said.
They warned that this could lead to a very large number of caste categories and make the data generated by the caste census difficult to use.“If the correct number of members of a community is not recorded, its situation will also be assessed incorrectly,” the two leaders said. They argued that inaccurate data could affect backward, extremely backward and other disadvantaged communities.
According to Rahul and Kharge, the impact could extend to government decisions on education, employment, welfare schemes and social justice.They also raised concerns over the lack of clarity about the size of country's Other Backward Classes (OBC) population. “We would not even know how large the OBC population is in India,” they said, pointing out that the term “backward class” is not included in the census process.
Another Congress leader Jairam Ramesh also targeted BJP-led Centre over census. Ramesh said, "Government's current efforts towards a caste census are just whitewash".

London agreed to provide Ukraine with the blueprints for SCALP missiles for production by Ukraine - media

Unknown Publisher

London agreed to provide Ukraine with the blueprints for SCALP missiles for production by Ukraine - media
Kyiv • UNN
Britain has allowed the blueprints for Scalp components to be handed over to Ukraine for missile production. Italy has withdrawn from military exercises within the coalition.
The UK government has agreed to hand over drawings of British components for the Scalp missile, the French version of the British Storm Shadow cruise missile, which will allow Ukraine to produce this long-range weapon domestically, the BBC reports, writes UNN.
Details
The BBC and Reuters report that on Monday the UK announced it would give Ukraine access to classified technology to begin its own production of Storm Shadow long-range cruise missiles, capable of striking deep inside Russia, and that France had already agreed to license this technology for the European missile.
The UK government, as the BBC points out, is allowing British defence company MBDA to declassify information about its components for the Scalp missile, as Ukraine and France seek to establish assembly lines in Ukraine.
Scalp missiles and their UK-produced version, Storm Shadow, have already been supplied to Ukraine by both the UK and France and used to strike Russian military targets, the publication notes.
In response, the Kremlin, Reuters notes, said that the use of secret British technology would "add fuel to the fire" of deteriorating relations, after warning London last week of "consequences" for supplying drones to Ukraine.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, during his first official visit to Ukraine in office, promised to continue putting pressure on Russia despite Moscow's "outrageous threats." He said the Coalition of the Willing "is doing everything possible," while calling on the US Congress to "step up" economic pressure on Russia.
In a joint declaration following the Coalition of the Willing meeting, the allies, as Euronews notes, condemned the "systematic and intensifying strikes on Ukrainian cities, critical infrastructure and civilians" and promised to strengthen Ukraine's air-defence system, calling this a "matter of the utmost urgency."
The leaders also pledged to share relevant technologies, including through the Coalition for Missile Defence, as Ukraine prepares for another winter of Russian strikes on its cities and energy infrastructure.
Large-scale joint military exercises will take place between October and November, aimed at testing the operational capabilities of the countries that have joined the format and preparing for possible intervention after the hostilities end, French President Emmanuel Macron said while speaking at a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing.
"We have made a decision," Macron explained, stressing that the exercises are intended to demonstrate the Coalition's operational readiness and its ability to act after the cessation of hostilities. The goal, the French president added, is also to strengthen the credibility of the security guarantees offered to Kyiv.
Italy took a position different from that of the others on this point. Rome will not participate in the military exercises announced by Macron. In the evening after the meeting, as Euronews writes, government sources confirmed this, saying that the choice reflects the line repeatedly articulated by Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni. Italy supports Ukraine and is part of the Coalition, but does not intend to send its service members to Ukrainian territory.
Italy's decision comes as the government prepares a new package of aid for Ukraine. According to sources in the executive branch, Italy is focusing primarily on hospitals, schools and energy infrastructure, as well as new defensive equipment, including generators and air-defence equipment.
For Macron, as noted, the exercises are becoming an element of a deterrence strategy and future security guarantees. "It is very important to continue demonstrating our determination and our readiness," the French president said.
Italy’s choice, however, the publication writes, introduces an important distinction within the Coalition: Prime Minister Meloni, who joined the summit remotely, confirmed Italy’s support for its partners and the negotiating path. But on the issue of the direct involvement of the Italian armed forces, the position remains unchanged: no participation in ground operations.

Belarus’ National Bank lowers standard risk calculation rates for September
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
07:42:00 UTC
16:42:00 KST

MINSK, 25 August (BelTA) – The National Bank of Belarus has decided to lower the standard risk calculation rates for September 2026, the National Bank press service told BelTA.
The standard risk rate for new investment loans extended to legal entities (excluding preferential loans) will decrease from 10.69% to 10.45% per annum. For new loans extended to legal entities (excluding preferential and investment loans), the rate will drop from 12% to 11.79% per annum.
For new loans extended to individuals (excluding preferential loans), the rate will decrease from 17.83% to 17.65% per annum. For new fixed-term irrevocable bank deposits of individuals in the national currency with a maturity of one to three years, the rate will fall from 12.9% to 12.6% per annum.
For new fixed-term irrevocable bank deposits of individuals in the national currency with a maturity of over three years, the standard risk rate will be reduced from 14.62% to 14.5% per annum.
Standard risk calculation rates are a tool used to ensure financial stability. As the National Bank previously explained to BelTA, this is one of the upper-bound constraints on interest rates, calculated as the average rate of systemically important banks plus a certain margin. This provides banks with a signal level, above which, based on National Bank assessments and market data, is considered an indicator of high-risk behavior. Such behavior is not prohibited by the National Bank, but banks are required to meet additional capital and reserve requirements - a buffer in case they encounter difficulties as a result of riskier practices.
