Rare tornado in southwestern France injures dozens, damages homes
PARIS, Aug 25 - A tornado swept through a village in the Aude region of southwestern France late on Monday, destroying homes and injuring 39 people, authorities said, describing it as a rare and traumatic event.
Two of the injured are in a critical condition and around 300 houses in the village of Pomas have been damaged, officials said. Everyone in the village has been evacuated while authorities verify if homes are still safe to live in, they added.
"It felt as though death itself was falling upon us," Severine, a Pomas resident who did not give her surname, told BFM TV.
Speaking in front of her house, now flattened by the tornado, she said on Tuesday that the car her family piled into was shaken by the tornado before they managed to speed up and escape.
"We fled, it was survival instinct," she said, as people helped the family of four sort through the ruins to see what could be salvaged.
Social media footage verified by Reuters also showed the tornado swirling above the nearby village of Verzeille in Aude, late on Monday. Many of the homes caught up in its path had their windows smashed.
The tornado struck as this summer's intense heatwave gave way this week to thunderstorms in many areas of southern France.
On Tuesday morning 1,400 households in the area were still without electricity, the local prefecture said.
"This is an exceptional event, and it is deeply traumatic for all the residents," senior official Marie-Helene Bouissac told reporters.
While France may have dozens of tornadoes a year, that is far fewer than the United States where more than 1,000 are recorded each year. Tornadoes in France are also usually mild, according to official weather forecaster Meteo-France. REUTERS

NexTech Solutions buys BOOMSLANG in latest counter-UAS expansion

- NexTech Solutions acquired BOOMSLANG Aerospace on August 7, adding the MONGOOSE counter-UAS system to its product lineup.
- The deal is NexTech's fifth acquisition since a 2023 strategic investment from private equity firm Clairvest.
NexTech Solutions has acquired BOOMSLANG Aerospace, a developer of unmanned aerial systems and counter-drone technology, the Huntsville, Alabama-based defense contractor announced August 24. The deal closed August 7.
The acquisition is the fifth NexTech Solutions has completed since 2023, when the company took a strategic investment from Clairvest, a Toronto-based private equity firm, to serve as a platform for growth in the defense technology sector.
BOOMSLANG brings a counter-UAS system called MONGOOSE, along with its broader family of unmanned aerial systems, into NexTech’s product lineup. The company’s engineering team has worked on UAS design and counter-UAS systems, according to NexTech.
NexTech said BOOMSLANG’s technology will be folded into its existing counter-UAS architecture, which already includes products such as MANTLE, VidTerra COMPASS and JEFF-K. The company described the combination as extending its coverage across detection, defeat and airborne mission sets, though it did not specify contract values, customer names or delivery timelines tied to the acquisition.
“BOOMSLANG Aerospace has built exactly the kind of technology our customers are asking for: cutting-edge, mission-ready, and purpose-built for the current threat environment at the edge,” said Joseph Paull, CEO of NexTech Solutions. “We are excited to integrate the MONGOOSE C-UAS system and BOOMSLANG UAS family of systems into our networked ecosystem of products.”
“Together, we can move faster from concept to fielded capability for the customers who need it most,” said Alan Cornett, president and co-founder of BOOMSLANG Aerospace.
“BOOMSLANG’s approach to unmanned aerial systems and their C-UAS technology aligns perfectly with the modular, requirements-driven C-UAS strategy we are building at NTS,” said David Pollman, director of counter-UAS operations at NexTech. Pollman previously served as deputy division chief of operations at the Department of War’s Joint Counter-UAS Office, where he worked on evaluating the department’s counter-UAS strategy before joining NexTech in 2024.
NexTech has operated for more than 13 years, providing systems engineering, testing and evaluation, and operational support to the Department of War and other U.S. government customers. The company has offices in Huntsville, Tampa and Northern Virginia.
Counter-UAS systems are designed to detect and, in some cases, disable or destroy small drones. Demand for such systems among U.S. military and government buyers has grown as adversaries and non-state actors have made increasing use of low-cost drones for surveillance and attacks.
NexTech has pursued a series of acquisitions and partnerships since the Clairvest investment. The company announced a counter-UAS partnership with Xtend and a separate collaboration with Monkton on secure mobility technology, and it has continued developing its MANTLE platform, including a mobile version for Android devices.

“No artist should face criminal punishment for creating work that challenges official narratives or encourages critical reflection on history.
“This trial demonstrates how broadly worded and politically motivated laws are used – and worse, in this case, used retroactively – to silence artists, activists and other individuals who dare to express views that differ from those of the Chinese government.”

Gao Zhen is part of the internationally known Gao Brothers artistic duo. The brothers are renowned for their contemporary artworks examining Chinese history, state power and social change.
There are also concerns about his health and well-being in detention. Gao Zhen, now 70, reportedly suffers from multiple health conditions, including lumbar spine disease and fluid accumulation in his knees. Radically Collective: The Legacy of Cuba's Microbrigadas Housing Program
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
07:30:00 UTC
16:30:00 KST

In the 1970s, Cuba faced a severe nationwide housing shortage due to population growth, rural-to-urban migration, and the degradation of existing housing stock. The government's answer was a system that pulled ordinary workers off their regular jobs and put them on building sites instead. This program, known as the Microbrigadas (microbrigades), reshaped entire districts of Havana, where they combined collective self-construction and state-backed technical knowledge, which left a mark on the urban grid of its capital city that persists until today.
A Microbrigada was a residential apartment building constructed by factory and office workers rather than professional construction laborers. Workplaces sent a mix of skilled mechanics, administrative staff, or general laborers into the field. To ensure overall structural integrity, the state assigned a small team of professional architects, structural engineers, and master builders to oversee each site, train the workers, and ensure structural stability. The reassigned workers then spent their time building apartment blocks, while their colleagues who stayed at the offices and factories absorbed their duties. A process known as "esfuerzo colectivo" or collective effort.

Nevada sues Trump administration over reduction in Colorado River water use
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
07:28:17 UTC
16:28:17 KST

Berk Kutay Gokmen
25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
The US state of Nevada has sued the administration of President Donald Trump over a federal plan requiring the state and two others to reduce Colorado River water use, marking the first legal challenge to Washington’s effort to prevent the river from reaching a critical point.
In its federal court filing on Monday, Nevada said the Interior Department’s drought management plan could cause “devastating environmental, socioeconomic, and health and human safety impacts to southern Nevada and its citizens.”
The plan was created after the seven Colorado River states failed to agree on how to respond to worsening shortages, according to The Washington Post.
The dispute centers on a river that supplies about 40 million people in the southwestern United States and Mexico. Nevada officials said the proposed reductions could cut as much as 71% of the state’s annual allocation. The river provides roughly 90% of the water used by Las Vegas and surrounding communities.
“This isn’t about political posturing,” Nevada Governor Joe Lombardo said. “This is a matter of survival for a community that represents about two-thirds of our state’s citizens and the lion’s share of its economy.”
Years of overuse and a severe drought worsened by climate change have pushed the river into crisis. Federal data show this year’s flow is about 37% of average, while Lakes Powell and Mead have reached record-low levels.
The federal plan requires the US states of Arizona, California, and Nevada to reduce use by about 20% over the next two years. It also allows for deeper cuts later if shortages persist, while imposing no mandatory reductions on the Upper Basin states.
Nevada’s lawsuit argues the plan violates rules governing the river and fails to adequately account for the economic consequences of reducing urban water supplies.

TOKYO, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- An exhibition on the Japanese military's production and use of poison gas during World War II (WWII) is being held from Aug. 23 to 28 in Yokohama City, Kanagawa Prefecture, Japan.
Organized by a Japanese civic group, the "Japanese Military Poison Gas Exhibition" aims to expose the atrocities committed by the Japanese military, specifically the wartime production of poison gas and the waging of gas warfare during its war of aggression against China, and to reveal the crimes against humanity perpetrated by Japanese militarism.
According to materials presented at the exhibition, Japan produced poison gas on Okunoshima Island in Hiroshima Prefecture, manufactured poison-gas shells in Kitakyushu City in Fukuoka Prefecture, and trained personnel for chemical warfare in Narashino City in Chiba Prefecture, among other locations during WWII. The Japanese military also conducted chemical warfare operations in various parts of China.
After Japan's defeat, some chemical weapons were left behind in China, continuing to cause harm to local people. The Japanese government, however, has neither issued a formal apology nor provided compensation.
The exhibition uses photographs and written materials to document the history, while Japanese civilian researchers, photojournalists and others involved in researching the subject have been invited to speak at the venue.
Japanese photojournalist Kenji Higuchi has investigated issues related to poison gas warfare on Okunoshima Island since 1970, documenting victims of poison gas as well as the remains of facilities where chemical weapons were produced through his lens.
Speaking at the event, Higuchi recounted his experiences reporting on the subject and called on the Japanese government to face history squarely.
"Conducting chemical warfare was an atrocity committed by the Japanese military in its war of aggression against China, yet the Japanese government seeks to erase this part of history," Higuchi told Xinhua. "They committed such evil acts, and it is a disgrace for the country. That is why they want to erase it from history."
Masao, a visitor from Yokosuka, said Higuchi's account at the exhibition made him realize that this part of history had remained largely unknown for a long time.
"I never learned about this history at school. They don't teach this at school. It was really shocking to see these materials for the first time," another Japanese visitor told Xinhua.
Higuchi stressed the importance of preserving and conveying the historical record. "This history must be made clear. What was wrong was wrong, and what was right was right. We must become people capable of distinguishing right from wrong," he said. ■

Feature: A menu simmered for a 26-year reunion feast on Chinese sand
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
15:26:04 CST
16:26:04 KST

HOHHOT, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- Twenty-six years had passed before Yin Yuzhen, a national-honored sand-control villager in China's Inner Mongolia, finally sat down to have a reunion feast with her American friend Ronald Sakolsky.
More than half a month before the reunion, she had already begun preparing a feast for Sakolsky, a retired teacher, making sure he could savor the homely, authentic flavors.
The night before their reunion, Yin still gathered around the table with her family, going over who would steam the cakes and how every dish should look and taste.
"Everything must be done properly. Each dish should look beautiful and taste delicious," she told them. "No chicken essence. Just the real flavor."
At noon on Monday, laughter filled Yin's home. Around the table sat Yin, her family and Sakolsky, sharing a long-awaited reunion meal after 26 years apart.
For each dish, Yin had chosen an auspicious meaning: boiled mutton, a symbol of desert generosity; braised fish for abundance year after year; stir-fried green beans for smooth sailing. One by one, she introduced them to her old friend.
The menu had been revised again and again prior to the reunion meal.
While waiting for her friend's visit, she slipped out to her vegetable garden whenever she had a spare moment, imagining stir-frying a plate of long beans for Sakolsky, or thinking how good steamed pumpkin would taste to her old friend.
When the desert roses had bloomed, Yin turned them into the filling of mooncakes. Her family made more than 5 kg of mooncakes to welcome Sakolsky as the Mid-Autumn Festival is approaching.
"I put roses in the filling so he can taste the sweetness of the desert," she said. "Mooncakes mean reunion. I want him to try a traditional Chinese food and take some back to his family in the United States."
By the time the menu list reached more than a dozen, she still felt it was not enough. "I wanted to bring out the very best of the desert to welcome him," she said.
For Yin, the menu was more than a list of dishes. It carried the taste of home, the warmth of an old friendship, and the landscape's quiet transformation. The once-barren desert has become a place of green and abundance.
The story behind the feast began in 1999, when Sakolsky taught English at a school in central China's Henan Province under a teachers' exchange program between the two countries.
By then, Yin had spent more than a decade battling desertification that had severely threatened her livelihood, even half burying her house during sandstorms. "I'd rather wear myself out planting trees than let sand defeat me," she vowed.
After watching a television news report about Yin's tireless work planting trees in the Maowusu Sandy Land, the fourth-largest sandy area in China, Sakolsky was deeply moved and raised 5,000 U.S. dollars to help Yin and her husband with their afforestation efforts.
At the time, the donation was a staggering amount that was enough for Yin to build a house, cover her children's upbringing costs, and even completely change the trajectory of her family's life.
The saplings bought and planted with that donation have since grown into a forest of more than 50,000 towering trees.
When they first met in 2000, Yin's family had little to offer. All she could prepare was a bowl of plain noodles. In those years, the sandy land yielded so little that a bowl of noodles was among the finest meals a family could offer. The sand storms were so strong that one could find a layer of sand settle at the bottom of the bowl by the time the noodles were finished.
Learning that Sakolsky remembered the taste all these years, Yin ground fresh-harvested wheat into flour and made him another bowl of noodles for the reunion feast. This time, she displayed some special culinary skills.
"I stretched a single strand of dough to fill an entire bowl. This is our 'long-lasting noodle,'" Yin said. In Chinese tradition, extra-long noodles symbolize enduring friendship.
"The noodles are the best," said Sakolsky. "This is all from the desert. She helped Mother Earth, and Mother Earth said thank you. That's very simple, and that's something else China taught me."
Indeed, over more than four decades, Yin and her family transformed some 70,000 mu (around 4,667 hectares) of barren sand into green land, turning desert into fields, vegetable plots, and orchards.
Before the reunion meal, Yin led Sakolsky through her yard, where colorful corn, red-skinned potatoes and plump pumpkins were laid out like a small harvest exhibition.
"Look at all these vegetables and fruits," she said. "This land once could not even grow a blade of grass."
Yin's story is part of a much larger picture. Over the decades, China has set up special funds, offered preferential tax policies, and mobilized farmers and locals in afforestation campaigns.
Today, beyond dedicated local farmers like Yin, China's afforestation campaign also attracts large numbers of environment-conscious volunteers, especially young urban dwellers and international students.
Official figures show that China has contributed about one-quarter of the world's increase in green vegetation and rehabilitated 152 million mu of desertified land between 2021 and 2025.
"Our results in sand control are not only visible but can be tasted," Yin said. "If you protect the earth, the earth will reward you." ■

An estimated 2,800 homes were left without electricity across 10 villages, officials said.
France sees several dozen tornadoes per year on average.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan follows the UN’s anti-corruption convention and uses international reviews to improve its policies, Justice Minister Cheng Ming-chien (鄭銘謙) said Tuesday.
Speaking at a review meeting for the Republic of China’s third national report under the convention, Cheng said the UN Convention against Corruption is a major international framework for preventing and fighting corruption. It covers preventive measures, criminalization and law enforcement, international cooperation, and asset recovery, CNA reported.
Taiwan voluntarily follows the convention and underwent international reviews in 2018 and 2022, Cheng said. He said the reviews help the government assess whether its policies are effective, identify weaknesses, and set priorities for reform.
For the first time, Taiwan’s third national report uses the same self-assessment checklist used by countries that have joined the convention. Government agencies reviewed how Taiwan has implemented each part of the convention.
Cheng said anti-corruption systems must keep pace with technological change. He said international reviews can help Taiwan respond to emerging risks and improve its laws and policies.
Minister without Portfolio Lin Ming-hsin (林明昕) said geopolitical risks, rapid advances in AI and digital technology, cross-border crime, and illegal financial flows are making anti-corruption work more complex. He said clean government, transparency, and the rule of law are important for public trust and national competitiveness, per UDN.
The government released its third national report in April. The report reviews Taiwan’s recent implementation of the convention and its response to recommendations from the second international review.
It highlights progress in 10 areas, including transparency, risk management, government procurement, whistleblower protection, corporate governance, money laundering prevention, and international cooperation. It also covers open data, law enforcement, and cooperation between the public and private sectors.
Lin said Taiwan scored 68 points in Transparency International’s 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index, ranking 24th among 182 countries and territories. He said international scrutiny can help demonstrate Taiwan’s anti-corruption progress abroad.
Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) said corruption is no longer only a domestic issue because money and criminal activity increasingly cross national borders. He said transparency, accountability, and clean government are important foundations of democracy and good governance.
Taiwan began implementing the UN Convention against Corruption domestically in 2015. Its third national report covers anti-corruption laws, preventive measures, asset recovery, criminalization and law enforcement, and international cooperation.
The international review will last four days and includes discussions among international experts, government agencies, and nongovernmental organizations. The review committee is scheduled to present its final recommendations Friday.

She said the operation was unlikely to have gone unnoticed, given the perimeter checks, construction supervision, and inspections of the materials used.
Ma also challenged the military’s assertion that the contaminated backfill does not affect training safety, urging the Army to release the results of load-bearing and other tests conducted on the roads. She called on prosecutors to investigate the flow of more than NT$1.3 billion (US$40.8 million) in alleged illicit gains attributed to Chen and his associates and determine whether any military personnel were involved.
The Army said the training center remained a victim of the scheme and that an investigation found no evidence it had conspired with the contractors, per CNA. Smaller businesses are also playing a growing role in greener supply chains. Green procurement reported by small and medium-sized non-manufacturing companies more than doubled last year, rising 113% from the previous year.
Participation is expanding beyond businesses to educational and medical institutions. Green purchases reported in the category covering these and other organizations increased 68% last year.
The initiative recognizes organizations with strong records. Among last year’s award recipients, 74 companies received awards for the third consecutive year, while 83 won for the first time.
Taiwan has set a target of NT$160 billion in combined green procurement by the public and private sectors by 2030. The ministry said the practice has evolved beyond purchasing decisions, giving businesses a way to encourage lower-carbon changes across their supply chains while supporting Taiwan’s goal of reaching net-zero emissions by 2050.
The ministry said it will expand the types of purchases eligible for reporting, including products with environmental certifications, resource-circulation products, and other environmentally friendly products. It also plans to include newer models such as leasing instead of purchasing.

Lawmakers question U.S. Navy’s handling of Iran deployment strain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
07:11:09 UTC
16:11:09 KST

- Senate Democrats are calling for an Armed Services Committee hearing on extended U.S. Navy deployments tied to operations against Iran.
- The USS Abraham Lincoln has been at sea more than 250 days, and the USS Gerald R. Ford suffered a fire and plumbing failures during its own extended deployment.
A group of Senate Armed Services Committee Democrats is asking Chairman Roger Wicker to hold a public hearing on extended deployments tied to U.S. military operations against Iran, according to a letter released August 24 by Senators Gary Peters (D-Mich.), Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) and Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.).
The letter cites conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, which left San Diego on November 21 and has remained at sea for more than 250 days without a scheduled return date. The carrier’s roughly 5,000 sailors and Marines went more than 200 consecutive days without a port call, according to Sen. Richard Blumenthal, a modern-day record for a U.S. Navy carrier.
Military Times reported August 11 that multiple sailors aboard the Lincoln had attempted to go overboard during the deployment, based on accounts from family members. CNN separately confirmed with U.S. officials that a sailor went overboard on August 3 and was recovered within an hour by a search-and-rescue helicopter, treated aboard ship and transferred for further care. A second overboard incident involving the same strike group occurred last spring, according to a sailor aboard the Lincoln and two U.S. officials who spoke to CNN.
Family members confronted Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao at a town hall in San Diego, with one spouse describing a message from her husband saying he hoped he would not wake up the next morning, according to Military Times and Stars and Stripes reporting cited in the letter.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has disputed the Military Times account, calling it “completely misrepresented.” The Navy has said no service members aboard the Lincoln have died and that the August 3 sailor was quickly and safely recovered.
The senators’ letter also points to the USS Gerald R. Ford, which suffered a laundry-room fire on March 12 that took more than 30 hours to extinguish, injured two sailors and damaged roughly 100 sleeping berths. The Navy initially described the fire as contained and said the ship remained fully operational. Later footage obtained by CNN showed more extensive damage, including burned bunks and exposed wiring in crew living spaces.
The Ford left frontline operations and sailed to Souda Bay, Crete, for repairs, then stopped in Split, Croatia, before returning to sea on April 2. The ship had also experienced recurring failures in its roughly 650-toilet vacuum waste system throughout the deployment. The carrier ultimately spent about 11 months at sea, exceeding the Navy’s typical seven-month deployment target, before returning to Norfolk in May for scheduled maintenance.
Both carriers were redirected from other missions to support Iran operations. The Lincoln had been headed for a routine Indo-Pacific patrol before its diversion to the Middle East in January. The Ford was pulled from a planned deployment to Europe, sent briefly to the Caribbean in connection with operations against Venezuela, and then routed to the Middle East.
“The toll this unauthorized, disastrous war is taking on our troops is unconscionable,” the senators wrote, characterizing the military campaign against Iran as illegal and citing what they described as a pattern of inadequate planning for extended deployments.
The senators asked the Armed Services Committee to examine morale conditions, financial strain on military families, and the Department of War’s plan for ending the extended deployments. They also requested that the department detail how it plans to sustain troops in the region if the campaign continues.
The USS George Washington has since been ordered to relieve the Lincoln, according to a U.S. official cited by CNN. As of the senators’ letter, no public timeline had been given for the Lincoln’s return to San Diego, and Chairman Wicker had not publicly responded to the hearing request.

Chinese factory workers accidentally caught on camera glasses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
07:10:39 UTC
16:10:39 KST

Camera glasses contain footage that appears to have been accidentally filmed inside Chinese factory
Factory workers who helped make a Chinese-brand of camera glasses appear to have been unknowingly filmed by the devices in accidental videos.
7.30 bought a pair of budget glasses made by Shenzhen-based company Oho Sunshine online and found footage already on the device, which appears to be from inside the factory.
The collection of four short videos, dated last year, shows a number of workers sitting at their desks inspecting the glasses, while listening to jaunty electronic music.
One video clearly identifies a worker lifting a pair and shaking them vigorously.
Another three videos, up to 10 minutes long and dated this year, show only black with atmospheric audio, suggesting the glasses were activated while inside a case or box.
The shoot button on the side of the frames is sensitive and easily switched on.
7.30 approached Oho Sunshine, with questions about the apparent privacy breach but received no response.
Oho Sunshine was founded in 2009 in the Chinese city of Shenzhen in Guandong province, north of Hong Kong, as a smart wearable technologies manufacturer, according to the company's website.
The accidental leak perhaps proves not even the workers who make camera glasses are safe from being filmed and provides a rare insight into the globalised production chain.
Rise of camera glasses
Camera glasses are enjoying a surge in popularity as cheap brands flood the market. Oho is just one of numerous companies manufacturing similar devices.
They look like ordinary glasses and allow you to record video and audio, largely without people knowing.
While some models have a built-in light to indicate filming, there are now services that remove the indicator cheaply.
The glasses can play music and make calls, with more high-tech versions allowing users to live-stream or swipe through messages on a display in the lenses.
Meta's fashionable Ray-Ban smart glasses can cost up to $700 a pair, but basic versions can be bought online for as little as $40.
Kmart Australia's $89 Anko brand of camera glasses recently sold out, prompting an online petition to stop their sale amid concerns about privacy and their use by male content creators recording women without their knowledge and uploading the videos to potentially millions of followers.
While filming in public places is generally legal, the devices have raised new concerns around privacy.
Filmed without consent on 'rizz cam'
Beth Knight, 18, found herself the subject of lurid commentary from online users after a man filmed her with camera glasses and uploaded it to social media without her knowledge.
At the time of the incident late last year, she was 17 and by herself at London's busy Waterloo station.
"I'd missed my train, so I had 40 minutes to wait in the station," Ms Knight told 7.30.
"Then pretty much immediately a man approached me and opened with, 'I've seen you, I found you attractive,' and I immediately shut him down and I said I had a boyfriend."
She discovered that their conversation had been turned into content after she heard about other cases.
"I started looking up buzzwords. I was looking up "picking up girls", "Meta glasses", "Waterloo", all of those into the TikTok search bar and that's when I found his page."
She saw a video of her interaction titled, "POV: You approach her instead of walking by".
"It was framed as a successful pick-up, like a win, when I know in the moment I was incredibly uncomfortable … because it was a strange man refusing to accept my soft hint of a no," she said.
"He had very much framed it as, 'Look, I've picked her up, I got her Instagram, I've won here,' and over the top of the video he was instructing men watching that when girls say they have a boyfriend they're lying."
Ms Knight was not lying and thought the man would get the message and leave.
The man is a content creator who touts himself as a pick-up artist and advertises male coaching on his social media account.
Digital extremism researcher Milica Stilinovic, from Sydney University, said such content was known as "rizz cam" — rizz being slang for charisma — when women are sometimes filmed without their consent.
"I would find it horrendous to be treated that way and then subjected to a global audience," she told 7.30.
Ms Stilinovic led a study that reviewed more than 350 Instagram videos filmed with camera glasses.
"Pick-up artists are adjacent to the manosphere, or part of the manosphere, and they have a dual purpose to exist," she said.
"One is to build the self-confidence of men, supposedly through the subjugation of women, and the second part is to sell male coaching, which is basically like a multi-level marketing scheme.
"Some of the worst examples included underage girls. Some of [the filmers] approached women who were inebriated. Some of them approached women who were semi-nude at beaches."
Ms Knight said her experience left her feeling angry.
"It's weird to watch it back," she said.
"But the anger definitely came from the fact that it was spun so heavily to look good on his part.
"I went home and sobbed to my parents."
She said she asked the content creator to take the video down, but he blocked her.
7.30 has contacted the creator for comment, but he did not respond.
Is it legal?
According to Australia's Privacy Commissioner, Carly Kind, the use of camera glasses in public is largely legal, with laws varying across states.
"Wearing smart glasses in public to capture images of things that happen in public is generally not illegal under Australian law," Ms Kind told 7.30.
"[But] when you are in a private premises or a private space, and that might include a private home, a vehicle, or potentially a semi-private space like a gym or a workplace, for example, then you're likely going to run up against laws that do prohibit the use of surveillance devices."
In Victoria, where filming inside a private business is generally allowed, one content creator known as "The Latte Bloke" uses camera glasses to review coffee around Melbourne.
He is not a pick-up artist, but his videos feature staff and customers.
One 19-year-old cafe worker said she did not consent to being filmed while serving him.
Her aunt, Tara Venn, told 7.30 her niece was upset after seeing herself in a video online.
She was new in the job.
"It was a bit affronting [for her]," Ms Venn said.
She said content creators should consider the ethics of filming someone.
"Common sense says you are polite and you ask if you are going to invade a person's privacy by filming them without them knowing,"
"I just want people to think and to actually use good manners and decency."
The content creator declined to be interviewed but told 7.30:
"Latte Bloke is all about filming the latte experience and having a bit of fun reviewing the coffee. The focus has never been on the staff or customers, and I'd never intentionally want to make anyone feel uncomfortable."
Potential real-world consequences
Attorney-General Michelle Rowland has asked Australia's Privacy Commissioner to make recommendations about camera glasses in Australia.
Ms Kind says she was already worried about them.
"If you think about their use in workplaces, there's a high likelihood that corporate espionage could be permitted through these kinds of glasses without proper control,"
"I think the theft of personal information through the use of the glasses is also a potential offence that we could see spiralling out here, and [there are] obviously real risks around vulnerable groups, women and children."
In New South Wales it is illegal to create or share sexually explicit videos or audio of someone without their consent.
Last year, new federal privacy laws made serious invasions of privacy an offence; however, the commissioner told 7.30 there was a high bar to prove it was intentional and caused harm.
In the UK, some pubs and restaurants have reportedly banned the devices, while in Germany, rights advocacy group HateAid has lodged a complaint to German prosecutors against Meta and other companies, claiming such devices breach the country's covert recording laws.
Ms Stilinovic wants camera glasses temporarily banned in Australia.
"I would suggest that we stop the rollout of smart glasses until regulation and policymakers have caught up to keep societies safe,"
Watch 7.30, Mondays to Thursdays at 7:30pm on ABC iview and ABC TV

Majority of South Koreans view US 'unfavorably,' 1st time in over 20 years: Survey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
07:04:30 UTC
16:04:30 KST

Aamir Latif
25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
For the first time in over two decades, a majority of South Koreans have an unfavorable opinion of the US, a survey showed.
Some 55% of the participants expressed an unfavorable opinion of the US, up from 39% last year, according to the survey conducted by the Washington-based Pew Research Center.
The survey, released Monday, revealed that 18% of respondents had a "very unfavorable view," up from 9% in 2025.
Fewer than half of South Koreans, 45%, have a favorable view of the US, marking a 16-point drop from 61% last year, and a 35-point drop from 2018, the second year of US President Donald Trump’s first term, when it stood at 80%.
The US has some 39,000 soldiers deployed in South Korea under a defense treaty with Seoul, according to Trump, who recently ordered the Pentagon to scale back annual joint military exercises with South Korea.
In response, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung reiterated his push for military independence from Washington.
Around six in 10 South Korean adults, 57%, consider the US a reliable partner. That’s down from 83% in 2022, during the Joe Biden administration.
There has also been a decrease in the share of South Koreans who think the US takes into account the interests of countries like their own when making international policy decisions. This year, 21% of South Koreans think the US does this a great deal or a fair amount. That’s down from 38% in 2023.
The share of South Koreans who say that Washington contributes a great deal or a fair amount to peace and stability around the world has also fallen, from 74% in 2023 to 47% this year.
Only 14% approve of Trump's handling of tariffs. Earlier this year, Trump threatened to raise tariffs on South Korean goods to 25% if the country’s legislature did not approve a proposed trade deal.
The South Korean parliament later approved the deal.
Around three-quarters of South Koreans disapprove of the way Trump is dealing with Iran. That includes nearly half, 47%, who strongly disapprove.
Despite viewing Washington less favorably this year, South Koreans still overwhelmingly name the US as their country’s most important ally. This share has decreased slightly since last year, 84% compared to 89%.

Uganda's Gaza 'stabilisation force' plan sparks debate in Africa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
07:04:24 UTC
16:04:24 KST

Breadcrumb
Uganda's participation in Gaza 'stabilisation force' sparks debate in Africa
Uganda's parliament approved the deployment of army troops to the" International Stabilisation Force" in the Gaza Strip at the beginning of August as part of US President Donald Trump's plan. The move marks the first official declaration by an African country of its readiness to participate in Gaza.
The approval came on 6 August after Ugandan Defence Minister Kiria Kiwanuka told lawmakers that Trump had asked President Yoweri Museveni in July for Uganda to contribute to the proposed international force in Gaza.
After the Ugandan parliament's approval, a Ugandan soldier in military uniform posted a video on social media in which he appeared alongside the words, "Gaza, we are coming", indicating that the idea of a military deployment had begun circulating within Uganda's military and media circles.
The Ugandan government has not yet specified the number of troops it may deploy to the territory or when they would be sent.
Israel's public broadcaster reported last Monday, 17 August, that senior officers from Uganda and Burundi had arrived at the US command headquarters in Kiryat Gat in the occupied Palestinian territories as part of advanced talks with the two countries to send hundreds of soldiers to the territory as part of the multinational stabilisation force.
The broadcaster also said last Thursday, 20 August, that Morocco had been chosen to train members of the force.
Ugandan forces in the Gaza stabilisation force has sparked debate inside the Ugandan parliament, with opposition lawmakers calling for more information about the nature of the mission, the number of troops, its funding, and the guarantees provided to soldiers and their families.
The opposition also warned of the security and political risks associated with sending troops to a devastated territory and under highly complex field conditions.
Uganda has extensive experience in peacekeeping operations, particularly in Africa, where its forces participate in missions in Somalia, South Sudan and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
The defence minister cited this experience to justify the Ugandan army's ability to participate in a new international mission.
Without African backing
The decision has also raised questions about Kampala's approval of it and whether it has broad African backing or bypasses African consensus by being taken without Uganda consulting its partners in the African Union.
The African Union has consistently supported the Palestinian cause in principle and calls for the implementation of a two-state solution.
However, Israel has built relations with several African countries over decades, viewing the continent as an arena of Arab-Israeli competition.
In 2021, the union accepted Israel as an "observer member", a move that prompted Palestinian and Arab protests and was later revoked.
Uganda's relations with Israel, meanwhile, have continued to grow.
The Ugandan judge Julia Sebutinde, vice-president of the International Court of Justice, has attracted attention after she was described as believing that "God relies on her to stand with Israel". Sebutinde opposed the six rulings imposed by the court in 2024 to protect Palestinians and stop the genocide in Gaza.
Ugandan military leadership also recently said that any attempts to "destroy" Israel, amid the US-Israeli war on Iran, could prompt Uganda to intervene in support of the occupying state.
Uganda is also one of the largest importers of military technology and spyware from the occupying state.
In this context, Sudanese writer and researcher Abbas Saleh, who is based in the Ethiopian capital Addis Ababa, told The New Arab that Uganda's potential participation in the proposed international force for the Gaza Strip reflects a renewed predicament facing the African Union.
Decisions and positions adopted by the continental organisation often appear non-binding on member states, which may adopt unilateral policies that conflict with the union's collective positions.
"Despite the clear positions adopted by the African Union on the Palestinian cause, its rejection of Israeli violations and its repeated calls for an end to the war and the protection of civilians, the involvement of some member states in international security arrangements linked to Gaza could weaken the unity of the African position and expose the organisation's limited ability to turn its political positions into practical commitments by its members," he pointed out.
According to Saleh, Uganda is among the countries whose name has for years been associated with a broad security and military role in Africa, as well as close relations with Western powers, particularly in the Great Lakes region and the Horn of Africa.
He explained that this role "has given it a prominent position in several regional security issues but has at times made its foreign policy a subject of debate over the extent to which its decisions are independent of the calculations of international powers".
"The Ugandan move is significant beyond the participation of a single country, as it could set a precedent encouraging other countries that had been hesitant or reluctant to join the proposed international force, particularly if they are provided with appropriate political and security guarantees or international incentives," Saleh opined.
He stressed that participation in a military mission inside Gaza carries significant risks, given the complexities of the security and political situation, continuing disagreements over the future of the territory and governance and security arrangements, and the sensitivity surrounding the presence of foreign forces in the Palestinian territories.
"Uganda's move places the African Union before a difficult test: how can the organisation maintain a unified African position on the Palestinian cause while each member state has broad scope to make its foreign and security decisions independently?" he added. "The union's ability to deal with these contradictions could be an important indicator of the effectiveness of its political positions, not only towards Palestine, but also towards international crises affecting the continent and the interests of its countries."
Contradictions, differences
Meanwhile, researcher on Sahel and Sahara affairs Mohamed Torshin told The New Arab that the participation of Ugandan forces in the peace process in Gaza clearly reflects the scale of contradictions within the African Union and its limited ability to impose or implement decisions taken collectively, whether at the level of the AU Commission, the Peace and Security Council or the General Assembly.
Although African Union decisions and collective positions are supposed to form a common political framework for member states, the Ugandan position, along with other previous cases, reveals clear differences in the positions of African countries towards several sensitive regional and international issues.
In many cases, these differences push some countries or regional blocs to adopt policies and approaches that conflict with the union's collective position.
According to Torshin, the repercussions are not limited to a particular issue but extend to the effectiveness of African decision-making in general.
When a member state, in his view, adopts a position that clearly contradicts the union's collective position, this weakens the organisation's ability to present itself as a unified political actor and limits its ability to exercise diplomatic influence on issues requiring a coherent continental position.
In this context, Torshin noted that the repetition of such cases could widen the gap between decisions issued by African Union institutions and the policies pursued by some member states at the national level.
"This would gradually weaken the ability of the AU Commission and its political bodies to turn collective positions and decisions into effective and binding policies, making African decision-making more vulnerable to fragmentation and differences between countries and regional blocs," he added.
Torshin pointed out that the lack of protocol and political coordination between different African countries, ministries and institutions, and the absence of unified positions and decisions on common issues, could create space for international parties with interests and programmes in Africa to deal with countries individually and implement their policies and projects according to their own interests, away from the collective frameworks and decisions of the African Union.
He argued that "as this divergence and the multiplicity of positions within the continental organisation continue, international powers may find themselves with greater room to manoeuvre and negotiate with African countries bilaterally, gradually weakening the union's ability to formulate and defend a unified African agenda".
"In the long term, the continuation of this fragmentation could affect the future of African integration, making the implementation of continental policies and projects more closely tied to the interests of countries and external partners, and less subject to the collective vision that the union is supposed to represent," Torshin warned.

OnlyFans owner Radvin̦skiy received $700 million in dividends before his death - FT
Kyiv • UNN
OnlyFans revenue grew to $1.6 billion, while profit rose to $715 million. Owner Leonid Radvin̦skiy received more than $700 million in dividends.
OnlyFans paid more than $700 million in dividends to its owner before his death earlier this year, according to the annual accounts of the British streaming platform, which will be filed in the UK this week, the Financial Times reports, writes UNN.
Details
"The results of Fenix International, which owns the British streaming platform used by sex-industry workers, show that revenue rose by one-tenth to $1.6 billion in the year to November 2025, while pretax profit increased by 5 percent to $715 million. The highly productive business has just 47 employees," the publication writes.
Most of the profit in the 2025 accounts reportedly "went in the form of dividends to its owner, Ukrainian-American entrepreneur Leonid Radvinsky, who died of cancer in the spring." His death preceded the sale of a 16 percent stake in the business to San Francisco-based private investment firm Architect Capital in April for $535 million, giving the company a valuation of $3.2 billion.
According to the company's accounts, "Radvinsky was paid $535 million in dividends in the 2025 financial year, compared with $497 million the year before. However, according to the accounts, a further $174 million was paid in several installments after the end of the financial year."
Some Wall Street advisers considered the sale valuation low for such a profitable company, which was attributed to investors' reluctance to participate in the business, the publication notes.
In 2025, the total number of creator accounts on OnlyFans grew by 9 percent to 5 million, while the number of fan accounts worldwide increased by 16 percent to 437 million.
Of the 5 million creator accounts, 2.5 million were classified as "active" because they were used during the financial year ending November 30, 2025, while there were 132 million active fan accounts.
Last year, creators were paid approximately $6.2 billion after OnlyFans took its 20 percent share of their revenue. The total amount paid to creators now stands at $30 billion since the platform was founded in 2016.
The site also hosts other creators, such as actors, musicians and sports stars, who seek to earn money directly from fans, often in exchange for accepting requests for certain types of content.
The reports, which will be filed with the UK corporate registry Companies House this week, confirm that the group is now controlled by a family trust headed by Kateryna Chudnovska, Radvinsky's widow.
OnlyFans is marking its tenth anniversary, having been founded in 2016 by British entrepreneur Tim Stokely and his father Guy, and then sold to Radvinsky in 2018. It remains based in the UK.
OnlyFans Chief Executive Officer Keily Blair said: "In the 10 years since the platform launched in 2016, OnlyFans has paid more than $30 billion to creators worldwide, including more than $1 million to over 5,000 creators. As a British business, we have also made a significant contribution to the UK economy, paying more than £600 million in corporate taxes from 2016 to the present."
The group's largest market is the US, where it generated $965 million in revenue in the latest financial year. The UK and Europe contributed $347 million, while the rest of the world contributed $241 million.

Poland receives first K2 tanks from new $6.5B deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
07:02:20 UTC
16:02:20 KST

- Poland received 28 K2 tanks, the first delivery from an August 2025 contract with Hyundai Rotem, assigning them to the 16th Mechanized Division.
- Future batches under the contract will include the K2PL variant, with 61 of 64 units to be assembled in Poland using domestic components.
Poland has received its first batch of tanks from a second, $6.5 billion contract with South Korea’s Hyundai Rotem, Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said Tuesday.
Twenty-eight K2 tanks arrived in Poland and will go to the 16th Mechanized Division, he said.
The contract was signed August 1, 2025, and covers 180 additional tanks. It follows an earlier deal for 180 K2GF tanks that Poland completed receiving in November 2025.
Kosiniak-Kamysz said the tanks delivered in this batch are standard K2 models, and that future shipments under the same contract will include the K2PL variant, a Polish-modified version built in part from domestically produced components. The second contract calls for 116 K2GF tanks between 2026 and 2027, followed by 64 K2PL tanks between 2028 and 2030. Of those K2PL tanks, 61 are set to be assembled in Poland at the Bumar-Łabędy plant in Gliwice, which belongs to the state-owned defense group PGZ.
The K2 Black Panther is a South Korean third-generation main battle tank armed with a 120 mm smoothbore gun and an autoloader. It also carries a 7.62 mm machine gun and a 12.7 mm heavy machine gun.
Kosiniak-Kamysz described the delivery as a step that expands Poland’s domestic production capacity and strengthens the country’s defense posture, tying the arrival of the K2PL variant to the broader technology-transfer terms of the contract.
The 16th Pomeranian Mechanized Division, based in northeastern Poland, has been the primary recipient of K2 tanks under the earlier contract, which equipped the 20th Bartoszyce Mechanized Brigade, the 9th Braniewo Armored Cavalry Brigade and the 15th Giżycko Mechanized Brigade. Six additional tanks from that contract went to the Land Forces Training Center in Poznań.
The second contract, worth roughly $6.5 billion, also includes 81 support vehicles based on the K2 chassis: 25 combat engineering vehicles, 25 armored bridge layers and 31 armored recovery vehicles, along with ammunition, a logistics and training package, and technology transfer. Brigadier General Artur Kuptel, head of Poland’s Armament Agency, signed the agreement on the Polish side at the Bumar-Łabędy facility, with Hyundai Rotem CEO Lee Yong-Bae signing for the South Korean company.
Poland’s tank purchases from South Korea are part of a broader rearmament effort that has included M1A2 SEPv3 Abrams tanks from the United States and continued operation of Leopard 2 tanks acquired from Germany. Poland had roughly 117 M1A2 SEPv3 tanks delivered as of early 2026. Officials have said Poland aims to field around 900 tanks across the three platforms by 2030, which would make it one of the largest tank fleets in Europe.

America proposes new US$103,265 H-1B visa fee, expanding charge beyond new arrivals
The extra upfront cost of hiring skilled foreign workers could make it far less attractive to sponsor Chinese and Indian professionals
The US Department of Homeland Security proposed the additional fee on Monday for every H-1B petition subject to the annual numerical cap of 85,000 visas. That figure includes the 20,000 visas reserved for people holding US master’s degrees or higher. Employers would pay the new charge when filing a petition, on top of existing fees.
Universities and certain non-profit or government research organisations would be exempt.
The new measure would also go further than an earlier one. A US$100,000 fee imposed by presidential proclamation in September 2025 mainly targeted new H-1B arrivals from overseas.
The US$103,265 charge would apply more broadly, including to cap-subject petitions filed for people already in the US seeking a change of status.
That means the new policy could have an impact on many international students working in the US under Optional Practical Training.

Finnish satellite firm ICEYE launches India subsidiary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
06:57:36 UTC
15:57:36 KST

- ICEYE formally established ICEYE India in New Delhi on August 24 to serve the country's defense and intelligence customers.
- The company plans to build satellite manufacturing capability in India using local suppliers and engineering talent, though no timeline has been disclosed.
ICEYE, the Finnish satellite operator, has formally established a corporate entity in New Delhi called ICEYE India, the company announced August 24. The move gives ICEYE a direct legal and operational presence in a market it has been supplying for several years without a local subsidiary.
ICEYE operates the world’s largest constellation of synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellites, a form of imaging that uses radar rather than visible light to capture ground data. SAR imagery works through cloud cover and at night, which sets it apart from optical satellite systems.
The company said ICEYE India’s immediate focus is giving Indian defense and intelligence customers access to its satellite imagery and related intelligence products. ICEYE also said it plans to engage more broadly with India’s space and defense sector through supply-chain participation, technology validation and local capability building.
The New Delhi entity will also serve as the base for ICEYE’s manufacturing plans in India. The company said it intends to build production capability in-country, drawing on local suppliers and engineering talent, to serve Indian defense, surveillance and environmental monitoring customers. ICEYE did not disclose a timeline, investment figure or planned facility location for that manufacturing effort.
“ICEYE India means real engineering and manufacturing capability on the ground. We’re excited to build this together with the government and local partners and to support India as it strengthens its own sovereign intelligence capability,” said Rafal Modrzewski, CEO and co-founder of ICEYE.
The company said it is exploring collaboration with Indian launch providers, electronics and component manufacturers, and other technology partners, without naming specific firms or agreements.
India has been building out its own space-based surveillance capacity, and the government has pushed a policy of domestic defense manufacturing under its Aatmanirbhar Bharat, or self-reliant India, initiative. ICEYE said its approach of building local industrial capability in each country it enters aligns with those goals.
The Indian subsidiary follows a similar move by ICEYE in Germany last month, where the company also set up a national entity. National subsidiaries have become a common structure among Western satellite and defense firms seeking to bid on government contracts that require some form of sovereign or in-country control.
ICEYE has built its business around small, relatively low-cost SAR satellites that can be deployed in larger numbers than traditional radar satellites, allowing more frequent revisits of a given location. The company’s satellites currently offer imagery resolution as fine as 16 cm.
ICEYE has supplied SAR satellites to Brazil’s Air Force since 2020 and provided tactical satellite imagery to Ukraine following Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. In 2025, the company signed a deal worth roughly $200 million with Poland covering radar satellites and ground infrastructure.

More porters, fewer passengers: What really caused Ben-Gurion Airport’s staff strike? - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
06:57:19 UTC
15:57:19 KST

Since the recent wildcat strike at Ben Gurion Airport, staffing at the Israel Airports Authority (IAA) has become the main flashpoint between management and the workers' union.
The union points to a critical deficit of roughly 500 employees across all departments, arguing that an unreasonable workload ultimately triggered the system's collapse. Union Chairman Pinchas Idan claimed there are simply not enough porters to handle luggage loading and unloading, forcing staff into grueling, consecutive 12-hour shifts in unbearable heat under inhumane conditions. He added that the severe shortage is exacerbated by employees serving on active military reserve duty.
The numbers tell a different story
Anyone spending ten minutes outside at midday can sympathize with the grueling physical strain of hauling heavy baggage between aircraft and luggage carts in the summer heat. However, data obtained by Walla reveals a contrasting picture: The number of porters at Ben Gurion Airport has actually grown over the past six years, even as overall passenger traffic declined.
The baseline for comparison is 2019, widely regarded as a peak year for passenger volume at Ben Gurion. In August 2019, 2.807 million passengers passed through the airport, serviced by a workforce of 386 porters. By comparison, August 2026 is projected to see approximately 2.675 million passengers, whereas the porter workforce has expanded to 402. This reflects a net addition of 16 porters alongside a decrease of roughly 130,000 passengers.
Furthermore, a source familiar with the matter told Walla that the union never formally submitted a written request to management regarding a worker shortage.
"A union always wants more workers, and that's fine," says a source familiar with the matter. "But in this case, there is no shortage of porters because there are actually more of them. Besides, operational needs on the ground are no justification for shutting down a country."
The workers' union firmly rejects these assertions, insisting that continuous appeals were submitted to management over two months ago.
Tenured vs. temporary staffing friction
However, another source suggests the core issue stems not from total headcount, but from an imbalance between tenured and temporary staff: "In 2019, there were more temporary porters at Ben Gurion Airport. Over the years, the proportion of tenured staff increased while temporary staff declined. Temporary workers experience less burnout, are more flexible, and show higher motivation, whereas tenured staff are less willing to work. The operational model needs an overhaul - something that must be executed in cooperation with the workers' union."
Despite that structural challenge, the likelihood of Idan permitting a shift from tenured positions toward temporary hiring appears virtually non-existent - particularly amid reports that management intends to push for his removal as union chief.
Chairman of the Israel Airports Authority Yiftah Ron-Tal declined to confirm any efforts to oust Idan from leadership. "I am currently focused on managing the crisis and am not dealing with that," he says. "I have established an inquiry team to investigate the incident and draw conclusions."

"Steps must be taken to prevent these acts from the start and protect Palestinian residents," he added.
Golan removes post calling for Sukkot's arrest

During the tour, residents shouted insults at Sukkot, including calling him "a complete zero" and asking, "What do you have to teach our children?" He was called a "provocateur" and told, "In Rahat? Go teach yourself."

Ben-Gurion management knew about employee shortages before crisis, IAA union rep. says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
06:57:00 UTC
15:57:00 KST

Ben-Gurion Airport management had known for months about the employee shortage, which led to the recent severe disruptions earlier this month, Attorney Naomi Landau, who represents the Israel Airports Authority (IAA) employees’ union, said on the 103FM program Where’s the Money on Monday.
At the beginning of the discussion, Yael Ayalon, editor of Where’s the Money, addressed how the disruptions began and the Histadrut labor federation’s involvement.
According to her, "this time, these labor disruptions were initiated by or coordinated between the workers’ union and employees on the ground. The Histadrut discovered the dispute and the chaos only after it had already started. Although it gave formal support to the move, even in the official statement by the Histadrut chairman that same day, during the first hours of the chaos, it was stated that no such instruction or directive had been issued by the Histadrut for a strike or labor dispute."
Ayalon also addressed the lack of an official labor dispute declaration, saying that, "The Histadrut chairman was abroad; the Histadrut was on recess. The chairman of the transportation workers’ union was also abroad. That does not prevent them from intervening, but the most significant point is that despite the Histadrut speaking out about the manpower shortage, it did not declare the issue a labor dispute. Essentially, the workers’ union had limited abilities from the outset, and it could not legally launch a strike, which is what happened in practice."
Later, Attorney Landau joined the conversation and sought to demonstrate that the manpower shortage at Ben-Gurion Airport had been known for months. She quoted remarks made by Pinchas Idan last May, when he said, "I don’t know how we will get through August; we need another 400 workers. I say with full responsibility, there will probably be lines in the coming period. Management is doing everything to recruit. But right now, many more workers are still missing."
Management faced difficulties recruiting for Ben-Gurion, despite known shortages
Landau argued that additional officials within the Airports Authority had also warned about the shortage in advance, emphasizing how difficult it was the recruit workers for the required positions. "The heads of departments warned about this, absolutely," she added.
"I am already saying that management tried to recruit, and it is very difficult to recruit workers for these positions during this period. These are challenging jobs, because being a baggage handler or a firefighter at Ben-Gurion Airport during this period is very difficult. In addition, even if workers are recruited, they must undergo training, complete additional requirements, and receive security clearance to work there."
Landau then pointed the finger at the Israel Airports Authority management, claiming that the decision that led to the closure of the counters was made by management.
"Management panicked," she said, further explaining that "once those 18 workers collapsed and left after nine hours of work in the heat, instead of moving other workers from other areas of the airport who could provide support, management decided to close the counters, and only management has the authority to do that. Pinchas himself was shocked by the matter."
Airport workers' union preferred negotiation over dispute
Landau also addressed why the workers’ union did not declare a labor dispute, claiming that Idan initially preferred to negotiate with management. According to her, "We considered it, and Pinchas decided to negotiate with management. He received promises. You do not enter a labor dispute so easily, because once you enter one, there is only one path that leads to a strike, and then the workers say, 'What did you do to me?' Pinchas Idan did not want to close the airport. What exactly would closing it in August give him? What would it give the workers’ union? It gives them absolutely nothing."
At the end of the interview, Landau addressed efforts to recruit additional workers and the dispute over responsibility for the events. "Management announced that it is recruiting nearly 100 workers who are currently on unpaid leave and will fill the ranks," she added.
"And still, even when there is a fully staffed shift, there is still a manpower shortage under these conditions. There was no strike, and the ones who closed the counters were management. There was no dispute between management and the workers, except that management claimed there was no shortage of workers."

North Macedonia has made strengthening relations with Israel a priority of its foreign policy and is seeking to expand cooperation in areas ranging from defense and investment to tourism and water management, Foreign Minister Timčo Mucunski told The Jerusalem Post during his first official visit to Israel.

Mucunski said the trend reflects a deliberate policy adopted by the government of Prime Minister Hristijan Mickoski.
Mickoski believes in stronger collaboration with Israel
“Prime Minister Mickoski himself believes that stronger collaboration with Israel is a necessity for our country to also be successful,” he said. “There are many things that we can learn from you. There are many common values that we share, both domestically and internationally.
“Since the formation of our government, we have made the bilateral relationship with Israel one of the priorities of our foreign policy,” he added.
Mucunski said he and Sa’ar communicate “on a fairly regular basis” and have remained in frequent contact despite Monday marking his first visit to the country.
Sa’ar, meanwhile, thanked North Macedonia for standing alongside Israel in international forums, particularly since the October 7 massacre.
“North Macedonia has demonstrated its friendship by standing up to these attempts in the international arena,” Sa’ar said. “We appreciate its voting record and its support for Israel. Israel values its friends who stand by it in difficult times.”
For Mucunski, one example of the relationship came following the deadly nightclub fire in Kočani in March 2025, which left 63 people dead, when Israel dispatched a medical delegation to Macedonia to help treat victims.
“Gideon Sa’ar was one of the first foreign ministers to call me,” Mucunski recalled. “I might not remember the content of the call, but I remember what happened very quickly after.”
A team of Israeli doctors arrived shortly afterward and began working alongside Macedonian medical teams, he said.
“They were performing surgery in our hospitals and helping our doctors with their experience and their in-depth knowledge, and helping to save the lives of many young individuals,” Mucunski said. “This situation was proof that Israel stands by my country.”
A European gateway for Israelis
Mucunski said North Macedonia now hopes to position itself as a destination not only for Israeli tourists but also for Israeli companies seeking access to European markets.
“We want to be a gateway for Israelis who want to visit Europe,” he said. “But we want to be a gateway not just for tourists, but also for Israeli businesses.”
He pointed to Macedonia’s position along two major European transport corridors, investment in energy connectivity, and its efforts to attract foreign investment.
“We can also be a gateway for Israelis who want to invest in a European market that hasn’t been fully utilized by the Israeli business community,” Mucunski said.
Monday’s visit lasted only around 24 hours, but Mucunski said he expected it to be the first of more visits to Israel.
“This is my first visit,” he said, “but I am absolutely sure that it will not be my last.”
The Jerusalem Post will publish a longer, in-depth interview with Foreign Minister Timčo Mucunski later this week.

President says Syria ‘shakes off dark stain’ with removal from US terror list
DAMASCUS – Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa hailed early on Aug 25 the United States’ removal of his country from the state sponsors of terror list, a major sanctions relief step.
“Today, Syria shakes off a dark stain and tears away a painful chapter of its past to embark on a path of development, reconstruction and rebuilding,” Sharaa said in a speech.
Washington’s decision on Aug 24 rescinded a decades-old designation that came with severe economic restrictions, marking another step in warming ties between the countries following the 2024 ouster of long-time Syrian ruler Bashar al-Assad.
The Treasury Department announced corresponding sanctions relief.
Sharaa expressed his “many thanks to the President of the United States of America, Donald Trump, and to all the friendly and supportive nations that stood by us”.
The US Department of State also revoked its designation of the al-Nusra Front – latterly known as Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham (HTS) – as a global terrorist organisation. Sharaa led that group, which spearheaded the blitz offensive that toppled Assad.
It was formerly the branch of Al-Qaeda in Syria before breaking ties with it in 2016.
Syria’s new authorities are trying to attract investment to support the country and rebuild its infrastructure, heavily damaged by more than a decade of civil war.
The United States had initially announced in July its intent to delist Syria as a state sponsor of terrorism, a move seen as a vote of confidence in Sharaa.
The Aug 24 move gave Syria’s “a path to prosperity”, according to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
The action “eliminates the final major barriers for private sector investment in Syria and promotes Syria’s economic recovery and reintegration into the global economy”, he said in a statement.
Syrian Foreign Minister Assad al-Shaibani described Washington’s delisting as a “historic milestone” and said it reflected “the new Syrian state’s commitment to international peace and security”.
Finance Minister Mohammed Barnieh described the move as a “success for Syrian diplomacy”, according to the official news agency SANA.
It “opens a major and long-awaited door to strengthening Syria’s integration into the global economic and financial system, attracting investment and modern technologies, and supporting development opportunities”. AFP
