Millions of Teslas recalled in China over door handle safety
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
06:30:27 UTC
15:30:27 KST

People work on the Tesla Model Y production line at the Tesla Gigafactory assembly plant during a media organized tour, in Shanghai, China (AP Photo)
Tesla is recalling nearly three million cars in China with interior door handles that could hamper a person's ability to exit their vehicle in an emergency, Beijing's national market watchdog said.
Eight Chinese carmakers also filed recalls over similar safety risks, China's State Administration for Market Regulation (SAMR) announced on Aug. 21.
Some recalls were effective immediately, while others began over the weekend and on Aug. 24.
Tesla's recall involves 2.9 million domestically-made units of its Model 3 and Model Y electric cars and begins on September 25.
The U.S. carmaker — which operates a huge factory in Shanghai — is also recalling around 46,000 imported units of its Model 3, Model X and Model S cars, the SAMR announcement said.
The recalled cars have inner emergency mechanical handles "similar in color to the interior, making them difficult to identify and operate" in emergencies, the watchdog said.
In Tesla's Model 3, for example, passengers must reach into a compartment inside the door pocket and find a release cable to manually open the rear door, according to the company's website.
"In extreme situations such as severe collisions causing the vehicle's low-voltage system to fail, (the handles) may affect passengers' ability to quickly open car doors for escape and rescue operations outside the vehicle," SAMR said.
SAMR said Tesla was separately recalling 2.7 million domestically-made Model 3 and Model Y EVs over issues with monitoring systems while a driver is using steering assist functions.
It was not clear whether some Teslas were counted in both recalls.
Chinese EV makers including Xiaomi, XPeng, Geely, Chery and Leapmotor are also recalling cars with handles that blend in with their interior.
Xiaomi began recalling around 390,000 units of its 2024 SU7 series on Aug. 21, and XPeng started recalling nearly 265,000 cars on Aug. 22.
Beijing-based BAIC BluePark, a subsidiary of state-owned automaker BAIC, on Aug. 22 began recalling around 46,000 Arcfox Kaola EVs over a "lack of dedicated text prompts" near the emergency mechanism on its right rear sliding door.
Beginning on Aug. 24, Geely is recalling around 92,000 cars from its luxury brand Zeekr.
Companies offered to attach warning labels near the handles for free, and some said they would remotely upgrade software involving lowering windows after a crash.
Safety concerns have risen in China recently over sleek car designs that are prone to losing operability in the event of a crash.
The mass recalls are in line with China's plan to ban hidden door handles on cars from January 1, 2027, local media reports said.
Those rules, announced in February by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, will require door handles to have both interior and exterior mechanical releases.
Electronic door handles were introduced with Tesla's 2012 launch of the Model S, later becoming popular with Chinese EV brands prioritising high-tech features.
Folding into the body of the car, such door handles provide a slight boost to efficiency by reducing drag while the vehicle is in motion.

NASA finds Earth microbes could survive on the Moon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
06:30:18 UTC
15:30:18 KST

NASA finds Earth microbes could survive on the Moon
- Date:
- August 25, 2026
- Source:
- NASA
- Summary:
- NASA scientists found that microbes brought by astronauts could survive in cold, shadowed niches around the Moon’s South Pole, potentially complicating future searches for pristine lunar chemistry. Some refuges may be no larger than a footprint, while one hardy fungus could even withstand limited exposure to sunlight.
- Share:
NASA scientists say some microbes carried into space by human explorers may be able to survive in sheltered, shadowed areas near the Moon's South Pole.
The findings, published on Aug. 19, 2026, in Science Advances, underscore the importance of understanding how long Earth microbes can persist in extreme lunar environments. As people establish a more permanent presence on the Moon, contamination from astronauts could make it harder for scientists to separate ancient lunar chemistry from material introduced by humans. Researchers say the same issue will matter when missions eventually search for signs of life on Mars.
"Humans are natural explorers, and with them come their voices, their memories … and their microbes," said Prabal Saxena, a planetary scientist who led the study from NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland. "For some scientists, myself included, that reality can be unsettling. But it also creates an opportunity to turn an imperfect situation into a useful experiment."
Microbial Hitchhikers Are Unavoidable
Humans inevitably carry microbes with them. On average, about 1 million bacteria live on every patch of skin roughly the size of a pencil eraser. Some of these organisms can escape from spacesuits and habitats into the surrounding environment.
That creates a challenge for scientists hoping to study chemical evidence connected to the Moon's ancient geology or possible biology. At the same time, the researchers argue that the Moon could serve as a valuable natural laboratory. Carefully monitored shadowed regions near the South Pole could allow scientists to test the real limits of microbial survival under conditions that are extremely difficult to reproduce on Earth.
Before those experiments can begin, however, researchers need to establish a clear baseline showing what contaminants humans introduce.
"We need to understand what was there before us, because when we go to Mars to search for signs of life beyond our planet, we will want to make sure it's not stuff we brought," said Andrew Needham, a NASA Goddard-based paper co-author who is an Artemis contamination-control scientist for lunar samples.
Some Microbes Are Surprisingly Tough
Even rigorous sterilization cannot eliminate every hardy organism. One example is Aspergillus niger, a fungus that commonly grows in warm, humid environments such as bathrooms and heating, ventilation, and air conditioning systems.
Astronauts have collected samples of the fungus aboard the International Space Station, and previous experiments have shown that it can also survive outside the station. Aspergillus niger was one of five microbes examined in the new study because of its demonstrated resilience in spaceflight conditions.
Scientists were surprised that microbes like these could endure exposure on the exterior of the space station. According to Aaron Regberg, a geomicrobiologist at NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston, these organisms are not usually classified as "extremophiles" capable of surviving conditions such as the vacuum of space.
"I would have expected these microbes to have dried out," said Regberg, who studies space station bacteria and was a co-author on the paper.
NASA can reduce biological contamination on robotic spacecraft by heating them to more than 400 degrees Fahrenheit. That approach is not possible for crewed missions, which means microbial contamination becomes a much more complicated issue when astronauts explore the Moon's south polar region.
Why Lunar Shadows Matter
To determine where microbes might survive, researchers first examined the unusual way sunlight reaches the lunar poles. In this study, survival means that a microbe remains alive for at least one Earth day. It does not mean the organism is able to grow or reproduce.
Because the Moon has only a slight axial tilt, the Sun appears to stay very close to the horizon when viewed from the poles. Its light sweeps across the surface almost like a flashlight lying flat on a table.
That low angle means crater rims, mountains, ridges, and even small surface bumps can block sunlight from reaching lower terrain. The result is a patchwork of shadowed areas that can stay extremely cold, preserve water, and protect delicate molecules and potential microorganisms from damaging radiation.
Testing Microbes at the Lunar South Pole
Using that environment as a guide, the researchers examined which Earth microbes could potentially withstand conditions near the Moon's South Pole.
They selected organisms found in spaceflight settings as well as microbes commonly associated with humans. In addition to Aspergillus niger, the group included Bacillus subtilis, Staphylococcus aureus, Deinococcus radiodurans, and several species of Fusarium.
Drawing on an analysis of earlier research, the team determined how much heat and ultraviolet (UV) radiation each organism could tolerate.
The scientists then modeled conditions in three locations near the lunar South Pole -- Nobile Rim, Connecting Ridge, and De Gerlache Rim. The simulations relied on detailed maps of elevation and temperature generated from data collected by instruments aboard NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, along with models showing how radiation reaches the lunar surface.
Microbial Refuges as Small as a Boot Print
The resulting maps identified "survivable niches" ranging from crater floors several miles across to areas no larger than an astronaut's boot print.
Aspergillus niger proved especially resilient. Because it was the most resistant to UV radiation, the fungus could potentially survive even in locations exposed to some sunlight. UV radiation is deadly enough to many microorganisms that hospitals routinely use it for sterilization.
"When we think of the Moon, we don't typically think of biology," said Heather Graham, a paper co-author at NASA Goddard who helps develop tools and techniques for detecting biology that may look nothing like Earth's. "But the Moon is a place where a cell can survive, so our first exploration of these sites should pay extra attention to our microbial hitchhikers and work hard to characterize lunar chemistry before our visits change what we will find."
The researchers emphasize that surviving is not the same as thriving. Some microbes may remain dormant in protected regions near the South Pole and potentially complicate future scientific studies, but there is no evidence that the Moon provides the conditions needed for them to grow and reproduce.
Among the missing ingredients is liquid water, which generally depends on the presence of an atmosphere and moderate temperatures.

Journal Reference:
- Prabal Saxena, Stefano Bertone, Heather V. Graham, Natalie M. Curran, Aaron B. Regberg, Andrew Needham, D. E. (Betsy) Puge, Noah E. Petro. Potential survivable niches for microbial life on the lunar south pole. Science Advances, 2026; 12 (34) DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aec0811

Donald Judd’s Artillery Sheds in Texas to Undergo Major Restoration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
06:30:00 UTC
15:30:00 KST

The Chinati Foundation has announced plans to restore the Artillery Sheds in Marfa, Texas, the former military buildings adapted by artist Donald Judd to house his 100 untitled works in mill aluminum, created between 1982 and 1986. Led by architect Troy Schaum of Schaum Architects, the multi-year preservation project is being developed with the Getty Conservation Institute and will address the historic buildings' envelope, accessibility, environmental performance, and landscape while preserving Judd's site-specific installation. The project follows the Artillery Sheds' inclusion in the National Register of Historic Places in 2025 as part of the expanded Donald Judd Historic District.
Located on the grounds of the former Fort D.A. Russell at the northeastern edge of the Chihuahuan Desert, the Artillery Sheds were constructed in 1939 by the US Army Corps of Engineers for large-scale mechanical work. Judd began adapting the two structures in 1980, replacing their garage doors with quartered glass windows of his own design and adding curved Quonset hut-style roofs that doubled the buildings' exterior height. He finalized the placement of the 100 aluminum works in 1986, the year the Chinati Foundation was established.
The restoration will repair the roofs, gutters, and facades and introduce more than 10,000 square feet of energy-efficient glass to provide additional protection for the artworks from Marfa's extreme weather conditions. The project will also improve accessibility through updated paths and access points and introduce rainwater harvesting systems to support native grasses and the surrounding Chihuahuan Desert landscape.
Related Article
Stefano Boeri Architetti Converts Former Rome Transit Depot Into Multifunctional Civic Space
The project team is working to limit interventions that could alter the relationship between Judd's works and their architectural setting. "The real ingenuity of the restoration is maintaining Donald Judd's vision and editing around the edges," said Troy Schaum, describing an approach that incorporates low-energy mechanical systems and other discreet interventions into the existing buildings.
As part of the restoration, Judd's 100 aluminum works will be moved for the first time since their installation in the 1980s. The works will undergo extensive documentation and material analysis before being reinstalled after construction. Chinati's conservation team, led by Head of Conservation Bogna Skwara, is working with Alfred Lippincott, co-owner of Lippincott's LLC and one of the original fabricators of the works, as well as the Getty Conservation Institute.
The restoration forms part of Chinati's Art as Intended capital campaign, to support collection stewardship, infrastructure improvements, visitor experience, and long-term financial sustainability. The 39th annual Chinati Weekend, taking place October 9–11, 2026, will be among the final opportunities to view the Artillery Sheds and Judd's installation before construction begins. The buildings will remain closed to visitors throughout the multi-year restoration, while other permanent installations across the Chinati site will continue to be accessible.
In other renovation news, Herzog & de Meuron has been selected to revitalize Tirana's Palace of Congresses, a 1986 building designed during Albania's socialist period. In Turin, MVRDV and Balance Architettura have unveiled their proposal to renovate the 1959 Civic Gallery of Modern and Contemporary Art (GAM), introducing flexible exhibition systems and publicly accessible storage while restoring the museum's connection to the city. Meanwhile, Stefano Boeri Architetti will transform Rome's former Depositi delle Vittorie transport depot into a mixed-use complex combining cultural, educational, commercial, and leisure spaces with new public areas and landscaping.

Calcutta HC protects Abhishek Banerjee from arrest and allows overseas travel for medical treatment.
NEW DELHI: The Calcutta high court has clarified that Trinamool Congress MP Abhishek Banerjee can travel abroad for medical treatment, subject to the conditions permitted by the Supreme Court.The clarification came in connection with a travel restriction imposed on Banerjee in a case involving an allegedly provocative speech made during an election campaign.
The development comes after Banerjee approached the Calcutta high court seeking permission to travel overseas for eye treatment. He had sought relaxation of the restriction to allow him to stay abroad for about a week.The matter was placed before Justice Saugata Bhattacharyya.Separately, the Calcutta high court has granted Banerjee protection from arrest until November 30 in three FIRs registered against him.The cases come amid multiple proceedings involving the Diamond Harbour MP and Trinamool Congress national general secretary.The developments also come as the CID continues its investigation into a case involving Banerjee's alleged ‘DJ’ remark during an election campaign.
A Bidhannagar court on Tuesday allowed the CID to collect Banerjee's voice sample as part of the probe. The magistrate accepted the agency's plea and scheduled the collection for June 30.
Banerjee had moved the Calcutta high court earlier seeking permission to travel abroad for eye treatment.The travel plea relates to restrictions imposed by a single bench of the high court in connection with the case involving his alleged speech during election campaigning.The latest clarification allows Banerjee to undertake foreign travel for medical reasons within the framework already permitted by the Supreme Court.

Economist: De-dollarization became sustainable, long-term trend in Belarus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
06:28:00 UTC
15:28:00 KST

An archive photo
                    
                    MINSK, 25 August (BelTA) – De-dollarization in Belarus has become a sustainable and long-term trend confirmed by statistical data, economic analyst Yulia Abukhovich told BelTA.
Yulia Abukhovich noted that the ruble’s share in broad money hit 68.6% in August 2026, compared to 63.3% in 2025, whereas retail term deposits in the national currency surged by a record 40.3% year-on-year. Ruble-denominated debt accounts for over 80% of the banking sector’s credit portfolio, meaning businesses have minimal exposure to foreign currency loans.
“A combination of factors that will persist and even intensify over the medium term indicates that this process is both sustainable and long-term. Domestic enterprises are shifting away from the U.S. dollar and other Western currencies in their settlements. Driven by sanctions, they have transitioned their trade contracts to friendly currencies, primarily the Russian ruble and the Chinese yuan,” the economist noted. “Keeping dollars and euros in bank accounts carries infrastructure risks, including freezes by correspondent banks and blocked transactions. Furthermore, banks impose high commissions on foreign currency accounts and cross-border transfers via intermediaries, making the dollar economically unviable for businesses.”
The expert added that the population is also abandoning the U.S. dollar as a standard of value, turning en masse to ruble-denominated accounts to safeguard their wealth. Today, interest rates on long-term non-callable ruble deposits outpace annual inflation rate (which stood at 4.4% in July) by nearly three times, whereas foreign currency deposits offer a nominal 0.5–2% that is completely eroded by inflation.
Yulia Abukhovich pointed out that over the last few years, the dollar has experienced periods of depreciation, so hoarding the U.S. currency at home has resulted in net losses in purchasing power for citizens. “The state is phasing out foreign currency from domestic transactions, including this spring’s ban on foreign currency loans and ruble-denominated loans pegged to foreign currencies between private individuals. History demonstrates that successful de-dollarization is a multi-year process taking from 5 to 20 years. To make the economy and the public abandon foreign currencies, not just the U.S. dollar, there must be solid economic incentives: tamed inflation, high interest rates on deposits in the national currency, and the clear unprofitability of storing foreign cash,” the expert concluded.

Over the past day, 209 battles took place at the front, Russia carried out 3,200 attacks — General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
Over the past day, 209 combat engagements took place; the Russian Federation launched missile and air strikes and carried out more than 3,200 attacks. The enemy's losses amounted to 1,230 servicemen.
Over the past day, August 24, there were 209 combat engagements at the front. The enemy launched two missile strikes using three missiles and carried out 80 airstrikes, during which it dropped 234 guided aerial bombs. This was reported by UNN, citing the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
Details
In addition, the Russian invaders deployed 9,641 kamikaze drones and carried out 3,203 attacks on populated areas and positions of Ukrainian troops, 83 of them using multiple launch rocket systems.
The populated areas of Bachivsk, Korenok, Ryzhivka, Tolstodubove, Ulanove, Volfyne, Budky, Shpyl, Rohizne, Kuch erivka, Bezzalivka, Vyntorivka, Havrylova Sloboda, Starykove, Atynske, Vovkivka, Malushyne, Seredyna-Buda and Yastrubshchyna in Sumy region; and Yanzhulivka, Bohdanove and Kliusy in Chernihiv region came under artillery fire. Tolstodubove was hit by an airstrike.
The aviation, missile forces and artillery of the Defense Forces struck 11 areas where enemy personnel were concentrated, five artillery systems, a UAV command post and one other important enemy target.
On the North Slobozhanskyi axis, eight combat engagements were recorded over the past day. The enemy carried out 74 attacks on the positions of our troops and populated areas, seven of them using MLRS. The enemy also launched one airstrike, using two guided aerial bombs.
On the South Slobozhanskyi axis, Ukrainian units repelled 11 enemy attacks. The invaders attempted to advance toward the populated areas of Kozacha Lopan, Hoptivka, Starytsia, Radkivka and Zarubynka.
On the Kupiansk axis, the enemy conducted one offensive action toward Kurylivka.
Attempts to break into the Ukrainian defenses were repelled on the Lyman axis, where the occupiers attacked 14 times toward the populated areas of Lyman, Novoselivka, Dibrova, Drobesheve and near Olhivka.
On the Sloviansk axis, the enemy conducted ten assault operations in the areas of the populated areas of Kryva Luka, Zakitne, Dibrova and Riznykivka, and toward Rai-Oleksandrivka and Mykolaivka.
On the Kramatorsk axis, the Russian invaders conducted no offensive operations.
Nineteen attacks were recorded on the Kostiantynivka axis. The occupiers conducted assault operations in the areas of the populated areas of Kostiantynivka, Ivanopillia, Illinivka, Novoselivka and Hruzke, and toward the populated areas of Vilne and Kucheriv Yar.
The enemy carried out 22 attacks on the Pokrovsk axis. The occupiers attempted to advance toward the populated areas of Novyi Donbas, Dobropillia, Vilne, Novooleksandrivka, Serhiivka, Muravka and Novopavlivka, and in the areas of Rodynske, Myrne, Kotlyne, Udachne and Novomykolaivka.
On the Oleksandrivka axis, the enemy carried out four attacks in the areas of Novyi Zaporizhzhia, Andriivka-Klevtsove, Oleksandrohrad and Krasnohirskyi.
On the Huliaipole axis, the occupiers attacked the positions of our defenders nine times. The enemy attempted to advance in the areas of Rizdvianka, Rivne, Dolynka, Hirke, Danylivka and Lisne.
On the Orikhiv axis, Ukrainian defenders stopped two attempts by the enemy to advance near Novoiakovlivka.
On the Dnipro River axis, the enemy conducted no assault operations over the past day.
Over the past day, Russian invader casualties amounted to 1,230 personnel. Nine armored combat vehicles, 48 artillery systems, two multiple launch rocket systems, one air defense system, ten ground robotic systems, 1,555 unmanned aerial vehicles, 448 vehicles and seven units of the enemy's special equipment were also neutralized.

UK, EU missions in Dhaka stress Rohingya right to return to Myanmar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
06:21:59 UTC
15:21:59 KST

Sm Najmus Sakib
25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
On the ninth anniversary of the mass exodus of Rohingya to Bangladesh, 16 diplomatic missions, including those of the UK, Australia, Canada, and the EU, in Dhaka on Tuesday recalled the Rohingya's right to return to their home country, Myanmar.
Bangladesh has been sheltering about 1.2 million persecuted Rohingya on the southeastern Cox’s Bazar coast after they fled a brutal Myanmar military crackdown and started crossing the border on Aug. 25, 2017.
However, nine years after the mass exodus, conflict is escalating across Rakhine and humanitarian needs are rising, according to the foreign missions’ joint statement.
“Deepening insecurity, airstrikes on civilian infrastructure and the Myanmar authorities’ blockades on aid and trade are worsening the humanitarian crisis,” the statement said, marking Rohingya Genocide Remembrance Day, observed on Aug. 25.
This instability is driving further displacement into Bangladesh, and across the region, leading to tragic loss of life through dangerous sea crossings, it said, adding that these conditions do not currently allow for voluntary, safe, dignified, and sustainable repatriation.
They said conditions for Rohingya return will require a strategic, coordinated, and long-term approach to address the root causes of displacement, build trust between communities, and support greater peace and stability in Myanmar.
They also said they will continue to work with Bangladesh to find pathways toward building the conditions for repatriation.
“As this crisis enters its tenth year, we must ensure that the Rohingya people are not forgotten. We will continue to amplify the voices of Rohingya communities, pursue justice and accountability, and work with Bangladesh and international partners to sustain global support,” the statement added.

The Richmond Football Club says players were not "referencing or making light of recent matters" in videos circulating from the team's post-season celebrations.
Media camped outside the venue filmed players spanking each other on the rear.
The venue that hosted the Tigers for their Mad Monday drinks has lauded them for being "extremely respectful".
The Richmond Football Club has denied its players were "referencing or making light of recent matters" in footage recorded during their post-season celebrations.
Tiger players were recorded during a drinking session at a Victorian country pub, with one player seen feigning shock after being spanked on his rear by a teammate.
Another teammate whips a fellow player on the back with a belt in footage captured by news outlets yesterday, leading to speculation they were referencing the ongoing Sydney Swans scandal.
The club denied that was the case.
"Richmond is aware of a video circulating from a player end-of-season gathering," a statement read.
"The club has spoken to the players who have expressed their embarrassment over their behaviour.
"The players are adamant they were in no way referencing or making light of recent matters."
The Tigers finished second last this season with a 3-20 win-loss record.
The pub that hosted Richmond's drinks said the controversy had been blown out of proportion.
"In our view, this has been blown out of proportion," the Garfield Hotel, 80 kilometres east of Melbourne, said in a statement posted on social media.
The hotel said it "could not speak more highly" of how players behaved.
"For such a young group, they were extremely respectful and a fun group of boys to deal with," the statement read.
"They enjoyed a few quiet beers to unwind after a long season and we see nothing wrong with that.
"They had booked out the venue for the afternoon, so they were the only patrons on site.
"They enjoyed their afternoon and moved on."
The hotel noted media were waiting for the Tigers players "in the hope of capturing a misstep, which we consider disappointing".

Libya factions draft initial election pact amid lingering mistrust
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
06:10:49 UTC
15:10:49 KST

Libya factions draft initial election pact amid lingering mistrust
A newly-formed committee has signed a preliminary agreement, but divided state institutions and legal voids threaten its execution.
Libyan negotiators have agreed to an initial election pact aimed at ending years of political divisions within the country.
The agreement covers electoral laws and the restructuring of the national elections commission, moving the process toward a highly complex and delicate implementation phase, experts and officials told Al Jazeera.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Can US, Middle Eastern powers unite Libya 15 years after Gaddafi overthrow?
- list 2 of 4One geography, two states: Saudi Arabia’s security approach to Sudan
- list 3 of 4Libya rivals test a new path towards unity, 15 years after Gadaffi downfall
- list 4 of 4Libya’s brain drain, 15 years after Tripoli fell
Since 2014, Libya has been divided between two bitterly opposed administrations that separately control the east and west of the country, with repeated United Nations-led efforts to end the crisis.
Current negotiations have been conducted by a committee consisting of four representatives from the House of Representatives, based in eastern Libya, and four representatives from the High Council of State, linked to the internationally-recognised Government of National Unity in Tripoli.
The United Nations-backed ‘4+4 committee’ signed the initial draft in Tunis on August 20, with the challenge now in getting other parties in Libya on board.
Legal expert Al-Mahdi Kashbour told Al Jazeera that there appears to be a gap between the powers of the parties that signed the agreement and the institutions with the authority to implement it.
Libya political analyst Elias Al-Barouni stressed that the pact does not make any concrete plans for the country’s elections. Even if legal hurdles are cleared, the problem then shifts to who governs Libya in the interim, he added.
This could be the most difficult test yet for the peace process, as the transitional authority would control state resources and have to navigate a highly sensitive security environment.
Key Libyan legislative bodies and politicians have strong reservations about the negotiations. Among them is Nuh al-Malati, a member of the High Council of State, an advisory body for the Government of National Unity.
“The council has not yet received an official copy of the agreement that was reached… these changes do not enjoy consensus within the council,” he told Al Jazeera.
Al-Malati claimed that the Government of National Unity-linked members of the ‘4+4’ do not represent the official position of the council.
Mohamed al-Menfi, the leader of the Tripoli-based presidential council, also criticised the ambiguity surrounding the basis of the talks.
“The success of any consensus is linked to the clarity of its basis, its jurisdictions, and its applicability, especially when it comes to sovereign institutions like the elections commission,” al-Menfi wrote on X.
There appears to be equal scepticism about the arrangement from members of the eastern authority.
Khalifa al-Daghari, a member of the House of Representatives, told Al Jazeera that lawmakers in this grouping did not participate in choosing negotiating team members.
“[They] followed the details of the committee’s meetings and the course of its talks through the media and official statements, without receiving any direct briefing on what took place in them or their outcomes,” he added.
He also claimed there was “secrecy over its proceedings”, and that the House of Representatives “cannot therefore determine its position on the agreement before officially reviewing its text and outcomes”.
Still, United Nations spokesman Mohammad al-Asadi told Al Jazeera that the pact was an “important step and a conclusion to the negotiations on all points under discussion”.
Amid criticism over the alleged secrecy of the negotiations, al-Asadi said the document will be made publicly available after the final signing.

China’s new traffic safety law set to clarify liability for fully automated cars
Lawmakers are set to establish clear liability standards for self-driving cars, a move that could open the floodgates for next-gen vehicles
Beijing could soon hold carmakers legally responsible for traffic violations when autonomous driving systems are in use, marking an important step towards clearing regulatory hurdles to wider commercialisation.
“The definitions of autonomous vehicles and driver-assistance functions would be clarified in the amendments,” Xinhua reported, without revealing when the revised law would enter into force.
Self-driving systems switched off during a journey would remain subject to existing rules and laws, according to Xinhua, while analysts noted that carmakers could be held accountable for accidents and traffic rule violations when such systems were activated in a vehicle legally recognised as autonomous.
“As they are required to shoulder the responsibilities for the cars’ operations on the roads, automotive companies will also be allowed to build and sell cars of this kind to attract consumers,” said Gao Shen, an independent analyst based in Shanghai.
“When the amended law is promulgated, dozens of new autonomous models will hit the streets.”

Australia’s music charts ban AI-made songs amid backlash over Madonna cover
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
06:00:38 UTC
15:00:38 KST

Australia’s music charts ban AI-made songs amid backlash over Madonna cover
Tracks that use AI in a ‘supporting role’ will still be eligible for inclusion in the official charts.
Australia’s official music charts have banned tracks mostly created by artificial intelligence (AI) following a backlash over a cover of Madonna’s “Like a Prayer” that relied heavily on the burgeoning technology.
“Wholly AI-generated” music will be excluded from the charts under the changes, while tracks that use AI in a “supporting role” will still be eligible, the Australian Recording Industry Association (ARIA) said on Tuesday.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4DRC’s constitutional battle: The fight over the 2028 vote
- list 2 of 4US plans to revoke business, tourism visas of 200,000 asylum seekers
- list 3 of 4Brutal gang attack on strategic Haiti hillside leaves at least 30 dead
- list 4 of 4Man killed in world’s largest annual bullfighting event in Mexico
AI-generated music will also not be considered for recognition at the annual ARIA Music Awards under the new rules, which are set to take effect on Friday.
ARIA said it would rely on a labelling system introduced by music industry groups last month to distinguish AI-generated tracks from those that use AI to complement human creativity.
Under the labelling rules announced by a coalition of organisations including the Recording Industry Association of America, tracks may be labelled “AI-Generated” or “AI-Assisted” depending on the level of human involvement in the writing and recording process.
Tracks are classed as “AI-Generated” if AI was used to create the “entirety or the primary portion of the creative elements of the recording” and “AI-Assisted” if the technology was used only for “some expressive elements”.
ARIA CEO Annabelle Herd said while the music charts should evolve to reflect the legitimate use of AI, they should not recognise music generated “wholesale” by technology that relies on other artists’ work.
“These changes reflect our intent to remain dynamic and promote the human nature of artistry in what is – to say the least – a rapidly developing space,” Herd said in a statement.
ARIA, whose members include major music labels such as Sony Music Entertainment Australia and Universal Music Australia, publishes more than two dozen weekly music charts in Australia, including the top 50 singles and top 50 albums.
The industry association’s decision comes after a Brisbane-based DJ’s chart-topping cover of Madonna’s 1989 hit Like a Prayer attracted a backlash over its use of AI-generated vocals and drums.
Josh Fawaz last month belatedly acknowledged using AI on the track after music fans and producers raised suspicions that it was not produced by a human.
The cover has racked up more than 48.5 million listens on music streaming platform Spotify and currently ranks number one on the ARIA Top 20 Australian Dance Singles Chart.
Fawaz, who has defended the use of AI as a “tool” in his music, described ARIA’s new rules as a “great move”.
“I understand that AI in music isn’t for everyone and that’s fine. Good to see Aussie artists killing it globally!!” Fawaz wrote in a social media post responding to the announcement.
Oliver Bown, an associate professor at the University of New South Wales who researches the relationship between technology and art, said the impact of AI on creative industries such as music demands urgent attention.
“Many large commercial AI music generation companies have assumed they can scrape training data without permission, and so are potentially predatory on artists,” Bown told Al Jazeera.
“I believe people can do great artistic work using AI respectfully, but there is also a predatory phenomenon whereby you can just go fishing for plays and profits,” he added.
“Many organisations have developed rules about AI use and an increasing number see the need to ban full-AI works. I think this is the right thing to do.”
Ivan Zavada, a senior lecturer in composition and music technology at the University of Sydney, said the changes have been widely viewed as a “necessary step” to protect “genuine human musical creativity and performance”.
“More work needs to be done on the legal and intellectual property fronts to enable more trust and clarity in these tools,” Zavada told Al Jazeera.
“AI will be an essential part of standard music production in the very near future. We are living a very exciting yet concerning transition period in the digital and electronic arts.”

Attiah fired for posts about Charlie Kirk's assassination

Turcios Juarez joined the military and became a US citizen in 2024 after a nine-month deployment to the Middle East, according to ABC News. He said he began pursuing citizenship for his wife, hoping his service would help expedite her naturalization process.
Father of USS Abraham Lincoln sailor detained amid Trump immigration crackdown

Trump has pursued an immigration crackdown that includes visa and green card revocations and an aggressive deportation drive. He says the crackdown aims to improve domestic security.
Rights groups say the crackdown has violated free speech and due process rights and created an unsafe environment, particularly for ethnic minorities, who have raised concerns about racial profiling.
While Trump campaigned in 2024 on a platform of stopping illegal immigration, his administration has also made legal immigration more difficult - for example, by imposing new and expensive fees for applicants of certain work visas.

Omega Just Released a Mini Moonwatch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
06:00:00 UTC
15:00:00 KST

I have skinny wrists. So skinny, in fact, that during the craze from the late 1990s to early 2010s, when watch cases started to tip over 48 mm, it became hard to find pieces that suited those of us not blessed (or cursed) with Schwarzenegger-sized forearms. Thankfully, watch case sizes have calmed down considerably since then, and now it's easy to find smaller models, particularly around that 38- to 40-mm Goldilocks zone.
This brings us neatly to Omega's latest collection of Speedmasters, all of which come in that ideal 38-mm size. The seven references in new color variations have been tweaked to improve the existing 38-mm Speedy collection. The most notable improvement? The oval subdials have been banished in favor of proper rounded versions seen on the Moonwatch. The bezels have also been overhauled in Moonwatch style and are now thicker with the essential Dot-Over-Ninety.
Across the new collection, two self-winding movements power the pieces. The Caliber 3330 powers the six references with date functions, including a $11,700 “cappuccino” style version with an ivory-color main dial, contrasting brown PVD-coated subdials, a stainless steel case, and an 18K Sedna gold bezel.
It's the seventh Black Dial reference with no date that's the pick of the bunch, however, powered by the Caliber 3332. Omega positions the $6,500 watch as much more “closely aligned with the signature look of the Moonwatch,” which it certainly is, compared to the existing black 38-mm model with a date window and inferior bezel design.
The reduced sizing, clean, uncluttered black matte-finish varnished dial, Moonwatch-style five-link bracelet, and much-improved black aluminum bezel bring to mind the classic Speedmaster Reduced from the late 1980s. A friend of mine has a Reduced, and I have coveted it for years as, when I see it, it always looks the perfect size on the wrist.
Launched in 1988, the Speedmaster Reduced had an ideal 38.5-mm case size, rather than the 38 mm in this new model. Other subtle differences include the crown position on the Reduced, which is lower and visibly offset from the pushers, and the bezel doesn't have the Dot-Over-Ninety, either.
The biggest giveaway that this is not a faithful reissue of the Reduced is that the subdials are in different positions. On the Reduced, the layout was running seconds at 3, 12-hour totalizer at 6, and 30-minute totalizer at 9. On this 38 mm, it's reversed, with the 30-minute totalizer at 3, and running seconds at 9, just as on the larger Moonwatch.
So perhaps it's best to think of this enticingly sized new 38-mm black Speedy as a “mini Moonwatch,” as it shares more design cues with the iconic Speedmaster, even if its diminutive dimensions conjure up memories of the Reduced models from the ’80s. Either way, the 38-mm’s price makes it the cheapest black-dial “Moonwatch” Speedmaster now available, which is most welcome—and it's a rare thing indeed to be rewarded for having skinny wrists.

China’s anti-corruption legal framework is about to extend beyond its borders
A draft law aimed at combating cross-border corruption has been submitted for its first reading by the country’s top legislature
On Tuesday, the draft Anti-Cross-Border Corruption Law was submitted for its first reading during the 24th session of the Standing Committee of the 14th National People’s Congress (NPC), which runs until Friday.
The text of the bill is not yet available to the public.
Enacting the law is a vital initiative to complete China’s foreign-related legal framework, protect national interests, promote compliant overseas business growth and “enrich the legal ‘toolbox’ for fugitive repatriation, asset recovery and handling foreign-related corruption cases”, according to state news agency Xinhua.
The law codifies a decade of anti-corruption practices to close jurisdictional loopholes and target offshore financial crimes, aiming to resolve long-standing systemic hurdles, specifically the “difficulty in detecting, collecting evidence, repatriating illicit assets” and prosecuting offshore offences, it said.
Comprising six chapters and 47 articles, the draft law establishes key principles, scope and national positioning regarding cross-border corruption.

Hsinchu Zoo earns environmental education certification
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
05:48:46 UTC
14:48:46 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Hsinchu Zoo is turning its historic landmarks and everyday activities into opportunities for environmental education, from a Japanese-designed entrance gate to postcards made from hippopotamus droppings.
The zoo recently received certification as an environmental education facility, becoming the second zoo in Taiwan to earn the designation after Taipei Zoo. Under Taiwan’s Environmental Education Act, certified facilities provide environmental education through trained staff, educational programs, and other organized activities, according to Friendly Seed.
The National Environmental Research Academy said the certification recognizes the zoo’s role in connecting environmental education with Hsinchu’s history. Founded in 1936, Hsinchu Zoo is Taiwan’s oldest zoo still operating at its original site. Taipei Zoo, founded in 1914, moved from Yuanshan to its current location in Muzha in 1986, according to the Ministry of Environment.
Among the zoo’s most recognizable landmarks is its entrance gate. Designed by a Japanese architect and modeled on the entrance to Hagenbeck Zoo in Germany, the gate features cast-iron sculptures that remain intact and have become a symbol of Hsinchu Zoo’s history.
The grounds also contain one of the world’s few remaining hemispherical aviaries. Built in 1936, the structure once housed pink-backed pelicans and grey herons. Today, the former aviary has been converted into a children’s playground, according to AJ Travel.
Another historic feature is a stone monument erected in 1921. Its front bears an inscription meaning “infinite life,” written by Li Yi-qiao (李逸樵), a well-known Hsinchu calligrapher at the time. The inscription on the back conveys the idea that all things eventually return to emptiness, according to the Bureau of Cultural Heritage.
The zoo has also developed an environmental education course that turns one of its waste products—hippopotamus droppings—into postcards. After the plant-fiber-rich material undergoes high-temperature disinfection, participants knead it and shape it into postcards with a grassy scent.

Fire severely damages hall at Taipei’s Zhinan Temple
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
05:48:29 UTC
14:48:29 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — A major fire severely damaged the Lingxiao Hall of Taipei’s Zhinan Temple in Wenshan District late Monday, with firefighters battling the blaze for more than four hours before extinguishing it shortly after midnight.
No injuries were reported. The fire broke out at about 8 p.m. Monday and was extinguished just after midnight, according to the Taipei City Fire Department. The blaze was concentrated on the first and second floors of the three-story Lingxiao Hall, which contains extensive wooden materials and flammable decorations, per UDN.
More than 100 firefighters and emergency personnel were mobilized, along with 34 fire and emergency vehicles. Firefighters also used drones to monitor the blaze and drew water from a pool at the temple to maintain their supply because of the temple’s mountainous location and limited access to water.
The first floor of the hall was almost completely destroyed, while about one-third of the second floor was damaged. A preliminary assessment found minor cracking around a stairwell, but officials said the main structural frame was undamaged and the building remained structurally safe.
Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) inspected the site Tuesday morning and thanked firefighters and volunteer firefighters for their efforts. He said the lack of casualties was fortunate and pledged city government assistance with the temple’s recovery and reconstruction, per CNA.
Chiang ordered the formation of a cross-department task force to assist with the restoration process. The city will conduct a structural safety assessment after the fire investigation and determine which portions of the building should be preserved and which may need to be removed. Officials will also document the site’s historical and cultural features before reconstruction begins.
“Zhinan Temple is one of Taipei’s most iconic temples,” Chiang said, adding that it holds memories for many residents and worshippers. He pledged that the city government would work alongside the temple throughout the restoration and reconstruction process.
Zhinan Temple was established in the late Qing Dynasty and is one of Taipei’s best-known Taoist temples. The temple complex includes several major halls and is located near Zhinan Temple Station on the Maokong Gondola.
Temple Chair Kao Chao-wen (高超文) said the temple would not close following the fire. Only Lingxiao Hall has been cordoned off, while visitors can continue to worship at the main hall and Daxiong Hall. Access routes have been adjusted to keep visitors away from the damaged area, per CNA.
Temple officials are expected to discuss a restoration and reconstruction schedule as the investigation and structural assessment proceed. The Taipei City Government describes the temple as an important religious and cultural landmark.

Japan’s famous bonfire monkey zoo to close for major revamp
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Japan’s famous bonfire monkey zoo to close for major revamp
During the closure, the zoo plans to use social media to post updates on its 700 monkeys and hold members-only events
Home to about 700 monkeys of around 50 species, the facility in Inuyama, Aichi prefecture, will open only on weekends and holidays from September, and close its gates from October 19. During the closure, it plans to use social media to post updates on the monkeys and hold events open only to registered members.
The zoo’s iconic bonfires date back to 1959, three years after it opened with funding from Nagoya Railroad, when staff burned trees that had fallen in a massive typhoon and resident monkeys were seen gathering around the fire.
It later became the first facility in Japan to keep mountain gorillas. Working with partners, including Kyoto University’s Institute for the Evolutionary Origins of Human Behaviour, it is regarded as one of the world’s leading primate care and research facilities.
Since 2014, the zoo has been run by a Kyoto University-linked non-profit foundation. Operating costs have been covered by admission fees and donations solicited under the name “Goshien” – a Japanese play on words combining “support” and “monkey”.

AfD could take power in German state for first time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
05:47:01 UTC
14:47:01 KST

Joerg Urban, leader of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) in the state of Saxony, speaks to voters at an AfD campaign rally prior to state elections in Saxony-Anhalt on Aug. 24, 2026 in Naumburg, Germany. (Photo by Sean Gallup/Getty Images)
Germany is preparing for the possibility that the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) could lead a state government for the first time, as the party holds a wide polling lead ahead of the Sept. 6 election in Saxony-Anhalt.
About 1.7 million people are eligible to vote in the eastern state.
Recent polls put the AfD at between 41 and 43 percent, well ahead of the governing Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which stands at between 22 and 24 percent.
With several smaller parties polling close to Germany’s 5-percent electoral threshold, that level of support could give the AfD an outright majority of seats, although the outcome remains uncertain.
If the party secures enough seats to govern alone, its lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund could become Germany’s first AfD state premier since the party was founded in 2013.
The prospect has prompted federal and state officials to consider how an AfD-led administration should be handled in sensitive areas, particularly intelligence sharing.
The AfD’s Saxony-Anhalt branch has been classified by the state’s domestic intelligence service as a “confirmed right-wing extremist” organization.
The party rejects the designation and is challenging it in court.
Thuringia Interior Minister Georg Maier has called for an AfD-led administration to be denied access to intelligence concerning right-wing extremist groups and counterespionage.
Maier said a state could not be excluded entirely from Germany’s joint intelligence network but argued that internal barriers could be introduced to restrict access to certain information.
He cited security concerns over the AfD’s contacts with Russia.
An AfD state premier would also participate in meetings of Germany’s 16 state leaders and their talks with Chancellor Friedrich Merz. Saxony-Anhalt is scheduled to assume the rotating chair of the Conference of Minister-Presidents in October, although it remains unclear whether a new state government will be formed by then.
The election will also test Germany’s political “firewall,” under which other parties rule out coalitions or structured cooperation with the AfD. With no prospective coalition partner, the party’s route to government largely depends on winning enough seats to govern alone.
AfD co-leader Alice Weidel criticized the firewall during an interview with public broadcaster ZDF on Aug. 23, calling it “the most undemocratic thing there is.”
Weidel said the AfD would enter government first at the state level and later nationally.
She also backed closing Germany’s borders and leaving the Schengen Area, defended her party’s position favoring an exit from the euro and rejected further measures targeting climate change.
The AfD’s Saxony-Anhalt campaign calls for a “180-degree turn” in migration policy, including tighter deportation rules and greater use of detention pending removal.

‘Grain’ revolution: How lost varieties of rice are coming back
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
05:44:23 UTC
14:44:23 KST

Decades after disappearing from Indian fields and kitchens, heirloom paddy is making a comeback.
Biryani made with Kaima instead of Basmati, payesh made with Badshahbhog, risotto made with Assam’s Bora. With heirloom rice vanishing from Indian kitchens faster than they could be documented, this seemed, until not very long ago, nothing more than nostalgia. The Green Revolution’s push for high-yield monoculture had, over the years, pushed out many old types of rice. But now, several of those varieties, thought long gone, are staging a comeback — thanks to the efforts of farmers, conservationists, NGOs, restaurateurs, and a bit of help from some state govts.
Guardians of the grain
In coastal Karnataka’s Nettanige village, Padma Shri awardee Sathyanarayana Beleri — everyone calls him ‘Seeding Sathya’ — nurtures more than 100 traditional paddy varieties in grow bags outside his house. It’s a small selection from his vast collection of over 650 seed varieties, collected from across India, Sri Lanka, Japan and the Philippines.He has strains of flood-resistant Edekunhi and Nereguli, the medicinal Dodda Byra Nellu, and Kalanamak (also called ‘Buddha Rice’). He’s distributed seeds to hundreds of farmers across Karnataka and Kerala, as well as to agricultural universities nationwide. “Rice”, he says, “can be cultivated in grow bags, just like vegetables at home.
As climate change reshapes agriculture, conserving traditional, climate-resilient varieties is no longer a choice. It is a necessity.”
Sathyanarayana Beleri with some of the more than 650 seed varieties he has collected from across India, Sri Lanka, Japan and the Philippines.
Further inland, entire families have turned conservation into a generational commitment. In Belthangady taluk, the Rao family has conserved 180-190 traditional varieties on 5.5 acres since B K Deva Rao started a seed bank in 1988. His son, Parameshwar Rao, points to a benefit beyond biodiversity. “Paddy cultivation is among the best forms of groundwater recharge and rainwater harvesting,” he says. “Strong field bunds can retain water for nearly a week. Even two cropping cycles can substantially improve the groundwater table.” Their prized variety, Kayame — a red rice — “has a flavour rarely found in modern commercial varieties,” he adds.Some 1,300km away in Chhattisgarh, Khemlal Dewangan, a maths teacher in Rajnandgaon district, started farming traditional paddy around 15 years ago. Dewangan started with a handful of desi strains. He now has a collection of around 70 varieties.His seed collection has grown through a nationwide network of farmers — brought together on WhatsApp — who test small quantities in their fields. “I now receive 10-15 enquiries a day from social media and word of mouth,” he says.For him, the appeal goes beyond the market: he says traditional varieties are healthier, as they take longer to mature, absorbing more soil nutrients.
Roots of a revival
None of this happened by accident. Back in 2004, the UN’s second International Year of Rice, Kerala-based NGO Thanal decided something had to be done about India’s vanishing rice varieties. They launched the Save Our Rice campaign through a workshop in Kumbalangi village. Thanal teamed up with Tamil Nadu’s CREATE (a non-profit organisation) to run it, and the campaign took root in Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Karnataka and Bengal, later spreading into Chhattisgarh.
Members of CREATE educate farmers about heirloom rice varieties on a farm in Tamil Nadu.
India had over one lakh varieties of rice in 1966, but by the time the campaign started, that number had dropped to around 30,000 — most locked away in university seed banks, rather than growing in farmers’ fields. The campaign has had a big impact on southern states. “In the last 15-16 years, there has been a revival of traditional seeds in these states,” says Jayakumar C, executive director at Thanal. “Today, there are more than 25 or 30 farmers or groups doing traditional seeds in different parts of Kerala. Thanal’s own centre in Wayanad now holds around 320- 330 varieties of rice.”That demand has started showing up in the market. Thanal runs a regular shop now in Thiruvananthapuram. Jayakumar says Kaima (also called Jeerakasala or Jeeraga Samba), a traditional variety, has become popular for biryani. Brands have caught on, too. Thondi, from a Wayanad farmer-producer company, sells online and via courier across Kerala’s cities, even as Mappila Chamba has built a following.“Traditional rice tends to be more filling,” says Jayakumar. You feel full after eating less, unlike white rice hybrids. Also, the longer shelf life and taste after cooking is winning over urban households, especially the older people.”
When state stepped in
In Tamil Nadu, govt push gave the revival momentum. According to Suresh Kanna, project director at CREATE Trust, state govt began promoting six native varieties some 10 years ago under the State Heritage Rice Mission: Mappillai Samba, Karuppu Kavuni, Thooyamalli, Poongar, Kaattuyaanam and Kichili Samba. “Today, they are liked by consumers and can be seen in organic shops across the state. They also fetch good income for the farmers. A Kavuni farmer can get up to Rs 200 for a kilo. My calculation is that more than one lakh farmers in the state are now cultivating traditional paddy varieties,” Kanna says.Even in Karnataka, grassroots efforts are now finding institutional backing. KVK Dakshina Kannada has begun field trials of 10 traditional varieties sourced from Beleri, aiming to identify strains suited to the coastal region, and reintroduce them into local food systems. Karnataka’s agriculture department has documented 2,164 traditional landraces (local, traditional varieties that evolved through natural and human selection to adapt to a specific geographic and climatic environment) across 20 crops, with paddy topping the list at 1,469 varieties, under its Conservation and Promotion of Landraces Programme. Rs 1.3 crore in incentives went to 490 farmers in 2025-26 for viable seed samples. The effort centres on custodian farmers who “continued cultivating them on small patches of land,” as department director GT Puthra puts it.The department is now supporting GI registration for varieties including Kagga paddy, Rajmudi paddy, Bijapur Jola, Joni Bella and Kumbi Mudli, and plans incentives for 15 “forgotten treasure” shops.
Farm to fork, fork to fame
A few restaurants are actively championing rare, indigenous rice over commercial varieties. Edible Archives in Goa works with regional grains like Thavala Kannan from Wayanad (a red rice from Palakkad, whose name means “frog’s eyes” in Malayalam), and Pokkali, which brings a distinct coastal terroir.The Kolkata-based Amar Khamar, both a heritage-grain retail brand and restaurant, is entirely built around Bengal’s native rice. Its signature is ‘Chhuti-r Bhat’, an 11-course meal following the traditional sequence of a Bengali meal, centred on heirloom varieties like Sugondhi Chine Kamini Aatap.
‘Chhuti-r Bhat’ in Kolkata’s Amar Khamar, which is an 11-course meal centred on heirloom rice varieties.
That influence has spread to other restaurants in the city. Sienna Cafe sources Chine Kamini, Radha Tilok, Kanakchur and Tulaipanji Atop from Amar Khamar; Yokocho, a Japanese alleyway-inspired bar and BBQ, draws on Kanakchur, Tulaipanji Atop and Karpurkanti; Red Bari incorporates Shatia, Mallifulo and Khejur Chhari.Juhi Punwani, head of kitchen operations at Amar Khamar, has built a career around collecting the many myths and stories behind Bengal’s native rice varieties. “Gobindobhog is not the only heritage rice in Bengal,” she says. A rice called Radhuni Pagol literally means “the cook gone crazy”, after lore that its fragrance once filled a kitchen so completely that the cook couldn’t think of anything else.Tulaipanji of North Bengal gets its name from how the cooked rice turns light and airy like cotton (tula); Khejur Chhari is named for the date palm its grains resemble; Radha Tilok’s dark-tipped grain evokes Radha’s tilak mark. “Every rice here has a beautiful story and a journey, and that’s what we’re trying to showcase,” says Punwani, whose team has worked to bring back over 100 varieties, keeping around 50 in active rotation.
A look at select traditional rice varieties and the regions they are associated with across India.
This past summer, that ambition crossed continents, as Amar Khamar toured France and Germany. In Paris, working with sommelier Rajat Parr, the team built an 80-guest, 10-course tasting menu entirely around rice. Kanakchur turned up as fritters with brown butter hollandaise, Sundarbansgrown Karpurkanti and Chine Kamini appeared as aatapan alongside a jackfruit-seed mung dal, Barddhaman’s Mohansal was served boiled, the meal closing with a Jhargram Fine Black Rice phirni.In Stuttgart, the team built a fully vegan Bengali tasting menu, rice carrying the meal from a humble jhal muri to a coconut-milk Badshahbhog payesh for dessert. A separate 200-guest winery event tested whether the format could scale — from Karpurkanti-paired lentils, a Chine Kamini peas pulao to Sunday lamb curry and Badshahbhog milk-rice. “None of this would be possible without the relationships we have built with a network of farmers,” says Punwani, who executed the menu in Europe.
The traceability problem
But as heritage rice travels from the farm into retail shelves, a different problem emerges: knowing whether what’s being sold is really what it claims to be. One store has built its entire business around solving exactly that. In Chennai’s Mylapore sits a store unlike any other. Spirit of the Earth calls itself a “retail store and experience centre”, where customers come to see, touch, feel and know the story of every rice. Opened in 2017, it’s the retail face of a project that Sheela Balaji, chairperson of NGO AIM For Seva, began over a decade ago, built on a principle she believes the heritage-rice surge often misses: traceability.“Unfortunately, certain grains are being sold as certain varieties, which is inaccurate,” says Balaji.“The minute you say heritage rice, people will just come and buy it. But who is taking accountability? How do you know if it’s really diabetic friendly? So, I started this project more than a decade ago, first and foremost by building a seed bank. All the rice that you see in our store is grown from our farm in Manjakkudi, a village in Tiruvarur.”
The 40-acre operation has grown as neighbouring farmers joined in, alongside a seed bank built from years of Balaji’s fieldwork with growers in Manipur, Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh.For Balaji, the mission is beyond nutrition or nostalgia. “Rice in our culture is Lakshmi,” she says. “And reintroducing its forgotten names and forms, one customer at a time, is as much about restoring that reverence as it is about the grain itself.”
Sheela Balaji and Parameshwar Rao explain the importance of rice and paddy cultivation.
Sneha Bhura is an Assistant Editor with The Times of India. She loves exploring stories at the intersection of culture and technology. She is also a published poet and podcaster. Her debut poetry collection 'Velvet Grapes' was released in 2021.

NSA Ajit Doval calls on Chinese Vice President Han Zhang ahead of border talks
NEW DELHI: National security advisor Ajit Doval on Tuesday met Chinese vice president Han Zheng in Beijing, with the two sides discussing ways to maintain peace and tranquillity along the border and further strengthen India-China relations across economic, political and multilateral platforms.The meeting came ahead of the 25th round of special representatives talks on the India-China boundary question between Doval and Chinese foreign minister Wang Yi later on Tuesday.Sharing details of the meeting, the Embassy of India in China said, "On 25 August, NSA and Special Representative on the India-China Boundary Question, Ajit Doval called on Han Zheng, Vice President of the People's Republic of China."The embassy said Doval and Han discussed ways to strengthen peace and tranquillity in the border areas and further improve bilateral ties "across economic, political and multilateral fora", in line with the consensus reached by the leaders of the two countries.Doval arrived in Beijing on Monday for a two-day visit to participate in the Special Representatives talks with Wang Yi, who is also China's Foreign Minister.
The talks are expected to focus on the boundary question, along with bilateral, regional and international issues.The Chinese Foreign Ministry has described the Special Representatives mechanism as the "main channel" for negotiations between the two countries on the boundary question and an important platform for communication on issues of mutual interest.
The mechanism was established in 2003 to address the India-China boundary dispute, which stretches across roughly 3,488 km.The 24th round of talks was held in August last year, when the two sides held what Beijing described as candid and in-depth discussions and reached several common understandings.The upcoming round assumes significance as India and China seek to stabilise ties following years of tensions along the Line of Actual Control.The discussions come amid efforts by New Delhi and Beijing to gradually improve bilateral relations after the 2020 Galwan Valley clash and the prolonged military stand-off in eastern Ladakh severely strained ties.Doval and Wang had also met in June in New Delhi on the sidelines of the BRICS National Security Advisers' meeting. The Ministry of External Affairs had described those discussions as "constructive and forward-looking".MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal had said, "The two sides reviewed recent developments in bilateral relations and noted progress towards gradual normalisation. NSA underlined that stable, predictable and constructive bilateral relations contribute to building trust and better understanding between the two sides. The discussions were constructive and forward-looking."The latest talks also come amid efforts by the two countries to build on a series of high-level engagements between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping.The leaders had welcomed positive momentum and steady progress in bilateral relations during their meeting on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Tianjin last year, after their previous meeting in Kazan in October 2024.
They had reaffirmed that India and China are development partners rather than rivals and that differences should not be allowed to become disputes."A stable relationship and cooperation between India and China and their 2.8 billion peoples on the basis of mutual respect, mutual interest and mutual sensitivity are necessary for the growth and development of the two countries, as well as for a multipolar world and a multi-polar Asia befitting the trends of the 21st century," the MEA had said after the leaders' meeting.Despite the gradual improvement in ties, differences over the boundary and Arunachal Pradesh remain sensitive issues between New Delhi and Beijing.Both Doval and Wang are designated Special Representatives for the boundary talks mechanism. While the process has not resolved the long-running border dispute, officials on both sides continue to regard it as an important channel for managing tensions and maintaining communication.The talks also come ahead of Xi's expected visit to New Delhi for the BRICS summit on September 12-13, which could provide an opportunity for another meeting between Xi and PM Modi and further discussions on the bilateral relationship.

Interview: China's key initiatives inspirational for global governance reforms in multipolar era, says former UNGA president
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
13:39:08 CST
14:39:08 KST

BELGRADE, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- The global governance system can draw inspiration from China's major global initiatives in a multipolar world, a former senior UN official told Xinhua in a recent interview.
"China's four initiatives give together a very important set of values and principles that, in my opinion, ought to be applied to the current system that we have in order to transform it," said Vuk Jeremic, who served as president of the UN General Assembly (2012-2013) and foreign minister of Serbia (2007-2012).
Jeremic currently leads the Center for International Relations and Sustainable Development, a global public policy think tank based in Belgrade.
He was referring to a series of major global initiatives proposed by China: the Global Development Initiative, the Global Security Initiative, the Global Civilization Initiative and the Global Governance Initiative.
Reviewing the evolution of the international landscape, Jeremic said the world is no longer unipolar. "There is no single center of power that dominates all others," he said. The world has moved toward multipolarity, he noted, but a new multipolar world order has yet to be fully established.
Jeremic said the emergence of a multipolar world does not mean a more cooperative international system.
He outlined three possible forms of multipolarity: competitive, managed and cooperative. Competitive multipolarity would see major powers compete fiercely without recognizing each other's legitimacy, increasing the risk of conflict. Managed multipolarity would involve competition within agreed rules and red lines to prevent misunderstandings and escalation.
Cooperative multipolarity, meanwhile, would see major powers recognize each other's existence, legitimacy and rights and work together to address common challenges such as climate change and the regulation of advanced technologies, including artificial intelligence.
"This third multipolar version, cooperative multipolarity, is something that we should all hope for," he said.
Jeremic also spoke highly of China's development over recent decades, describing it as "the most successful exercise in the history of human development."
He cited lifting hundreds of millions of people out of poverty and increasing opportunities to participate in economic and social development as major achievements. He also highlighted China's technological achievements, noting that the country has become a leading tech power.
It is in this broader context, Jeremic said, that China's four global initiatives have particular significance.
He identified the four initiatives as important components of China's approach to global challenges, stressing how the Global Governance Initiative is people-centered and action-oriented.
Global governance, he said, should be "not just for governments around the world, not just for certain blocs, but for the people."
"For somebody who comes from a very small country, this respect for international law and the sovereign equality of nations that is deeply embedded in the Global Governance Initiative is something very appealing," he said.
In his view, these principles are particularly relevant, given that the existing multilateral system faces significant challenges and that international institutions fail to better reflect today's realities.
"We do have a multilateral system that is not terribly functional these days," he said. "We need to change it, we need to reform it."
Though transforming the international system would be a lengthy process, Jeremic said China's global initiatives provide principles for countries worldwide to explore a more cooperative multipolarity. ■

‘Constitutional monstrosity’: P Chidambaram attacks One Nation, One Election Bill
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

‘Constitutional monstrosity’: P Chidambaram attacks One Nation, One Election Bill
Edited by: Yashasvi Vasistha / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Aug 25, 2026, 11:09 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
File photo: Congress MP P Chidambaram
NEW DELHI: Senior Congress leader and Rajya Sabha member P Chidambaram on Tuesday said simultaneous elections to the Lok Sabha and state assemblies cannot be held in 2029 even if Parliament passes the proposed One Nation, One Election (ONOE) legislation.Chidambaram, who appeared before the Joint Parliamentary Committee (JPC) examining the ONOE Bills, said his basic submission before the panel was that the proposed legislation violated the basic features of the Constitution, particularly parliamentary democracy in a federal country.
In a post on X, Chidambaram said he was not permitted to disclose his evidence before the JPC but outlined the thrust of his argument.“I am grateful for the opportunity to present my views to the JPC on O.N.O.E. I am not at liberty to disclose my evidence to the JPC but the basic thrust of my deposition was that the Bill violated the basic features of the Constitution, especially the tenets of parliamentary democracy in a federal country,” he wrote.
Chidambaram disputes 2029 timeline
Chidambaram also rejected the reported assertion by JPC chairman PP Chaudhary that simultaneous elections could be held in 2029.
“I have read the reported statement of the Chairman, JPC, that simultaneous elections are possible in 2029 I am afraid his view is wrong and goes against the text of the Bill,” he said.According to Chidambaram, the Bill provides that the “appointed date” can only be a date that comes after a general election. Since the next Lok Sabha election is due in 2029, he argued that simultaneous polls cannot be conducted in that year.“Even if the Bill is passed (which is very unlikely), the 'appointed date' under the Bill can only be a date 'after a general election'. The next general election will take place in 2029. Hence, simultaneous elections are not possible in 2029, which is a blessing,” he said.Chidambaram added that the Congress and other Opposition parties would launch a nationwide campaign against the legislation, calling it a “Constitutional monstrosity in parliamentary democracy in a federal country.”
JPC receives suggestions on deferring state polls
Meanwhile, the parliamentary committee examining the ONOE legislation received several suggestions during its deliberations on Monday.According to sources cited by news agency ANI, two public policy institutions proposed replacing subjective discretion in deciding whether to defer state assembly elections with defined and judicially traceable grounds, along with fixed outer limits for such deferrals.The Constitution (One Hundred and Twenty-Ninth Amendment) Bill, 2024, seeks to facilitate the proposed synchronisation of Lok Sabha and state assembly elections. The Union Territories Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2024, forms part of the broader legislative framework for implementing simultaneous polls.Both Bills were introduced in the Lok Sabha on December 17, 2024, and subsequently referred to the JPC for detailed examination.The panel has since held meetings with subject-matter experts and undertaken study visits, with its most recent study visit taking place in Lucknow in July.
Chidambaram had opposed Bills before panel
Chidambaram had appeared before the JPC on Monday and strongly opposed the proposed simultaneous-election framework.He argued that curtailing the five-year tenure of elected legislatures would violate the Constitution's basic structure.He also said he could not support the Bills on grounds of conscience and contended that the government did not have the two-thirds majority required to pass the proposed constitutional amendments, according to sources cited by news agency PTI.JPC chairman PP Chaudhary said Chidambaram had provided “good inputs” but noted that he represented a particular political party. Chaudhary maintained that the proposal to hold simultaneous elections was not against the basic structure of the Constitution.
The ONOE Bills were formulated after a high-level committee headed by former President Ram Nath Kovind recommended holding Lok Sabha, state assembly and local body elections simultaneously in a phased manner.Historically, Lok Sabha and state assembly elections were held together from 1951-52 until the cycle was disrupted by premature dissolutions of some state assemblies in 1968 and 1969, followed by the early dissolution of the Fourth Lok Sabha in 1970.

BEIJING, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- Chinese lawmakers on Tuesday began reviewing a draft revision to the Enterprise Bankruptcy Law, with the second draft incorporating refinements to rules on individual bankruptcy, bankruptcy protection, restructuring and cross-border bankruptcy.

US removes Syria from state sponsors of terrorism list
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
05:36:52 UTC
14:36:52 KST

The United States on Aug. 24 formally removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism and lifted Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham’s (HTS) remaining U.S. terrorist designation.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio authorized the rescission after the mandatory 45-day congressional notification period ended.
He also revoked the designation of al-Nusrah Front, also known as HTS, as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist organization.
The Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) simultaneously removed HTS from its Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List.
The State Department had already revoked HTS’s separate designation as a Foreign Terrorist Organization in July 2025.
Syria had been on the state sponsors list since December 1979. The designation carried restrictions on U.S. assistance, defense exports and sales, certain dual-use exports and financial dealings.
Rubio said the decisions reflected steps and commitments by President Ahmed al-Sharaa’s government to distance Syria from international terrorism. He said the changes removed “the final major barriers” to private-sector investment and supported Syria’s economic recovery and reintegration into the global economy.
Al-Sharaa welcomed the decision, saying Syria was leaving behind a painful chapter and moving toward development and reconstruction. He thanked U.S. President Donald Trump and countries that had supported Syria.
Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani called the decision historic, saying the designation had been linked to the policies of the ousted Assad government and had never been the Syrian people’s choice.
Türkiye’s Ambassador to Syria Nuh Yılmaz said the move had removed “the final obstacle” to Syria’s integration with the world and would support stability and development in both Syria and the wider region.
