DRC’s constitutional battle: The fight over the 2028 vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
00:34:29 UTC
09:34:29 KST

DRC’s constitutional battle: The fight over the 2028 vote
President Tshisekedi’s reform push is fuelling a battle over DRC’s 2028 succession.
Kinshasa, DR Congo – President Felix Tshisekedi is due to leave office in 2028 under the current Constitution of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Yet with more than two years to go, a battle over the rules governing what happens when his mandate ends is already reshaping Congolese politics.
In May, Tshisekedi said he had not sought a third term but would accept one if the Congolese people wanted him to continue. The remarks revived opposition fears that constitutional reform could eventually open a path beyond the existing two-term limit.
Under the current constitution, the president is elected for five years, renewable once, while the number and length of presidential terms are protected from constitutional revision.
Tshisekedi’s camp says the country needs institutional reform. Opponents of the reform fear the process could ultimately be used to change the rules governing presidential succession.
The dispute is unfolding as the DRC fights a rebellion in the east led by M23, an armed group that operates within the broader Alliance Fleuve Congo (AFC), a political-military coalition that controls Goma and Bukavu, the capitals of North Kivu and South Kivu.
With an opposition mobilisation planned for September and Tshisekedi preparing to outline an inclusive national dialogue, the confrontation is entering a critical phase.
The referendum battle
The confrontation accelerated in June when the Parliament of the Democratic Republic of the Congo passed legislation setting out conditions for organising a referendum.
The Constitutional Court ruled in July that the law complied with the constitution, while raising concerns about some of its provisions. On August 10, Tshisekedi formally asked the presidents of the National Assembly and Senate to reconsider the legislation in light of the court’s observations. The National Assembly said the fresh deliberation would be placed on the agenda for its September session.
The legislation provides for a constituent assembly followed by a referendum in the event of what it describes as a “major dysfunction” of state institutions.
Critics of the process say the mechanism could eventually be used to alter provisions that currently prevent Tshisekedi from seeking a third term. The government, meanwhile, has presented constitutional reform as a broader institutional issue rather than an explicit bid to extend the president’s tenure.
The main opposition group campaigning against the process is known as C64, or the Article 64 coalition. Its name refers to Article 64 of the DRC’s constitution, which calls on citizens to oppose anyone who takes power in violation of the constitutional order.
C64 says it will resist any attempt to use constitutional reform to extend Tshisekedi’s mandate beyond 2028. The coalition announced a nationwide mobilisation for September 15, with demonstrations in Kinshasa expected to converge on the Palais du Peuple, the seat of parliament.
Taking the fight to parliament
The dispute has already spilled onto the streets.
Thousands demonstrated in Goma and Bukavu on July 28 against proposed constitutional changes and any attempt to extend Tshisekedi’s time in office.
In Kinshasa, protesters are expected to converge on the Palais du Peuple.
For C64, the destination is deliberate: the coalition wants to take its protest to the institution at the centre of the constitutional process.
Jean-Marc Kabund, a Congolese opposition politician, told Al Jazeera that no constitutional revision, referendum or legal manoeuvre should be allowed to circumvent the current constitution.
He warned that this happening while the country is at war could deepen divisions and threaten national cohesion.
A constitutional fight during a war
The constitutional dispute is unfolding alongside a conflict that has transformed eastern Congo.
M23 and the AFC have seized large areas of territory, including Goma and Bukavu. The Congolese government accuses Rwanda of supporting M23, a charge that Kigali denies.
The war is also raising questions about the 2028 elections.
Tshisekedi has warned that elections may not be possible if the fighting continues, arguing that it would be difficult to organise a credible vote while parts of the country remain outside government control.
Emmanuel Bugama, a Congolese political analyst based in Bunia, told Al Jazeera that national interests should come before political disputes.
“The nation’s best interests should take precedence over these political squabbles,” he said.
The view from Goma
In Goma, the argument is being watched from a city no longer under Kinshasa’s control.
Gentil Mulume, a civil society activist in Goma, told Al Jazeera that any constitutional change extending Tshisekedi’s mandate would not be recognised in territory controlled by M23 and the AFC.
“If Tshisekedi dares to amend this constitution to extend his term of office, it will not be recognised here,” he said.
Mulume said the dispute was part of a deeper divide between Kinshasa and the east. He argued that continued Tshisekedi rule could be viewed there as a form of domination and that self-determination should be part of the political debate.
His comments illustrate how a constitutional confrontation in Kinshasa is being interpreted in territory already beyond the government’s effective control.
What do ordinary Congolese know?
There is also a more basic question: how much do ordinary citizens understand about the proposed changes?
Kevin Kalala, a 30-year-old mobile-credit retailer in Kinshasa, told Al Jazeera that he does not know enough about the constitution to take a position.
“We do not know what our constitution entails,” he said. “The Congolese state should start by teaching us about our constitution.”
Kalala said citizens should first be shown which provisions need changing, why they need changing, and what the benefits would be.
“I am neither for nor against amending the constitution,” he said.
An offer of dialogue
As tensions rise, Tshisekedi has proposed an inclusive national dialogue involving political parties, civil society and religious groups.
While in Libreville, Gabon, on August 16, he said he would soon address the nation to set out his vision and the contours of the talks. The date and format of the dialogue have yet to be announced.
Tshisekedi has ruled out sitting with people he accuses of siding with Rwanda or the armed rebellion.
Martin Fayulu, who challenged Tshisekedi in the 2018 presidential election, has called for former President Joseph Kabila and Corneille Nangaa, the political leader of the AFC, to participate.
For now, the constitutional dispute is running alongside the war in the east and the uncertainty over the 2028 elections.
The question is no longer only whether the constitution will change. It is whether Congo’s political forces can agree on the rules for what happens when Tshisekedi’s current mandate ends.
“We are certainly heading towards one of the most decisive periods in our recent history,” Bugama told Al Jazeera. “The country is under the control of an armed group, whilst the government in Kinshasa is posturing over constitutional reform instead of tackling what matters most.”

Want to keep a big dog in Hong Kong? Experts share what you should know
Concerns about responsible handling of big dogs raised after attacks last week
Heat, humidity and crowded living spaces could pose challenges for Hongkongers hoping to keep large or aggressive dogs as pets, experts have said, urging potential owners to consider the needs of such animals before deciding to house them.
They issued the warning after a woman and two small canines were mauled in two separate attacks last week.
The woman was found collapsed in Ping Yeung Tsuen, hours after she was attacked at a dog training centre by a canine suspected of being a mixed-breed fighting dog. She was certified dead at the scene.
The smaller dogs were mauled to death in Yuen Long by an unleashed 60kg (132lbs) mastiff-type canine earlier that week.
Discussing the importance of correctly caring for big dogs, Lau Yun-yu, chairman of the Hong Kong Society for Pet Nutrition, said large canines, particularly those with thick coats, could face greater challenges in Hong Kong’s hot and humid climate.
“Dogs rely primarily on evaporative cooling through panting rather than sweating,” he said, adding that sustained high humidity could significantly reduce their ability to cool themselves.

Nevada sues US government over cuts to Colorado River access
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
00:21:00 UTC
09:21:00 KST

Nevada sues US government over cuts to Colorado River access
- Nevada has sued the US government to block planned cuts to its Colorado River water allocation, which could reduce its share by two-thirds and threaten Las Vegas's water supply.
- The federal plan cuts water use for lower-basin states Arizona, California, and Nevada by up to 3.7 billion cubic metres annually, while upper-basin states keep their current levels.
- The cuts respond to ongoing drought and overuse, with federal officials warning that without agreement, hydropower dams on the river could fail, and other states like Arizona may also file lawsuits.
AI generated
LOS ANGELES - Nevada on Aug 24 launched legal action against the administration of US President Donald Trump over a plan that would cut the state’s access to the vital Colorado River.
The river, which originates in the Rocky Mountains, makes farming possible in large tracts of the arid American south-west, and provides drinking water to the 40 million people who live there, including in cities like Phoenix.
But decades of over-use, coupled with years of drought, have put crippling strain on a watercourse whose management has always been based on an over-allocation of available resources.
Last week the federal government announced it was imposing cuts on the amount of water the so-called “lower-basin states” – Arizona, California and Nevada – can use, while leaving the allowances for the “upper basin states” of Colorado, New Mexico, Utah and Wyoming unchanged.
The plan envisages slashing the three states’ collective water consumption by up to 3.7 billion cubic metres per year until 2036 – the equivalent of 1.5 million Olympic-sized swimming pools.
Now Nevada has launched legal action seeking to block the change, which state officials say could reduce their allocation by two-thirds, potentially devastating the desert city of Las Vegas, which depends on the river for 90 per cent of its water.
“This isn’t about political posturing,” Nevada Governor Joe Lombardo, a Republican, said on Aug 24.
“This is a matter of survival for a community that represents about two-thirds of our state’s citizens and the lion’s share of its economy.”
Federal officials say their plan to cut usage is necessary because the seven states that lie on the river have been unable to agree amongst themselves.
They say without an agreement, dams on the river that are used to generate hydropower could cease to function.
Experts say Nevada’s lawsuit, lodged in a US district court, is unlikely to be the only legal action, with Arizona – which faces the deepest cuts – expected to launch its own challenge.
The federal government directive and the resulting legal action come after Lake Powell and Lake Mead, America’s two largest reservoirs, and which are fed by the Colorado River, fell to record low levels.
Scientists say human behaviour, including the unchecked burning of fossil fuels, is warming the global climate and interrupting weather patterns.
This leads to more sustained droughts in some parts of the planet, and more ferocious storms in others. AFP

Search continues in Tunisia as migrant boat sinking sparks protests
Tunisia’s Ben Guerdane reels from violent protests after boat carrying 15 people sinks, killing at least 12.
Tunisia protesters march after deadly migrant boat sinks
Volunteers in Tunisia have continued the search for two people still missing after a boat carrying 15 migrants sank off the country’s southeastern coast, as the city of Ben Guerdane reeled from violent protests sparked by the tragedy.
Footage, verified by Al Jazeera, showed volunteers in the city of Zarzis heading out to sea on fishing boats on Monday to search for the missing.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Tunisia recovers 11 bodies after boat carrying migrants sinks, 3 missing
- list 2 of 3Antigovernment protesters take to Tunisia’s streets for second month
- list 3 of 3Tunisia sees protests after migrant boat sinking kills eight
The migrant boat, believed to be headed towards Italy, sank late on Friday after setting off from a location between Zarzis and Ben Guerdane with 15 mostly young people on board. It sank about 14 nautical miles (26km) off the coast of Zarzis.
Only one person survived, having drifted at sea for about 48 hours before being rescued by a commercial vessel, according to Tunisian media.
The bodies of 12 people were recovered by Sunday, the Tunisian National Guard said.
The deaths have sparked a wave of grief and anger, triggering violent protests in Ben Guerdane on Sunday night. According to the Tunisian National Guard, some 14 people on the boat were from Ben Guerdane, and one was from Zarzis.
The protesters burned tyres and blocked roads, while police responded by firing tear gas to disperse the crowds. The protesters demanded better living conditions and economic development, saying a lack of opportunities and years of marginalisation are pushing young people to undertake dangerous sea crossings to Europe in search of a better life.
Mostafa Abdelkebir, the head of the Tunisian Observatory for Human Rights, said those on board included seven members of the same family. He told the Reuters news agency on Monday that a hospital in Ben Guerdane has received at least 19 bodies of migrants recovered from the sea over the past two days.
It was not clear if all the bodies were from the boat that sank. Abdelkebir told Reuters that genetic testing was being carried out to identify the bodies and determine how many had been on board the boat.
Some in Tunisia have called for a national day of mourning over the deaths.
Imad Oulad Jibril, a lawmaker, on Sunday called it “the tragedy of a nation that sees its youth fleeing the hardships of the land only to be swallowed by the sea”.
The opposition Democratic Bloc party tied the sinking to Tunisia’s economic strains, saying: “When crossing the sea becomes easier than living in Tunisia, we must ask: Who is at fault?”
Tunisia has seen similar tragedies in recent years, including the Kerkennah disaster, in which more than 100 people died or went missing in 2018 after the sinking of a migrant boat. The incident led to the dismissal of the then-interior minister. In Zarzis in 2022, at least 18 people died after another migrant boat sank, sparking weeks of protests.
Tunisia’s southeastern coast lies just 145 km (90 miles) from the Italian island of Lampedusa.
The central Mediterranean is considered the deadliest migration route in the world, according to the International Organization for Migration, which says at least 821 migrants have died or gone missing on the route this year – more than double the toll over the same period last year.
Across the Mediterranean as a whole, at least 1,065 people have died or gone missing, according to the group.

US state probes OpenAI over rogue AI hack
WASHINGTON – ChatGPT-maker OpenAI faces an investigation by the US state of Alabama after the company revealed in July that its models went rogue and hacked an artificial intelligence (AI) platform during testing.
In mid-July, two OpenAI models escaped their confined testing environment and gained access to the internet, where they found and attacked Hugging Face, a site AI developers use to store and share models and data sets.
The incident raised alarm about the dangers of AI systems acting autonomously and breaking guardrails set by human programmers to prevent safety violations.
In a 14-page order, the office of Alabama Attorney-General Steve Marshall demanded OpenAI hand over internal records about the July incident, along with a long list of other material, including the identity of every employee involved in the intrusion or in the testing that led to it.
The investigation comes in response to “the company’s complete lack of oversight and adequate safeguards”, Marshall’s office alleged in a statement.
It is the first known state investigation into whether an AI system attacking another company’s infrastructure amounts to a violation of consumer protection law – a finding that would expose the company to major litigation across the US.
On Aug 3, Alabama and 14 other states wrote to OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman asking the company to preserve records on the incident and halt any internal cybersecurity evaluations of its models.
OpenAI has not responded to that August request, a spokesperson for the Alabama attorney-general’s office told AFP.
OpenAI did not immediately respond to an AFP request for comment.
However, OpenAI said in a statement to the tech news site TechCrunch that it was “conducting a thorough review along with external advisers”.
“Once the review is complete, we will share a technical report with relevant government authorities and publish our findings publicly,” it added. AFP

The Supreme Court has cleared the way for US President Donald Trump to move ahead with his executive order restricting mail-in voting, though it remains unclear how much his administration can implement before the fast-approaching midterm elections.
The decision on Monday appears to leave room for additional court challenges that could further slow Trump's order.
And with some states beginning to send mail ballots to voters in just a few weeks, time is running short to impose major changes.

The case could be one of multiple voting-related challenges before the justices. The Justice Department had filed an emergency appeal asking the high court to allow work on implementing the changes before the midterms.

In June, Judge Indira Talwani ruled that the president lacked the authority to order changes in how states administer federal elections, noting that under the US Constitution, states have the role of determining voter-eligibility requirements.
The judge also noted that federal agencies lack the ability to compile accurate lists of citizens for each state.
The states contend that their claims are not hypothetical and that the administration's "rushed effort to change the rules of mail voting on the eve of the November midterms risks disenfranchising a substantial number of voters."
The judge rejected the administration's arguments, finding that the suit was not filed too soon and that the states had legal standing because they would face election administration disruption, compliance costs and a credible threat of criminal prosecution.

Viral false claims about quakes, Hiroshima expose Japan’s online conspiracy problem
Claims that a deadly quake was artificial and Hiroshima was not hit by an atomic bomb have alarmed experts tracking Japan’s online spaces
In the aftermath of the July 28 earthquake in Kumamoto prefecture in southern Japan, a social media user claimed that seismic data from the National Research Institute for Earth Science and Disaster Resilience showed the tremor was “not an earthquake but an artificial explosion waveform”.
The post, published about 30 minutes after the magnitude 7.1 quake, was later listed by Yahoo Japan’s real-time search as a popular post, with more than 2,100 reposts and 6,300 likes. Other posts pushed a related claim that the quake had been triggered by HAARP, a research facility in Alaska that has long been a target of disaster-related conspiracy theories.
Days later, as Japan marked the August anniversaries of the Hiroshima and Nagasaki bombings and the end of World War II, NHK reported that false claims denying the atomic attacks were gaining traction online, with some posts on X and TikTok drawing more than 1 million views and one YouTube video claiming the bombing was a lie attracting more than 300,000 views.
“Both the theory that the earthquake was artificially triggered and the denial of the atomic bombings lack scientific basis, but the contexts in which these conspiracy theories take root differ,” said Yuzuru Kido, a former J-CAST News deputy editor and internet media researcher who tracks Japanese social media discourse.

The leaders of Britain and France pledged to provide Ukraine with stronger military support, including access to classified technology and faster deliveries of air defense missiles, at a meeting of allies to mark Kyiv's independence day celebrations.
Burnham, in Kyiv on his first foreign visit since taking office last month, urged the gathering of the "Coalition of the Willing" to "do everything we can" to bolster Ukraine's defenses against Russian air strikes.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky had earlier praised the resilience of the Ukrainian people during more than four years of war.
At the United Nations in New York, dozens of countries issued a joint statement reaffirming support for Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity and urging Russia to accept an immediate, full and unconditional ceasefire.
Ukraine acquires tech to make Storm Shadow missiles
"Ukraine absolutely wants peace, but it is not ready to simply surrender," Zelensky said, adding that Russia would not halt its aggression even if Ukraine ceded to its demands for more territory in the country's east.
Wearing a traditional Ukrainian embroidered shirt, Zelensky thanked foreign leaders for traveling to Kyiv to show their support on the 35th anniversary of Ukraine's break from the Soviet Union.
Standing alongside Zelensky and European Council President Antonio Costa, Burnham said his choice of Kyiv for his first foreign visit showed the importance he attached to assisting in Ukraine's defense.
"We are with you in this struggle all the way, heart and soul," Burnham said, vowing to continue that support "despite Russia's outrageous threats to my country."
"This is the moment to keep up the pressure on Russia. The moment to squeeze their ability to fund this illegal war," Burnham said, calling for further economic sanctions.
Britain announced on Monday it would allow Kyiv access to classified technology to start its own production of Storm Shadow long-range cruise missiles, capable of carrying out strikes deep within Russia. France has already given its assent to license the technology for the European missile.
In response, the Kremlin said the use of classified British technology would "add fuel to the fire" of their worsening relations, after it warned London last week there would be "consequences" for supplying drones to Kyiv.
With Russia escalating its ballistic missile attacks on Ukrainian cities, Kyiv is suffering an acute shortage of the US-made Patriot air defense interceptors, the only weapon in its arsenal capable of downing such missiles.
Zelensky said Ukraine needed at least 300 interceptors to make it through the winter, and he appealed to allies to deliver an air defense package before Russia renews its strikes on his country's energy infrastructure.
French President Emmanuel Macron, co-chairing the coalition meeting via video link, said that a string of deadly attacks on Ukrainian cities in recent weeks had shown that allies needed to step up the deliveries of interceptors and France would do its part.
"I think it's very important that all of us accelerate in terms of delivery," Macron told the meeting, urging countries not to back down in the face of Russian intimidation. "The bottom line is, for me, very clear: keep calm and carry on."
Zelensky told the meeting that Ukraine's war effort was complicated by a $27-billion defense funding gap this year and appealed for additional financial support. He suggested that Russia's frozen overseas assets could be used to finance the deficit.
Paying tribute to Ukrainian people and soldiers defending Ukraine in the war, Zelensky called on allies to give it "everything" needed to stop the war.
"We are not asking you to fight for us," he said.
In a joint statement, more than 50 countries at the UN called on Russia to accept an unconditional ceasefire. "This senseless war and the immense human suffering could end immediately," the statement said.
"Russia simply needs to accept the unconditional ceasefire that Ukraine and the international community has been calling for for over a year and a half now."
Russia's UN ambassador, Vassily Nebenzia, accused Western countries of using Ukraine as a tool for exerting pressure on Moscow while falsely portraying themselves as peace advocates.
Drone demonstration marked celebrations
Hundreds of thousands of people have been killed, and swathes of Ukrainian territory have been laid waste, since Russia launched its full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022.
US-led peace talks to bring a lasting end to the war fell apart earlier this year as Ukraine refused Russian demands to cede more territory. Fighting continues along a 750-mile (1,200-km) front line and Ukraine has succeeded in bringing Russian advances overall to a virtual halt this year.
Hovering in the sky above Kyiv, a squadron of aerial drones carried out a demonstration of Ukrainian military technology, which has helped to keep Russian forces in check.
Naval drones swept along the Dnipro river, while unmanned ground vehicles, some equipped with heavy machine guns, trundled in formation along one of the city's main historical avenues.
Ukraine has increased its long-range attacks on Russian refineries and logistics infrastructure, aimed at undermining Moscow's war effort.
It hit four logistics hubs owned by Russia's second-largest online retailer Ozon in southern Russia in drone strikes on Monday, the company said.
In a somber moment, the Ukrainian leader rewarded fallen soldiers with state awards, which he presented to their mothers and family members.
He also announced the return of 10 Ukrainian servicemen, who were previously listed as missing in action, as part of a special prisoner exchange with Russia.
"We remember each and every one who remains in captivity," Zelensky said, promising to do everything possible to bring them home.

US State Dept. sanctions Iranian military activities, fuel export in Operation Economic Outcast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
00:10:21 UTC
09:10:21 KST

The US State Department implemented sanctions against Iranian military activities, cyber threats, and illicit oil trade, State Department Spokesperson Tommy Pigott announced on Monday evening.
"Today, the United States took sweeping action against multiple entities, individuals, and vessels enabling the Iranian regime’s destabilizing activities," Pigott said.
"The measures target Iranian military officials responsible for procuring weapons and directing attacks against US service members and regional partners, Iran-based entities that gathered intelligence for targeting US forces and allies, and a procurement ring supplying Iran’s military and missile programs," he added.
"The US will continue to disrupt, expose, and dismantle Iran’s military and proliferation activities, procurement schemes, malicious cyber operations, and illicit oil trade that sustains the regime’s malign behavior."
Sanctions target groups for supporting Iranian military actions
The sanctions targeted two Iran-based groups that were involved in procuring images used to attacks US forces and bases located across the Middle East.
DadeNegar Startup Studio and the Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Cyber-Electronic Command (IRGC-CEC) were named in the sanctions package.
DadeNegar was sanctioned for supporting the "targeting of US and partner facilities in the Middle East for the Iranian military during Operation Epic Fury." The State Department said DadeNegar used commercial Chinese satellite imagery to support Iran's military in its efforts to target and damage US forces and bases in the region.
The IRGC-CEC was sanctioned due to obtaining information about US forces and bases that was used to support Iran’s targeting of US assets during the conflict.
Both groups were designated "for having engaged, or attempted to engage, in any activity that materially contributes to, or poses a risk of materially contributing to, the proliferation of arms or related materiel or items intended for military end-uses or military end-users, including any efforts to manufacture, acquire, possess, develop, transport, transfer, or use such items, by the Government of Iran."
Individuals also sanctioned by US State Department
Monday's announcement also targeted seven individuals responsible for directing the use of conventional weapons against US forces.
Sanctions targeted members of Iran's Supreme National Council, several commanders of various military branches of the IRGC, the country's deputy defense minister, and the spokesperson for Iran's Defense Ministry.
Former secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr was targeted for having "an active role advocating for Iran’s continued support of its so-called Axis of Resistance."
Zolghadr "was designated by the UN Security Council in Annex I of UN Security Council resolution (UNSCR) 1747 (2007), reimposed on September 27, 2025, in response to Iran’s 'significant non-performance' of its nuclear commitments," the statement added.
IRGC head Ahmad Vahidi and Ali Abdollahi, the newly appointed head of Iran's conventional military and previously commander of the Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters, the Iranian government branch responsible for wartime operations, were sanctioned for their roles in driving military decisions Iran made during Operation Epic Fury.
Sanctions also targeted IRGC Aerospace Force Chief Hossein Mousavi Eftekhari, and Artesh [Iranian army] Chief Amir Hatami. Both were sanctioned due to their responsibility for Iran’s ballistic missile and drone programs.
Deputy Defense Minister for Industrial and Research Affairs Mahdi Farahi was sanctioned by the US for "directing the procurement of arms and related materiel and has demonstrated in-depth knowledge of various missile systems, including those that Iran has reportedly used against US forces and allies."
Reza Talaei-Nik, spokesperson for Iran's main defense ministry body, was sanctioned for "engaging in activity that materially contributes to the supply, sale, or transfer, directly or indirectly, to or from Iran, or for the use in or benefit of Iran, of arms or related materiel, including spare parts."
US sanctions also target fuel exports, shadow fleet
The State Department also sanctioned companies that "engaged in the illicit trade of Iranian petroleum and petrochemical products, activities that have generated millions of dollars in revenue for the Iranian regime," the statement said.
"These Iranian petroleum, petroleum products, and petrochemical cargoes," the statement added, "are frequently transported by shadow fleet operators, including vessel management companies that regularly engage in dark activity and other deceptive shipping practices, endangering other vessels and trade flows."
Sanctions targeted both Iranian and international companies that facilitated the trade of petroleum and petrochemical products with Iran.
Implications of the sanctions
The sanctions come following US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's announcement of the start of Operation Economic Outcast and the implementation of an "economic D-Day" against Iran.
Monday's sanctions mark the start of US action aimed "to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone," said Bessent.
"We are no longer managing the Iranian threat," he emphasized. "We are ending it."
Iran promised to retaliate to sanctions
Before the announcement, Iran threatened both a possible military response and further reduction in oil exports from the Gulf in response to any US economic measures. Afterward, Iranian Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh said, "We are fully prepared for the US sanctions."
"Naturally, the enemies intend to launch an economic terrorist attack on us, but we also have our own tools and know how to play the game. Our defense is no longer so defensive; the enemies should wait for an attack," Madanizadeh told state television.
He also said neither China nor Russia had "accepted" the US measures, and predicted other countries would resist them.
IRGC spokesperson Brigadier-General Hossein Mohebbi vowed heavy blows to US vital interests and energy chokepoints if Iran's infrastructure is threatened, Press TV reported.
Reuters contributed to this report.

US eyes China overcapacity tariffs of 7.5% before Xi-Trump talks

- The tariff move follows investigations under Section 301 and faces legal challenges, with negotiations ongoing about exact rates and suspension periods.
- The US aims to extend the current trade truce with China, while balancing tariffs on allies and justifying duties through forced labour and overcapacity probes.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – The US is set to impose a 7.5 per cent tariff on Chinese goods over allegations of excess manufacturing capacity before a planned summit between Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump in September, according to sources familiar with the matter.
The move would restore Trump’s second-term duties on China to around 20 per cent, a level Beijing has previously said is consistent with its trade truce with Washington. Those come on top of other levies imposed during Trump’s first term and extended during the Biden administration.
It would mark the latest step by Trump to resurrect his protectionist trade agenda after the Supreme Court struck down his previous import taxes on products from China and dozens of other economies, while stopping short of escalating the trade conflict with Beijing beyond the agreed-upon threshold.
Exact rates have yet to be finalised, said the sources, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
Trump is also known to make last-minute demands or changes to trade announcements. One option under consideration is announcing a higher duty rate for China but suspending part of it to reduce the effective rate to 7.5 per cent, a source familiar with the deliberations said.
The details of what rates would be suspended and for how long are still under negotiation, the sources added. Beijing and Washington are also looking to extend their so-called trade pact, which established a one-year truce that is set to expire on Nov 10, they said.
In March, the Trump administration launched an investigation into more than a dozen major trading partners under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 over excess capacity concerns. It was one of two probes that the President’s team used to replace his prior tariffs with more durable ones.
September summit
Administration officials hope to publish the results of the excess capacity inquiry before Trump and Xi are due to meet in Washington on Sept 24. The details of the overcapacity report have proven legally challenging, according to sources familiar with the matter.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told Bloomberg Television in July that the excess capacity investigation would take longer than another on forced labour because of its complexity and that the delay had nothing to do with efforts to maintain the truce with Beijing.
Asked about the tariff plans, a White House official said any announcements will come directly from the administration and that any reporting or discussion of them should be considered baseless speculation. The Office of the US Trade Representative did not immediately respond to a request for comment. China’s Ministry of Commerce did not respond to a fax for comment.
The Trump administration’s approach to China, its foremost geopolitical rival, stands in stark contrast to its stance towards some of the US’ biggest traditional allies.
While the President has been keen not to upset his tariff truce with China, his administration applied a 50 per cent levy on billions of dollars of Canadian products and has mused about tearing up the North American trade agreement he renegotiated during his first term.
Trump is rebuilding a tariff wall that was struck down when the Supreme Court in February ruled that his global levies, issued under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, violated the US Constitution. The President’s temporary 10 per cent global tariffs expired in July and were also deemed illegal by a trade court.
The administration is justifying its new global duties under the findings of its investigations into forced labour and industrial overcapacity in the economies of dozens of trading partners.
As part of that campaign, the administration in July imposed a 12.5 per cent tariff on Chinese goods, citing inadequate efforts to address forced labour practices.
While Beijing criticised the move, it stopped short of announcing retaliatory measures, instead saying Washington had agreed to cap any additional duties on Chinese exports at 20 per cent. That clarified earlier comments that referenced tariff ceilings discussed during trade talks in 2025.
Malaysia deal
“We hope that the US will honour its commitments, ensuring that regardless of the reasons given for imposing or replacing tariffs on China in the future, US tariffs on China will not exceed the levels outlined in the Kuala Lumpur trade consultations,” China’s Ministry of Commerce said in a May statement.
Section 301 allows the US Trade Representative, under the direction of the President, to impose tariffs in response to other nations’ trade measures that it deems discriminatory to American businesses or in violation of US rights under international trade agreements. But efforts to implement the levies have already come up against legal challenges.
A coalition of 25 states, including New York, California and Illinois, filed a lawsuit earlier in August at the US Court of International Trade, adding to similar proceedings by small businesses that claim the levies are illegal. The states allege Trump unlawfully invoked Section 301 to replace tariffs struck down by the Supreme Court, using the forced-labour rationale as a pretext.
The administration has said the duties under Section 301 are legally sound and that the provision has been supported by previous court rulings. BLOOMBERG

Judge postpones U.S. trial for man accused in deadly 1988 Lockerbie bombing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
00:08:50 UTC
09:08:50 KST

Judge postpones U.S. trial for Libyan man accused in deadly 1988 Lockerbie bombing, citing new evidence
A federal judge on Monday postponed a trial in the United States for a former Libyan intelligence official charged in the 1988 bombing of Pan Am Flight 103 over Lockerbie, Scotland, citing the discovery of new evidence that defense attorneys want to examine in the nearly 40-year-old case.
Abu Agila Mohammad Mas'ud Kheir Al-Marimi is charged in the U.S. with making the bomb that downed the airplane, killing 270 people, most of them Americans. Jury selection was scheduled to begin Wednesday for his federal trial in Washington, D.C. — the first trial in the U.S. for the Dec. 21, 1988, bombing.
U.S. District Judge Dabney Friedrich's order didn't specify the nature of the newly discovered evidence.
Al-Marimi's lawyers say prosecutors disclosed the new evidence to them on Saturday and added that their "constitutional and ethical obligations require the defense to investigate this development." Defense attorney Laura Koenig, an assistant federal public defender, declined to elaborate in response to an Associated Press inquiry.
The judge scheduled a Sept. 1 hearing in Washington to discuss the status of the case. Friedrich's brief order cited the complex nature of the case, the newly discovered evidence and "the need for the defense to determine how best to defend this case" as reasons to postpone the trial.
Flight 103 was 31,000 feet over Lockerbie when a bomb in the plane's forward cargo area exploded 38 minutes after takeoff from London Heathrow Airport. The flight was bound for John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York.
The blast killed all 259 passengers and crew members and 11 people on the ground in Lockerbie, where the wreckage destroyed an entire city block. Citizens of 21 countries were killed, including 190 Americans and 43 from the United Kingdom. The passengers included 35 Syracuse University students returning home from a semester abroad.
The FBI says that, prior to 9/11, the Pan Am Flight 103 bombing "was one of the world's most lethal acts of air terrorism and one of the largest and most complex acts of international terrorism ever investigated" by the agency.
Kara Weipz, board president of the nonprofit Victims of Pan Am Flight 103, said her organization had received no details about the new evidence that prompted the trial delay. Weipz's brother, Richard Monetti, was among the Syracuse students killed.
She called the delay a shock and noted that some victims' relatives were already packing to head to the trial.
"At the same time, for almost 38 years we've been seeking the truth of what happened," Weipz said. "If that's what this is, then that's a good thing, and this delay is worth it. ... It's important to hear all the facts."
Prosecutors allege Al-Marimi and others carried out the bombing at the direction of Libyan leader Muammar Qaddafi, who was ousted and killed during a 2011 civil war.
Al-Marimi, now in his mid-70s, is charged with two counts of destruction of an aircraft resulting in death. He faces a maximum penalty of life in prison if convicted. In February 2023, public defender Whitney Minter entered a not guilty plea on his behalf in the U.S. District Court in Washington, D.C.
Two other Libyan intelligence agents were tried by a panel of Scottish judges on a former U.S. military base in the Netherlands in 2000. The tribunal convicted one official and acquitted the other, but the bombmaker's possible identity remained a mystery for years.
According to prosecutors, Al-Marimi worked for the Libyan intelligence service as an explosives expert from approximately 1973 to 2011, rising to the rank of colonel, and had ties to Libya and Tunisia.
Prosecutors believe he brought a suitcase containing a bomb to an airport in Malta and gave it to co-conspirators for a flight to Frankfurt, Germany. The suitcase traveled from Frankfurt to London, where it was loaded onto Flight 103, according to investigators.
Al-Marimi was first charged in 2020 and later indicted in December 2022 before he was transferred to U.S. custody.

What is celebrated on August 25 in Ukraine and around the world
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
03:07:56 EEST
09:07:56 KST

What is celebrated on August 25 in Ukraine and around the world
Kyiv • UNN
On August 25, thematic observances, Uruguay's Independence Day, and Miner's Day are celebrated around the world. Believers honor Photius and Anicetus.
August 25 is World Chicken Day and the Birthday of the Tin Can. Meanwhile, according to the new calendar, believers commemorate the Day of the Holy Martyrs Photius and Anicetas, UNN writes.
World Chicken Day (World Chicken Day / unofficial global initiatives)
A date dedicated to the role of poultry farming in the global food industry and culinary traditions.
Birthday of the Tin Can
A commemorative date dedicated to the patent obtained for preserving food in a tin can by British entrepreneur Peter Durand in 1810, which revolutionized food storage.
Linux Software Birthday
A landmark date in the IT sector dedicated to Linus Torvalds's publication of the first message about creating a new free operating system in 1991.
Independence Day in Uruguay
The country's main national holiday, dedicated to Uruguay's declaration of independence from Brazil in 1825. Nationwide celebrations, parades, and historical reenactments take place throughout the country.
Miners' Day
A traditional commemoration honoring workers in the coal and mining industries who ensure energy security.
National Park Second-Guessing Day
A day dedicated to reconsidering plans for the future and analyzing the steps taken.
Day of the Holy Martyrs Photius and Anicetas
According to the new calendar: on August 25, Orthodox believers commemorate the Holy Martyrs Photius and Anicetas and many others who suffered for the Christian faith during the persecutions of Emperor Diocletian. In the folk calendar, this day was often called "Fostius and Anicetas" or marked the beginning of active preparations for autumn fieldwork.
According to the old calendar: on August 25, the memory of Hieromartyr Alexander, Bishop, as well as the Martyrs Pamphilus and Capiton, is commemorated. Among the people, this day was called "Wounded Photius" or the day when people traditionally put their barns in order and prepared for the arrival of the first autumn birds.

How the French language contributed to the US-Canada trade war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24

How the French language contributed to the US-Canada trade war
- The US-Canada trade war has escalated into a cultural conflict centered on protecting the French language and Quebec culture, which Canada views as fundamental rights.
- Canada faces new US tariffs worth US$20 billion and has vowed to retaliate equally, with strong support from Quebec residents for defending their cultural identity.
- Quebec's recent laws on French-language content and product labelling challenge US companies, while the US downplays language issues but objects to financial rules favouring Canadian competitors.
AI generated
MONTREAL – The trade war between the United States and Canada has taken on the flavour of a culture war after the collapse of negotiations last week.
According to Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, the dispute with the nation’s largest trading partner was not just about tariff demands but what he called unacceptable “threats” to the French language and “Quebec culture”.
Those are not typical sticking points in trade negotiations, but emotive ones in Canada, particularly in the French-speaking eastern province of Quebec, which has long sought to preserve its distinct identity.
Carney said Canadian subsidies for Francophone culture, the role of Francophone online media and bilingual labeling of products sold in Canada were among the issues at stake.
He described these as “fundamental rights” and said there was “a huge gap between Canadian and American perspectives”.
The Prime Minister also contended that the US wanted to destroy Canada’s automotive, steel and aluminum industries, and restrict Canadian trade deals with other countries.
After the breakdown of talks, Canada now faces additional tariffs on some US$20 billion (S$25.4 billion) worth of its US exports and double tariffs on Canadian vehicles, while Carney has vowed to match the US tariffs “dollar for dollar”.
In Quebec, Carney’s decision to break off negotiations was widely supported.
A poll published on Aug 23 by the Angus Reid Institute found that 85 per cent of Quebecers supported the move – the highest approval rate among the 10 Canadian provinces.
“Our identity is not negotiable,” Quebec Premier Christine Frechette wrote on Aug 23 in a social media post.
She faces a re-election battle in October and is currently trailing in polls to the leader of a Quebec separatist party.
According to the Canadian media, Frechette said Washington wanted concessions on Quebec’s rules for appliances and instruction manuals, as well as its law promoting French-language cultural content.
Recent legislation by Quebec allows it to regulate how much French-language content digital platforms offer and how prominently it appears, which can add to the cost of doing business for US companies, the Montreal Gazette reported.
In an interview on Aug 24, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer played down the language issue in the trade talks as a “funny fake story”.
“What we don’t like is a situation where Canada, the federal government, forces American tech companies to take their earnings and give a percentage to their competitors in Canada,” Greer told CNBC.
“But I understand why the Quebecois want to have French language content and all of that. And we think that’s a really valuable thing.” AFP

U.S. Supreme Court lifts lower court ruling that blocks Trump's order to restrict mail-in voting
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
07:45:17 CST
08:45:17 KST

WASHINGTON, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday lifted a lower court's ruling that blocked part of U.S. President Donald Trump's executive order to restrict mail-in voting, but it remains to be seen whether such measures would be implemented before the November midterm election.
"The Court's disposition of this application does not mean that any measure taken by the Government to implement the Order will necessarily be lawful. On that score, time will tell," the nation's highest court said in a ruling.
"But the Order itself does not harm the States, so the District Court lacked jurisdiction to bar the Government from trying to implement it. And for the reasons discussed, that injunction is likely to irreparably harm the Government if it remains in place while the appellate process runs its course," the court continued.
The ruling marks the latest court action in the legal fight over Trump's order rolled out in March, which calls for the Department of Homeland Security to develop state lists of adult U.S. citizens and for the United States Postal Service to obtain lists of eligible mail voters from states.
U.S. media believe that it remains to be seen whether such measures would be implemented before the November midterm election.
CNN report noted that additional legal challenges could hinder implementation of Trump's plan before the midterm elections.
"It remains unclear what impact the high court's order will actually have on eligible mail-in voters," according to a report from NPR.
"The legal fight is far from over, with a separate set of lawsuits led by Democrats and voting rights groups continuing to play out as this fall's election draws closer," the NPR report said. ■

Calls grow for US to deny visa to RSS chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
23:38:12 UTC
08:38:12 KST

More than 1,000 people across the US have written to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, calling on the State Department to deny or revoke a US visa for Mohan Bhagwat, the head of India’s right-wing Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, or RSS.
The letters, collected by the Indian American Muslim Council (IAMC) alongside allied organisations, call on Washington to cancel Bhagwat's scheduled August 29, appearance at Madison Square Garden in New York City amid widespread public opposition.
"Mohan Bhagwat does not represent Indian Americans, and Madison Square Garden should not present him as though he does. The State Department has the authority to deny him a visa, and a federal commission has already recommended it. They must act before August 29," said Mohammed Jawad, President of the IAMC.
Sanctions calls
In March, the US Commission on International Religious Freedom (USCIRF) recommended targeted sanctions against the RSS, including asset freezes and visa restrictions on its leadership, citing its involvement in "acts of extreme violence and intolerance against members of minority groups for decades."
The Congressional Research Service classifies the RSS as a "hardline Hindu nationalist" organisation.
Human Rights Watch has identified the RSS and its affiliates as "most responsible" for violence against Christians and "directly responsible" for the 2002 anti-Muslim violence in Gujarat.
International watchdogs, including Genocide Watch and the US Holocaust Memorial Museum's Early Warning Project, have repeatedly raised alarms over state-tolerated mob violence, bulldozer demolitions of Muslim properties, and the systemic disenfranchisement of India's religious minorities.
Global pushback
The US petition follows actions in Canada, where more than 40 civil society, human rights, and faith groups urged Ottawa to bar Bhagwat, and Canadian MPs called for a ban on the RSS.
The RSS, founded in 1925, serves as the ideological parent organisation of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
Amid mounting scrutiny, senior RSS leaders, including General Secretary Dattatreya Hosabale, have recently conducted outreach tours across the US, Britain, and Germany to counter international criticism and oppose calls for Global Magnitsky sanctions.
IAMC has urged Madison Square Garden management to cancel the event and has called on New York officials to condemn the platforming of the RSS leadership.

A former member of Pussy Riot claimed to have collaborated with the FSB for three years
Kyiv • UNN
Rita Flores said that the FSB forced her to spy on activists and prepared her to abduct Pyotr Verzilov. She fled Russia.
Former Pussy Riot member Rita Flores said that she had been cooperating with the FSB since 2023, and that the Russian security service had tried to involve her in the abduction and murder of Pyotr Verzilov. Flores told this to lawyer Dmitry Zakhvatov in an interview published by Port, Meduza reports, according to UNN.
Details
According to Flores, after a search of her apartment on February 17, 2023, two FSB officers forced her to cooperate, threatening her with criminal prosecution, the murder of her relatives, and the activist’s own disappearance.
The security service gave her the operational alias "Harley," took away all her documents except her internal passport, and provided her with a work phone. Flores’s main task was to collect information about artists and political activists, including members of Pussy Riot.
The FSB allegedly prepared an operation against Verzilov
Flores claims that she took part in the "development" of artist Filip Kozlov, performance artist Pavel Krisevich, and Maria Alyokhina. According to her, the FSB later tried to involve her in the abduction and murder of Pyotr Verzilov.
After receiving the assignment concerning Verzilov, Flores contacted lawyer Dmitry Zakhvatov. According to her, together they managed to postpone the operation, after which she fled Russia. Zakhvatov said that Flores contacted him in the summer of 2025, and that they managed to get her out of the country approximately 10 days ago.
Flores said that she spoke about her cooperation with the FSB in order to help other people in similar situations.

Ozon will pay compensation for destroyed goods only if they are insured against the risk of damage resulting from UAV attacks
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
02:27:03 EEST
08:27:03 KST

Ozon will pay compensation for destroyed goods only if they are insured against the risk of damage resulting from UAV attacks
Kyiv • UNN
Ozon will compensate sellers for losses only if they have insurance with Ingosstrakh. Since the attacks began, the company's shares have fallen by 27%.
The Russian marketplace Ozon said that sellers whose goods were damaged or destroyed as a result of Ukrainian drone strikes on the company's warehouses will be able to receive payouts only if they have the relevant insurance coverage. The Moscow Times reported this, UNN writes.
Details
This concerns sellers who insured their goods with Ingosstrakh against the risk of damage resulting from drone attacks. The amount of the payouts will be determined after an inventory of the damaged warehouses, while instructions on receiving compensation are to be sent to sellers through their personal accounts.
According to Ozon, warehouses in Krasnodar and Makhachkala were damaged, with fires still burning there at the time of the report. The fires in Chapayevsk and Orenburg had already been extinguished, while the logistics centers in Adygea and Nevinnomyssk, according to the company, were not damaged and are expected to resume operations.
Among the measures to support sellers, Ozon also cited the free transportation of goods from closed facilities to other warehouses. Goods headed to the affected logistics centers will be redirected at the company's expense, while storage fees for products at the damaged sites will not be charged from the time of the incident.
According to The Moscow Times, the attacks on Ozon warehouses began on August 22. Over three days, drones attacked six of the company's facilities, and on August 24, Ozon shares on the Moscow Exchange fell 27% at one point—to 2,112.5 rubles per share—the lowest level since August 2023.
Since the beginning of the year, Ozon's market value has fallen by 47%, or approximately 376 billion rubles. Ozon is Russia's second-largest marketplace after Wildberries, whose warehouses have also been struck. According to The Moscow Times, since July 18, 12 large Wildberries logistics centers have been disabled or destroyed, while the reported damage from the attacks has approached 1 trillion rubles.

Breadcrumb
German court convicts siblings over looted Egyptian artefacts
A German court on Monday convicted two siblings of money laundering over the illegal sale of ancient Egyptian artefacts, and ordered the confiscation of 32 million euros ($37 million).
The brother and sister, who were not identified, were also hit with hefty fines in the case related to the objects, which allegedly came from illegal excavations in Egypt.
The artefacts, which were sold for millions of euros to museums, included a bust of Cleopatra, a stone slab associated with King Tutankhamun and items from a princess's grave.
Sentencing the pair, a judge at a regional court in the northern city of Hamburg said "unique cultural treasures" were involved in what was a "highly complex legal case".
The man and woman were accused of acting with other suspects, who are being prosecuted separately. The pair are the children of one of the main alleged perpetrators, reportedly an archaeologist from Hamburg.
The male defendant is said to have been involved in illegally trading the artefacts since 2013, according to prosecutors.
He was accused of bringing several sarcophagi from the princess's grave to Germany, having them restored and then reselling them to a museum in the United Arab Emirates, concealing their origins.
A few years later, he was involved in the illegal sale of the bust of Cleopatra, Egypt's last pharaoh, and the Tutankhamun slab to museums in the UAE.
The court ordered the confiscation of 26 million euros from the male suspect, and that he pay a fine of more than 90,000 euros.
He was however cleared of the more serious charge of working with a gang to deal in stolen goods, because of insufficient evidence.
Some of the sale proceeds flowed through the account of the female defendant.
The court ordered that six million euros be confiscated from her, and fined her 30,000 euros.

TWG Global has tapped veteran Goldman Sachs lawyer David Markowitz to be its chief legal officer, as federal investigators probe how two insurers that are part of TWG CEO Mark Walter's sprawling business empire classified loans to companies the billionaire controls.
Markowitz, while at Goldman, was a major player in the team that negotiated settlements worth billions of dollars to resolve the corruption scandal involving Goldman and its Malaysian subsidiary in connection with the Malaysian state-owned development company 1MDB. The scandal led to criminal and regulatory cases alleging Foreign Corrupt Practices Act violations by the bank.
"We are pleased to welcome David to TWG Global," Walter, who also owns the Los Angeles Dodgers, said in a statement Monday.
"His deep legal experience and proven leadership will be invaluable as we continue to strengthen the legal framework that supports our growth and allows us to execute on our long-term strategic priorities," Walter said.
Walter has not been charged with wrongdoing in the insurance probe.
Bloomberg first reported Markowitz's hiring by TWG, which is a holding company with interests in financial services, insurance, artificial intelligence and technology, and sports and media.
Markowitz's hiring comes nearly two weeks after Walter shocked the sports world by agreeing to sell his controlling stake in the Los Angeles Lakers — which he acquired last October — to Joshua Kushner and Bob Iger in a deal that valued the basketball team at $12.5 billion.
That sale revived attention on the parallel investigations into Walter's businesses by the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York and the Securities and Exchange Commission.
The probes are focused in part on Delaware Life Insurance Co. and its affiliate, Clear Spring Life and Annuity, two Group 1001 insurers ultimately controlled by Walter, and how they labeled about $20 billion in loans to companies that were part of Walter's empire in regulatory filings.
The insurers reclassified billions of dollars of investments as affiliated or related-party transactions after receiving grand jury subpoenas and conducting internal reviews. Lending to affiliates is not illegal.
But Delaware Life, in a reclassification of its audited 2025 financials, said its affiliated investments stood at about 42% of invested assets, up from the 3% originally stated.
TWG last week announced it had agreed to exchange up to $6.5 billion of affiliated investments held by Delaware Life Insurance Co. for an equal amount of nonaffiliated assets.
"Under the agreement, TWG Global takes on investments tied to the performance of affiliated entities and the insurers receive assets that are independent of any affiliate," TWG said in a statement.
Markowitz joined Goldman in 2011, and most recently was the bank's global co-head of litigation and regulatory proceedings.
Before that, Markowitz spent eight years at the Securities and Exchange Commission's enforcement division and later had senior roles in the New York Attorney General's Office.
"I have long admired TWG Global's unique position across some of the world's most cutting-edge industries and its ambitious vision for transforming category-defining businesses and building enduring value," Markowitz said in a statement.
"I look forward to working with the incredible leadership team and helping grow the company's existing legal structure," he said.

Al-Marimi is charged in the US with making the bomb that downed the plane.

Literacy Owns AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
23:15:16 UTC
08:15:16 KST

Despite recent hiccups and doomsday warnings, AI will continue to develop and become part of our everyday lives in much the same way that the internet has since the dotcom bubble burst over 20 years ago. Fears that widespread use of AI will make many job functions obsolete are well founded, but it will also create many opportunities for people skilled in its operation, especially those who can clearly communicate instructions and break down ideas into text. These skills are more than AI literacy, they are skills that we acquire through reading, listening, writing, and speaking—advanced literacy skills.
We need to recognize what AI is good at and what makes it work best for us—how it can automate mundane tasks and streamline processes, but not replace perspective or lateral or critical thought.
AI won’t replace communication or critical thinking, but it is replacing many entry-level jobs.
To make the most of AI, language and critical thinking are prerequisites. You can’t construct prompts to give AI instructions without using precise language. Nor can you check output without careful and critical review. So, if we are to provide our next generation of AI natives with the skills they need for success, we should focus on developing advanced literacy in middle and high school and then increase our attention on humanities like English, World Languages, Linguistics, and Philosophy.
Courses combining AI and philosophy are surging in popularity in China, Hong Kong, and the Philippines, driven by the demand from employers for graduates who can understand and use generative technologies as well as critically evaluate them.
In France, philosophy is strictly compulsory for all students in their final year (Terminale) across general academic tracks, and university applicants must take a philosophy exam to pass the baccalauréat.
Just a few weeks ago, The Economist reported that AI companies are hiring philosophers in large numbers, as philosophy plays a key role in improving the reasoning ability, safety, and ethical judgment of AI models. According to data released by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York earlier this year, the unemployment rate for computer science majors in the US was 7% as of 2024, but for philosophy majors it stood at just 5.1%.
This is not to say that all students need to focus on philosophy. Studying language and literature is another, more practical, route to acquiring many of the same valuable skills—comprehension, reasoning, argument, and communication.
While we must continue to focus on helping ALL children achieve basic literacy in the early grades, we also need to recognize the importance of developing ALL students’ literacy skills as they advance through their schooling and make the most of their linguistic assets.
To work effectively with the latest technological tools in their learning and their work, today’s students need to articulate complex ideas, concepts, and functions; understand detail and nuance; and produce output that speaks to our increasingly multilingual and multicultural society. Our educational policymakers need to react to a world where AI is the ubiquitous tool by encouraging students developing their communication and literacy skills throughout their elementary, high school, college, and work careers.
Daniel Ward

Tens of Thousands of Nevadans Evacuated in Latest Wildfire of Record-Breaking Year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
23:01:47 UTC
08:01:47 KST

The ongoing “Hawk” fire outside the city of Reno, Nevada, has prompted the evacuation of tens of thousands of people in yet another devastating blaze contributing to one of the worst U.S. wildfire seasons in recent history.
Roughly 42,000 people have been evacuated around Reno, while an additional 45,000 were warned that they may also have to flee. The evacuation is among the largest prompted by a U.S. wildfire this year, following the fires around Spokane, Washington, in early August during which roughly 60,000 people were evacuated.
The Reno evacuations mark another flashpoint of a record-breaking fire season. The fire is dwarfed in acreage by larger blazes from this year, at roughly 15,000 acres burned so far, but its direct effect on civilians is one of the largest in recent years, and demonstrates the potential risk that worsening wildfires may have on people and their communities in years to come.
Here’s how fires around the U.S. have set new records, and why they have been so bad this year.
More acres burned and more entrapments
Compared to the past 10 years, more acres have been burned this year in the U.S. to date.
The National Interagency Fire Center (NIFC) posted on Monday that firefighters have responded to 50,784 wildfires that have scorched over 7.8 million acres this year: 168% of the 10-year average for acres burned, and 129% of the average for total fires.
Around the same time last year, roughly 4 million acres had been burned, around 50% of the current acreage for 2026 so far, according to NIFC tracking.
The U.S. has also been at the highest level of “fire preparedness” for 38 days, since July 18th, at a five out of five, which means that federal resources are strained and may not be available to address every new fire.
The 10-year average for fire preparedness in August is four. The last time the fire preparedness level was at a five for the entire month of August was in 2021.
Meanwhile the 10-year annual average for days spent at level four and five combined is 48 days, and so far, the U.S. has already spent 57 days within that range, after reaching level four in late June.
There has also been a 20-year high of firefighter entrapments, life-threatening situations in which firefighters’ safety zones and escape routes are compromised. According to a Reuters report, there had been 12 entrapments in 2026 as of Aug. 13, more than the year-total average of nine in the last 20 years. This year’s entrapments also marked the highest year-to-date figure since 2006.
Six out of 13 firefighter deaths have involved entrapments, the report shows. An average of 17 firefighter fatalities occur each year from wildfires.
Hotter, drier, and windier conditions
Wildfire trackers often use the “30-30-30” rule to identify conditions that can lead to extreme wildfires. The rule refers to when the temperature is at least 30 degrees Celsius (86 Fahrenheit), humidity is at 30% or lower, and wind speeds are at 30 kilometers per hour or more (roughly 19 miles per hour). When combined, these hot, dry, and windy conditions can produce extremely large and destructive fires, as they have this year.
Reno has experienced an average daily high temperature of 92.8 degrees Fahrenheit (33.7 Celsius), 27% humidity, and 18 miles per hour (29 kilometers per hour) daily maximum wind speed over the last 10 days, including the week before the “Hawk” fires began on Saturday and the three days since as the blaze continues.
Although the 30-30-30 rule is a metric for local weather conditions’ effect on wildfires, increases have been exhibited this year compared to past years across the U.S. in each of its categories—temperature, dryness, and wind speed.
When it came to temperature, the average in the contiguous U.S. from January through July was the second warmest in 132 years, at 4.2 degrees Celsius (55.5 Fahrenheit), according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).
July in particular was the hottest month on record in the U.S., with an average of 76.9 degrees Fahrenheit (24.9 Celsius). Nevada specifically had one of its warmest July’s on record, according to NOAA.
Wind speeds generally fluctuate the most by region, but from January through June of this year, they averaged 0.5% above the 20-year average during 2005-2024, according to an S&P Global analysis.
These hotter, drier, and windier conditions have set the stage for an active wildfire season.
One underlying explanation for increasingly fire-prone conditions is climate change, which has contributed to longer-lasting fire seasons, now lasting for six to eight months in some areas, compared to what used to be roughly four months in past decades.
“Generally we're having drier summers and higher winds,” Peter Sunderland, professor of fire protection engineering at the University of Maryland, previously told TIME. “We are seeing more and more climate extremes.”
