Shame and fear of false accusations deter male victims of intimate partner violence from seeking help
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
22:00:05 UTC
07:00:05 KST

Men who experience abuse by a female partner encounter a range of shared obstacles when trying to seek help, but the specific challenges they face often vary depending on their racial and ethnic backgrounds. New research details how concerns like shame, fear of false accusations, and institutional bias shape the decisions of Black, Latino, and White men who have been victimized. The findings were published in Psychology of Men & Masculinities.
Intimate partner violence affects people across all demographics. A survey covered by PsyPost in 2024 indicated that a large majority of men have experienced at least one instance of sexual victimization by a woman. Despite high rates of abuse, men who are victimized are much less likely to ask for support than women.
When they do look for help, they often find themselves alienated in systems that were designed primarily with female victims in mind. These institutional structures can reinforce the idea that male victimization is rare, leaving men without tailored resources.
Earlier research identified the common hurdles that prevent male victims of abuse from seeking help. A 2019 study showed that male victims frequently avoid reporting abuse because they fear society will not believe them or will instead view them as the actual aggressor. That same year, a systematic review confirmed the widespread difficulties and stigma men face when trying to find support for domestic abuse.
Adding to this context, a study covered by PsyPost in 2025 found that societal sexism often leads people to outright deny or minimize the fact that men can be victims of relationship violence. These roadblocks can leave men trapped in abusive situations.
Most of the previous research on this topic focused on predominantly White samples or lumped all men together without looking at racial differences. This dynamic led a research team to investigate how these barriers might differ among specific groups.
The research, led by Lyric N. Russo of George Mason University, involved 1,194 men in the United States between the ages of 18 and 59. The participants were recruited through an online survey platform and were roughly divided into three groups: 596 Latino men, 299 non-Latino Black men, and 299 non-Latino White men.
To participate, all the men had to report having experienced aggressive, controlling, or coercive behavior from a female romantic partner at some point in their lives. The sample represented men who had endured high rates of abuse. Almost all the participants (95.8%) reported being subjected to coercive control, such as a partner keeping them from seeing friends and family, and 84.6% reported experiencing physical abuse.
The men answered questions from a 17-item scale designed to identify specific reasons why they might not have asked for help. The survey also included an open-ended question allowing the participants to describe their unique obstacles in their own words.
Across all three groups, the men reported similar core obstacles. Over half of the total sample (55.7%) viewed the abuse as a private or personal matter, making it the most common reason for not seeking help. Nearly half of the participants reported feeling shame or embarrassment (49.2%).
Similar numbers expressed concerns that their partner would falsely accuse them or seek revenge (47.8%), that they would be blamed (47.5%), or that they simply did not know how to tell anyone (47.3%). Nearly 40 percent doubted whether resources could actually help them.
The pattern of obstacles shifted when looking at specific racial and ethnic groups. Latino men reported a higher total number of barriers on average than Black men. They were more likely than both Black and White men to report that they did not know how to disclose their experiences.
They also expressed more concern about bringing shame or dishonor to their families. Compared to White men, Latino men were more likely to cite language difficulties, concerns about revealing their immigration status, and a fear that their partner was actively preventing them from seeking help.
Black men in the study were less likely than both Latino and White men to worry that others would not believe them or would be biased against them. The authors note that this finding requires context to be properly understood. Rather than feeling confident that they would be supported, the lower concern about bias might reflect societal stereotypes about Black women.
Because 73.2% of the Black men in the study reported that their abusive partner was a Black woman, racialized gender stereotypes portraying Black women as aggressive might cause society to find the men’s reports of abuse more believable, even if institutional support remains inadequate.
White men reported their own distinct challenges. Based on the open-ended responses, White men were more likely than Latino men to express difficulty recognizing or labeling their experiences as abuse. Traditional gender norms that emphasize toughness and self-reliance can make it hard for men to realize that a partner’s behavior is actually abusive, leading them to interpret the harmful actions as normal relationship conflict rather than mistreatment.
The study relied on a specific sample of men recruited through an online panel, meaning the results might not represent all men in these demographic groups. Men without internet access or those less comfortable sharing personal experiences online were likely not included. The research also captured a snapshot in time rather than tracking the men over a longer period. This approach makes it impossible to determine how barriers to seeking help might change as a relationship progresses or as a person’s life circumstances shift.
The data comes entirely from self-reported surveys, which can be influenced by a person’s willingness to disclose sensitive information. The study focused exclusively on men abused by female partners. Men who experience abuse from male or nonbinary partners might encounter a different set of obstacles, shaped by different social stigmas and available resources. Future research could explore how different types of relationships and community contexts alter a person’s ability to access support services.
The study, “Barriers to Help-Seeking Among Male Victims of Female-Perpetrated Intimate Partner Violence: Insights From Black, Latino, and White Men,” was authored by Lyric N. Russo, Denise A. Hines, Jennifer L. Mezzapelle, Chiara Sabina, Kerry A. Lee, and Emily M. Douglas.

====================================================================================================

Air Force ‘Closely Following’ Navy’s New Long-Range Air-to-Air ‘Malice’ Missile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
21:57:01 UTC
06:57:01 KST

A new Navy missile could fill a long-range air-to-air need for the U.S. Air Force’s fourth-, fifth-, and sixth-generation fighters.
The Navy’s portfolio acquisition executive for munitions posted information on the AIM-424 Long Range Air-to-Air Missile online on Aug. 22, the same day it unveiled the project at the service’s annual Tailhook Symposium in Reno, Nev.
The Raytheon missile is geared for Marine and Naval aviators’ fighter platforms, from the Boeing F/A-18 Super Hornet to the Lockheed Martin F-35 Lightning II, with a range “in excess of 250 nautical miles.”
“Also known as Malice, the LRAAM directly supports the Department’s contribution to integrated deterrence by increasing range, lethality, and combat effectiveness for Marine and Naval Aviation forces that are defending our fleets, our interests, and our homeland,” according to a Navy statement emailed to media. “Further details regarding specific capabilities and deployment timelines remain classified to protect operational security.”
Malice’s advertised range is well more than that of the Lockheed Martin AIM-260 Joint Advanced Tactical Missile, said to be beyond 120 miles, and the Raytheon AIM-120D Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile, around 100 nautical miles. The Air Force is taking the lead in developing JATM for itself and the Navy.
“With increased range, lethality, and combat effectiveness for naval forces, the AIM-424 delivers a generational leap in long range air-to-air combat capability that can out range any threat,” Phil Jasper, president of Raytheon, said in an email statement.
Malice Data
- Contractor: Raytheon
- Propulsion: Solid-propellant rocket motor
- Length: 13.5 feet
- Diameter: 13.5 inches
- Wingspan: 26.2 inches
- Weight: 1,500 pounds
- Range: In excess of 250 nm
- Warhead: Blast fragmentation
Source: Navy
But while Malice represents a major increase in range over current missile programs, it falls short more ambitious efforts early in development like the Air Force Long Range Weapon, which seeks distances of more than 1,000 nautical miles. The Air Force first revealed plans for the AFLRW in June.
“The Air Force is closely following the progress of the Navy on the AIM-424 Long Range Air-to-Air Missile Program,” an Air Force spokesperson told Air & Space Forces Magazine on Aug. 24. The spokesperson declined to answer additional questions.
The two services often partner on missiles for their aircraft, such as JATM, AMRAAM, and the AIM-9X Sidewinder.
“The Navy and Air Force have different operational requirements, but in areas such as fighter-launched offensive weapons, each can benefit from the other’s technological advances, testing, and development,” said retired Air Force Col. John “JV” Venable, senior resident fellow at the Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies. “Malice appears to be another example of how parallel efforts can accelerate capability and produce benefits across the Joint Force.”
The Navy has also developed the AIM-174B Gunslinger, which has a range of 150-200 nautical miles, but that missile won’t fit in the internal weapon bays of the F-35 and F-22, limiting its usefulness to the Air Force.
The new Malice missile, on the other hand, is meant to go a wide range of aircraft, including sixth-gen fighters like the Navy’s not-yet-named F/A-XX and the Air Force’s parallel project, the Boeing F-47.
“The long-range missile fight is much like a jousting contest: the fighter with the longer lance has a major advantage,” said Venable, a former F-16 pilot and commander. “Chinese beyond-visual-range missiles are assessed to outrange many current U.S. weapons, potentially giving Chinese fighters the opportunity to shoot first by dozens of miles.”
The Malice missile would “extend U.S. engagement range, improve first-shot opportunities, and help restore our tactical advantage against peer adversaries,” he said.
Beyond the tactical level, Venable noted, having a missile like Malice in the fighter community’s quiver would give commanders greater flexibility in operational planning and offset numerical disparity with a potential peer fight.
“The People’s Liberation Army Air Force (PLAAF) already holds a significant advantage in the numbers of fighters it can generate over Taiwan compared with the U.S. and allied forces,” he said. “We need every technological advantage available to offset that numerical disparity.
Roots
Aviation Week reported that Malice has a two-stage design—reminiscent of a decade-old program known as the Long Range Engagement Weapon, developed in the mid-2010s under then-Secretary of Defense Ash Carter.
Flight Global reported at the time the LREW effort was also a two-stage design that would eventually transition to multiple services. The Air Force was known to be working on the weapon while also developing the JATM – both efforts sought to replace the decades-old AMRAAM, which debuted in the mid-1980s.
The JATM is seen as a direct replacement for fighters to carry instead of the AMRAAM. But the LREW’s two-stage design promised a far greater range.

BRATISLAVA, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- Slovakia's minimum wage will rise to 972 euros (1133.5 U.S. dollars) per month in 2027, up from 915 euros (1067.1 U.S. dollars) in 2026, Slovak Labour, Social Affairs and Family Minister Erik Tomas announced on Monday following a meeting of the tripartite council.
"The minimum wage next year will be 972 euros (1133.5 U.S. dollars), bringing it closer to the symbolic threshold of 1,000 euros (1166.2 U.S. dollars)," Tomas said. The minister also presented a qualified estimate for the minimum wage in 2028, when it is expected to exceed 1,000 euros (1166.2 U.S. dollars) per month and could reach 1,016 euros (1184.8 U.S. dollars). Extra payments for night and weekend work will also increase, as they are linked to the minimum wage.
The minimum wage in Slovakia is regulated under Act No. 663/2007 Coll. It is set annually for the following calendar year and applies as a monthly and hourly amount. Under the law, the minimum wage is set at 60 percent of the average nominal salary from two years earlier. According to Slovak Statistics Office, the average nominal salary in 2025 stood at 1,620 euros (1889.2 U.S. dollars).
Tomas added that approximately 120,000 employees are paid the basic minimum wage in 2026. If all six minimum-wage levels based on job difficulty are taken into account, the measure will affect approximately 160,000 people in 2026, some 6 percent of the country's labor force. ■

GABORONE, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- Botswana's Ministry of Higher Education and the China-invested Khoemacau Copper Mining company on Monday signed a collaboration agreement to establish a Mining Center of Excellence at Maun Technical College in North West District of the southern African country, to train technical workers for the local mining sector.
Speaking at the event held in Gaborone, the capital of Botswana, Minister of Higher Education Prince Maele said the partnership shows "a new way of thinking about skill development, technical education, relationship of education and industry," to fill the industry skill gap.
The agreement is meant to produce graduates who are "skilled, employable, innovative, adaptable and globally competitive," bringing the classroom closer to the workplace so that "theory must meet practice," and knowledge translates into productivity, said Maele.
He said the goal is for young people to leave school ready to work, cultivating not just job seekers but problem-solvers and entrepreneurs equipped to enter the workforce with practical, industry-relevant skills. He noted that he is "looking forward to a productive, enduring, and mutually beneficial relationship" with the project.
Chen Dexin, chairman of China Minmetals Corporation, parent company of Khoemacau Copper Mining company's investor MMG, termed the mine project as a bridge of friendship between China and Botswana, and pledged the corporation's long-term commitment to the country's socio-economic development.
The mining center of excellence aims to build local capacity through world-class training and produce a substantial pool of skilled workers, he added, describing its purpose as extending far more than running training courses to include lasting community and regional benefit.
Minister of International Affairs Phenyo Butale said the country's relationship with China has evolved beyond financial assistance toward skills transfer, which is successful in China's development. He described the center as a step toward building a pipeline of Batswana technicians and engineers who will eventually lead, not just work in, the mining sector.
Minister of Minerals and Energy Bogolo Kenewendo said the government is focused on making work-based learning standard and letting industry help shape curricula, pointing to the Kalahari Copper Belt and other base-metal deposits as key to diversifying an economy long dominated by diamonds.
Botswana's Minister of Labor and Home Affairs Pius Mokgware and Chinese Ambassador to Botswana Fan Yong also attended the event, which featured traditional music and song performance of Botswana. ■

Feature: Polish farmers find cheer in harvest despite tough growing season
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
05:55:27 CST
06:55:27 KST

by Yue Yuanyuan, Guo Shuang
WARSAW, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- Folk music filled the air as people in traditional costumes danced, local residents sold agricultural products and handicrafts, and families wandered among stalls at a harvest festival in Warsaw over the weekend.
The festival is one of Poland's long-standing rural traditions, held after the main fieldwork and harvests are completed.
Traditionally, farmers give thanks for the crops they have gathered and celebrate the end of months of work in the fields.
Yet behind this year's festive atmosphere lies a difficult growing season marked by sharp weather swings.
Poland experienced unfavorable weather conditions for agriculture this year, according to Statistics Poland.
In its preliminary estimate released in late July, the agency put production of basic cereals and cereal mixtures at 25.3 million tonnes this year, down about 4.9 percent from 2025.
Rapeseed production was projected to fall 14.4 percent, while fruit harvested from trees was expected to decline by 18.6 percent and output from fruit bushes and berry plantations by 6.5 percent.
The Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development has said frosts in April caused temperatures near the ground to fall as low as minus 10 degrees Celsius in some areas, damaging sour and sweet cherries, raspberries and currants.
Drought added another layer of pressure.
Poland's agricultural drought monitoring system found drought conditions affecting a wide range of crops between March and July, including cereals, rapeseed, fruit bushes and maize.
Stanislaw and Barbara Wojcik, an elderly farming couple who grow wheat and rye and sell homemade bread at the festival, said "We harvested less wheat and rye than last year. There was too little rain at some stages, and the heat also affected the crops."
The picture emerging from the harvest festival, however, was not entirely bleak.
Alexander Sobolev, who sells bottled freshly pressed fruit juice and has lived in Poland for four years, said "apples are expected to be very good, and there were a lot of strawberries."
For beekeeper Krzysztof Tomkielski, the changing weather brought more gains than losses. Sunny weather was particularly favorable for buckwheat honey. "There was more honey than last year," he said.
The sector's resilience is also supported by government measures. Poland has 2.4 million bee colonies, the second-largest number in the European Union after Spain, and nearly 100,000 active beekeepers, according to the Polish government.
Funding for this year's beekeeping support programs has been increased by 20 million zlotys (about 5.4 million U.S. dollars).
The harvest may have been uneven, but the difficulties of the growing season did little to dampen the festive spirit. Music played, children watched folk performances, and farmers stood behind their stalls smiling and talking with visitors.
"It is not only about having a very good harvest," said Sobolev. "People come here to be thankful for what they have and celebrate the work of the whole season." ■

U.S. threatens "economic D-Day" sanctions on Iran
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
05:55:20 CST
06:55:20 KST

This photo taken on Aug. 24, 2026 shows the U.S. Department of the Treasury in Washington, D.C., the United States. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday threatened Iran with "an economic D-Day," announcing a wave of new sanctions aimed at further isolating the country. (Xinhua/Li Rui)
NEW YORK, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday threatened Iran with "an economic D-Day," announcing a wave of new sanctions aimed at further isolating the country.
"We are launching an economic onslaught against Iran's financial connections around the globe," said Bessent at a press conference. "Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline" that sustains the country, he said.
The U.S. Treasury Department said in a press release that the new sectoral sanctions determinations target five critical sectors -- digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping -- that the U.S. says Iran has relied on to prop up its economy.
The measures marked the beginning of "a sustained and systematic campaign to close every financial resource" that supports Iran, the department said. It added that "any entity that facilitates money laundering or sanctions evasion on behalf of Iran risks being cut off from the U.S. financial system."
The department is expanding the categories of "Iran-related conduct" that the United States might sanction in the future, and said "every country will be given a defined timeline to shut down the Iran-related activity" the United States has identified.
Bessent disclosed that U.S. President Donald Trump has been calling world leaders with specific requests to cease their interactions with Iran.
Simultaneously, the department's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) sanctioned nearly 60 entities, individuals, and vessels in multiple jurisdictions that enable Iran's activities, including illicit nuclear and missile technology procurement, cyber operations, and oil-revenue generation networks.
OFAC also suspended several general licenses that previously authorized certain remittance payments to Iran and Iranian access to the U.S. cultural and academic system.
Additionally, the Treasury Department released additional guidance on the sanctions risks associated with complying with Iranian demands regarding shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.
In a post on X, Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf responded to U.S. economic threats against Tehran by saying that, "Iran's trading partners, both in the media and through messages sent to us, have made it clear that they don't take these statements into account anywhere."
"They cannot cut off our financial lifelines," Iran's Minister of Economic Affairs and Finance Seyed Ali Madanizadeh said in another X post, adding that Tehran has been "planning for some time to counter the sanctions." ■

US set for largest mass visa revocation, targeting up to 200,000 foreigners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
21:53:42 UTC
06:53:42 KST

US targets up to 200,000 foreigners in largest-ever mass visa revocation
State Department prepares mass revocation of tourist and business visas for foreigners seeking asylum
The Trump administration is preparing to revoke the business and tourism visas of up to 200,000 foreigners who have applied for or are currently seeking asylum status in the United States. If it happens, the move would be the largest single mass revocation of visas in US history and would likely face legal challenges.
Unless challenged or revised, the State Department was expected to announce in the coming weeks the revocation of so-called B1 and B2 visas issued between 2016 and 2026 whose holders have sought asylum or are now seeking asylum, according to State Department documents obtained by Associated Press and two US officials. The action would be taken in coordination with the Department of Homeland Security.
“We are coordinating with DHS to identify and revoke the nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently,” said State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott.
He declined to comment on the number of visas that might be revoked, saying “as the process will be ongoing, the number of revocations remains dynamic and will be done on a rolling basis”.
The revocations would not necessarily result in their immediate deportation, the officials said. Most of those with asylum cases currently pending would be recategorised but would lose their status as business or tourism travellers, according to the officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because the revocations are not final yet.
Since US President Donald Trump took office for his second term last year, his administration has steadily ramped up restrictions on visa applicants — demanding more information about their social media histories, requiring the posting of expensive bonds for the processing of visas, and outright banning the issuance of visas to citizens of certain countries.

Israel bars two Swedish MEPs from West Bank visit
Israel said Monday that it had refused entry to two left-wing Swedish deputies in the European Parliament who wanted to visit the occupied West Bank.
Jonas Sjostedt and Hanna Gedin, members of Sweden's Left Party, were turned away Sunday at Israel's Ben Gurion Airport, the primary gateway for visitors to the Palestinian territory.
Israel's foreign ministry said the pair had "consistently acted against Israel", including by calling for international legal proceedings against Israelis.
"On various public occasions, they have spread false accusations against Israel, including allegations of genocide, deliberate starvation and the intentional targeting of children and medical personnel," the ministry said in a statement.
United Nations investigators, who do not speak for the global body as a whole, charged in June that Israel was deliberately targeting Palestinian children in an ongoing "genocide" in Gaza.
Israel fiercely rejected the finding and accused Hamas of using Palestinian children as human shields.
Sjostedt in a Facebook post said that the two MEPs planned to meet human rights and charitable organisations, including Save the Children, and to see refugee camps.
"We continue to work against Israel's illegal occupation, the displacement of Palestinians, and genocide," Sjostedt wrote.
He added that Sweden had issued a protest.
But Swedish Foreign Minister Maria Malmer Stenergard, while noting the Swedish embassy assisted the pair, said that every country "has its own entry regulations" and that Sweden has a travel advisory in place for Israel and the Palestinian territories.
"Why Jonas Sjostedt and Hanna Gedin nevertheless choose to travel there is something they themselves need to answer," she told the Dagens Nyheter newspaper.
Rawhi Fattouh, president of the Palestinian National Council, the West Bank-based legislative body, called on European parliaments to speak out against the exclusion of critical voices.
The denial of entry is "an attempt to impose silence by force and turn criticism of the occupation into an accusation, in clear disregard for international law and the moral immunity afforded to parliamentary work", he said.

US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Monday that Washington is not ruling out further military strikes on Iran, even as the Trump administration intensifies economic pressure on Tehran.
Asked whether kinetic strikes were currently on pause, Hegseth said: “No. If we need to use kinetic strikes, we'll use them.”

Hegseth also declined to discuss reports that US stocks of ATACMS long-range missiles had been significantly depleted in ongoing conflicts, saying the military had “plenty” available.

“To the sailors and families of the Lincoln, I say godspeed on a historic mission. Congratulations, you're on your way home,” he said, describing the deployment as “tough” and longer than most.
The Lincoln has spent more than eight months without making a port call, setting a US Navy record. Families of sailors have reported worsening conditions and morale aboard the carrier, though Hegseth has said such claims have been “completely misrepresented.”

Supreme Court allows Trump's plan to regulate but not block use of mail ballots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
21:38:04 UTC
06:38:04 KST

Supreme Court for now allows Trump to plan new mail ballot rules. California to sue again
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta said his office expects to sue again within days.
- About 30% of the nation’s voters — and 80% of Californians — cast their ballots by mail in 2024.
WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court cleared the way Monday for President Trump to continue seeking new limits on the use of mail ballots, though their implementation remains in dispute as the November election rapidly approaches.
California leaders immediately noted the limits of the high court ruling and said they would file a lawsuit to prevent Trump’s desired changes from taking effect.
“The Supreme Court just let the Trump administration move ahead (for now) with its plan to disenfranchise voters across the country. California will be suing AGAIN to block these Orwellian rules from being implemented,” Gov. Gavin Newsom said in a statement.
Acting by a 6-3 vote, the court’s conservatives granted an emergency appeal from Trump’s lawyers and set aside a lower judge’s order that blocked federal agencies — including the Department of Homeland Security and the U.S. Postal Service — from advancing new federal regulations on states and their use of mail ballots.
Trump called for those regulations in a March executive order directing Homeland Security to compile its own lists of eligible citizen voters in each state and the Postal Service to restrict its processing of mail ballots to those submitted by individuals on those Homeland Security lists.
The high court’s ruling allows those agencies to move forward with their work to comply with Trump’s order, but reaches no conclusions as to the legality of those pending rules.
Across California and the nation, Democratic leaders and voting rights advocates are ramping up coordination and gaming out responses to a raft of potential actions by the Trump administration to subvert the November vote or deny its outcome.
“The Court’s disposition of this application does not mean that any measure taken by the Government to implement the Order will necessarily be lawful. On that score, time will tell,” the high court wrote.
The unsigned order spoke for the six Republican appointees. The three liberals, all Democratic appointees, dissented in two separate opinions.
Lauren Bis, a White House spokeswoman, called the ruling a “major win for the security of American elections” in a statement to The Times.
“These are commonsense measures that protect the security of mail-in ballots and ensure only Americans are electing American leaders,” Bis said. “This Administration will continue to lawfully enact the agenda President Trump was elected on — which includes the safety and security of our elections.”
California officials stressed that the court’s ruling does not allow final implementation of the rules requested by Trump.
California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta, who helped lead the coalition of states challenging Trump’s order, called the ruling “somewhat disappointing” but “purely procedural” and far from the final word on the issue.
“It doesn’t address the merits. And we think that when the merits are addressed — and we will bring a lawsuit to address the merits of this case — that we will prevail, because the president has zero authority to determine the time, place and manner of elections, and he is through an executive order trying to exert a very significant amount of authority,” Bonta said.
He said the court found the state’s lawsuit was not “ripe” to bring because there was no final Postal Service rule in place implementing new controls on mail ballots. He said the Postal Service issued a final rule Friday — and “now that the final rule’s in place, we’ll sue, and we’ll start from the beginning.”
The 95-page new rule implements parts of Trump’s executive order by requiring a new design for mail ballots and the envelopes they go in, as well as procedures for how data are collected from them by the federal government.
Bonta said his office expects to sue again within days. He expects a lower court will block the Trump-ordered changes again, and for that ruling to stand through November. He said if the high court does weigh in again before the midterms, he expects it to acknowledge that the president has no authority to dictate election policy.
Dean Logan, registrar-recorder and county clerk for Los Angeles County, also said the issue is far from settled.
“As we approach the issuance of the first ballots for the November General Election, it is important to recognize that these regulations are still subject to active litigation and interpretation,” Logan said in a statement to The Times. “In response, we will intensify our voter outreach and educational initiatives to ensure individuals are fully informed and aware of any adjustments to the voting process.”
The Supreme Court found in part that the lower court order blocking the agencies from working toward Trump’s order was invalid because that work had yet to cause any harm to the states that sued, including California.
It wrote that Trump’s executive order “is internal directive from the President to his subordinates mandating that certain agencies pursue certain policies. It neither requires nor forbids anything of anyone outside the Executive Branch.”
About 30% of the nation’s voters — and 80% of Californians — cast their ballots by mail in 2024. Trump, however, has long maintained that voting by mail leads to fraud, including voting by noncitizens.
With the court’s ruling Monday, Homeland Security may compile state-by-state lists of citizens who are 18 and over and eligible to vote. However, California and other states “are not required to use the Lists,” the court said.
The Trump administration has acknowledged potential law enforcement applications for the lists and warned state election officials across the country that they could face legal consequences if they don’t work to ensure that noncitizens aren’t able to vote in their elections.
President Trump signed an executive order Tuesday purporting to place new federal controls on voting by mail in states such as California.
Such warnings from the administration were mentioned by Justice Sonia Sotomayor in her dissent as evidence of the harm suffered by the states already, and reason for the lower court’s ruling halting implementation to hold.
She wrote that the administration has acknowledged that a state’s “refusal to consider” the Homeland Security lists “could conceivably, depending on the circumstances, be relevant evidence of an intent to violate, or to facilitate the violation of, the federal laws prohibiting non-citizen voting.”
She also made the limits of the majority’s ruling clear.
“Today’s decision does not address whether the President’s attempts to interfere with States’ administration of the November 2026 elections are lawful,” Sotomayor wrote in a dissent joined by Justice Elena Kagan. “Nor does it suggest that the Executive Branch has any constitutional or statutory authority to implement the President’s directives. Instead, today’s decision merely postpones adjudication of those challenges.”
Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, in her own dissent, also noted the limits of the majority’s ruling and criticized it for failing “to explain when, exactly, is the right time to bring a meritorious election-rule claim challenging unconstitutional interference with electoral processes.”
Jackson wrote that the ruling “needlessly injects chaos and uncertainty into the upcoming midterm elections. It also lets another shoe drop in the Kafkaesque nightmare that our precedents have been steadily creating for certain plaintiffs who seek to bring election-related challenges.”
Trump’s executive order said it was aimed at “ensuring citizenship verification” in federal elections. California and 22 other Democratic-led states sued a few days later and said Trump sought to use the Postal Service to impose new restrictions on voting by mail. They also argued the Constitution gives states and Congress the power to regulate elections, not the president.
A federal judge in Boston and the 1st Circuit Court agreed with the challengers and blocked Trump’s executive order from taking effect for the November elections.
The case on appeal was Trump vs. California because Bonta was a leader of the Democratic state attorneys who sued.
Logan, of Los Angeles County, said the Trump administration’s “ongoing efforts to modify the electoral process amid an election cycle are deeply troubling and frustrating,” and that one of the “most significant risks we face” as a result is “the possibility of voter confusion and diminished participation — outcomes that run counter to the principles of free and fair elections.”
“Our team is dedicated to minimizing any adverse effects on voters, and we will work diligently to safeguard their ability to make their voices heard and ensure their votes are properly recorded,” Logan said.

US public support for Iran war falls as Trump approval at record low: Poll
Falling Republican support, rising gas prices, and fears of a long conflict drive a decline in backing for the Iran war.
Support in the United States for the war on Iran has fallen as President Donald Trump’s approval remains at a record low, a Reuters/Ipsos poll suggests.
Public backing for the war has dropped to its lowest level since the early stages of the conflict, with declining Republican support contributing to the shift, according to the poll released on Monday.

Just 31 percent of Americans surveyed said they support US military action against Iran, down from 37 percent in March and 34 percent earlier this month. Support among Republican respondents fell to 69 percent, compared with 77 percent in March.
The war is also continuing to weigh on Trump’s standing with the public, the poll suggests. For the second consecutive Reuters/Ipsos survey, 33 percent of respondents said they approved of Trump’s performance as president, matching the lowest approval rating recorded in the polling series across his first and second terms.
Trump has defended the military campaign as necessary to prevent Iran from developing a nuclear weapon. The conflict began on February 28 with US and Israeli attacks on Iran.
But the economic effects of the war remain a concern for Americans. Iran has maintained a de facto blockade of oil exports from the region, contributing to a rise in US petrol prices to near record highs.
The Trump administration has also announced recent pledges to increase economic pressure on Iran. Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent said on Monday that the US would target all of Iran’s sources of revenue, including oil, with the aim of preventing other countries and companies from doing business with Tehran. The campaign is dubbed “Operation Economic Outcast”.
A growing majority of Americans expect the war to continue for some time, the poll suggests. Eighty-three percent of respondents said they believe the conflict will last for an extended period, up from 80 percent earlier this month.
The prospect of a lengthy war presents a challenge for Trump, who campaigned for the presidency in 2024 on promises to bring down inflation and to adopt an “America First” strategy of avoiding foreign military engagements.
Six months into the conflict, petrol prices are more than $1 per gallon (3.8 litres) higher than they were before the war, adding to economic pressure ahead of November’s midterm elections.
The higher fuel costs could also create difficulties for Republicans defending narrow congressional majorities.
The poll suggests that independent voters favour Democrats over Republicans when asked which party they would support in a congressional election held today. Among independents, 33 percent said they would vote for a Democrat, compared with 19 percent who said they would choose a Republican.
The Reuters/Ipsos survey questioned 1,215 adults across the United States over four days and has a margin of error of 3 percentage points in either direction.

US Supreme Court gives Trump temporary win on mail-in ballots as midterms loom
Decision permits Trump administration to enforce restrictions for now, leaving final judgment pending as Democrats vow new lawsuits
The US Supreme Court gave President Donald Trump a temporary victory on Monday, lifting a lower court block on his executive order curbing the use of mail-in ballots.
The Republican president signed an order in March seeking to restrict mail-in voting ahead of the November midterm elections but it was immediately met with multiple legal challenges.
Democratic-led states sued the administration on grounds that under the US Constitution, states – and not the federal government – retain broad control over the administration of elections.
A district court in Massachusetts blocked implementation of the executive order but the Supreme Court on Monday lifted the judge’s stay, allowing parts of Trump’s directive to go ahead for now.
“The District Court lacked jurisdiction to bar the Government from trying to implement” the executive order, the Supreme Court majority said in an unsigned opinion.
But the justices withheld final judgment on the merits of the case pending further litigation.

Why all the fuss on a Triple Zero campaign from telcos?
Why are telcos sending us messages on how 000 works? Nobody cares how it works. If my network is down I just want to know if I dial 000 I’ll get connected. Sounds like they’re just going to give us all the excuses why it might not work .
- Phillip
Hi Phillip,
That's the whole point of the campaign — because in the event your network is down, they want you to know you can still dial Triple Zero (000) if there's an emergency.
Since outages are (thankfully) pretty rare, not everyone knows that they can still call Triple Zero and be connected to the relevant emergency service. But during an outage, the only difference is that the call can take slightly longer to connect to the other network (we're talking 40–50 seconds) due to how the "camp-on" process works.
In other words — if you called Triple Zero during an outage, you might not hear the usual or expected ringing initially, but the call is still going through.
Optus in particular has been leading the push for this campaign after their outage in 2023.
"This campaign provides Australians with practical information about how their phone connects to emergency services and what they should do if their usual network is unavailable," an Optus spokesperson said.
"By raising awareness of safeguards such as emergency camp-on and providing simple guidance people can use in a high-pressure situation, we're helping Australians better prepare for the moments when reliable access to Triple Zero matters most."
Key Event
AI brands seeing mounting distrust levels amongst Australians
Australians are increasingly distrustful of artificial intelligence brands like OpenAI and Palantir, according to Roy Morgan's latest risk monitor report.
The findings show that in the year to June, Optus is still the most distrusted brand, followed by Meta, Temu, Woolworths and Coles.
While their positions haven't changed, Roy Morgan's research shows that OpenAI (including ChatGPT) and Palantir have seen the "most consequential declines".
OpenAI is the 16th-most distrusted brand due to privacy concerns and personal data risks, while Palantir is now the 30th-most distrusted brand in the country.
"The latest results from the ongoing trust survey show distrust in both brands has grown quickly — despite neither facing a definable and definitive scandal," said Roy Morgan CEO Michele Levine.
"Australians are increasingly citing concerns about AI companies such that the customer interfaces don't protect users' privacy, the companies are unethical and dishonest, they're too motivated by profit and greed, and also that the large electricity requirements to run the data centres these companies rely on are environmentally irresponsible."
As for the brands Australians trust the most? There have been no changes there: Bunnings, Aldi, Kmart, Commonwealth Bank and Apple are still topping the list.
Key Event
eHarmony engaged in misleading conduct about pricing and subscriptions
The Federal Court has ruled that online dating site eHarmony misled customers about the "pricing, renewal and duration" of its memberships.
Almost three years ago, the ACCC announced it was suing the dating site over what it described as a "subscription trap" and alleged the company broke consumer law in the process.
But the Federal Court has today ruled that the dating site did breach Australian Consumer Law by engaging in misleading or deceptive conduct by:
- offering free dating when a consumer could not engage in ongoing communication with other people for free
- the automatic renewal of memberships
- one-month memberships, when the minimum period consumers could sign up for was six months
- consumers not being able to cancel their subscription early
- stating monthly subscription prices that did not mention an additional mandatory fee to pay monthly.
eHarmony was also found to have broken Australian Consumer Law by failing to display the minimum total amount a customer would pay for their subscription as a single price.
"The ACCC is committed to taking action against businesses that engage in misleading conduct in the digital economy, including by using subscription traps and other dark patterns that unfairly impact consumer choice," ACCC Commissioner Luke Woodward said.
"The Court's ruling underscores that when businesses advertise a price for a subscription divided into instalments, such as a price per month, the minimum total cost must also be clearly and prominently displayed."
In a statement, eHarmony says it has been cooperating with the ACCC throughout the case and is "carefully reviewing the Federal Court's judgment and considering [its] options".
The matter will return to court at a later date to determine penalties and compensation for customers.

Have you gotten a reminder from your telco provider this week about reaching Triple Zero even when your phone doesn't have any connection?

Key Event
RBA considered rate hike at August meeting
The minutes from the RBA's latest monetary policy meeting earlier this month have just been released, and have revealed the central bank considered lifting interest rates by 0.25 percentage points.
That would have taken the cash rate to 4.6%, the highest level since late 2011, but unanimously voted to leave it on hold at 4.35%.
In explaining its consideration to potentially lift rates the minutes referred to the "assessment of the risks to the inflation forecast".
"Members noted that if the risks around the inflation forecast were judged to be significantly skewed to the upside it may be appropriate to mitigate those risks somewhat by tightening monetary policy pre-emptively," it said.
Those risks included:
"A prolonged conflict in the Middle East could cause oil reserves to dwindle to very low levels and oil prices to rise sharply; widespread cost pressures … could be passed into consumer prices more fully than assumed; the AI and data centre investment boom could prove to be larger than anticipated, globally and/or in Australia; aggregate demand in Australia more generally could be more resilient than forecast; and productivity growth might not pick up as assumed in the forecasts."
Ultimately though, the RBA "judged it appropriate to leave the cash rate target unchanged at this meeting, while remaining alert to the upside risks to the inflation outlook and being ready to act should they materialise".
That said, the RBA reiterated that it won't hesitate to lift rates again if it deems it necessary to "deliver price stability and full employment" and those upside risks to inflation materialise.
The RBA's next interest rates decision will be handed down on September 29.

Forcing women to drink at business dinners has no place in modern China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
21:30:06 UTC
06:30:06 KST

Forcing women to drink at business dinners has no place in modern China
The alleged assault of a female employee in Hangzhou exposes how such unsavoury practices persist amid Beijing’s anti-extravagance campaign
Reports of a female employee allegedly being assaulted at a drinking party in Hangzhou brought back a version of myself from more than a decade ago. Back then, I was one of those young women routinely invited to business dinners.
Seating followed an unwritten rule, with the most powerful person taking the seat of honour, flanked by two young women. Everyone knew what we were there to do: keep the conversation lively, entertain the guests and, above all, keep raising our glasses.
I’ve always been a terrible drinker. Yet under the familiar pressure – “Everyone else is drinking. Why aren’t you?” – I would force down a glass or two. I developed little tricks. Baijiu is clear, so I could sometimes discreetly spit it into a napkin without anyone noticing.
However, that didn’t always work. Once, I was told to drink what they called a “red apple”, or a full glass of red wine. There was nowhere to hide it. I drank it, blacked out later, vomited three or four times and spent the next day with a splitting headache.
What I remember most vividly is not the physical misery. It’s a strange sense of shame. Why could everyone else drink but I couldn’t?
The ability to drink was seen as an important professional skill. The women who could drink without flinching seemed admirable. They knew when to stand, whom to toast and, above all, how to manage the mood of the table. I felt that my own body and personality were holding me back.

Syria hails its removal from US terrorism list as ‘result of transformation brought by Syrians’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
21:30:01 UTC
06:30:01 KST

Abdulsalam Fayez and Mohammad Sio
25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
Syria on Monday hailed its removal from the US list of state sponsors of terrorism as the “result of the transformation brought about by the Syrian people,” saying the decision reflects the new Syrian state’s commitment to international peace and security.
 
“We congratulate the Syrian people on this historic milestone,” Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani said on the US social media platform X, referring to the removal of Syria from the list after 47 years.
 
Shaibani said the designation was associated with the policies and practices of the former regime, which was toppled in late 2024, and “was never the choice of the Syrian people, nor was it befitting of Syria and its history.”
 
“This step is the result of the transformation brought about by the Syrian people,” he stressed, adding that it also reflects the new Syrian state’s commitment to international peace and security and to cooperation and partnership with the US and countries around the world.
 
Under President Ahmad al-Sharaa’s guidance, “we will continue our efforts to overcome the legacy of isolation and foster an environment based on transparency, mutual interests and respect, in support of development and stability in Syria and the region,” Shaibani said.
 
Shaibani thanked US President Donald Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, US Envoy for Syria and Ambassador to Türkiye Tom Barrack, the US administration, members of Congress and others who contributed to the decision.
 
In a separate statement, Syria’s Foreign Ministry welcomed the US decision as opening “a new chapter” in the country’s international relations, saying it would support economic recovery, help create conditions for reconstruction and strengthen stability and security in Syria and the region.
 
Damascus also expressed hope for further US steps to lift remaining restrictions hindering its recovery and said it looked forward to deeper strategic partnerships and broader cooperation with Washington and the international community.
 
Hours earlier, the US State Department announced that it had removed Syria from the list of state sponsors of terrorism and revoked the designation of the al-Nusrah Front, also known as Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham, as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist Organization. The Treasury Department also endorsed the move.
 
Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham was one of the most prominent armed groups opposing Bashar al-Assad’s forces during Syria’s civil war. The group was led by Ahmad al-Sharaa, who became Syria’s president after Assad’s ouster in December 2024.
 
Syria had remained on the US list of state sponsors of terrorism since 1979, during the decades-long rule of the former regime.
 
Damascus sees the removal of the designation as opening the way for greater economic transactions, investment and international cooperation as well as eliminating restrictions linked to the designation. Other US restrictions remain subject to separate legal processes.

Former world snooker champion Graeme Dott has been convicted of sexually abusing two primary school children in Scotland in the 1990s and early 2000s.
Dott, 49, was found guilty of abusing a girl from 1993-96 and a boy from 2006-10 after a five-day trial at the High Court in Glasgow. The judge ordered Dott to be held in custody ahead of his sentencing on September 29.
The woman, now in her 40s, testified that Dott sexually abused her on multiple occasions, "caressing" her bottom over her clothing, exposing himself and touching her with parts of his body, including his penis.
The man, now in his late 20s, said he was abused on multiple occasions, with Dott touching him inappropriately, kissing him and performing sexual acts.
"Dott is a dangerous individual, and I hope this conviction provides some measure of comfort to those impacted by his crimes," Detective Inspector Gary Smillie from Police Scotland said.
Snooker's governing body suspended Dott in April 2025 after he was charged in the case. The Scot was ranked number 56 in the world at the time and dropped from the rankings after the season.
On Monday, the World Professional Billiards and Snooker Association revoked Dott's membership following an emergency board meeting. The WPBSA also said it wrote to the World Snooker Tour to request his immediate removal from the WST Hall of Fame.
Dott won the World Snooker Championship in 2006 and was a runner-up twice.

US Supreme Court lifts a judicial hurdle to Trump's mail-in ballot curbs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
21:13:37 UTC
06:13:37 KST

US Supreme Court hands a win to Trump over mail-in ballot restrictions
NEW YORK – The US Supreme Court on Aug 24 lifted one court order blocking President Donald Trump’s administration from implementing an executive order restricting the use of mail-in ballots ahead of the November midterm elections.
But the fate of Trump’s order remains uncertain, as a separate injunction blocking a key part of the plan remains in place.
Republicans are locked in a tight battle to retain control of Congress in the midterms.
Restricting mail-in ballots would stand to disproportionately benefit Republicans given that Democratic voters traditionally have been more likely to use mail-in ballots.
The Aug 24 ruling from the Supreme Court’s 6-3 conservative majority applied to a June injunction from Boston-based US District Judge Indira Talwani.
A coalition of 23 mostly Democratic-governed states and the District of Columbia had sued to stop the executive order over mail-in ballots.
The Supreme Court on Aug 24 said it was too soon for the states to challenge the order but left the door open for them to sue again as the midterm contest approaches.
Trump’s March executive order
Trump’s executive order, issued in March, directed the Department of Homeland Security to compile and transmit to the states a list of US citizens eligible to vote in each state, and the Justice Department to prioritise investigating and prosecuting state and local election officials who issue ballots to people deemed “not eligible” to vote in federal elections.
It also required the US Postal Service to deliver ballots only to voters on each state’s approved mail-in ballot list.
Trump has vowed to end the use of mail-in ballots nationwide before the midterms, and has long cast doubt on the security of such ballots, although evidence of voter fraud is rare.
The court on Aug 24 did not act on another injunction from Talwani that blocked the US Postal Service nationwide from enforcing the directive’s tighter rules for voting by mail.
The judge issued that order on Aug 11 in a separate lawsuit filed by voting-rights groups.
Judge ruled Trump lacked authority
Trump’s executive order is part of his wider efforts to make fundamental changes in US elections.
Trump, who has made false claims of widespread fraud in US elections including his 2020 loss to former Democratic president Joe Biden, has pressed the Republican-controlled Congress to pass a contentious package of voting restrictions called the SAVE America Act.
In June, Talwani ruled that the president lacked the authority to order changes in how states administer federal elections, noting that under the US Constitution, states have the role of determining voter-eligibility requirements.
The judge also noted that federal agencies lack the ability to compile accurate citizen lists for each state.
Despite Talwani’s action, USPS on Aug 21 released a finalised rule to implement Trump’s order, which would require states to provide it with lists of voters who received mailed ballots, as well as unique barcodes on outbound and return ballot mail envelopes.
In the Aug 24 decision, the conservative majority agreed with the Justice Department that the lawsuit challenging Trump’s directive was premature and that the states did not have the required legal standing at this stage to sue.
The agencies have not yet taken concrete actions that impact the states and so any harm they allege is speculative, the court said. Trump’s order itself “does not harm the states”, the court added.
California Governor Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, said on Aug 24 : “The Supreme Court just let the Trump administration move ahead (for now) with its plan to disenfranchise voters across the country. California will be suing AGAIN to block these Orwellian rules from being implemented.”
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The USPS declined to comment.
Justice Sonia Sotomayor, joined by fellow liberal Justice Elena Kagan, said that the states should not have to wait to challenge the order.
“Today’s decision does not address whether the president’s attempts to interfere with states’ administration of the November 2026 elections are lawful,” Sotomayor wrote. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson also wrote a separate dissent.
The states contend that their claims are not hypothetical and that the administration’s “rushed effort to change the rules of mail voting on the eve of the November midterms risks disenfranchising a substantial number of voters”.
“This decision is a painful setback, but it will not be the final word,” New York Attorney-General Letitia James said in a statement. “The right to vote is sacred, and no administration should be allowed to put that right in jeopardy by making it harder for eligible voters to cast their ballots.”
In her June ruling, Talwani rejected the administration’s arguments, finding that the lawsuit was not filed too soon and that the states had legal standing because they would face election administration disruption, compliance costs and a credible threat of criminal prosecution. REUTERS

Ukraine to Produce French-British Storm Shadow Cruise Missiles Domestically
Ukraine will begin producing Storm Shadow long-range cruise missiles domestically after the United Kingdom approved the transfer of relevant technology. British and French defense companies will also participate in the effort, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said during a visit to Kyiv, according to RBC-Ukraine on August 24.
Burnham said Britain had been the first country to provide Ukraine with long-range weapons in 2023 and that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had since asked London to share Storm Shadow technology to enable Ukraine to develop the capability independently.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Storm Shadow, jointly developed by Britain and France, is an air-launched cruise missile designed for precision strikes against high-value targets at long distances. France operates the missile under the name SCALP-EG.
Burnham said the decision was intended to further strengthen Ukraine’s ability to conduct long-range strikes as Russia continues missile attacks against Ukrainian cities and civilian infrastructure.
According to the British prime minister, Russian leader Vladimir Putin is seeking to prevail through what he described as a campaign of terror involving ballistic missile attacks against Ukrainian civilians.
Burnham said Russia must be prevented from launching missiles by imposing sanctions that disrupt its supply chains and by supporting Ukraine’s long-range strike campaign.
Several hours earlier, Britain had authorized missile manufacturer MBDA to share classified technical information on British-made components incorporated into SCALP missiles.
The authorization allows the Franco-British defense company to provide Ukraine with technical documentation covering UK-origin components used in the missile, paving the way for the establishment of local assembly and production capabilities.

In Romania, near the border with Moldova, fragments of a drone were found that had presumably crossed the airspace of the neighboring country after a Russian attack on Ukraine. This was reported by Romania's Ministry of National Defence, writes UNN.
Details
The drone was discovered on August 24 in the yard of a house in the village of Chushlya, Vrancea County, not far from the border with Galați County. The area within a radius of 300 meters was evacuated, and specialists examined the device that had been found.
After the checks were completed, it was established that the drone did not carry an explosive charge
According to the ministry, the items found most likely belonged to a drone that entered Romanian airspace from Moldovan territory on the morning of August 24. Its exact origin and model have not yet been established.
Moldovan airspace was temporarily closed
Earlier, Moldova's Ministry of Defence reported that an unidentified drone entered the country's airspace at 05:55 from the direction of Odesa region. It was heading toward Vulcănești, and at 06:09 it left Moldova's territory in the direction of Romania.
Because of the drone's appearance, airspace in southern Moldova was restricted for approximately 15 minutes. Moldova's Ministry of Defence said that the device flew over the country's territory after Russian airstrikes on Ukraine overnight.
In Romania, after radar signals were detected, two F-16 fighter jets from the 86th Air Base in Borcea and an IAR-330 SOCAT helicopter were scrambled. At 06:12, a RO-Alert message was issued to residents of the area.
Christian Popoviciu, a representative of Romania's Ministry of Defence, said that the last radar contact with the drone was recorded at 06:37.
We cannot confirm either its origin or its model, but we are continuing the investigation, and when we have all the details, we will release the information

"Things won't change with the GST. I've made that very clear."
Federal MPs condemn 'disturbing' footage showing Richmond players
Two federal MPs have condemned footage appearing to show Richmond football players re-enacting scenes relating to the Sydney Swans sexual assault allegations.
The footage appears to show a Tigers footballer pulling down his pants and covering his mouth in shock as a shirtless fellow player whips him on the buttocks four times.
Speaking to Channel Nine, Liberal MP Aaron Violi says the footage is "disturbing" and looks "very inappropriate".
"End of season obviously the players have the right to let their hair down but they can do that in a more appropriate way," Violi says.
"They're in the spotlight, they're role models and it looks like they've missed the mark on this one."
Labor MP Dan Repacholi says it's not the right look.
"This is bloody ridiculous with what's going on with the Swans right now with sexual assault allegations are terrible," Repacholi says.
"These guys out there doing this sort of thing and mocking and taking the piss generally is just not the right look for AFL or for anyone."
Albanese faces further GST backlash after standing by lucrative WA deal
Anthony Albanese is facing further pressure from Labor and Liberal states to overhaul the GST carve-up after declaring he was sticking by Western Australia's lucrative funding deal.

Federal Labor expects to settle new rules for how data centres use energy at Wednesday's national cabinet, despite opposition from Queensland.
Queensland and the Northern Territory have flagged they will not sign on to a standard that ties data centres to renewable projects at the exclusion of coal and gas.
The shadow energy minister has told ABC Radio National Breakfast the Coalition has demonstrated that it can work with the government on NDIS and gambling advertising.
"What we need is the government to reach across the table and say to us they're prepared to work with us in the national interest to meet the types of principles that we think are absolutely fundamental," Tehan says.
"So far, we haven't seen the government do that but we have said and made it quite clear that we're prepared to do it."
Tehan says Victoria receives fair share of GST despite landmark report's concerns
Shadow Energy Minister Dan Tehan says he thinks his home state of Victoria is getting its fair share of GST revenue.
The Productivity Commission's interim report into the GST found the carve-up had cost the federal budget $23 billion in its first six years, $22 billion of which had flowed to WA.
But speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, Tehan says Victoria needs to use its own natural resources to grow its economy.
"What we've seen in Victoria is it's locked down all its natural resources and hasn't been able to develop the state like it was in the past," Tehan says.
Resources minister takes issue with Productivity Commission GST report
Madeleine King says the Productivity Commission's interim report into the GST carve-up had no halfway solution.
The Productivity Commission's interim report found the deal struck with WA eight years ago to boost its GST share is costly and inequitable and must be changed.

To further isolate Iran's economy, U.S. rolls out 'D-Day' sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
21:05:13 UTC

To further isolate Iran’s economy, U.S. rolls out ‘D-Day’ sanctions
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Iranian officials downplayed the significance of the pressure campaign, and suggested it could shut down all oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz.
- Bessent’s plan to potentially squeeze major economies like China and India over their ties to Tehran could pose a diplomatic risk to the U.S.
WASHINGTON — The United States unveiled plans Monday for new sanctions against Iran that Trump administration officials said are designed to sever Tehran from the global financial system as the nearly six-month conflict between the two countries drags on.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who previewed the announcement last week as “economic D-Day,” described the measures as the opening of an all-out financial assault on the Iranian government and its trade partners — a group that includes China, India, Turkey and the United Arab Emirates.
“To those who enable Tehran, do not discount the cost of testing Washington’s resolve,” Bessent said at a news conference. “No nation should expect to enjoy the rewards of our system while helping those who seek to destroy it.”
Bessent said it was time for world leaders to “make a decision” between “America and Iran,” adding that President Trump has already been calling foreign leaders to make specific requests ahead of the new sanctions.
But when asked whom the president had been talking to, Bessent said he would not “name names.” He also said the secondary measure would not take effect immediately, arguing that the administration is trying to give “everyone the opportunity to remedy bad behavior.”
“Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” Bessent said when a reporter pressed him on why the sanctions weren’t immediate. “We believe that it is important to level set and give people a cure period, but they should know that that will move very quickly and that we are serious.”
After trade negotiations collapsed, President Trump’s 50% tariffs on scores of Canadian imports kicked in over the weekend. A look at what that means.
The pressure campaign will build on a naval blockade and other sanctions the Trump administration has already imposed in its effort to force Tehran into a deal that ends the war on U.S. terms.
Trump’s latest economic push against Iran revives a familiar strategy from presidents of both parties, using financial leverage to pressure Tehran toward more serious negotiations over its nuclear program. Sanctions helped bring Iran to the table before a 2015 nuclear deal brokered by President Obama, but the agreement was widely criticized as weak by Republicans. After Trump withdrew from the agreement in his first term, a new “maximum pressure” campaign failed to secure a new deal.
Trump’s decision to return to a strategy of economic coercion has signaled to Iran that the fighting phase of the war is probably over, for now, with the U.S. administration choosing a path “neither of war nor of peace,” Masoud Pezeshkian, Iran’s president, said this week.
Iranian officials, who had been anticipating the move, pushed back on Washington’s strategy even before Bessent began speaking Monday.
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told Iranian state media over the weekend that the sanctions amounted to a repackaged version of decades-old American pressure tactics that Tehran has already learned to withstand. Esmail Baghaei, Iran’s foreign ministry spokesman, warned of “grave consequences” for any countries cooperating with what he said was “illegal behavior” by the United States. And Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme Security Council, suggested that the economic pressure could shut down oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz, a threat that would ripple through global energy markets.
That defiance underscores the central gamble of Washington’s strategy. Rather than aiming sanctions at Iran alone, Bessent’s plan to potentially squeeze major economies like China and India over their ties to Tehran could pose a diplomatic risk to the U.S.
The fallout could also reach beyond foreign diplomacy as a hit to global markets also risks compounding Trump’s troubles at home ahead of the midterm elections, as Americans grow unhappy with the economy and their support for the conflict in the Middle East plummets. The Iran sanctions also land as the administration wages a separate trade fight with Canada, adding uncertainty to global and domestic markets.
Whether Washington will be able to apply pressure on Iran’s trade partners remains an open question.
China alone shares nearly $10 billion in bilateral trade with Iran, and paid roughly $31.2 billion for unreported Iranian crude oil imports in 2025, according to the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission. That makes China the largest buyer of Iranian crude oil by a wide margin, accounting for more than 90% of Iran’s oil exports, according to the commission.
It is unclear whether Trump has spoken to China’s leader, Xi Jinping, about the sanctions. But the two leaders are set to meet in Washington next month, adding to the diplomatic dynamics of the moment.
Other trading partners have already made some moves.
The UAE said last week that it was suspending trade with Iran, a decision that followed accusations that Tehran had fired two ballistic missiles at the Emirates.
Afra Al Hameli, a spokesperson for the Emirati Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said in a post on Aug. 18 on X that all trade, commercial exchanges and financial transactions with Iran have been halted until further notice. She added that the Emirates was “firmly committed to safeguarding the integrity of the international financial system.”
Bessent said Monday that he expects other countries will “take similar actions as we continue our engagement.”
In an opinion article written for the Financial Times last week, Bessent has cast the new measures as the “single greatest financial offensive ever marshalled against an adversary.”
Bessent wrote that countries that “sever Iran’s remaining financial and commercial connectivity” will see their economies reinvigorated, and those who don’t will experience the end of their “lasting prosperity.”
President Trump is betting ramped-up economic pressure against Iran’s trading partners can finally force Tehran to accept a peace deal on U.S. terms. But, as with similar efforts before, Iran may be impervious to such pressure.
“Any nation that serves as a financial artery of a withering regime should expect to share in its isolation,” he wrote. “To become a sanctuary for terror is to become, in the eyes of the United States, a global pariah.”
Ahead of the announcement Monday, Trump posted on Truth Social that Iran was “completely collapsing.”
Meanwhile, Iran’s central bank governor, Abdolnaser Hemmati, said the U.S. had already done all that it can against Iran and that the central bank had been shoring up its foreign currency reserves for months. Last week, he said Iran’s crude exports had “virtually stopped.”
“[The Americans] have done everything, so what else can they do?” he said in an interview with Tasnim News.
Despite his assurances that the central bank was working on preventing a devaluation of the Iranian rial, the currency has struggled to remain above a black market exchange rate of 2 million per dollar — a record low. The Central Bank rate stands at roughly 1.5 million rial to the dollar.
Though experts question the effectiveness of additional economic pressure on Tehran, Bessent’s threat to target Iran’s trading partners — especially the UAE, China and Turkey, who together comprise almost three-quarters of Iran’s foreign imports — will undoubtedly be painful for Iranians.
For example, Iran uses the UAE as a reexport hub and buffer, and receives vehicle spare parts from China, according to the Observatory for Economic Complexity. Iranian economic experts say both the agricultural and pharmaceutical sectors also rely on imports from countries such as Brazil and Turkey.
Ceballos reported from Washington and Bulos from Beirut.

Trump administration plans to revoke visas of foreigners seeking asylum
- The US plans to revoke business and tourism visas of up to 200,000 foreigners who have applied for or are seeking asylum, marking the largest visa revocation in US history.
- The revocation targets B1 and B2 visas issued between 2016 and 2026, coordinated with the Department of Homeland Security, but does not mean immediate deportation.
- The move follows claims that the asylum system is overwhelmed by frivolous cases, sparking criticism from rights groups over due process and racial profiling concerns.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – President Donald Trump’s administration said on Aug 24 it planned to revoke the non-immigrant visas of foreigners who have applied for or are currently seeking asylum status in the United States, marking its latest step in a sweeping immigration crackdown.
A State Department spokesman said it was coordinating with the Department of Homeland Security “to identify and revoke the non-immigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently”.
The State Department statement did not specify the number of visas that will be revoked in the process.
The Associated Press put the number of foreigners whose business and tourism visas is planned to be revoked at up to 200,000, which if materialised, would be the largest single mass revocation of visas in US history.
The AP cited State Department documents and two US officials.
The State Department will revoke so-called B1 and B2 visas issued between 2016 and 2026 whose holders have sought asylum or are now seeking asylum, the AP report added.
The B1 and B2 non-immigrant visas are issued for business and tourism travel.
The visa revocations would not necessarily result in immediate deportation, the AP report said, adding that most of those with asylum cases currently pending would be re-categorised but would lose their status as business or tourism travellers.
Earlier on Aug 24, Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau alleged on X that the American immigration system “has long been swamped by frivolous asylum claims”.
The State Department said earlier in August that under the Trump administration, it has revoked more than 175,000 visas of foreign nationals.
Trump has pursued an immigration crackdown that includes revocations of visas and green cards and an aggressive deportation drive.
He says the crackdown aims to improve domestic security.
Rights groups say the crackdown has violated free speech and due process rights and created an unsafe environment, particularly for ethnic minorities, who have raised concerns about racial profiling.
While Trump campaigned in 2024 on a platform of stopping illegal immigration, his administration has also made legal immigration more difficult – for example, by imposing new and expensive fees for applicants of certain work visas. The government’s crackdown has faced legal challenges. REUTERS

In a first, Census 2027 will not record data on begging
Unknown
