In a first, Census 2027 will not record data on begging
Bharti Jain / TNN / Updated: Aug 25, 2026, 08:42 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
The number of beggars in the country will no longer figure in census tables.
NEW DELHI: In a departure from previous exercises, Census 2027 will not record data on begging separately, with the questionnaire having omitted the category 'beggars and vagrants etc' from the list of 'non-economic activity'. This, as per sources, is due to the very less return in this category in the last census; just around 3.8 lakh non-workers and marginal workers declared themselves as 'beggars and vagrants' in Census 2011.Another key change in is the inclusion of 'natural calamities' as a 'reason for migration', in addition to work, business, education, marriage, moved after birth, moved with household and 'any other'.
While the 2011 census and earlier had listed 'beggars and vagrants etc' as marginal and non-workers engaged in 'non-economic activity' - in addition to students, household duties, dependents, pensioners, rentiers and others - they will now be counted among 'others'; as a result, the number of beggars in the country or their classification by age, religion, state/UT, educational status etc will no longer figure in census tables.Sources said the count of 'beggars and vagrants' returned by previous census exercises was not considered reliable, as many respondents in this category were reluctant to return themselves as such due to associated social stigma. "Census rules require the enumerator to record the occupation/non-economic activity as declared by the respondent," an officer said. The count of non-worker beggars/vagrants was thus recorded at around 3.8 lakh in Census 2011, 6.3 lakh in Census 2001 and around 5.4 lakh in Census 1991.
As for the new census fields 'father's particulars' and 'mother's particulars' - which will capture date and place of their birth as well as religion - sources said they need to be filled only where the mother and father are not listed in the same household or are no longer alive. The enumeration form already records the religion and date and place of birth of each member of the census household, including parents.
Sources told TOI that some of the trends that may emerge from recording religion of both parents include generation-wise prevalence of inter-faith marriages and history of religious conversion. Also, date and place of birth of parents will give the aggregate data on how many Indians fulfil citizenship criteria as per Citizenship Act.While the latest questionnaire seeks details like mobile number, Aadhaar, voter ID and Indian passport number, where "available", technically requiring every individual having these documents to share their number, sources said the enumerators have been trained to only persuade the respondents to do so, by assuring them that all individual data will remain confidential. If the respondent is still reluctant, the enumerator shall leave these fields empty."Even blank fields will enable the census team to cull out data on which of the documents - Aadhaar, voter ID and passport number - respondents are most reluctant to share due to privacy concerns," an official told TOI.
Bharti Jain is senior editor with The Times of India, New Delhi. She has been writing on security matters since 1996. Having covered the Union home ministry, security agencies, Election Commission and the ‘prime’ political beat, the Congress, for The Economic Times all these years, she moved to TOI in August 2012. Her repertoire of news stories delves into the whole gamut of issues related to terrorism and internal strife, besides probing strategic affairs in India’s neighbourhood.

The United States removed Syria from the list of state sponsors of terrorism after 47 years

The United States removed Syria from the list of state sponsors of terrorism after 47 years
Kyiv • UNN
Washington officially removed Syria from the list of state sponsors of terrorism. The decision is expected to pave the way for investment and economic recovery.
On August 24, the United States officially removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism, where the country had been listed since 1979. The decision paves the way for new investment and is expected to promote Syria’s political and economic stability. This was reported by the U.S. Department of the Treasury, UNN writes.
Details
According to U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, removing Syria from the list should create conditions for attracting investment and the country’s economic recovery. The decision was another step by Washington toward deepening engagement with Syria’s new authorities following the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s regime in late 2024.
Syria remained on the list of state sponsors of terrorism for more than four decades. The United States added it to the list in December 1979 because of the support provided to terrorist organizations by the Syrian regime at the time.
The U.S. decision regarding Syria
In July, Washington announced its intention to remove Syria from the list. The final decision took effect after a 45-day review period by Congress.
Syria’s removal is viewed as a sign of trust in the country’s president, Ahmad al-Sharaa, who met with U.S. President Donald Trump last month. According to Reuters, as part of the agreements, Syria also promised to significantly reduce its imports of Russian oil.
At the same time, the Syrian authorities are seeking to attract foreign investment to rebuild the economy after years of war. Removal from the list of state sponsors of terrorism eliminates one of the key obstacles to international business and financial cooperation with Syria.
Who remains on the list
After Syria’s removal, Cuba, Iran, and North Korea remain on the U.S. list of state sponsors of terrorism. For countries on this list, Washington imposes restrictions, including on foreign assistance, arms trade, exports of dual-use goods, and certain financial transactions.
The change in U.S. policy toward Syria came after the overthrow of Bashar al-Assad’s regime in late 2024. Assad left the country with his family, after which power passed to a new administration headed by Ahmad al-Sharaa.

Ocean temperatures hit 'very troubling' record high, spurred by El Niño
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
20:56:26 UTC
05:56:26 KST

The world's ocean temperatures hit 21.1 degrees Celsius on Friday and Saturday, narrowly edging out the record set in March 2024.
Scientists say a supersized natural El Niño and human-caused climate change have spurred the record.
Normally, sea surface temperatures peak in March and April due to most of the ocean being in the southern hemisphere.
The world's oceans have reached their highest temperatures on record and are likely to warm even further in the next few months, putting stress on life in the water and on land.
Spurred by a still-growing but already supersized natural El Niño and human-caused climate change, the world's ocean temperatures hit 21.1 degrees Celsius on Friday and Saturday, narrowly edging out the record set in March 2024, Samantha Burgess, strategic climate lead for European climate service Copernicus, said.
"This is yet another sign of our climate system under strain and the ocean under immense pressure," Ms Burgess said.
Jane Lubchenco, an oceanographer and former chief of the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, called the record "very troubling".
"An ocean this warm destabilises weather patterns and threatens food security, economic prosperity and marine life," Dr Lubchenco said in an email.
"A warmer ocean is not our friend."
Warmer water means worse storms and hotter nights
When the ocean warms, it becomes more acidic and carries less oxygen, which hurts food industries that rely on the seas, Ms Burgess said.
She said it also changed ocean currents and weather patterns, giving more juice to storms, making them rainier and making storm surges bigger.
"When we have a warmer ocean such as we've had in Europe this summer, it amplifies the impact of heat waves because you don't get the cooler night-time temperatures with the sea breeze coming off the ocean when the ocean is very warm," she said.
Normally, because most of the southern hemisphere is ocean, the world's sea surface temperature peaks in March and April, as the southern summer draws to a close. But this year, the record was set in August, Ms Burgess said.
She said this meant the oceans would keep getting hotter until the current El Niño — a natural, temporary warming of parts of the Pacific that warps weather and raises temperatures globally — reached its peak, which was expected sometime between November and January.
The current El Niño is already as big as recent ones and it is still growing. It is expected to reach unprecedented levels at its peak.
Ms Burgess said it was responsible for a good chunk of the heat in the oceans, alongside long-term warming from burning coal, oil and gas, which had warmed the waters by 0.8C.

The Deauville Sport Images Festival, organized by the municipality, explores sport through social, cultural, artistic, and historical perspectives. The photo was among images included in the festival's program highlighting contemporary sporting events.

White House Policy Sets Goal of Supporting 1,000 Rocket Launches a Year by 2030
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
20:49:08 UTC
05:49:08 KST

A new White House policy calls for the Pentagon to craft plans for additional space launch facilities to support a projected increase in launch demand that could see the U.S. supporting as many as 1,000 launches by 2030, more than a fivefold increase from 2025.
The memo, issued Aug. 20, is the first official update to the National Space Transportation Policy since 2013. In the 13 years between updates, launch rates have spiked and proliferated constellations with hundreds and even thousands of satellites are in the works. The U.S. had 19 launches for all of 2013; in 2026, it hit that number by mid-February.
“Access to, from, and within space is a vital national and economic security interest,” the new policy states. “American space transportation capabilities underpin the global economy, and commercial space innovation flourishes with affordable, reliable, and safe space transportation.”
Of particular interest for the Pentagon, the document calls on the Department of Defense to work with the Department of Homeland Security, NASA, and other government agencies to explore options to build additional spaceport infrastructure on federal property. The agencies will brief the White House in February on their findings as well as any policy changes, resourcing, or authorities needed to move forward with launch range infrastructure projects.
It also directs both the Pentagon and NASA to “prioritize and coordinate on infrastructure investments that optimize launch and reentry capacity, flexibility, agility, resilience, and economies of scale at Federal launch and reentry facilities and ranges.”
Today, the Space Force manages two major spaceports at Vandenberg Space Force Base, Calif., and Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Fla. Activity at the two ranges accounts for the bulk of U.S. commercial and military launches, and together they supported 175 launches in 2025.
The Space Force has acknowledged those sites are running out of room to handle the demand that’s forecasted over the next five to 10 years. In congressional testimony in May, Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said the service needs a third launch facility that can handle the larger heavy and super heavy-class rockets. And outgoing Chief of Space Operations Gen. Chance Saltzman said in July the Space Force may need to put a cap on the number of missions it can support each year without additional funding.
The service is building new facilities and trying to make the most of limited real estate—particularly at Cape Canaveral—but without more resources, its infrastructure is approaching capacity limits.
“We don’t want to put a cap on the number of launches that we can support from our ranges, but we have to consider that our existing resources will fail if we don’t consider a cap,” Saltzman said. “And I think that’s kind of where we are right now.”
Short of infrastructure investments, the White House also directs DOD and NASA to implement more efficient range scheduling processes at their spaceports and to be more transparent with the public and industry about launch schedules.
The new policy also addresses other major trends in the spacelift industry. Another provision calls on the Pentagon and other departments to identify what “regulatory, programmatic, operational, and technological barriers” hinder efforts to provide more responsive and resilient access to space. That’s familiar territory for the Space Force, which has been trying to refine its processes for rapid launch in recent years.
In its most recent exercise in June, the service and its industry partners demonstrated the ability to launch a satellite just 16 hours and 42 minutes after receiving orders and then conduct a series of maneuvers in orbit involving multiple spacecraft. The service has more missions in the works that will further explore rapid launch timelines as well as orbital maneuver and in-space propulsion—another area the White House highlighted in its memo.
The document directs DOD and NASA to pursue in-space transportation capabilities for missions like on-orbit logistics or servicing and to factor in those platforms and services when designing new architectures. It specifically calls for “diversity of transportation types,” to include spaceplanes, like the Space Force’s X-37, which to date has largely conducted classified and experimental missions for the military and NASA.

The United States has launched an unprecedented economic campaign against Iran and expanded sanctions

The United States has launched an unprecedented economic campaign against Iran and expanded sanctions
Kyiv • UNN
The United States has launched the “Economic Outcast” campaign and expanded sanctions against nearly 60 organizations, individuals, and vessels. The restrictions cover oil, cyber operations, and technology.
On August 24, at the direction of President Donald Trump, the U.S. Department of the Treasury launched a large-scale economic campaign against Iran and networks associated with it, simultaneously imposing sanctions on nearly 60 organizations, individuals, and vessels. The U.S. Department of the Treasury reported this, UNN writes.
Details
The department called the campaign "Operation Economic Outcast" and said its aim was to cut off the financial channels supporting the activities of the Iranian regime and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. According to U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Washington intends to systematically dismantle Tehran’s economic ties around the world.
Today, in the same spirit, we are launching an economic offensive against Iran’s financial ties around the world. Our goal is to interrupt every economic path that supports this tyrannical regime until Tehran is left alone
U.S. expands sanctions pressure
As part of the new campaign, the U.S. Department of the Treasury expanded the categories of activities for which foreign companies and individuals may face secondary sanctions. These include five key sectors of Iran’s economy: digital assets, technology, gold, aviation, and shipping.
The Treasury Department said Iran uses cryptocurrencies to evade sanctions, seeks access to advanced technologies for military programs, uses gold to support its currency, and uses the aviation and maritime sectors to transport weapons, technology, oil, and other resources.
The United States has imposed sanctions on five key sectors of Iran24.08.26, 21:23 • 3412 views
In addition, the U.S. Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control imposed sanctions on nearly 60 organizations, individuals, and vessels across several jurisdictions. The restrictions target networks linked to the procurement of nuclear and missile technologies, cyber operations, the illicit sale of Iranian oil, and the financing of IRGC activities.
OFAC also suspended several general licenses that had previously allowed certain money transfers to Iran and Iranian citizens’ access to the U.S. cultural and academic systems. Separately, the department issued guidance on sanctions risks for companies that comply with Iran’s shipping requirements through the Strait of Hormuz.
Oil and cyber networks targeted by sanctions
The U.S. sanctions also target networks that provide Iran with revenue from oil sales and help it evade international restrictions. According to the U.S. Treasury Department, brokers, companies, and vessels in countries across the Middle East, Asia, and Europe are involved in such schemes.
Separately, Washington imposed restrictions on participants in a network that the United States links to the procurement of sensitive technologies for Iran’s nuclear research and missile programs. According to the U.S. side, more than 20 organizations and individuals in countries across the Middle East and East Asia helped Iran obtain dual-use technologies through front companies and intermediaries.
Iran rejected U.S. threats of new sanctions against its partners24.08.26, 22:00 • 3294 views
Iranian cyber operators whom the United States accuses of attacking American companies and government institutions were also sanctioned. According to the Treasury Department, since late 2023, members of the relevant networks have compromised the systems of U.S. critical infrastructure companies, particularly in the energy, defense, healthcare, technology, and financial sectors.
The U.S. department also said it was targeting Iran’s "shadow fleet," which facilitates the transportation of oil to international markets. The sanctions target companies and vessels that, according to the United States, transported millions of barrels of Iranian oil and petroleum products to China and other countries.
The U.S. Treasury Department emphasized that Washington expects other countries to take immediate action to terminate activities linked to Iran. Foreign companies and financial institutions that continue helping Tehran evade sanctions or conduct prohibited transactions risk being subjected to secondary sanctions and losing access to the U.S. financial system.

====================================================================================================

Can You Kill Salmonella in Eggs Without Cooking Them? I Tried It
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
20:45:52 UTC
05:45:52 KST

It may finally be safe to eat lettuce again after June’s horrifying—and bagged-salad-trust-destroying—cyclospora outbreak. But the summer of ’26’s foodborne illness train rolls on with a new rash of recalls: for salmonella.
The FDA has reported multi-state salmonella bacteria outbreaks tied to jalapeños, granola, dog food, alfalfa sprouts (also featuring E. coli), and something most people probably have in their refrigerator at this very minute: eggs.
Though the eggs being recalled are only from one supplier, Midwest Poultry Services, they were sold under five brand names, including two distributed by one of the country’s largest grocery chains: Kroger and Simple Truth. While this July recall only concerned Kroger stores in Texas, why wait for the next one?
With the advice of two infectious disease experts, I tested what may be the easiest, most universally applicable way to ensure the eggs in your refrigerator are salmonella-free and safe to use—even in raw or near-raw preparations like Hollandaise and pasta carbonara. All it requires is an immersion circulator, a pot of water, and about an hour and a half of your day.
Are All Eggs at Risk?
Salmonella, which can cause fever and severe diarrhea, is not a new problem for eggs.
In fact, “eggs remain the single food commodity most associated with outbreak illnesses,” says Alan Bulbin, director of infectious disease at Catholic Health’s St. Francis Hospital and Heart Center in Roslyn, New York.
Chickens and other poultry commonly carry Salmonella enteritidis, the bacterium most commonly responsible for salmonellosis in people, which can be transferred to the shell from contact with droppings or even deposited inside the egg itself from an infected chicken's ovaries.
It's difficult to tell just by looking if a chicken has salmonella, which is easily transmitted by rodents or wild birds. In fact, at one point, the USDA estimated that 1 out of every 20,000 eggs was thought to be contaminated with salmonella. That means out of the 67 billion eggs produced in the US each year, 3 million eggs could conceivably have dangerous bacteria in or on them. The USDA enacted a 72-page egg safety requirement in 2009 in hopes of eradicating contamination, but clearly, it hasn't happened.
It's good practice to always keep your eggs refrigerated at 42 degrees Fahrenheit or less and wash your hands before and after handling. It's also worth noting that cooking eggs kills salmonella bacteria. As long as your eggs are “cooked thoroughly, with a firm yolk and white,” according to Bulbin, salmonella shouldn't be a concern.
The Raw Truth
But what if you (like me) have kids who cook for themselves, who you know for a fact will never wash their hands after handling eggs? And more commonly, what if you're not fully cooking the eggs? Many recipes, from mayonnaise and aiolis to eggnog and royal icing for cookies, call for eggs that will be consumed uncooked. How can you make sure they're safe to use?
While in-shell eggs aren't pasteurized, all liquid eggs are—the kind in the carton. However, these are just egg whites, not yolks, which means they won't work for many of the above recipes.
If you want to be certain a whole, raw shell egg is free of bacteria, the only way to ensure this is to pasteurize it, which means heating the egg for a long period of time at 130 to 140 degrees Fahrenheit, but not cooking it. Because this is tricky, the vast majority of eggs sold in the US are not pasteurized—if they are, you'll know it, as they're more expensive and the carton will indicate as much.
However, there is a way you can pasteurize your own eggs at home—any store-bought eggs, or ones from your backyard flock—with a simple kitchen tool that happens to also make a mean steak or vegetable side dish.
Sous vide immersion circulators actually originated in laboratory settings as a way to incubate cultures and sterilize testing equipment, but chefs discovered them in the 1970s and ’80s as a solution to easily overcooked foods like vegetables and chicken. Vacuum-sealing a chicken breast and letting it cook gently in a water bath results in meat that stays juicy and tender instead of stringy or rubbery.
Part of the challenge with pasteurization is maintaining a precise and consistent temperature without producing a hard- or soft-boiled egg, since eggs cook quickly. (It's also worth noting that pasteurizing eggs denatures the proteins, and so will affect egg whites’ performance—don't expect to be making any pasteurized-egg soufflés or pavlovas.)
I attempted to pasteurize some eggs I bought at Costco using the 3.0 immersion circulator model from Anova, a company that WIRED reviewer Joe Ray says has been “building water baths for the industrial and scientific community since 2003, and circulators since 2007.” He gave this model's predecessor a 9/10 rating in 2013, praising its touchscreen and dishwasher-safe parts.
Though Bulbin said he does not have direct experience with an immersion circulator, he added that it is possible to use it to kill salmonella if used for long enough. “If used correctly,” says Bulbin, “salmonella can be killed in eggs; however, the egg center must be maintained at a similar temperature to pasteurization (135 degrees) for close to one hour. The ‘come up’ time for the circulator to reach the appropriate temperature does not count and will not kill salmonella.”
Sous Vide Solution
With this “come up” time in mind, I set the eggs' time in the circulator bath for 90 minutes—the same time recommended by Anova and Serious Eats, and deemed “sufficient” by Kristin Burkholder, a microbiologist and assistant academic director at the University of New England's School of Biological Sciences.
“We can say that sous vide process will make eggs safer for human consumption,” Burkholder said. “However, it’s important for people to realize that sous vide may not kill all of the salmonella that might be present in the eggs, so people who are immunocompromised or otherwise more susceptible to salmonella infection might want to consider other cooking options to be truly safe.”
She also notes that eggs should be stored in the refrigerator prior to the sous vide process, “because this helps to keep any salmonella that may be present in the eggs from replicating, thus ensuring that starting levels of salmonella are low.”
I attached the Anova to a clean pot filled with water and selected 135 degrees Fahrenheit on the touchscreen. (Burkholder notes that circulators can vary by at least 1 degree, so it's a good idea to double-check with a probe thermometer—and possibly adjust the time for small versus large eggs.)
Once the water reached temp, the circulator beeped, and I added six eggs. The Anova's touchscreen only shows time elapsed, so I set my phone timer and went about my business. (The device has an app, but most features, including timer notifications, are a paid upgrade.) When my phone timer went off, I added the eggs to an ice bath, and once they were cool, cracked one to see how cooked it was.
To my surprise, not much at all—there was some cloudiness to the egg white, but it was pretty minor. I was able to use the eggs just as I would a “normal” raw egg, though due to the denatured proteins, I wouldn't expect any stellar foaming or stiff-peak performance. In all, the immersion circulator is pretty set-it-and-forget-it—it would not be difficult to do this for every dozen eggs I bring into my house, even just for peace of mind.
The Anova is user-friendly and about as simple as it gets—just clip it on a pot full of water and you’re good to go. And it’s not just great for eggs; with a vacuum sealer, you can slow-cook just about any kind of meat or vegetable, with most of that time being hands-off. For the cautious and thrifty among us, a pot is free, of course. Just note that maintaining a steady 135 degrees Fahrenheit for that long requires careful monitoring with an accurate thermometer.

Your $100 Marketplace sale could raise an unexpected question
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
20:45:49 UTC
05:45:49 KST

In brief
- When does selling your unwanted items on Marketplace go from hobby to business?
- When do you actually need to start declaring your earnings from Marketplace?
It’s now easier than ever to sell your unwanted clothes or household items online in Australia. Many popular sites, from eBay, Depop, Facebook Marketplace to newly arrived competitors like Vinted, have either scrapped or limited their seller’s fees, depending on the location, value and number of items sold.
So when do you need to declare your online sales income to the Australian Taxation Office and pay tax on it?
The answer can be as messy as your wardrobe. Be aware there is no minimum value of sales that triggers taxation obligations in Australia.
Digging into the law reveals key questions to consider whether you’re spring cleaning your wardrobe to get some cash for the latest fashion, selling a more valuable asset, or starting to run a business.
Tracking 600 million transactions a year
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Two of the biggest online sales sites, eBay and Amazon, are required to provide lots of transaction data to the tax office.
What about selling goods on other platforms? The tax office may be tracking that too. Its tentacles are vast, with more than 600 million transactions reported and matched to taxpayers every year from a wide variety of private and public sources.
Even if a platform is not required to report, the transactions may still be captured through credit and debit card payment systems, such as Stripe or Square.
The tax office can also request information from the banks. It may even gather information via insurers on unexplained wealth based on "lifestyle assets" – such as cars, boats or art – you may own. There are also examples of taxpayers being caught out with unexplained deposits leading to hefty tax bills.
Is it just a hobby?
Let’s say you found a dress in your wardrobe that you bought for A$250, wore once, but don’t like. So you decide to sell it on eBay or Amazon, rather than giving it away.
You list it and sell it for $100. While you’ve now got $100 more than before, you have really lost $150 overall.
This is not a sound business model. Anything you sell actually comes at a cost to you; think profit, not just sales.
The tax office is unlikely to be interested in these types of occasional, low-value, generally loss-making personal-type activities.
In this scenario, where you’re just cashing in on your existing wardrobe, the tax office is likely to consider it private in nature and just a "hobby".
This is unlikely to create a tax bill. However, you still may need to declare certain activity and have records to support your position.
When does online selling become a business?
What happens when you go from selling just a few old dresses to spotting a market opportunity? Perhaps you start to develop a pattern of buying vintage clothes from friends, family and op shops and selling them at a markup?
Now you’re putting in time and money with the aim of making a profit.
That sort of activity makes it more likely for the tax office to see it as a "business".
A business typically involves repeated and continuous activities. For example, regularly buying items to resell online for profit would be more likely to be considered a business.
Another factor to consider is how systematic you are being. Are you acting in a "business-like" manner? For example, the kind of records you keep, and whether you advertise beyond family and friends, will both be relevant.
No minimum sales to be a business
While the value of sales can be a factor, be careful, as there is no clear dollar threshold for when activities will be considered a business.
But what data the tax office collects from eBay and Amazon provides a clue as to when you’re more likely to be asked questions. Amazon and eBay both share data for people who sell goods worth a total of A$12,000 or more in a particular year.
Earning more or less than that amount does not rule you in or out of running a business, and whether your activities are taxable or not. But if you are earning more than $12,000, you will be on the radar of the tax office – and more likely to be asked to explain your activities.
If you are running a business, you will need to declare income and can claim allowable expenses. You need to pay tax on the net business income.
Consider other tax obligations too. For instance, do you need an Australian Business Number (ABN)? Should you register for the goods and services tax (GST)? If you’re unsure, the federal government’s business website has useful resources.
When in doubt, get advice
Even if you only sell online occasionally, the tax office may be more interested if it involves higher valued goods — such as jewellery originally purchased for more than $500, or other personal items purchased for more than $10,000 – which you’re now trying to sell.
For these more valuable sales, any gain you make – if you managed to sell it for more than you originally paid – is taxable.
However, it gets a little murky if you have made a loss. In general, the tax office restricts how to use losses for these higher valued personal items.
If you’re still unsure whether your online selling is just a hobby, if you’re about to sell a valuable asset, or think you might have crossed over into running a business, don’t risk it — speak to a registered tax practitioner for advice.
Elizabeth Morton is a senior lecturer at Curtin Law School, Curtin University.
She has previously been contracted to co-facilitate a short-term training contract for tax and crypto facilitated by UNSW for the Australian Taxation Office and is currently a member of the ATO's Crypto Industry Working Group. This is unrelated to this article. Elizabeth has not received grant funding directly related to the content of this article. Elizabeth is a chartered accountant, fellow of the Tax Institute and member of the Institute of Public Accountants.

Removing Syria’s US terrorism designation is ‘decisive step’ toward partnership, stability: US envoy

Mohammed Ragawi, Mohammad Sio
24 August 2026•Update: 24 August 2026
Removing Syria from the US list of state sponsors of terrorism is a “decisive step” in the country’s transition from isolation to partnership and from being viewed as a source of terrorism to becoming a committed partner in combating it, US Special Envoy for Syria Tom Barrack said Monday.
Barrack made the remarks in a post on US social media company X after the US State Department formally announced that it had removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism.
He called the decision “another historic milestone” in US President Donald Trump’s “bold vision to give Syria a chance,” hailing it “another decisive step in Syria’s remarkable journey from isolation to partnership, and from a source of terrorism to a committed partner in the global fight against it.”
Barrack said the designation had served as a “another wall separating the Syrian people from the investment, enterprise, and opportunity necessary to rebuild their nation,” adding: “Today, another wall comes down.”
With the designation removed, “capital can replace conflict, enterprise can replace isolation, and commerce can continue to triumph over chaos,” he said.
Barrack, who also serves as ambassador to Türkiye, said the decision was not simply the removal of a restriction but a “another foundation stone in a new U.S.–Syria relationship built on shared interests, mutual security, and shared prosperity.”
He said the move demonstrated Trump’s vision of “security first, prosperity next” vision becoming reality, adding: “Promises made. Promises kept. Syria has been given a chance — now the work is to turn that chance into enduring peace and prosperity.”
Hours earlier, the US State Department announced that it had removed Syria from the list of state sponsors of terrorism and revoked the designation of the al-Nusrah Front, also known as Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham, as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist organization. The Treasury Department also endorsed the move.
Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham was one of the most prominent armed groups opposing Bashar al-Assad's forces during Syria's civil war. The group was led by Ahmad al-Sharaa, who became Syria's president after Assad's ouster in December 2024.
Syria had remained on the US list of state sponsors of terrorism since 1979, during the decades-long rule of the former regime.
Damascus sees the removal of the designation as opening the way for greater economic transactions, investment, and international cooperation, as well as eliminating restrictions linked to the designation. Other US restrictions remain subject to separate legal processes.

biosphere 2: what happens when humans try to recreate earth?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
20:35:19 UTC
05:35:19 KST

In 1991, eight people entered Biosphere 2, a vast glass enclosure in the Arizona desert designed to test whether humans could live inside a materially closed ecosystem. Conceived by Space Biospheres Ventures as both an experiment in ecological engineering and a possible prototype for long-duration space habitation, the complex brought rainforest, savanna, desert, ocean, agriculture, laboratories, and living quarters under one envelope. What happened inside over the following two years was an unusually revealing account of how ecological, architectural, technological, and human systems become entangled when there is nowhere else to go.
exterior view of the University of Arizona’s 40-acre Biosphere 2 campus in Oracle, Arizona | all images courtesy of University of Arizona
Biosphere 2 used ‘lungs’ to regulate its enclosed atmosphere
Biosphere 2 emerged from an optimistic period in which ecological thinking, counterculture, systems theory, and space exploration increasingly overlapped. John P. Allen, working with Texas businessman and philanthropist Edward P. Bass, developed the project around the idea that a contained ecological system could be studied at a scale large enough to include people. The ambition was simultaneously terrestrial and extraterrestrial: to understand Earth’s cycles by reproducing them in miniature while exploring whether similar principles could eventually support human life on the Moon or Mars.
That proposition made the building itself part of the experiment. Constructed in Oracle, Arizona, between 1987 and 1991, Biosphere 2 was housed within a steel-and-glass envelope that looked like a greenhouse filled with plants, enclosing approximately 200,000 cubic meters of atmosphere, while a stainless-steel liner beneath the site was intended to prevent uncontrolled exchanges with the surrounding soil and water. Extensive piping, pumps, heat exchangers, air systems, and water-recycling infrastructure formed a hidden technosphere beneath the visible landscape.
Because the sealed structure heated and cooled under the Arizona sun, its internal atmosphere expanded and contracted. Engineers therefore installed two enormous variable-volume chambers known as the ‘lungs.’ Flexible diaphragms moved in response to changes in air volume, helping regulate pressure without simply venting the atmosphere to the outside. The system is an important reminder that Biosphere 2 was as much a machine for managing atmospheric physics as it was a miniature world.
The project attempted to compress ecological diversity into a relatively small footprint. A tropical rainforest occupied a high glass volume, while savanna, mangrove, ocean and reef, and fog desert environments formed a sequence of contrasting habitats. An agricultural zone was intended to provide much of the food for the crew, while residential spaces and laboratories were integrated into the same closed environment. The underlying strategy was to create enough biological complexity that the ecosystem could begin to organize itself. But the experiment quickly demonstrated that biodiversity cannot just be assembled from a list of species and expected to reproduce the relationships of a mature ecosystem.
When the atmosphere stopped behaving
After the first crew entered the enclosure on September 26th, 1991, oxygen concentrations began falling. By January 1993, atmospheric oxygen had dropped from approximately 20.9 percent to 14.5 percent. The conditions placed considerable physiological stress on the crew and eventually required oxygen to be introduced into the supposedly closed system. The problem was not simply that the plants were producing too little oxygen but that the artificial ecosystem contained a vast reservoir of organic matter in its soils. Microorganisms consumed this carbon through respiration, using oxygen and producing carbon dioxide. Photosynthesis was expected to compensate for that exchange, but the balance was disrupted by reduced light levels inside the structure and unusually cloudy conditions during the first winter.
The use of concrete for the building was another variable that had not been adequately accounted for. Carbon dioxide produced by microbial respiration reacted with calcium compounds in the structure’s concrete, effectively removing part of the gas from the atmosphere and resulting in a peculiar imbalance in which oxygen continued to disappear while much of the corresponding carbon dioxide failed to remain in the air.
Biosphere 2’s rainforest biome recreates a dense tropical environment beneath the glass enclosure
The ecosystem was not a miniature Earth
Other failures were biological. Pollinating insects and several introduced vertebrate species disappeared, while opportunistic species such as ants and cockroaches flourished. Aggressive vines spread through the rainforest and crop production became difficult as pollination, pests, disease, weather, and available light interacted in ways that were difficult to predict from individual ecological components.
The agricultural system nevertheless supplied a substantial proportion of the crew’s food. But the shortfall contributed to the human body adapting to scarcity, another experiment unfolding alongside the ecological one.
The crew lived under conditions of confinement, restricted food availability, altered atmospheric composition, intensive work, and continuous observation. Roy Walford, the mission physician, also used the enclosure as an opportunity to study caloric restriction, placing the crew on a nutritionally dense but low-calorie diet. Weight loss, fatigue, hunger, and physiological adaptation became part of the experiment’s lived reality.
This is where Biosphere 2 becomes more interesting than a simple story of an engineering project that did not work.
The experiment was trying to reproduce an ecosystem, but it also had to reproduce the conditions under which humans could function inside one. That meant that governance, psychology, nutrition, maintenance, labor, and interpersonal relationships became environmental variables.
Biosphere 2 is set against the Santa Catalina Mountains in Oracle, Arizona
The human system proved impossible to seal
As the mission continued, the eight biospherians became divided over how strictly the rules of the experiment should be maintained. One position prioritized material closure and experimental purity; another favored interventions when human health or operational continuity was threatened. The distinction was philosophical as much as practical. If oxygen had to be added, food imported, or mechanical systems used to compensate for ecological shortcomings, was the enclosure still a closed system?
A supposedly autonomous world required constant human care, while the humans inside it were themselves increasingly dependent on technological intervention. The social consequences became inseparable from the ecological ones. Confinement, hunger, physical exhaustion, atmospheric stress, competing interpretations of the mission, and intense external scrutiny contributed to fractures among the crew. The experiment revealed that a closed habitat is a problem of collective governance.
The second mission, begun in 1994, ended amid management disputes and a breach of the enclosure. By then, the original proposition of a fully closed human world had become increasingly difficult to sustain.
the main glass structure encloses Biosphere 2’s rainforest biome
From failed utopia to scientific instrument
The later history of Biosphere 2 may be the most useful part of the story. Under Columbia University and, subsequently, the University of Arizona, the facility was transformed from a prototype for closed human habitation into an open, highly controlled laboratory for Earth-system science. Researchers used its biomes to investigate questions around elevated carbon dioxide, ocean acidification, plant respiration, drought, and ecosystem response. Later, the Landscape Evolution Observatory introduced another form of experimental landscape through three artificial hillslopes designed to observe hydrological, geological, and biological processes as they developed over time.
Biosphere 2 began by attempting to construct a self-sufficient world and ended by becoming a place for studying the systems that make Earth’s world difficult to reproduce. The original experiment showed how many variables are hidden inside apparently stable environments and how quickly those variables become visible when planetary buffers are removed.
Biosphere 2 belongs to a lineage of utopian projects that treat buildings as instruments for producing alternative ways of living. Its glass envelope, artificial landscapes, pressure-regulating lungs, buried infrastructure, agricultural systems, and controlled atmosphere turned architecture into an operational ecosystem. But the experiment’s most enduring insight may be more modest.
A future habitat on Mars, the Moon, or elsewhere cannot be designed as a perfectly autonomous machine that simply keeps its occupants alive. It has to accommodate maintenance, failure, adaptation, unequal dependencies, ecological unpredictability, and the people operating it. The more completely a habitat is sealed from its surroundings, the more consequential every small imbalance becomes. Biosphere 2 therefore remains compelling not because it achieved its utopian promise, but because it made the promise testable.
Its glass walls separated eight people from the Arizona desert, but they could not separate biology from architecture, technology from ecology, or environmental stress from human behavior.

the project reads as an artificial landscape
the glass structures form a sequence of distinct volumes across the site
the scale of the experimental complex becomes apparent against the surrounding desert terrain
dense vegetation climbs around the path inside the rainforest biome
a landscape that feels closer to a tropical forest than the Arizona desert outside

Spike in Turkish military flights to Pakistan raises concerns over possible weapons transfers
NEW DELHI: An unusual increase in Turkish military transport flights to Pakistan in the last few days has raised hackles in Indian defence circles.Open-source flight trackers noted a 60-hour surge of Turkish military transport flights, including Turkish C-130 Hercules and A400M aircraft (such as one with call sign TUAF526), landing at Pakistani air bases like Nur Khan, Masroor, and Murid between August 19 and 21.There is speculation in defence circles that the flights may have carried Turkish military hardware, including unmanned aerial systems (drones) and air-defence equipment like Baykar (next-generation kamikaze UAV K2) and Asisguard systems (drone systems) to Pakistan. The aircraft movements were seen soon after after the signing of the tripartite Mecca Joint Defence Agreement between Pakistan, Turkey, and Saudi Arabia on Aug 7. The agreement establishes a collective defence pact, stating that an armed attack against any one of the three member states will be considered an attack against all of them.
However, neither Pakistan nor Turkey has officially confirmed the precise nature or cargo of these transport operations.With Turkish aircraft landing in Pakistan, questions are being raised in defence circles whether Pakistan is gearing up for another conflict with India.
Before Operation Sindoor in May last year, China and Turkey had allegedly supplied Pakistan with advanced military hardware, including Chinese PL-15 air-to-air missiles and HQ-9 air defence systems, and Turkish-origin Bayraktar (Yiha) and Asisguard Songar kamikaze drones. They also provided real-time battlefield data and tactical support.
During the four-day conflict last year, the Indian armed forces tackled these attacks using their multilayered air defence grid and integrated command and control strategy, successfully intercepting all incoming aerial threats before reaching critical military or civilian infrastructure.The Indian forces deployed indigenous technology and advanced anti-access frameworks to crush the Pakistan defence network and also thwarted its offensive attacks. The IAF used long-range capabilities of Russian-acquired S-400 Triumf air defence system and indigenous Akash-NG missiles to thwart missile and UAV attacks. The IAF also used the S-400 to shoot down a high-value Pakistani Saab 2000 Erieye AEW&C surveillance aircraft from around 314 km away — which stands as one of the longest-range combat surface-to-air missile engagements in military history.

Netanyahu has two sons and a daughter. It remains unclear which of his sons was allegedly targeted.
His elder son, Yair, 35, has spent extended periods in Miami since early 2024, reportedly under Shin Bet protection.
His stay in the US has attracted controversy in Israel over the cost to taxpayers of providing security, while some residents in south Florida have expressed concern that his presence could make the area a target for attacks by Israel's enemies.
Shortly after Netanyahu's remarks became public on Monday, prominent Israeli journalist Amit Segal wrote on his Telegram channel that the alleged assassination attempt had been known for "months" but was subject to a gag order.
Israel killed Iranian supreme leader Ali Khamenei in the opening salvo of US-Israeli strikes on February 28, along with some of his family members.
His son Mojtaba, one of Khamenei's six children, was named the new supreme leader a week later.
In a message read out on his behalf on state TV, Mojtaba Khamenei said that in addition to his father, he had lost his wife, his sister, her child and his brother-in-law.
Mojtaba Khamenei has not been seen in public since his appointment, and was reportedly wounded in the same strikes that killed his father.
In another message attributed to him and published on the occasion of funeral ceremonies for his father, the new leader pledged to "avenge the blood" of Ali Khamenei.

Violent museum heists on the rise across Europe: Europol
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
20:25:50 UTC
05:25:50 KST

Ayhan Şimşek
24 August 2026•Update: 24 August 2026
Museum heists across Europe are growing more violent, more targeted and increasingly tied to criminals who move between illicit markets, Europol said in a report Monday.
The EU's law enforcement agency said thefts from museums, long seen as a largely nonviolent form of organized crime, are showing "a shift in both methods and targeting."
Thieves increasingly use "sledgehammers, explosives and firearms to breach premises and intimidate staff," while targeting precious metals, gemstones and culturally significant artifacts, the agency said.
Europol described the trend as "an alarming shift toward aggressive methods, targeted attacks, and the involvement of cross-market criminal networks."
Precious metals such as gold and silver have become especially attractive because they can be melted down, erasing much of the trail for investigators, Europol said.
Jewelry set with precious stones can also be broken apart and resold, the agency said.
Both categories appeal to criminal networks because of their "visibility, accessibility" and the perception that museum security is weaker than protection at jewelry stores, according to the report.
Europol also warned that "new criminal actors" are entering the field, including ad hoc groups recruited through social media.
Some may be "opportunists from other criminal sectors," drawn by what they see as a low-risk, high-profit crime, the agency said.
The report said the pattern differs sharply from traditional networks trafficking cultural goods, which typically operate as a tight core group organized around a single leader.

The Best Kitchen Gadget to Prevent Salmonella Is a Good Meat Probe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
20:22:35 UTC
05:22:35 KST

It is the summer of salmonella, it seems. Multiple overlapping salmonella outbreaks now sprawl across at least 30 states as of late August, even as cases of prodigious-poop-causing parasite cyclospora seem to be receding. Hundreds have been sickened, and simultaneous recalls are in effect for products as diverse as eggs, granola, jalapeño peppers, greens powders, nut butters, and dog food.
Salmonella, and its attendant havoc on the GI tract, are these days a hallmark of American summer—not just in meat and eggs but, increasingly, fresh produce, as climate change brings warmer and wetter summers. Foodborne bacteria enjoy the same weather as corn and tomatoes and are happy to hitch a ride.
“When we see warmer temperatures, that is going to create conditions that are favorable for bacteria like salmonella or parasites like cyclospora to grow,” Ellen Shumaker, a food safety expert at NC State Extension, told WIRED this month.
Luckily, there's already a simple preventive technology known to be wildly effective against salmonella. It's called “cooking.” While anything above the USDA-recommended food-safe temperature of 140 degrees Fahrenheit can kill salmonella if cooked for long enough, the bacterium is dead nearly immediately above 165 degrees.
Heat is the last, best line of defense against salmonella. I'm the WIRED Reviews team's lead reviewer for cooking technology, and I consider my food thermometer the single most important food safety item in my kitchen.
And yet, while most Americans own a food thermometer, more than 70 percent don't regularly use it to assess food temp, according to a recent food safety survey. This is a statistic that would terrify my mother.
I have convinced myself that the problem is that your thermometer is terrible. A lower-cost thermometer, like this $14 quick-read thermometer my editor has in her kitchen, will give you an accurate enough internal temperature for your meat or lasagna. But it'll take as long as seven or eight seconds to get a useful ballpark reading, which can feel like a lifetime when hovering over a pan or an open oven door.
The best meat thermometer is the one you'll actually use. For more than a decade, the WIRED Reviews team has been recommending an instant-read food thermometer that costs seven or eight times the price of a “fast-read” thermometer on Amazon.
The reason is simple: speed. The above Thermapen One offers a stable digital readout of food's internal temperature within just a couple seconds. This difference is pivotal, because it means you're likely to actually use it rather than dread using it. This gives the Thermapen a much better claim to hang out in the important real estate next to the stove rather than jumbled somewhere nearby in a drawer.
What Food Temperatures Can Kill Salmonella?
If you're looking for the maximum reduction in your risk of salmonella, you need to “introduce a kill step,” said Jerold Mande, an adjunct professor of nutrition at Harvard’s School of Public Health. And in the case of bacteria, your kill step likely involves temperature.
Salmonella and other dangerous bacteria thrive, and propagate, in the temperatures between 40 degrees and 140 degrees Fahrenheit. To be safe, food must be either placed in the fridge or cooked and held at temps higher than 140 degrees.
To kill bacteria, the FDA recommends that red meat be cooked to 145 degrees or above and rested for three minutes. Eggs and ground meat should be cooked to 160 degrees Fahrenheit or higher. Poultry should be 165 degrees Fahrenheit.
Wireless Options
For stovetop purposes, an instant-read thermometer like the Thermapen One is going to have the most utility. But for oven-cooked meats, for air-fried wings, and even for thicker produce like potatoes or layered dishes like casseroles and lasagna, I tend to prefer a wireless temperature probe.
The most reliable I've used, especially if you also plan outdoor cooks in thick-walled smokers, is the Typhur Sync Gold series, which offers the best mix of easy use and admirable signal strength. In addition to being a food safety tool, the Typhur's predictive function can be a useful helper in hitting precise temp targets on long cooks, and the Sub-GHz (915 MHz) signal can travel a good ways down the block before fading.
But if you're just planning to cook indoors in a space with a good Wi-Fi signal, I've also found the TempPro TempSpike Pro ($130) to be convenient at a lower cost, with a digital temperature monitor that has a magnetic back so I can mount it on the fridge. The app's not as fancy as Typhur's, and the signal range also isn't as good if you're trying to take this outside. But the accurate ambient temperature readings are a lot more precise than the thermostat in my range oven; the internal temps are likewise reliable. But especially, the TempSpike's fridge-mounted digital temp readout makes it the probe I often reach for.
And (say it with me): The best meat probe for food safety is the one you actually use.
More Food Safety Gear
Lately, increasing reports about tomatoes and onions and jalapeños had me worried: Do I need to use a meat thermometer for veggies now?
Deaths from acute food-borne illnesses range from the hundreds to the low thousands in the US, and foodborne illnesses have declined significantly since the turn of the millennium. Compared to the long-term chronic disease risks of avoiding fresh produce and eating processed foods, the acute risk posed by your lettuce and carrots can look comparatively insignificant, Mande said.
This said, each person's risk tolerance is, well, personal. This is true especially if you're a parent, or an older or immunocompromised person. Those worried about salmonella outbreaks in the news should first consult local public health authorities to determine whether an outbreak is active in their area, Mande said.
Washing produce helps, though it's not foolproof. So does using separate cutting boards for meat and produce and avoiding cross-contamination of cooked and uncooked food. Most food safety experts tend to recommend that the best cutting board for raw meat is a less-porous, high-density cutting board like this one from Great Jones, which WIRED reviewer Louryn Strampe loves for its juice groove and easy portability.
I don't like piling up extra cutting boards. And so I use an ingenious, svelte, steel-reinforced dual-sided cutting board from Steelport, which has end-grain walnut on one side for veggies and a high-density, non-porous polymer on the other side for meats.

PM faces further GST backlash after standing by lucrative WA deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24

Albanese faces further GST backlash after standing by lucrative WA deal
In short:
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has faced more backlash over the GST carve-up after recommitting to a lucrative deal with Western Australia.
The 2018 deal boosted Western Australia's share of the GST, but the Productivity Commission has urged the government to scrap it.
What's next?
Mr Albanese will meet with state leaders at national cabinet this week, putting him on a collision course with premiers who want change.
Anthony Albanese is facing further pressure from Labor and Liberal states to overhaul the GST carve-up after declaring he was sticking by Western Australia's lucrative funding deal.
The prime minister promised on Monday not to change the 2018 arrangements that boosted the resource-rich state's share of the GST.
This was despite a Productivity Commission report recommending the government scrap the deal, warning it had cost billions more than anticipated and was worsening inequality between states.
Mr Albanese is set to meet with state leaders at national cabinet on Wednesday, putting him on a collision course with premiers demanding a GST shake-up.
Victoria's Labor treasurer, Colin Brooks, said the Productivity Commission's interim findings had "backed up exactly what Victoria has been saying for years".
"The current system isn't working. It leaves other states like Victoria exposed and goes against the core purpose of fair distribution," he said.
Queensland's LNP treasurer, David Janetzki, also hit out at the existing funding arrangements, saying his state was looking for a "consistent approach".
"I do have concerns that the inequity of the GST distribution, the consistent cost-shifting from the federal government to the state government, is threatening the integrity of the federation," he said.
"If the prime minister shows up for Western Australia and acknowledges their unique character as a resources state, the same should be applied to Queensland."
Tasmania's Liberal treasurer, Eric Abetz, warned his state faced possible significant reductions in GST revenue unless the 2018 decision was reversed.
"Australia was built on a simple concept: a fair go. This sense of fairness is what underpinned GST when it was first introduced," he said.
"The prime minister has told the nation that doesn't exist anymore. Western Australia has been told it can keep its lucrative and disproportionate deal."
PM defends WA deal
On a visit to Western Australia on Monday, Mr Albanese said the state deserved its funding allocation and promised no changes while he was prime minister.
It was the first time he had made the guarantee since the Productivity Commission handed down its interim report earlier this month.
"The important thing that sometimes isn't understood from some of the critique of WA getting its fair share of the GST is that those additional payments have not come from states and territories," Mr Albanese said.
"They have come from the Commonwealth. I am comfortable with that.
"What I say to premiers and chief ministers, though, is that you need to bear that in mind when you're discussing federal-state financial relations."
Mr Albanese's announcement was welcomed by Western Australia Premier Roger Cook, who previously lashed out at "east-coast clowns" when the Productivity Commission report was released.
Federal resources minister and WA MP Madeline King said those comments were "fair enough" and also cast doubt on the commission's report.
"I don't actually quite agree that it [the Productivity Commission] has gone through it as methodically as it might have," she told ABC's Radio National.
"The report also doesn't acknowledge that no state has suffered from the current arrangements. No state has had any money taken from them or any less of it.
"I respect the work of the commissioners. And I also note there are no Western Australians on the Productivity Commission."
Independent economist Saul Eslake, a critic of the 2018 deal, said he was disappointed but not surprised by the prime minister's decision.
"Since becoming prime minister, Mr Albanese's approach has essentially been what Western Australia wants, Western Australia gets," he said.
"Mr Albanese knows that his initial accession to the prime ministership was delivered by Western Australia.
"Although he doesn't need Western Australia's votes in the current parliament, it's likely that he will need them to retain government at the election that's due in 2028."
Federal Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie, who represents a Western Australian seat, also welcomed Mr Albanese's announcement that he would stick by the 2018 deal.
"We will always stand up for WA, and the Coalition is committed to the current arrangements," he told ABC's 7.30.
"I think the way it [the GST carve-up] was arranged before our change in 2018 was fundamentally unfair.
"It was punishing productive and prosperous states like Western Australia."

Space Force Honor Guard Gets a New Uniform with Blue Accents
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
20:18:59 UTC
05:18:59 KST

Space Force Honor Guard members recently unveiled the unit’s ceremonial service dress uniform, the latest step in the new service’s journey to create its own distinctive visual appearance.
The uniform is an evolution of the new Space Force service dress uniform, which is intended to replace the modified Air Force uniform Guardians have worn since the service was first established in 2019.
But the Honor Guard’s new uniform features distinctive light blue accents to the outer belt and service cap band as well as a light blue rope that’s worn over the left shoulder to help the uniform stand out to the public, according to an Aug. 21 Space Force press release.
“Having a dedicated ceremonial uniform ensures that our Guardians present a unified, unmistakable presence during high visibility global missions,” Chief Master Sgt. Ross Koehler, senior enlisted leader for the Space Force Honor Guard, said in the release. “The updated uniform reflects the force’s evolving individual culture and pride in those who wear it.”
The guidance for the new uniform was released Jan. 13 and took eight months for the Honor Guard to make finishing touches to its new uniform, according to the release.
“There have been many adjustments that we have seen on paper over the past several months,” Honor Guard member Spc. 3 Amelia Olsen said in the release. “To be able to see it, wear it, and finally be able to show it to the public now feels rewarding.”
Honor Guard members debuted the new uniform for the first time publicly Aug. 23 at the Freedom 250 Grand Prix Event in Washington, D.C.
“The Space Force is honored to share a history with the Air Force, but our mission to the space domain is concentrated and strategic,” shared Koehler, “It requires further establishing a distinct identity.”
The Space Force didn’t wait long to begin developing its unique appearance. Two years after its establishment, the service unveiled the prototype of the service dress uniform at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber Conference in September 2021.
The new ensemble featured a dark blue coat, upturned collar, and diagonal row of buttons, but feedback from Guardians prompted Space Force to make several design adjustments that included better fitting pants, a redesigned collar, and a better-draping fabric that resulted in an improved overall fit.
Outgoing Chief of Space Operations Gen. Chance Saltzman said in January that the new uniform will service as a “significant step in establishing the service’s unique culture and visual identify.”

Grim signs the globe is about to run short of food
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
20:18:58 UTC
05:18:58 KST

analysis
Climate, wars and fuel shortages foster famine fears
Now for round two.
Just as the global economy was adjusting to higher fuel prices, a new inflationary wave is about to hit.
This time, the shortages will revolve around food, and the poorest nations on the planet will be the worst affected.
A deadly trifecta of higher input costs, disrupted trade routes, and a changing climate has combined to drastically reduce food supply, particularly grains and especially wheat.
Global food exporters, including Australia, are suffering in a vice-like grip, caught between soaring prices for refined fuel and fertiliser just as a supersized El Niño gathers strength.
Meanwhile, two wars, one in the Middle East and the other in Eastern Europe, are having a devastating impact on food distribution from the recent northern hemisphere harvest.
But rapidly changing weather patterns – fire and drought across key food bowls in Europe and North America even before the long-anticipated El Niño unleashes its wrath – are adding to the problem as farmers reduce planting programs.
As seasoned campaigners, Australian farmers are already bracing for El Niño.
While many have adapted to the vagaries of producing grain on the world's driest inhabited continent, the shifts in weather patterns that result from El Niño – severe drought across much of northern and eastern Australia – are becoming more erratic.
Australian farmers scaling back
Wheat is the largest single crop on the planet, by area.
Along with rice and corn, which both produce more tonnage of finished crop, it is a staple that is essential for human nutrition.
In a normal year, Australia supplies 10 to 15 per cent of the world's wheat market.
But this year is expected to be anything but normal.
The total winter crop, including wheat, barley and canola, is likely to be about 21 per cent down on last year.
According to the Australian Bureau of Agriculture and Resource Economics and Sciences (ABARES), the area planted is forecast to fall by 12 per cent to 10.9 million hectares, the smallest in six years.
"The Middle East conflict has caused significant disruption to the global supply of liquid fuels and fertiliser," ABARES reported in June.
With almost all our fertiliser imported from the Middle East, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz for much of this year severely affected local agriculture.
"To date, disruptions have resulted in significantly higher input costs rather than physical shortages, although some short-term fuel outages occurred earlier in the planting window," it said.
Those higher prices have squeezed growers' profit margins. Combine that with extremely dry conditions in northern cropping regions and little wonder some farmers are unwilling to take big risks with planting.
While well below record levels, Australia's total winter harvest is likely to be respectable. But the onset of El Niño is likely to hit summer crops such as sorghum and rice, while concerns remain for next year's winter crop.
Diesel prices soaring again
Since the breakdown in negotiations between the US and Iran to end the war, oil prices have surged back above $US90 a barrel, which, while elevated, is well below the $US126 a barrel peak earlier this year.
But, as the graph below shows, the global price of refined fuel has surged back to the exorbitant levels of the early days of the Iran war when oil and refined fuel supplies from the Middle East ground to a halt.
That's because Ukraine's continued bombardment of Russian oil refineries has removed one of the world's largest suppliers of diesel from the market.
Despite the trade sanctions, Russia usually ships vast quantities of diesel to Türkiye, which then redirects it to European markets. Now, Russia has been forced to import supplies as angry citizens queue for fuel.
Diesel is the primary fuel choice for agriculture, and price shifts like those above have a huge impact on planting decisions as margins are whittled to the bone.
In addition, the Ukraine attacks have also disrupted global wheat shipments.
Between them, Russia and Ukraine account for almost a third of the global wheat trade. But shipments from the Black Sea have now ground to a halt.
Russian attacks against Ukraine's port in Odesa have been answered by a lethal Ukrainian bombardment of Russia's export facilities in Novorossiysk.
Shifting weather patterns are also playing a role.
Ukraine had been using the Danube River as an alternative route to export its grain. But severe drought has rendered the waterway impassable.
Those same extreme weather conditions led to a sharp reduction in yields from European producers, particularly France and Germany.
US drought and Trump's tariffs
When Washington was shrouded in Canadian brushfire smoke during the FIFA World Cup, it should have been a stark warning to even those in the White House that the global climate was changing.
Together, the US and Canada account for between 25 and 30 per cent of global wheat exports.
America, however, is on track for its worst wheat harvest in more than half a century, with the Great Plains, scene of the great US dust bowl during the 1930s depression, again experiencing a severe and debilitating drought.
Given bumper crops in recent years helped build reserves, global wheat prices, while edging up, have yet to respond to the impending supply shortfalls.
And war of a different kind has also contributed to the disrupted global food trade.
Donald Trump's strong-arm trade tactics forced many smaller nations to strike purchase agreements with the US for wheat supplies.
Loading
Bangladesh, Indonesia and Israel all agreed to preference US wheat purchases over other suppliers as part of an offset agreement to avoid tariffs on their own exports.
But the arrangement means they will need to accept whatever price US wheat is trading at rather than being able to purchase on the open market. Many within Bangladesh have denounced the deal and are attempting to renegotiate it.
Indonesia's arrangement is even worse. It has agreed to purchase up to 2 million tonnes of US wheat per year, just so its tariffs could be lowered to 19 per cent.
Already under intense pressure, the Indonesian economy is unlikely to withstand a huge lift in basic food prices.
The pain is expected to be even greater in drought-ravaged nations across North Africa and the Middle East, where food shortages would exacerbate intense political instability.

Berlin Stretches 45-Meter Anti-Drone Net by Brandenburg Gate to Show Ukraine’s Frontline Reality
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
20:18:23 UTC
05:18:23 KST

- Category
- World
Berlin Stretches 45-Meter Anti-Drone Net by Brandenburg Gate to Show Ukraine’s Frontline Reality
A 45-meter anti-drone net was stretched across central Berlin near the Brandenburg Gate on August 24, bringing a striking piece of everyday life in Ukraine’s frontline communities into the heart of the German capital for Ukraine’s Independence Day, according to Deutsche Welle on August 24.
The installation at Pariser Platz was organized by Ukrainian civil society organization Vitsche to demonstrate how civilians living close to the front have been forced to adapt to the constant threat of Russian drones.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Across frontline areas of Ukraine, protective nets have increasingly appeared above roads, streets and public spaces in an effort to prevent low-flying Russian drones from reaching civilians, vehicles and critical routes.
For one day, organizers recreated that reality in one of Berlin’s most recognizable public spaces.
The installation was intended to highlight the stark difference between what looking toward the sky means in Germany and in wartime Ukraine. For most people in Berlin, the sky remains part of ordinary daily life. For millions of Ukrainians, it can mean air raid alerts, incoming drones and missiles.
Beneath the net, organizers presented an exhibition dedicated to Ukrainian civilians targeted in what has become known as Russia’s “Human Safari,” a pattern of deliberate drone attacks against ordinary people.
“Every intercepted missile or drone represents a life saved. The impact of technology depends on whose hands it is in. Russia uses drones to terrorize civilians through a human safari, while Ukraine uses innovation to protect lives—from interceptor drones that shield cities from aerial attacks to technologies that help evacuate the wounded and save soldiers on the front line. This experience is invaluable for the security of all Europe,” said Kateryna Mykhalko, Managing Director of New Age Defence.
Organizers stressed that the net itself is not presented as a solution to Russia’s aerial attacks. Instead, it illustrates the extraordinary improvised measures Ukrainians have been forced to adopt simply to move through their towns and cities more safely.
The broader message is that real protection must come before Russian missiles and drones reach civilians in the first place through stronger air defenses, interceptor technologies and other systems capable of stopping aerial threats.
The installation was followed by a protest march through Berlin, running from Potsdamer Platz to Pariser Platz.
Organizers said the demonstration was intended to reinforce a wider political message: protecting Ukrainian cities is not only a question of Ukraine’s survival but also part of safeguarding European security.
Previously, the European Commission approved a new €6.1 billion defense support package for Ukraine on August 24—Independence Day—directing the funding toward urgently needed air and missile defense systems, missiles, ammunition and radars.

Ukraine unveils MV11, largest naval drone in MAGURA naval family
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
20:12:54 UTC
05:12:54 KST

- UFORCE unveiled the MV11, the largest drone in its MAGURA naval family, during Ukraine's Independence Day parade on August 24.
- The ocean-going platform carries up to 2,200 kg of payload with seven-day endurance and is designed to launch and support other unmanned systems far from shore.
Ukraine’s Independence Day parade in Kyiv on August 24 included a new naval drone, the MV11, from the Ukrainian company UFORCE. It is the largest vessel yet built in the company’s MAGURA family, an unmanned surface vessel line credited with helping push Russia’s Black Sea Fleet back from Ukrainian waters.
The parade marked the first time Ukraine has staged a dedicated public display of unmanned systems for its Independence Day, held this year on the Dnipro River as part of the country’s 35th anniversary. The MV11 appeared alongside other current MAGURA models.
Unlike earlier MAGURA vessels built primarily for strike missions, the MV11 is designed as a transport and support platform. It is built to operate in open ocean rather than coastal waters, and it carries a payload of up to 2,200 kg (4,850 pounds) with an endurance of up to seven days at sea.
UFORCE said the vessel is meant to launch, resupply and support other unmanned systems far from shore, functioning as a mobile base for maritime operations. The company said the MV11 is intended for reconnaissance, surveillance, support of amphibious operations and resupply of fuel and equipment to other naval drones.
The MV11 was developed by UFORCE’s design and research bureau in Portugal, with international investment, as an addition to the MAGURA line.
“We are proud to present the MV11 on Ukraine’s Independence Day. This is not just the largest naval drone, it is a platform that delivers multi-domain capability: a single carrier that transports and launches other unmanned systems far from shore, enabling operations across all domains,” said Oleg Rogynskyy, CEO of UFORCE.
The MAGURA family has been UFORCE’s primary naval product since it entered combat use in 2024. Ukrainian officials have said MAGURA drones contributed to the sinking or damaging of at least a dozen Russian naval vessels, part of a campaign that forced much of Russia’s Black Sea Fleet out of its former operating areas near Crimea. A MAGURA V7 variant carried out what Ukraine described as the first successful naval drone strike against an aerial target in late 2024, using AIM-9 Sidewinder missiles.
UFORCE has been expanding beyond Ukraine this year. In July, the company signed a memorandum of understanding with the U.S. boatbuilder ReconCraft to manufacture MAGURA vessels in Oregon and South Carolina, following a ceremony at the Embassy of Ukraine in Washington. ReconCraft co-founder Joe Silkowski has said the partnership is intended to eventually produce hundreds, and later thousands, of MAGURA vessels annually for the U.S. market. The value of that agreement has not been disclosed.
MAGURA vessels also took part in the U.S.-Philippines Balikatan exercise in April 2026, where the drones reportedly sank a target ship during a live-fire demonstration in the Luzon Strait.
Rogynskyy has framed UFORCE’s role in broader terms in past statements tied to the MV11 unveiling.
“Russia out-produces us in every classical category. Men, shells, missiles, armour. So we made the speed of change itself our main weapon,” Rogynskyy said.
UFORCE was formed by consolidating nine Ukrainian unmanned systems developers into a single company, combining Ukrainian wartime engineering with Western financing and governance. By early 2026, the company had more than 1,000 personnel across manufacturing, software development and field support, with a supply chain spanning more than 15 locations in six allied countries.
UFORCE has not disclosed a production timeline or unit cost for the MV11, and the company has not said how many vessels have been built or ordered. The standard MAGURA V7, by comparison, is about 7.6 meters long, carries over 770 kg of payload across distances exceeding 560 km, and costs under $500,000 depending on configuration.
