US removes Syria from terrorism sponsor list, lifting major investment obstacle
DAMASCUS, Aug 24 - The United States removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism on Monday, lifting what Damascus says was the last major impediment to investing in the country as Washington deepens ties to the new Syrian government.
The removal, posted on the U.S. Treasury's website, took effect after a 45-day congressional review period triggered when Trump formally notified Congress on July 8 of his intention to rescind the designation.
“These actions were all taken in recognition of the positive actions taken and further commitments by the Syrian government under President Ahmed al-Sharaa to fully distance Syria from acts of international terrorism,” U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement.
Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shibani told Reuters on Saturday that the government hoped removing what he called the "last obstacle" would help reconnect Syria to the global financial and economic system and boost investment. "There is no longer any obstacle to investment, doing business and rebuilding economic life in Syria," he said.
Syria had been on the list since 1979, when Washington accused the government of former President Hafez al-Assad of supporting militant groups. The designation remained throughout the rule of his son Bashar al-Assad, who was toppled by rebels led by current President Ahmed al-Sharaa in December 2024.
CUBA, IRAN, NORTH KOREA REMAIN
Monday's announcement also removed the designation of the Nusrah Front as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist organization, leaving Cuba, Iran and North Korea as the three countries designated by Washington as state sponsors of terrorism.
The designation carries restrictions on U.S. foreign assistance, defense exports and sales, certain dual-use items and financial transactions, and had remained a major deterrent for banks and investors even after Washington dismantled its broader sanctions program on Syria.
Trump's administration terminated comprehensive U.S. sanctions on Syria in July 2025, while maintaining targeted sanctions against Assad and his associates, rights abusers, drug traffickers, Islamic State and al Qaeda affiliates and Iranian proxies.
The U.S. Treasury has since said American financial institutions can provide services to Syria, process payments involving Syrian banks and establish correspondent banking relationships with them, provided sanctioned parties are not involved.
But the terrorism designation remained a source of legal and compliance risk for firms considering entering Syria, whose government is seeking billions of dollars in investment to rebuild after nearly 14 years of war.
Signs of interest had grown ahead of the removal. Syria's finance ministry said this month that Finance Minister Mohammad Yisr Barnieh held talks with Bank of America executives over potential cooperation and Syria's reintegration into the international financial system. Bank officials expressed willingness to visit Syria and continue discussions, according to the ministry.
Mastercard has gone further, announcing in May that it was working with QNB Group and Syria's central bank to prepare infrastructure for international card payments in the country. The company has described itself as an early investor in Syria and said it wants to help connect Syrian consumers and businesses to global payment networks.
CONTINUED COOPERATION
Trump notified Congress of his decision after meeting Sharaa in Ankara in July, telling the Syrian president in a letter seen by Reuters that he had promised to "remove all barriers" preventing Syria from rebuilding.
The delisting also followed months of negotiations between Damascus and Washington over Syria's economic and foreign policy.
Reuters reported this month that Damascus agreed to drastically reduce imports of Russian oil during discussions with Washington over lifting the terrorism designation, according to three sources familiar with the talks.
Trump has increasingly embraced Sharaa, the former commander of al Qaeda's Nusra Front who broke ties with the global jihadist network in 2016 and led the rebel coalition that overthrew Assad.
Washington has praised cooperation by Sharaa's government against Islamic State and said easing restrictions is intended to give Syria an opportunity to stabilise, attract investment and rebuild. REUTERS

No Tanks, No Troops—Ukraine Sends Its Robot Army Through Kyiv in World-First Drone Parade
Unknown

2026-08-24

04:28:06 KST

- Category
- Defense Tech
No Tanks, No Troops—Ukraine Sends Its Robot Army Through Kyiv in World-First Drone Parade
Ukraine marked its 35th Independence Day with a radically different kind of military display, sending combat robots down Kyiv’s main street, naval drones across the Dnipro River and UAVs into the skies in what Defence Blog described as the world’s first military parade centered entirely on unmanned systems.
The August 24 demonstration replaced the traditional columns of tanks, armored vehicles and marching troops with some of the technologies that have come to define Ukraine’s defense against Russia’s full-scale invasion.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Dozens of unmanned ground vehicles rolled along Khreshchatyk in central Kyiv, showcasing robotic platforms designed for combat, reconnaissance, logistics and other frontline missions.
On the Dnipro River, Ukrainian naval drones including the Magura and Sea Baby were displayed. Both families of unmanned vessels have become closely associated with Ukraine’s campaign against Russia’s Black Sea Fleet.
The maritime display included reconnaissance platforms, strike drones and versions equipped with air defense missiles, demonstrating how Ukraine has expanded the role of unmanned vessels far beyond their original use as explosive attack craft.
Ukrainian drones also appeared above the capital, including reconnaissance systems, strike UAVs and interceptor drones developed to destroy incoming Russian aerial threats.
The display offered a snapshot of how deeply Ukraine’s military has changed since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Drones that initially played mostly supporting roles have evolved into central elements of Ukrainian operations on land, at sea and in the air. Kyiv has since institutionalized that transformation by creating the Unmanned Systems Forces as a dedicated branch of its military.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed legislation establishing the branch in 2024, making Ukraine the first country to build a separate military service specifically around unmanned warfare. June 11 has since been designated as the annual Day of the Unmanned Systems Forces.
The Independence Day demonstration brought many of those technologies together in the center of the Ukrainian capital.
Ukraine had not staged a conventional military parade during the full-scale war. In previous years, Khreshchatyk instead became known for displays of destroyed Russian tanks, armored vehicles and other equipment captured or knocked out during fighting.
Previously, reports emerged that Ukraine is expanding its fleet of unmanned ground vehicles, aiming to produce at least 50,000 combat and logistics robots this year to reinforce infantry units and bridge manpower shortages along the frontline.

Türkiye on Monday established four subcommissions to coordinate implementation of legislation aimed at strengthening national unity and social cohesion, according to a board overseeing the process.
The Monitoring and Evaluation Board, chaired by Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz, made the decision at its first meeting.
The meeting of the board, established under the National Solidarity and Strengthening Social Cohesion Law, focused on coordinating the work of state institutions involved in the process and establishing procedures and principles governing the board’s activities, according to a statement shared by Yilmaz on US social media platform X.

The board established the Legal and Judicial Affairs Coordination Subcommission, Monitoring and Assessment Subcommission, Social Compliance and Integration Subcommission, and Disarmament and Strategic Coordination Subcommission.
The statement said the process aimed at completely eliminating terrorism and violence from Türkiye and the region, removing weapons from the agenda and strengthening fraternity has reached an “important milestone.”
It said the law was adopted by the Turkish Parliament with “a high level of social and political consensus” and reflected the will of the Turkish people.
“Türkiye will continue to implement these historic steps with determination, in full coordination among all its institutions, to strengthen social integration,” the board said.

General Atomics Plans ‘Wildfire’ Drone for Pentagon’s Low-Cost MMA Program
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
19:14:47 UTC
04:14:47 KST

General Atomics Aeronautical Systems predicts the new drone it plans to pitch for the military’s “Massed Modular Aircraft” program will exceed many of the military’s requirements for a successor to the MQ-9 Reaper.
Wildfire, as General Atomics has dubbed it, “meets every wish on the [MMA] list and exceeds most of them,” company spokesman C. Mark Brinkley said in a statement, though he declined to specify the drone’s expected capabilities or cost. Aviation Week first reported the company’s plans for Wildfire.
MMA is intended to be a low-cost, attritable drone that could fly in groups if needed and take on some missions now performed by the MQ-9 Reaper, which was also made by General Atomics. The Defense Innovation Unit released a solicitation July 7 asking companies to submit ideas for the new drone concept, which is meant “to execute missions that the MQ-9A performs today.”
The Air Force is partnering with DIU on the MMA effort, which it said “will directly inform the requirements for the MQ-9’s successor.”
DIU’s solicitation called for drones to be able to carry a payload of at least 2,800 pounds—roughly the weight of one Long-Range Anti-Ship Missile, or LRASM—and have an unrefueled combat radius of at least 2,300 nautical miles, while carrying a payload, as well as being able to fly a one-way ferrying flight of at least 8,000 nautical miles.
The Pentagon wants MMA drones to be able to launch weapons, collect intelligence, conduct electronic warfare, or relay communications while staying airborne for long periods. DIU said that is intended to exhaust an enemy and force them to burn through pricey anti-aircraft missiles and other resources.
While General Atomics did not detail what Wildfire—a medium-altitude long endurance drone—will be able to do, Brinkley’s statement hinted at some of the goals the company set out to achieve.
“How do we come out of the box, day one, with a 10,000 nautical mile ferry range?” Brinkley said. “Can we carry four LRASMs? Can we swarm 100 aircraft under semi-autonomous control? Can we fuse all of that data into a highly effective common operating picture? Can we do that at scalable, affordable mass?”
The Air Force has lost dozens of MQ-9 drones since operations against Iran launched in late February. The Washington Post reported earlier in August that about 45 Reapers have been lost, in some cases shot down, during Operation Epic Fury.
In its original solicitation, DIU said that with adversaries increasingly using low-cost antiaircraft capabilities to create layered defenses, the military won’t be able to rely on “exquisite” aircraft with price tags north of $30 million. For that reason, DIU and the Air Force said, the military needs drone capabilities that can weather some losses while still being able to accomplish their missions.
The Air Force and DIU want these new drones to be modular so they can be quickly updated with payloads like full-motion video sensors, so an MMA could carry out some of the MQ-9’s current missions. An Air Force official told reporters earlier in August that the service wants to start awarding contracts by the end of this year.
DIU also wants contractors to be able to flight test a full-scale prototype 21 months after receiving the award and to be able to deliver 20 mission-ready aircraft by fiscal 2031.
Brinkley said General Atomics “can deliver Wildfires years earlier than the current schedule.”
However, Brinkley said, the military has an “immediate, critical ISR gap” that Wildfire would not be able to fill in the short term. General Atomics has options that could serve as an interim bridge, he said, and the company is now discussing those with Pentagon decision-makers.
General Atomics did not reveal any imagery or concept art for Wildfire.

‘Mom, I’m coming home’: Belarus hosts Russia, Ukraine prisoner exchange
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
19:12:00 UTC
04:12:00 KST

Screenshot of the video from the First News TV channel
                    
                    MINSK, 24 August (BelTA) – Ten Ukrainian citizens and ten Russian servicemen have returned home following a prisoner swap, BelTA learned from the First News TV channel.
Belarus carried out an important humanitarian mission to help its neighbors return home at a difficult time. Following a personal instruction from Belarusian President Aleksandr Lukashenko, ten Ukrainian citizens who had been in Belarus in violation of migration laws were handed over to the Ukrainian side. Based on the principle of family reunification, they were given an opportunity to return home. As agreed earlier, the Ukrainian side also handed over to Belarus ten Russian servicemen who had been on its territory. Thus, a total of 20 people were reunited with their homes and loved ones on 24 August. 
 
 
“I feel as if I have won some kind of lottery of life. Peace comes at a very high price, but that is what you want most of all. You want to wake up without anxiety, with the desire and determination to live, that is the most important thing. When you truly realize that you only get one life, you start cherishing every moment,” another Ukrainian said. “I am happy inside now. It may not show much on my face, but I am immensely glad that this long-awaited moment has finally arrived and home is so close.” 
The return was accompanied by touching phone calls to relatives: mothers, wives, daughters. Tears of joy and relief could be heard in every conversation. “Mom, everything is fine, calm down. We’ve been swapped, we’re in Belarus now, at the border,” one of the Russian servicemen said with a smile. 
19-year-old Daniil, the youngest of the Russians, also made his mother his first call: “I’m coming home, everything is fine.” 
Irina Kostevich, Chairperson of the Standing Committee on Labor and Social Affairs of the House of Representatives, who is overseeing humanitarian mission and repatriation issues on the instructions of the head of state, stressed: “The main goal and task set by the president is to save lives. It does not matter whether someone is Ukrainian or Russian, first and foremost, they are human. Human life and family reunification are the top priorities. This humanity is historically inherent in the Belarusian people.” 
Dmitry Usov, Secretary of the Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War at Ukraine’s Main Intelligence Directorate, noted that Ukrainian citizens are returning home thanks specifically to the decision of the Belarusian president. “These formats are taking place. And work will continue to return our citizens and transfer Russian servicemen to the Russian side,” he said. 
The Russian servicemen brought to Belarus have injuries of varying severity. As part of its peacekeeping mission, Belarus promptly arranged their transportation to healthcare facilities in the Gomel Oblast. Specialists are currently providing the servicemen with all necessary qualified medical assistance, from initial surgical treatment to intensive care and comprehensive high-tech examinations. 
Belarus has once again confirmed its status as a reliable partner by providing safe corridors and a platform for humanitarian missions. Both Ukrainians and Russians received equal treatment and protection, guaranteed by international humanitarian law, providing yet another confirmation that dialogue is possible for the sake of saving human lives.

PNG Chiefs' latest signing Joey Manu says a conversation with Papua New Guinea's prime minister was part of the reason he chose to join the expansion side.
Manu is currently playing rugby union in France, but has signed for the Chiefs' maiden NRL season in 2028.
What's next?
The PNG outfit will officially be able to hit the open market in November, with all eyes on whether Nathan Cleary or Sam Walker will still be available at that point.
Joey Manu has revealed how a conversation with Papua New Guinea's prime minister helped convince him to return to the NRL and join the Chiefs in 2028.
The two-time premiership winner will be 31 by the time the two-year deal starts, and will arrive with the ability to play fullback, centre or even five-eighth in the club's first year.
Manu toured PNG last month and met with Prime Minister James Marape while there, before signing the deal from France on Sunday.
"Talking to the prime minister and how passionate he was about making it not just a PNG team, but a Pacific team and trying to get the Pacific nations behind this team, I think it's going to be special," Manu said.
"I'm a really proud Cook Island and Māori man, and I know my family's real proud back in Tokoroa in New Zealand and also in the Cook Islands too.
"It's a big decision to make, but bringing that positive impact to PNG but also young Pacific Island kids (is big).
"There's so much talent in the Pacific Islands, and rugby league is taking over the islands, so it's really cool to have a Pacific team."
Manu's signing means he follows Jarome Luai, Alex Johnston, Connor Watson, Brian To'o, Zac Lomax and English Test prop Matty Lees as Chiefs signings.
The PNG outfit will officially be able to hit the open market in November, with all eyes on whether Nathan Cleary or Sam Walker will still be available at that point.
Canberra second-rower Hudson Young also shapes as a potential target, given he is yet to agree to terms for an extension at the Raiders.
"Just joining the Chiefs is pretty special in the first year," Manu said.
"With how it can affect the country, that's why I wanted to go there.
"It's got a lot of positives about how passionate the country is, and what we can do for the country and how we can make a positive impact on people's lives."
Manu left the Sydney Roosters for rugby union at the end of 2024, initially to Japan's Toyota Verblitz before moving to Racing 92 in France.
His current deal expires next May, meaning it is possible he could sign for an NRL club for the second half of next season before joining PNG.
"I still keep a close eye on a few games and I get to watch a few games when I can," Manu said.
"You miss certain things when you're watching. I'm just grateful that I get to come back and play.
"I really enjoy playing rugby league, so I'm excited.
"Rugby league is a special game for myself, and to come back and play in the NRL is very special."

Houthis strike Saudi tanker Amzan in Red Sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
19:11:23 UTC
04:11:23 KST

ALBAWABA- Yemen’s Houthi group on Monday claimed responsibility for a ballistic-missile strike on the Saudi-flagged oil tanker Amzan in the Red Sea off Yanbu, escalating its campaign against Saudi-linked shipping and threatening a key route for the kingdom’s oil exports.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the tanker was hit directly, causing a fire and prompting nearby vessels to leave the area. The group said the attack was part of its declared blockade of Saudi-linked maritime traffic and its policy of “blockade for blockade.”
Saudi shipping company Bahri confirmed that the Amzan was involved in a security incident in the Red Sea but did not attribute responsibility for the attack. It said all crew members were safe and that no injuries had been reported. Earlier, the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency reported that a tanker had been struck by an unidentified projectile about 63 nautical miles west of Yanbu, causing a fire on its main deck. No environmental impact was reported.
The Houthis also claimed two separate attacks against Saudi-backed forces inside Yemen. According to their statement, ballistic missiles and drones targeted a large military convoy in the Al-Abr and Al-Wadi'ah areas, allegedly destroying more than 10 trucks carrying weapons and military equipment.
A second operation targeted Saudi-aligned forces in Al-Kanais, with the Houthis claiming casualties among commanders and officers and the destruction of weapons depots. Local sources confirmed the strikes and reported that vehicles belonging to civilians were burned as a result of the Houthi attack on the Wadi’ah area.
The latest escalation comes amid a broader deterioration in Yemen’s fragile security environment. The conflict had remained largely frozen since the 2022 UN-brokered truce, but tensions have intensified in recent weeks amid renewed Saudi-Houthi confrontation and stalled Omani-mediated efforts to reach a political settlement.
The escalation also coincides with the wider US-Iran confrontation and disruptions to regional shipping. Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on Red Sea routes such as Yanbu to move oil while traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains severely disrupted.

European gas prices hit highest level since January 2023 amid Iran sanctions concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
19:09:24 UTC
04:09:24 KST

Mücahithan Avcıoğlu
24 August 2026•Update: 24 August 2026
European natural gas prices climbed nearly 4% on Monday to their highest level since January 2023 after the US launched a sweeping campaign to isolate Iran from the global financial system, heightening concerns over further disruptions to Middle Eastern energy supplies.
The September futures contract at Dutch-based TTF, Europe’s benchmark gas trading hub, rose around 4% to €68.45 ($79.85) per megawatt-hour.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced Operation Economic Outcast, an “unprecedented” sanctions campaign targeting Iran’s aviation, shipping, gold, technology, and digital asset sectors.
“Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone,” Bessent told reporters.
He warned that any entity facilitating money laundering for Tehran would be permanently removed from the US dollar system and signaled that a major financial institution could be sanctioned by the end of the week.
The measures follow US President Donald Trump’s warning last week that Washington could sanction countries continuing to trade with Tehran.
Iran rejected the threats as a sign of desperation and argued that further sanctions would fail to force the country into submission.
European gas markets remain particularly vulnerable to developments in the Middle East, as tensions have kept the Strait of Hormuz largely closed and delayed Qatari liquefied natural gas shipments to Europe.
The disruption has coincided with stronger cooling demand during the summer heatwave, slowing the pace at which European countries are replenishing inventories.
The combination has raised pressure on storage levels and heightened concerns about whether Europe will enter the winter heating season with an adequate supply buffer.

WASHINGTON - US public approval of the war with Iran fell to its lowest level since the conflict’s early days, helping to hold President Donald Trump’s popularity at a record low, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll that closed on Aug 24.
The four-day poll showed just 31 per cent of Americans support US military action against Iran, down from 37 per cent in a March Reuters/Ipsos poll and 34 per cent earlier in August.
The decline was driven by fewer self-identified Republicans backing the conflict.
Some 69 per cent of Republican respondents support the war, compared with 77 per cent in March.
The war has been dragging on Trump’s public standing in 2026, and for the second survey in a row just 33 per cent of respondents said they approved of the Republican’s performance in the White House, the lowest level in polls from Trump’s first or second term.
Trump has told Americans that the war - which started with US-Israeli attacks on Iran on Feb 28 - is necessary to keep Tehran from developing a nuclear weapon.
The conflict has cooled in recent months but Iran has kept in place a de facto blockade of oil exports from the region, which has pushed US petrol prices near record highs.
Trump has vowed to ramp up economic pressure on Iran and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Aug 24 announced a possible expansion of sanctions on countries doing business with the country, but stopped short of actually imposing penalties, a sign of how thorny the conflict has become for the administration.
Some 83 per cent of the country thinks the war will go on “for an extended period of time”, the Reuters/Ipsos poll found, up from 80 per cent earlier in August.
Trump campaigned ahead of the 2024 presidential election on promises to control inflation and avoid lengthy military conflicts.
Six months into the war with Iran, US petrol prices are more than a dollar higher per gallon than they were before the war.
That is weighing on Trump’s Republican allies who will be defending narrow congressional majorities in the Nov 3 midterm elections.
Independent voters in the poll favoured Democrats over Republicans - 33 per cent to 19 per cent - when asked who they would vote for in congressional elections if the election were held today.
The poll surveyed 1,215 US adults nationwide and had a margin of error of 3 percentage points in either direction. REUTERS

German prosecutors identify likely suspect in deadly 1970 Munich Jewish center arson
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
19:07:55 UTC
04:07:55 KST

The Munich Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office has closed the case involving a previously unsolved antisemitic arson attack on a Jewish community center after 56 years, the Munich Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office and the Munich Police Headquarters (MPD) confirmed on Monday to The Jerusalem Post.
On the evening of February 13, 1970, the building of the Jewish Community of Munich at 27 Reichenbachstrasse in Munich, which is also a retirement home, was set alight using a petrol mixture. Seven Jewish residents who were Holocaust survivors died as a result of the arson attack. A further 15 people were wounded, four of them seriously.
Following a new tip-off from the public, the Munich Public Prosecutor’s Office reopened the investigation in April 2025 after the case was closed by the Federal Public Prosecutor in 2017.
A witness provided the prosecutor with credible information about the suspect. According to this information, the suspect had been in close contact with one of her relatives in the 1970s. The suspect then died in 2020.
Shortly after this relative’s death, the informant revealed what she knew about the matter. In order to verify the suspicion, investigators from the Munich Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office and the State Security Division of the MPD examined the archived files of the Munich I Public Prosecutor’s Office and the Federal Public Prosecutor’s Office, and interviewed witnesses from the suspect’s circle.
According to the findings of the new investigations, the prosecutor said there were compelling grounds for believing that the deceased suspect was the perpetrator.
Investigators link deceased suspect to far-right circles
At the time, the suspect, a German man, was 25 years old.
On the evening of February 13, 1970, he is said to have remarked, in the immediate vicinity of the crime scene and with a view of the Jewish retirement home, that “the Jews have everything” and that he wanted to “set them on fire.”
About 15 minutes later, the building was engulfed in flames. This information is based on the credible statement of the informant, who in turn was repeating the remarks made by her deceased relative. Other family members confirmed the remarks.
The prosecutor subsequently found that the suspect had been linked to far-right circles. Witnesses described him as an antisemite with a “Hitler obsession.” In his youth, he is said to have listened to Hitler’s speeches on records and practiced shooting in the former “Führer’s restricted area at Obersalzberg.”
A former schoolmate described the suspect’s hostility toward Jews as a defining characteristic.
A headteacher highlighted that the suspect had “a coldly calculating, attention-seeking manner” and reported a physical altercation during which the suspect was alleged to have used a dagger given to him by his father, which had belonged to the Hitler Youth.
Death of suspect leaves case without prosecution
Furthermore, the offender profile drawn up by the Bavarian Operational Case Analysis Unit on behalf of the Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office matched the deceased suspect.
Overall, the prosecutor said the new investigations strongly suggest that the suspect was responsible.
However, it is not possible to reach a definitive legal conclusion because dead defendants cannot be legally prosecuted in Germany.
Since the investigation did not reveal any reliable evidence of the involvement of other individuals, the Munich Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office closed the renewed investigation.

AI-generated music to be banned from ARIA charts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
19:07:55 UTC
04:07:55 KST

In short:
Australia's main music charts have announced a ban on AI-generated music to start this week.
The Australian Recording Industry Association says wholly AI-generated tracks will not be eligible for the ARIA Charts, though recordings using AI in a supporting role will remain eligible.
It comes after a song produced with AI became the most-played track on Australian radio and reached number four on two ARIA charts in July.
Songs created mostly or entirely by artificial intelligence will be excluded from Australia's official music charts from this Friday, under new rules set down by the recording industry.
However, AI-assisted recordings can still chart if they are substantially human-made.
The Australian Recording Industry Association (ARIA), which runs the charts of the most popular music in Australia, has updated its Charts Code of Practice to put it in line with principles put out by the global recording industry.
The updated code excludes music that has used generative AI unless it is "substantially human-made" and "raises no stream or chart manipulation concerns".
The new code lets ARIA remove ineligible recordings, alter chart positions and revoke chart awards. Artists and representatives can contest exclusions.
The change will apply to the charts released on Friday.
ARIA chief executive Annabelle Herd said while artists were already using AI tools, music generated wholly by services built on artists' recordings was a different matter altogether.
"This gives everyone who releases music in Australia a clear rule to work to," she said.
"We call on all parties who have a role in deciding the music played and promoted to Australian audiences, particularly radio, to support human artistry and implement similar changes across their own codes."
AI-generated music storming up the charts
The decision follows scrutiny of Queensland DJ and producer Josh Fawaz's cover of Madonna's Like a Prayer, which became the most-played song on Australian radio and reached number four on two ARIA charts in July.
The track attracted criticism from music figures who believed generative AI had been used.
Fawaz said he used AI "as a tool" and later updated the track listing on Spotify to say the vocals and drums were AI-generated.
ARIA's move draws from the principles published in July by the global body representing the recorded music industry, which said more than 20 official chart programs were adopting rules intended to distinguish human-created recordings from wholly AI-generated material.
An ARIA spokesperson told the ABC that the International Federation of the Phonographic Industry (IFPI) rules would likely disqualify music with lead vocals or key instrumentals that were AI-generated, suggesting Fawaz's song may not qualify under the new rules.
IFPI said its concerns included AI models trained on artists' music without authorisation from rights holders.
Loading...
Spotify has taken a different transparency measure when it comes to AI music.
It has pledged to badge AI personas and exclude them from recommendations by default, however that badge applies to just the identity behind an artist profile, not whether AI was used to make a particular recording.
ARIA's move comes amid a wider dispute between creative industries and AI companies, many of which have built their technology using copyrighted material without artists' permission.
The federal government is working on new rules for AI and data centres that would include "strong copyright protections for Australian creators".

Israel is using Qusra to show Palestinians the price of staying
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
19:06:52 UTC
04:06:52 KST

Breadcrumb
Israel is using Qusra to show Palestinians the price of staying
For more than two weeks now, the Palestinian town of Qusra has been under an Israeli-imposed siege as the displacement of Palestinian families there persists. What began with Israeli settlers armed with military-issued weapons transformed into a joint military-settler operation.
At the beginning of the attack and siege, Israeli settlers had cut off water and electricity from the Palestinian residents in the town, with the purpose of driving them out and taking over their homes and lands. After some media attention and international recognition of the depravity happening in Qusra, the Israeli army moved in in lieu of the settlers, declaring the area a closed military zone and imposing their own restrictions. But in reality, this distinction between the army and settlers obscures what is happening in Qusra and in the West Bank generally.
They may wear different clothes, but in the end what is happening is that armed Israelis are imposing the same political reality, one where Palestinians cannot exist or live freely in their own homes.
What Qusra does offer us is not another story of settler impunity, but a clear showcasing of how dispossession can happen through the division of labour.
The siege: different forms of enclosures
When we speak of a siege, there may be a tendency to imagine something with a perimeter. A barricade, soldiers surrounding the city, tanks stationed at entrances and exits, and darkness as a population is completely cut off from the outside world. Yet what we see in the West Bank is a much more dispersed form of enclosures.
Over the last couple of years, the West Bank has witnessed record-high restrictions on movement affecting all 3.4 million Palestinians. As of December 2025, there is a 43% annual increase in movement obstacles affecting Palestinians. The Israeli security apparatus, in coordination with Israeli settlers, has erected gates at the entrances and exits of every Palestinian town and village, designated dozens of roads as forbidden to Palestinians, hoisted hundreds of military-controlled checkpoints, declared dozens of acres as closed military zones, approved dozens of new outposts, and reclassified Palestinian lands as Israel.
What this has done is make movement conditional. The enclosures do not have to be continuous to be effective. What they have meant for daily calculations is that Palestinians may leave their homes, but not go through that road (and instead endure an hours-long detour with the possibility of being stopped and beaten at a checkpoint), that they may reach their farmlands, but not this week.
It means they may go to work and school, but at risk of being attacked by armed Israelis who have decided to gather at a major roundabout. In the case of Qusra, it means you may remain in your home, but someone could come and make remaining there progressively impossible.
Looking at these dynamics, it becomes clearer that the West Bank is a large open-air prison. One which may not operate as a conventional prison but as a prison whose walls can move, randomly and repeatedly.
This is perhaps the most striking aspect of highlighting Qusra without context. It inadvertently suggests that this besiegement of families across three homes is an aberration in an otherwise functioning territory.
The shrinking distance between home and frontier
The case of Qusra should emphasise and magnify to the world exactly what Palestinians encounter across the West Bank, and that is a relentlessly shrinking distinction between home and frontier. This has been Israel’s strategy of anticipation where it engineers the expectation of expulsion, and is even using Qusra as an instrument to punctuate this reality.
What is being said, through this organised state violence, is that any Palestinian home or land can become a target. If it is not taken over by Israeli settlers, it is declared a military zone and taken by the army, and at best it becomes a case of “contested land,” which can protract for weeks, months, or even years.
What we see is not a simple act of controlling territory, but a new geography of occupation where it becomes about altering the conditions of reality under which Palestinians can inhabit these lands. So, rather than expel an entire village and obliterate entire cities as was the case in Gaza, Israel is teaching Palestinians what staying will cost.
Right now, what Israel is doing in Qusra and elsewhere in the West Bank does not stop at displacement. It is forcing Palestinians to consider: “Is this house still worth living in?” “Can my children safely grow up here?” “If I leave for work this morning, will I be able to return in the evening?”
Qusra exposes an architecture of colonialism in which the West Bank is experienced as one large enclosure without the need for a wall. While Gaza has made the word “siege” synonymous with a territory encircled from the outside, Qusra and the West Bank require that we recognise another form of siege. One which advances from the inside of the territory where the perimeter is constantly redrawn around Palestinian lives.
We must understand that Qusra is not an isolated incident of settlers and military between settlers and three families. It is three families against one of the strongest and most brutal regimes of our time, and it doesn’t end with them. It extends to all Palestinians in the West Bank facing a large-scale transformation which not only seizes lands and homes, but holds captive Palestinian lives.
The world needs to move not just for Qusra, but for Palestinians and what remains of Palestinian lives and will to persist. The walls of this prison do not stand still; they move around us, compressing spaces in which life can be ordinary, where even our own homes become Israel’s battlefields.
Displacement and dispossession are not sudden events of violent expulsion; they are the acts of siege that happen in Palestinian daily life.
Mariam Barghouti is a writer and journalist based in the West Bank. She has been covering the region as a reporter and analyst for ten years, served as the senior Palestine correspondent for Mondoweiss, and is a member of the Marie Colvin Journalist Network.

Vance claims Canada is reliant on US defence umbrella to deter foreign invasion

2026-08-24
19:00:02 UTC
04:00:02 KST

US Vice President JD Vance has said that Canada has failed to invest in its military and would be invaded by another country without the protection provided by the United States.
"Canada is a country that has underinvested in its military that quite literally would get invaded by a foreign country were it not for the umbrella of protection provided by the United States of America," Vance told an audience on Monday in Brewer, Maine, a northern state bordering Canada.
Vance also criticised Canada over recent trade tensions with the US, accusing Ottawa of making unreasonable demands during negotiations.
"They came in with a bunch of unreasonable last-minute demands," Vance said.
"I think that we should have a deal, but I think that we need to send a message loud and clear to the prime minister of Canada: stop taking advantage of the people of Maine. Stop taking advantage of America. It’s over. We expect fairness in our trade policy."
His remarks come as President Donald Trump has repeatedly pressed Canada and other US allies to increase defence spending while seeking more favorable trade terms.
Trump has imposed tariffs on Canadian goods and repeatedly criticised Ottawa over trade practices, while Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has sought to negotiate with Washington to ease tensions between the two neighbours.
Canada is a member of both NATO and NORAD, a joint US-Canadian organisation responsible for monitoring and defending the airspace and maritime approaches of North America.
Ottawa has pledged to increase defence spending as geopolitical tensions grow, including amid Russia's war in Ukraine and rising strategic competition in the Arctic.
Trade talks collapse
The comments came as trade tensions between Washington and Ottawa escalated further. New US tariffs of 50 percent on about $20 billion worth of Canadian goods took effect on Saturday after trade talks collapsed.
Trump on Monday threatened an additional 50 percent tariff on Canadian automobiles, auto parts, and steel starting on January 1, 2027. Canada has vowed to retaliate.
Earlier on Monday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent during a press conference in Washington DC was asked if President Trump is still interested in making Canada the 51st US state.
"I think he would like Canada to come to the table and negotiate in good faith. They were offered quite a good deal last week. They chose to reject it," Bessent answered.
He accused Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney of rising to power on an "anti-American, anti-Trump platform", and questioned why Carney, a former Bank of Canada governor, would reject the deal if he truly has the Canadian people's interests at heart.
Carney said on Monday that the goal of trade talks with Washington "has always been to get the best deal for Canadians, never a deal at any price or on any time frame."
"We learned that, during the negotiations, the Americans wanted to destroy our major industries — including the automotive, steel, and aluminum sectors — through unfair negotiating terms. And that is one of the main reasons why we said no," he added.
He stressed that building domestically and diversifying trade abroad has been "plan A from the start."
Canadian officials also said that trade talks with the US collapsed after Washington sought to impose restrictions on Ottawa regarding trade deals with other countries.

The San Francisco 49ers had not immediately issued a statement on the case.
York has been with the 49ers organization since 2008 and served as the team's CEO for many years. He became the franchise's principal owner in 2024.
During York's tenure, the 49ers have reached three Super Bowls and seven NFC Championship Games.
The arrest came less than three weeks before the start of the 2026 National Football League regular season, with the 49ers scheduled to open their campaign against the Los Angeles Rams on Sept. 10.

Belarusian institute cultivates grape collection of almost 600 varieties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
18:58:00 UTC
03:58:00 KST

The Institute of Fruit Growing of the National Academy of Sciences of Belarus boasts a rich grape collection of nearly 600 varieties. It is a true national treasure - the result of more than 30 years of work by specialists who have proven that even in our capricious climate, which is not always favorable to this heat-loving crop, it is possible to obtain decent yields of both table and wine grape varieties. What does Belarusian grape taste like, how widespread is the domestic community of winegrowers, is Belarusian grape wine a myth, and what should those planning to take up this crop know? BelTA correspondents found out by visiting the institute.
Northern Grapes
Vladimir Ustinov, a researcher at the Department of Breeding of Fruit Crops, Nut-Bearing Plants, and Grapes, is truly passionate about his work and can talk about grapes for hours. His interest in the crop began during his first year at Vitebsk State University, where Viktor Kukharev, considered one of the pioneers in northern viticulture, taught.
“I have always been drawn to the unusual and the opportunity to harvest crops in our latitudes that are not typical for them, having studied the specific nuances of cultivation - it is, above all, a creative endeavor. Viktor Kukharev worked together with Doctor of Agricultural Sciences Romuald Loiko, who paid great attention to crops such as apricots, walnuts, and grapes, and was one of the founders of the Northern Grapes club. Back in the 1990s, he brought together grape enthusiasts who showcased their achievements and literally showed off clusters grown on their backyard plots, proving that grapes grow in Belarus,” Vladimir Ustinov said.
At that time, winegrowers focused primarily on table varieties, taking pride in being able to grow high-quality, environmentally safe produce. They have many followers today as well: table grapes are grown both for personal consumption and for seasonal sales, albeit in small volumes, at markets and stores across the country.
“But it is important to understand that table grape varieties here are primarily greenhouse crops. And this method of cultivation has been gaining popularity in recent years. Our institute also has its own greenhouse facility, where about 150 grape varieties are being studied. These greenhouses are unheated, made of polycarbonate, and are quite tall - 50–60 cm higher than standard tomato greenhouses. The grapevine grows rapidly and needs plenty of both air and light. Even in such conditions, the plants require winter protection for the root system, which is highly sensitive to frost,” Vladimir Ustinov explained.
According to the specialist, cultivating table varieties on a large scale in Belarus is a highly costly and labor-intensive process. It is also risky, as severe frosts, sometimes accompanied by a lack of snow cover, can lead to the loss of an open vineyard, primarily due to the vulnerability of the root system.
“Roots can withstand frost down to minus 11-12 degrees Celsius, while the above-ground part of the vine, depending on the origin of the species, can tolerate minus 15-18 degrees (Central Asian varieties), and minus 20-24 (Western European varieties). Amur and North American labrusca varieties have above-ground winter hardiness reaching minus 25-30 degrees, with some forms up to minus 40. I should note that even for us, this harsh winter proved to be a real test. Although we traditionally mulch the root zone in our greenhouses and, during heavy snowfall, also add snow to create a protective cover. Many varieties that performed well in previous years suffered frost damage. They did not die, but they are now recovering, and there is virtually no harvest this year,” Vladimir Ustinov said, emphasizing that this is how experience with specific varieties is built, which will later be summarized in specialist recommendations.
The institute also has not only greenhouses but also open vineyards covering about 3 hectares. In the protected environment, they work not only with grapes but also experiment with exotic crops - figs (with about 50 varieties collected), passion fruit, persimmons, thornless blackberries, German medlar, pawpaw (banana tree), kiwifruit, and silverberry.
Enormous interest
Despite such high risks, the number of people wishing to engage in viticulture in our latitudes is constantly growing.
“There are many enthusiasts of this crop, and with the development of the internet, hobbyists have gained access to a wealth of useful information, including from primary sources. Moreover, the number of cultivated varieties has noticeably increased. In the 1990s, the institute’s collection included just over 300 grape varieties, including those at the Pinsk support station, where they worked with heat-loving crops. Now, after last year’s inventory, we have 550 grape accessions, and by the end of this year, several dozen more will be added. Our collection is a true national treasure. Overall, there are over a thousand accessions across the country,” Vladimir Ustinov said.
And this number is constantly growing: enthusiasts bring in the most diverse grape varieties from around the world and try to settle them on their plots, observing how they behave in our climate.
“There is interest in both technical varieties and exotic table varieties with the most unusual flavors, completely atypical for grapes. The flavor spectrum of grapes is so wide that each time you marvel at its shades. Strawberry, pineapple, mango, blueberry, blackberry, citron, muscat, muscat-floral, and honey - the range of flavors is immense. And if you add the possibilities of processing the berries, where they reveal even more flavor nuances and notes, it makes the crop even more attractive,” the viticulturist said.
Krasotka, Lored, and Minsk Muscat 
Currently, 18 table and technical grape varieties are included in the state register. All have been tested in our conditions, and specialists have prepared recommendations on them. 
“Among the latest varieties prepared for the register are the table variety Krasotka and the technical red grape variety for winemaking - Lored, named in honor and memory of our scientist Romuald Loiko. We have also completed work on the technical white wine variety Minsk Muscat, which should become the 19th variety to enter the register. It should be noted that our scientists actively collaborate with Russian colleagues, and some of the varieties in the register are the result of joint work. When analyzing these figures, it is important to understand that with such an abundance of grape varieties in the world, viticulture in our country remains largely a hobby, as it involves high risks. Our goal is to support the interest of winegrowers in this crop,” the specialist said.
It should be noted that the institute has spent three years implementing a project to study the suitability of technical grape varieties grown in Belarus - such as Lored and Minsk Muscat - for processing.
“The experiment was conducted by our department together with the Storage and Processing Department. The latter’s specialists even traveled to the Magarach Institute in Crimea for training,” Vladimir Ustinov said.
Galina Novik is one of those who took part in the project. And 2024, with the research beginning in 2021, proved to be the most successful: September gave winegrowers a fourth month of summer, and the berries reached their optimal ripeness.
“We produced a good wine with its own unique flavor and character, distinguishing it from winemaking products of other countries. But the main conclusion was that even in our conditions, by working with the right varieties, it is possible to produce grape wine. Although the project is complete, work on studying technical varieties continues,” the researcher said.
Advice for beginners
According to the specialist, those wishing to start growing grapes on their plots should opt for proven varieties, as the grape “wonders” offered by breeders from around the world can be utterly disappointing in our conditions and kill any interest.
“Take those that have been well-known for about a decade, or those included in the register. For these varieties, you can get recommendations specific to our region. These include, for example, table varieties such as Tsetrin, Antratsit, Mars, Jupiter, and technical varieties like Solaris, Regent, as well as North American varieties bred using wild forms with enhanced winter hardiness, among others. But it is also important to understand that in the south of Belarus these varieties will feel more comfortable than in the north, so caution is needed. The chance of a good result often depends on a favorable September, and with a short summer and a cold September, the berries may simply not reach optimal ripeness,” Vladimir Ustinov noted.
In any case, one needs not only patience but also a certain amount of money for planting material, trellis construction, greenhouse installation, tools, crop protection products, and covering materials.
“This crop requires constant attention. The more care it receives, the better the result - from early spring to late autumn. And with large areas, the season never really ends. So, once you have decided on the scale and assessed your capabilities, you need to get to work, and with the right approach, it will certainly bear fruit. And harvesting them is a great joy,” Vladimir Ustinov added.
Traditionally, winegrowers of Belarus will gather at the Institute of Fruit Growing for the next festival with an exhibition of achievements, which will take place on 4 September.
“At the exhibition, you will be able to see record-sized clusters, taste the berries, and purchase surplus produce and planting material. You will also be able to make important contacts among experienced winegrowers,” Vladimir Ustinov said.

US removes Syria from state sponsor of terrorism list
- The US removed Syria from the state sponsor of terrorism list, easing investment restrictions and signalling support for political and economic stability.
- The US also revoked the terrorist designation of Al-Nusrah Front, now known as Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham, which broke ties with Al-Qaeda in 2016.
- The move aligns with President Trump's promise of sanctions relief and occurred alongside his meeting with Syrian leader Ahmed al-Sharaa after Assad's 2024 toppling.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – The US on Aug 24 removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism, rescinding a decades-old designation that came with severe economic restrictions and marking another step in warming ties between the countries.
The US Department of State also revoked its designation of Al-Nusrah Front – latterly known as Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham (HTS) – as a global terrorist organisation.
The Treasury Department announced corresponding sanctions relief.
Rebels led by HTS overthrew long-time Syrian ruler Bashar al-Assad in December 2024, with the group’s leader Ahmed al-Sharaa taking over as president as the country rebuilds after more than 13 years of civil war.
“Today’s action will help foster additional investment in Syria to promote political and economic stability,” US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement.
The Treasury said the moves were “in line with President (Donald) Trump’s promise to deliver sanctions relief to Syria”.
But the agency stressed that its removal of restrictions on Syria “does not change Treasury’s posture with regard to countering global terrorism and our commitment to hold bad actors in Syria accountable”.
HTS was earlier known as the Al-Nusra Front and was formerly the branch of Al-Qaeda.
It broke ties with the jihadist group in 2016.
The US initially announced in July its intent to delist Syria as a state sponsor of terrorism, a move seen as a vote of confidence in Sharaa.
On the sidelines of a NATO summit in Turkey, Trump met the Syrian president, a former jihadist who has sought to recast himself as a unifying figure after the toppling of the Assad family – which ruled with an iron fist for a half-century.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the Aug 24 delistings gave Syrians “a path to prosperity”.
The action “eliminates the final major barriers for private sector investment in Syria and promotes Syria’s economic recovery and reintegration into the global economy”, he said in a statement.
Top officials in Damascus hailed the delisting as a major opportunity for the country, still economically devastated after more than a decade of war that rights groups say killed more than half a million people.
Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani described Washington’s delisting as a “historic milestone” and said it reflected “the new Syrian state’s commitment to international peace and security”.
Finance Minister Mohammed Barnieh described the move as a “success for Syrian diplomacy”, according to the official news agency SANA.
It “opens a major and long-awaited door to strengthening Syria’s integration into the global economic and financial system, attracting investment and modern technologies, and supporting development opportunities”.
Central bank chief Safwat Raslan lauded the development, adding that his institution was “working to build a modern and reliable financial system capable of evolving with developments and taking advantage of all opportunities”. AFP

He also called on the Sudanese people to ignore claims by “malicious actors” regarding the imposition of a no-fly zone over Sudan, vowing to continue what he called the “battle for dignity” until “every inch of Sudanese land” is liberated.

====================================================================================================

Iranian Rial Hits Record Low as the U.S. Unveils New Sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
18:49:49 UTC
03:49:49 KST

Iran’s currency plummeted in value Monday, hitting a record-low open-market rate of 2.02 million rials to the dollar, amid the White House’s launch of “Operation Economic Outcast,” which aims to force concessions from Iran through isolation and a financial stranglehold.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned Sunday that an “economic D-Day” was coming, and he shared a first sense of what that might look like at a press conference the following day.
"D-Day marked a historic campaign with our allies,” Bessent said Monday. “Today, in that same spirit, we are launching an economic onslaught against Iran's financial connections around the globe."
The U.S. announced sanctions on more than 60 targets while expanding sanctionable sectors to digital assets, technology, gold, aviation, and shipping—which Bessent described as some of the country’s “most vital lifelines.”
The government may also impose secondary sanctions on Iran’s trade partners, Bessent said, adding that those sanctions could roll out in a matter of weeks.
The threat is meant to deter countries from bolstering the country’s waning economy and “collapse every last option for Iran,” Bessent said, describing it as "economic asphyxiation."
Read More: The U.S.-Iran War: By the Numbers
Though Bessent didn’t identify which Iranian partners might be targeted by a new round of sanctions, he did name one financial institution: Bank Melli, the Iranian government-owned bank with branches in about a dozen countries. Bessent said that “every branch” of the bank must be “shuttered and dark” or it will lose access to the U.S. dollar. The Treasury has previously claimed that the bank provides services to entities that support Iran’s nuclear and ballistic programs.
Since the start of its war with Iran on Feb. 28, the Trump Administration has applied both military and economic pressure to achieve its goal of dismantling the nation’s nuclear program.
Bessent’s remarks elaborate on President Donald Trump’s announcement on Aug. 19 that the U.S. would launch “the most crushing economic operation ever mounted” against Iran.
Iran initially dismissed the threat. Its foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, on Sunday called the U.S. “desperate.” And Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, told state television on Aug. 22 that Iran would turn against any neighboring Gulf states that yield to the U.S. in what he called an “economic war.”
“Any country that takes part in imposing economic restrictions on us will be regarded as an enemy,” he said.
Given Iran’s sustained control over passage through the Strait of Hormuz, any retaliation could push Brent crude oil above Monday’s closing price of about $92 per barrel or the wartime high of about $120 per barrel.
In a war that has been largely defined by its threat to the global economy, experts wonder whether sanctions against Tehran’s trade allies will further isolate it—and if that will succeed in forcing Iran to capitulate to the demands of the United States.
Could U.S. sanctions force Iran to end the war?
The Trump Administration has argued that in tightening sanctions against Iran, the country will face unprecedented isolation and economic pain.
But Trita Parsi, the executive vice president of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, tells TIME that the move doesn’t guarantee compliance.
“We really need to keep in mind here that Iran has been under U.S. sanctions for the last 40 years, and we've had several moments in which we have done some sort of a major escalation,” he says. “And each time, it has failed to translate into a policy change from Iran.”
Parsi notes that neither Bessent nor Trump has outlined specific demands for Iran—focusing more on maximum isolation rather than defining clear, achievable diplomatic terms.
Because of this, he argues that Iran is even less likely to succumb to increased pressure.
“What we know of the pattern in the past is that the Iranians will not capitulate—they will escalate,” Parsi says. “This is the same miscalculation Trump made when he thought that the threat of war would cause them to surrender, and instead they prepared themselves for war, and they fought back. And six months later, we're here.”
Further complicating matters is the fact that Iran is meeting with its neighbor, Oman, about regulating passage through the Strait of Hormuz, through which one-fifth of the world’s oil formerly passed. Oman’s foreign minister, Sayyid Badr Albusaidi, is visiting Tehran on Tuesday to continue high-level talks on “bilateral and regional issues.”
Controlling the waterway—a pain point for the global economy—has been Iran’s greatest strength in the war. Any agreement could affect Iran’s leverage over the waterway, although Oman has not publicly endorsed Tehran’s broader demands.
Trump last week threatened that the U.S. would target Oman next if it cooperated with Iran on this matter, telling Fox News: “We’ll bomb the s— out of them.” Experts have said, however, that this is an idle threat and that bombing Oman would be a mistake.
Continuing to enforce its blockade on the Strait does, however, come at a cost to Iran. A June analysis from the Foundation for Defense of Democracies estimated that Iran may be incurring economic damages of about $435 million per day while enforcing it.
How is the plummeting value of the rial affecting Iranians?
Ryan Costello, the policy director at the National Iranian American Council, tells TIME that implementing additional sanctions may not achieve the desired result—but will likely hurt Iranians.
“Regrettably, it has had very harsh impacts on ordinary Iranians—pushing millions out of the middle class, which is often seen as an engine for successful democratic change over time,” Costello says. “This currency depreciation has a real cost for ordinary Iranians, making their life ever more unaffordable.”
According to the International Monetary Fund, Iran’s average annual inflation rate is projected to reach 68.9% in 2026. The depreciation of the rial—which was already the world’s least valuable currency before it dipped this week—will strain Iranian citizens who are already struggling to buy groceries and pay for monthly living expenses.
There is a “real risk” of greater global market destabilization the longer the Strait of Hormuz is closed, Costello says.
“Iran's leadership is signaling that it will respond to intensified economic pressure by further restricting energy flows, and it appears to have the capacity to act on their threat,” Costello says.
In addition to its command of the Strait, he explains: "Iran and other aligned forces are demonstrating an ability to strike energy targets with missiles and drones, both in the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf. So Iran and/or its allies could target commercial ships, as well as pipelines, ports, refineries, and other critical energy infrastructure."
And there’s a second major risk if the U.S. places sanctions on certain global powers who buy Iranian oil—particularly economic powerhouse China.
“China could take steps to punish the U.S. economy in turn,” Costello explains.
He says that both risks could be “very damaging,” with economic ramifications that span the globe.
Why Trump is escalating economic pressure on Iran
The U.S.-Iran war is nearing its six-month mark, and peace negotiations have effectively stalled.
The memorandum of understanding established in June—which gave the nations 60 days to work out terms for Iran’s nuclear program and renew uninterrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz—expired Aug. 17. It unraveled in July as the U.S. struck hundreds of targets in Iran, and Tehran retaliated against its allies in the region, including Kuwait and Bahrain. But as the U.S. continued to draw down its munitions stockpiles, Iran held steady with its blockade of the Strait.
Now, Trump has changed his tactics.
“This is where the real problem is: He's going back to economic warfare because military warfare didn't work,” Parsi says.
If additional sanctions fail to force Iran to yield to some of Trump’s demands, Parsi says the President may be running out of options.
“The only exit out of this is actually through diplomacy,” he says. “Otherwise, the U.S. is just going to go back and forth between economic and military action.”
One route to relief may come by way of Pakistan, which helped mediate the June ceasefire between the U.S. and Iran. It dispatched a high-level delegation, led by Field Marshal Asim Munir, to Tehran this week to encourage its leadership to work toward a more lasting peace agreement.
But Parsi contends that the stream of threats from the U.S. may make Iran even less likely to reconcile, saying: “This does not end up becoming the end of the conflict. It just ends up becoming another cycle in the escalation spiral.”

Breaking Down the Ending of Spooky in Love
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
18:48:32 UTC
03:48:32 KST

Extraordinary Attorney Woo’s Park Eun-bin and Doona!’s Yang Se-jong star as ghost-whispering hotel heiress Cheon Yeo-ri and ace prosecutor Ma Gang-uk, respectively, in the supernatural romance series Spooky in Love. In the Korean drama, which broadcast domestically on tvN and was distributed globally by Netflix, Yeo-ri and Gang-uk are initially brought together by their shared desire for justice. For Yeo-ri, this takes the form of helping the ghosts she alone can see. For Gang-uk, it means doing a good, by-the-book job as an investigator. But when Gang-uk learns Yeo-ri’s secret, the two grow closer.
While Spooky in Love starts out with a strong, ghost-of-the-week format, the second half of the drama leans more into corporate in-fighting and family drama as context for Yeo-ri and Gang-uk’s romance. When Chairwoman Baek insists that Yeo-ri get engaged in order to secure a more stable future for the hotel and resort company, Yeo-ri side-steps the advances of family friend and fellow chaebol Kang Min-hwan (Ong Seong-wu) to announce she is engaged to Gang-uk. What starts as a fake relationship to keep Yeo-ri’s grandmother off of her back soon develops into the real thing. But can Yeo-ri and Gang-uk’s love survive Min-hwan’s machinations to take control of both Yeo-ri and her company? Here’s everything that happens in the Spooky in Love finale.
Yeo-ri’s supernatural powers, explained
Yeo-ri wasn’t born with the ability to see ghosts. She developed it 12 years prior to the start of the series, when she nearly died in the mysterious yacht accident that killed her boyfriend and Min-hwan’s little brother, Kang Ji-hwan (Kim Min-chul). The condition has ghosts constantly nagging Yeo-ri for help, and also keeps her isolated from the land of the living. If she touches hands with someone else, they will temporarily gain the ability to see ghosts for a month. As a result, she wears gloves constantly, and keeps a physical distance from her friends, family, and co-workers.
The stakes of Yeo-ri’s secret are intensified due to the power her family holds. Yeo-ri is the heir to the Reina Group, a corporate hotel chain that wields immense wealth. Yeo-ri’s grandmother, Baek Kyung-ja (Ye Soo-jung), plans to pass the baton to Yeo-ri—rather than step-daughter Ok Gye-hui (Baek Ji-won) or her adult children, Ha-ri (Cho Hye-joo) and Don-jun (Lee Dal). However, if Chairwoman Baek, or the larger public, finds out that Yeo-ri is haunted by ghosts, it could call her ability to run the family corporation into question.
Still, Yeo-ri’s sense of justice runs deep. In Spooky in Love’s early episodes, Yeo-ri is visited by the ghost of Jang Eun-ju (Yoon Hye-rim), a young woman who was murdered by her boyfriend, Park Seung-jae (Kim Do-wan), after she becomes pregnant with their child. Seung-jae is well-connected. Not only is he a rich pro golfer, but his father is one of the leading contenders in the next presidential race. When he is initially tried for murder, with Gang-uk acting as prosecutor, he is acquitted due to his father’s immense influence. It is only when Gang-uk and Yeo-ri team up that they are able to gather more evidence, and definitively pin the murder on Seung-jae.
What happened on the yacht?
Yeo-ri grew up close to Kang Ji-hwan and Kang Min-hwan, brothers poised to inherit ownership of CL Raymond Group. Though both brothers had feelings for Yeo-ri, Ji-hwan was the first to ask her out. For Min-hwan, this intensified the jealousy he had long felt of his little brother. Jin-hwan, who looked up to his brother, didn’t realize that he was often treated better by some members of the family compared to Min-hwan, who was adopted. When Jin-hwan started dating Yeo-ri, it was the final straw for Min-hwan.
On the day of the accident, the brothers are out on a yacht with their friends, including Yeo-ri and fellow rich kid Park Seung-jae. We learn in the penultimate episode that when the yacht hit a rock and Jin-hwan was thrown over the side, Min-hwan had the chance to pull his brother back onboard, but let the pleading Jin-hwan fall into the water below instead. Jin-hwan dies, and Yeo-ri, who also went overboard in the accident, is rescued from the water. She is wearing a protective pendant gifted to Jin-hwan by his grandmother. He asked her to wear it while they were on the boat, joking that, if something should happen, she should live and he will die.
Later, Yeo-ri and Gang-uk seek out the shaman who made the pendant. The original maker is dead, but her daughter informs them that the power of the pendant changed Yeo-ri and Jin-hwan’s fates. That power, paired with Yeo-ri’s inability to let Jin-hwan move on in the immediate aftermath of the accident, led to Yeo-ri’s ability to see ghosts. The shaman tells Gang-uk and Yeo-ri that, in order for Yeo-ri to stop seeing ghosts, she owes the afterlife a life.
Gang-uk’s connection to Jin-hwan
Gang-uk, who was raised by his grandmother, did not grow up in the same social circles as Yeo-ri, Min-hwan, and the other members of the chaebol class. However, he shares a unique connection to Jin-hwan. When Jin-hwan died, a sick Gang-uk was given Jin-hwan’s heart. The transplant allowed him to live on. Ever since, Jin-hwan and Min-hwan’s mother, Song Hee-won (Kim Seo-ra) has kept tabs on Gang-uk through his grandmother. Though she lost one of her sons, it makes her happy to see Gang-uk doing well.
Min-hwan’s crimes escalate
This truth of Jin-hwan’s death is known only by Min-hwan for more than a decade. Yeo-ri doesn’t remember what happened during the accident and, even if she did, she didn’t witness what occurred between the brothers that day. However, when Seung-jae temporarily gets out of jail to attend his father’s funeral, he happens to stumble upon a camcorder memory card with footage of Min-hwan choosing not to save Jin-hwan. Seung-jae attempts to blackmail Min-hwan with the evidence. When the two meet up in an abandoned warehouse, Min-hwan kills him for it.
Gang-uk finds Min-hwan’s cufflink at the scene of the crime, but Min-hwan counters. He hires someone to hit Gang-uk with a truck. Yeo-ri pushes the man she loves out of the way at the last second, saving his life and putting her own in grave danger. She is hit by the truck, and ends up in a coma. As Yeo-ri’s life hangs in the balance, we see her traverse a beautiful kind of purgatory. The ghosts she has helped in the past 12 years, including Eun-ju, are waiting for her there. They lend her some of their warmth to keep her from crossing to the other side.
Yeo-ri and Jin-hwan balance the scales
Still, Yeo-ri finally does make it to a Styx-like river, a boundary between the world of the living and the world of the dead. Before she can step onto the boat that would bring her across, the ghost of Jin-hwan appears to take her place. The two share a teary conversation in which they process Jin-hwan’s death. Yeo-ri apologizes for living instead of him, but Jin-hwan doesn’t see it that way. He says she still has so much to live for, and that the ghosts she has helped are rooting for her. When Yeo-ri wakes back up, she no longer has the power to see ghosts. Jin-hwan has crossed to the other side; the afterlife has been given the soul it was robbed of 12 years prior.
Min-hwan is brought to justice
Unbeknownst to Min-hwan, Seung-jae has hidden the memory card in a hollow golf ball at the warehouse. When Yeo-ri and Gang-uk are investigating, they find the card and have the evidence to take Min-hwan down. In the most dramatic way possible, Yeo-ri reveals the evidence to Min-hwan’s mother and the other people gathered at Jin-hwan’s memorial service. More than losing his power or going to jail, Min-hwan seems most distraught at the idea of his mother discovering his betrayal. A year later, when she visits her remorseful son in jail, she tells him that after he has finished serving his time, she will be waiting for him. Min-hwan, who always thought his mother’s love for her biological son diminished her love for her adopted son, can perhaps finally see otherwise.
Does Spooky in Love have a happy ending?
Spooky in Love has the happiest of endings. A year following the main events of the series finale, Yeo-ri is announced as the new chairwoman of Reina. Yeo-ri and Gang-uk are happily together. Gang-uk, who had been transferred out of Seoul after reporting internal corruption at the prosecutor’s office, has just received a promotion back in the capital city where Yeo-ri lives. The two visit Siena Hall, the Reina wedding property that symbolizes Yeo-ri’s late parents’ love for one another, and walk together, hand in hand.
When the two first started falling for one another, Yeo-ri had said that her greatest wish was to walk hand-in-hand with the person she liked. Then, she was too afraid to touch anyone, burdened by the certainty she would pass her curse onto them. Now, she does so, unafraid. The simple scene doesn’t just demonstrate the love between Yeo-ri and Gang-uk; it demonstrates the intimacy and warmth Yeo-ri is able to let into her life more broadly. She is no longer alone, and Gang-uk is only one part of that reality.

The UN has condemned the killing of two peacekeepers in an ambush in South Sudan’s Jonglei State.
“The Secretary-General (Antonio Guterres) strongly condemns this attack in no uncertain terms,” spokesperson Stephane Dujarric told reporters on Monday.
He confirmed that the two peacekeepers killed were Ethiopian nationals. Seven others were injured, including three UN peacekeepers, two South Sudanese police officers and two civilian staff members.
Guterres extended his condolences to the families of the fallen peacekeepers and to the people and government of Ethiopia, Dujarric said, adding that the UN chief wished all those injured a speedy recovery.

Asked about the nature of the incident, Dujarric said available information indicated that the peacekeepers appeared to have been intentionally targeted.
He noted that the incident brought the number of peacekeepers killed in “malicious acts” since January 1 to nine.
The UN mission deployed a quick reaction force to secure the area and assist in the emergency response.
Dujarric emphasised that attacks on UN personnel may constitute war crimes under international law.
Anita Kiki Gbeho, head of the UN peacekeeping mission in South Sudan (UNMISS), called for a prompt investigation to ensure that the perpetrators are brought to justice.
“Such deadly violence targeting UNMISS personnel who are serving to support peace in South Sudan is unacceptable,” she said.
